Writer Yiyun Li lost both of her sons. When words fell short, she turned to music
If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
Writer Yiyun Li does not talk about "grief" or the "grieving process." To her, those words make it sound that at some point you emerge from grief. Instead, Li prefers to use the word "abyss," which, she says, is where she expects to be for the remainder of her life.
Li's teenage sons both died by suicide six years apart, Vincent in 2017 at age 16, and James in 2024 at age 19. Her Pulitzer Prize-winning 2025 memoir, Things in Nature Merely Grow, chronicled the loss of her sons and her effort to go on.
"James' death taught me to suffer better," she says. "To say, 'I can do it, and I can live with my pain and sorrow without ever wanting to stop feeling.'"
Li's new novel, Music Against the Night, is set in the late 1700s and early 1800s and centers on two prodigies who are brought together by music, and drawn apart because of their aspirations. The novel focuses on music, which sits outside of words.
"I think I've had the feeling both times after my children's death that words often fall short, and falling short doesn't mean not succeeding, falling short doesn't mean failing," she says. "But when I start a new project, I would like a subject [where] words naturally fall short. So music is that choice."
Li grew up in China and served a year in the Chinese military before coming to the U.S. to study immunology. She eventually left her Ph.D. program to become a writer. Li is now a professor in the creative writing program at Princeton University.
Interview highlights
On the decision to set Music Against the Night in a different time period
I was in the middle of the novel when James died. This is a novel far from my usual interests or concerns, and the reason I think I went back to history is I would like to live again through history, through historical figures, through my characters living in the late 18th and early 19th century. ... I'm making the past into a new now for myself and possibly for my readers.
On how playing piano connects to her grief
I began my piano lessons at the end of 2023, purely to get to know how to play the piano. And James died in February 2024, so two months into my piano lessons he died, and it occurred to me that piano or music is a good way for me to count time — because music is about time. It's about counting the measure, counting the rhythm. And also music is about ... be[ing] engaged with something else. You can sit in your sadness all day long, do nothing, or crying. Or, like me, I could just sit there and just play the same drill again, and again, as a way to know I was, in a way, staying in touch with the world. ...
I'm not a concert pianist, but somehow I find it liberating and healthy to do something that you absolutely love but cannot do well. Every time I go to my piano lesson, I'm so intimidated. I'm sweating because I just can't do it. I can hear other people do it, I cannot do it myself. But I think that's, again, acknowledging the limit of my capacity.
On raising two gifted children
Both my children could be called prodigies, but James, my younger son, especially was extraordinarily odd and brilliant. ... We were greatly baffled. I remember he was 5 or 6, he said, "Mommy, you will never see the world. I see it full of dots and squiggly lines." And that again was a strange perception of the world [that] we adults did not have access to. …
What is the responsibility or the difficulty of bringing up a child [who is] very brilliant? … Some people would say, well, you really have to train him to be the next Einstein, but we did not want him to be the next Einstein, we want him to be a normal, happy boy living in an ordinary life.
On her son Vincent
He was a brilliant painter and we still have all his paintings around the house. He was an oboist and when he wanted to learn the oboe, the oboe teacher said he was a bit young, because he was 8 when he want to learn oboe, but he was certain. ... [He had] started on the piano and he could articulate that piano was not his instrument. He wanted to play the oboe. But mostly, he wrote beautiful poetry. He was a great poet. And he was a greater reader. I wouldn't call him an outlier, as James was, but he was brilliant and fun and interesting.
On struggling with suicidal ideation
Sometimes I think people have all sort of thoughts about or against people who have chosen suicide, and people who've chosen or attempted suicide are often called selfish. But my experience is oftentimes people [are] in great pain, whether it's great mental pain or great physical pain. And sometimes people in deep depression cannot tell the difference between mental pain and physical pain, because everything together is a great kind of suffering. I think it's not that people who experience that kind of suicidal urge, it's not that they want to die or they want [to] use this to hurt other people.
On becoming a writer
I was born with innate curiosity and also sensitivity to things that did not quite make sense. So I grew up in China. And for instance, when I was little, all the adults would say, since you're a child, you have no right to decide who you want to be or what you want to do. And my mother even had a saying, something along the [lines] that an adult decides and the child follows. I was quite young, you know, 4 or 5. I just couldn't make sense of all of these teachings because I thought I was as capable of thinking as the adults, and why did I have to follow them? So I think that sort of sensitivity to things that are very, very nonsensical, I think maybe that's one thing that made me into a writer.
Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

అక్టోబర్ 10న ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద భారీ నిరసన చేపట్టనున్నట్లు కాక్రొచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) ప్రకటించింది. ప్రత్యేక సమగ్ర ఓటర్ల జాబితా సవరణ (SIR) ప్రక్రియను వెంటనే నిలిపివేయాలని, 2025 జూన్ 25 నుంచి ఓటర్ల జాబితా నుంచి తొలగించిన పేర్లన్నింటినీ తిరిగి చేర్చాలని కూడా CJP డిమాండ్ చేస్తోంది. లెఫ్ట్ వింగ్ విద్యార్థి సంఘాలు కూడా ఈ నిరసనలో పెద్ద సంఖ్యలో పాల్గొంటామని ప్రకటన విడుదల చేశాయి. జంతర్ మంతర్లోకి ప్రవేశించేందుకు ప్రయత్నించిన సీజేపీ (CJP) నేతలను పోలీసులు అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, సోషల్ మీడియాలో ఒక వీడియోను (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) షేర్ చేస్తూ, 2026 అక్టోబర్ 10న ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన నిరసనలను ఇది చూపిస్తోందని ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారు. దీని వెనుక ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ఈ వీడియో 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఢిల్లీలో ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ జరిగిన నిరసనలను చూపిస్తుంది.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఢిల్లీలో జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ జరిగిన నిరసనలకు సంబంధించింది కాదు. ఈ వీడియోను ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో చిత్రీకరించారు. అయితే, ఈ వీడియోను ఖచ్చితంగా ఎప్పుడు, ఏ సందర్భంలో చిత్రీకరించారో తెలియదు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేస్తున్న వాదన తప్పుదారి పట్టిస్తుంది.
వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, ఒక ఫుట్ ఓవర్బ్రిడ్జిపై “Diyandi Festival” అనే పదాలతో ఉన్న హోర్డింగ్ కనిపించింది. దీని గురించి వెతికితే, ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో ప్రతి సంవత్సరం సెప్టెంబర్లో దియాండి పండుగను జరుపుకుంటారని తెలిసింది. నగర సంరక్షకుడైన సెయింట్ మైఖేల్ ఆర్చ్ఏంజెల్ గౌరవార్థం నిర్వహించే ఈ పండుగ సెప్టెంబర్ 29న ముగుస్తుంది.
వైరల్ వీడియోలో “Shann Gadget” అనే పేరుతో ఉన్న బోర్డులను కూడా గమనించాం. గూగుల్ మ్యాప్స్లో వెతకగా, ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో రోక్సాస్ అవెన్యూలో, గైసానో సిటీ సూపర్మాల్కు ఎదురుగా ఈ దుకాణం ఉన్నట్లు తెలిసింది.
గూగుల్ స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూలో పరిశీలించగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపించే ప్రదేశానికి, స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూ చిత్రాల్లోని ప్రదేశానికి మధ్య పలు పోలికలు కనిపించాయి. దీంతో ఈ వీడియోను ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలోనే చిత్రీకరించినట్లు నిర్ధారించాం.
అయితే, ఈ వీడియోను ఖచ్చితంగా ఎప్పుడు చిత్రీకరించారు, ఏ సందర్భంలో చిత్రీకరించారు అనే విషయాలను మేము గుర్తించలేకపోయాం. అందుబాటులో ఉన్న ఆధారాల ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియోను ఫిలిప్పీన్స్లోని ఇలిగన్ నగరంలో చిత్రీకరించారు. దీనికి ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన నిరసనలకు ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు.
చివరిగా, ఫిలిప్పీన్స్కు చెందిన ఒక సంబంధం లేని వీడియోను, ఢిల్లీలో జరిగిన CJP నిరసనల వీడియోగా తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు

Speciality chemical manufacturing startup Scimplify has raised $25 Mn (around ₹238 Cr) in a fresh funding round led by Hitachi Ventures, the venture capital arm of Japan's Hitachi Group. The round also saw participation from existing backers such as Accel, Bertelsmann India Investments, 3one4 Capital and Omnivore. New investors including Teknor Apex, Henkel and an undisclosed Japanese chemical company also joined the round. The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its research, processing and manufacturing capabilities across rare earth and critical metals purification. The funds will also go towards scaling its semiconductor chemicals and battery chemicals businesses. A chunk of the capital will also be used to strengthen SciNode, Scimplify’s agentic AI platform that connects research, process development, control and physical manufacturing. Founded in 2023 by Sachin Santhosh, Salil Srivastava, Dheeraj Dhingra and Hersh Manek, Scimplify is a B2B platform that specialises in end-to-end sourcing and manufacturing of speciality chemicals. It also offers contract research and commercial chemical manufacturing for agro-chemicals, active pharmaceutical ingredients and fragrances. The startup currently operates R&D facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, with its SciNode software platform supporting its manufacturing operations. Its network comprises more than 500 manufacturing partners and thousands of scientists and technical partners. Prior to this, Scimplify had secured $40 Mn in its Series B funding round, co-led by Accel and Bertelsmann Investments, in March last year. “In the 18 months since our initial investment, Scimplify has grown from serving 600+ customers across 16 countries to building a global platform with 1,000+ customers across 40+ countries,” Accel partner Rachit Parekh said. Scimplify's customers include Henkel, Coromandel, Dr Reddy's, Coherent, Holcim, BASF, Sanyo, Marubeni, among others. The startup claims to operate across five countries and serves more than 1,000 customers across over 40 countries. Going forward, Scimplify plans to expand its presence in the US, initially focusing on sectors where domestic processing capabilities remain limited. These will include rare earth and critical metals purification and processing as well as high-purity semiconductor and battery chemicals. Scimplify's latest fundraise comes as India looks to strengthen its position in the global chemicals value chain. Earlier this week, Bengaluru-based speciality chemicals startup NuSynth Technologies raised ₹36.5 Cr in a seed round co-led by Avaana Capital and Shastra VC. Scimplify operates in the broader Indian deeptech sector, which continues to draw investor attention on the back of regulatory push, subsidies, innovative local solutions, a thriving talent pool and growing local demand. Overall, Indian deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals in Q3 2026, a 176% increase from $105 Mn across 29 deals in the year-ago period. The sector outpaced the broader Indian startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn.

During my 10+ years of clinical experience in various States and with numerous patient populations, I have seen that dental anxiety is a constant challenge. I have seen this phenomenon in children clutching their parents’ hands before their first cleaning and in accomplished professionals quietly cancelling appointment after appointment in the hope that the problem will somehow resolve itself.
It doesn’t.
In my experience, the longer you leave a fear unchecked, the greater the clinical and human cost becomes. Dental anxiety is not a moral failing. This is a well-documented psychological response—and one with important, measurable public health consequences.
How severe is it?
Roughly a third of people have significant dental anxiety, and roughly a tenth have a clinical phobia. That’s not a little footnote. That means a lot of the population is actively avoiding or delaying care that could prevent serious disease. The downstream consequences of this avoidance are visible daily in my clinical work: infections tolerated for months, decay advanced far beyond what early intervention would have required, and patients presenting with pain that could have been prevented years ago.
Knowing where it starts
Dental anxiety typically has a definite source. A painful or poorly done procedure in childhood can be a source of dental anxiety. A provider who was in a hurry or didn’t tell the patient what was happening. The specific sensory environment of a dental office—the sounds, the smells, and the physical vulnerability of lying back with your mouth open—can leave powerful imprints, especially in young patients. That memory is not just wiped out; it impacts behaviour for decades. For some, it’s not just one event but an accumulation. Years of avoidance layered on top of embarrassment about how their teeth look now, and a fear of judgment prevents them from asking for help. This cycle of shame avoidance is one of the hardest patterns I see clinically. When these patients do come in, they need much more intervention than if they had come in sooner, and this becomes an instance of the very fear that kept them away.
The health price of avoidance
Research literature teaches us, that oral health is not an island. Untreated dental disease is a chronic inflammatory load on the body. It has been linked to cardiovascular risk, dysregulated blood sugar, and impaired immune function. When a patient avoids dental care for years, it is not just their smile that is at risk; they are carrying a preventable health load that will rise elsewhere in time.
In addition to the system effects, the impact on quality of life is immediate and real. A toothache interferes with sleep. It impacts nutrition, concentration, and the ability to speak with confidence. These are not trivial consequences; they affect how people show up in their professional and personal lives every day.
What works in practice
The most significant change I’ve made in my practice is making communication a priority before any procedure begins. When patients feel informed and in control, it greatly reduces their dental anxiety. A stop signal—a raised hand that stops everything instantly—can alter the psychological dynamic in the room. It shifts the patient from passive recipient to active participant, and that shift matters enormously. I also allow extra time for anxious patients. The problem is not that procedures take longer, but that rushing them increases anxiety. I explain everything before it happens, check in frequently, and never minimise what a patient is feeling. These should not be luxury accommodations; they should be routine parts of effective care.
For patients with more severe anxiety, pharmacological support is appropriate. Nitrous oxide is safe, effective, and rapidly reversible. There are also oral sedation choices if needed. These are clinical tools, not last resorts, and patients should feel comfortable asking about them.
A message to patients
If fear has kept you from the dentist, remember you are not alone, and you are not too far gone to be helped. What I ask of patients in this situation is one small step—not a treatment plan, not a procedure, simply a conversation. Come in and tell us about your nervousness. A good provider is a good listener and will start there. There is no need to be afraid of the dental chair. With the right approach, it can be a place where you take difficult things and make them manageable—and where the relief on the other side is worth it.
(Dr. Sowjanya Gunukula is a U.S.-licensed dentist with international training who focuses on preventive and evidence-based oral healthcare and contributes to advancing community and public health dentistry. sowji.gunukula@gmail.com)

Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say
- Published
Pope Leo XIV's recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is "progressing as expected", his doctors have said.
The 71-year-old pontiff has started to walk and has "resumed a normal diet" following the roughly 90-minute procedure, the medics said in an update shared by the Vatican.
The Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
Blood tests and an X-ray early on Wednesday showed his recovery was "proceeding normally", the doctors said, and he has also undergone respiratory physiotherapy.
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before spending a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
The pontiff is expected to remain there for about a week as he recovers.

He had announced that he would be admitted for the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
A Vatican source told news agency AFP that further tests were carried out to see whether the cancer had spread.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.
The news has shaken Catholics worldwide, many of whom will have recent memories of Pope Francis's hospital visits.
Pope Leo's predecessor, who died last year, also had part of his lung removed in his youth before suffering a series of respiratory infections later in life.
What is lung adenocarcinoma?
Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer.
The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person's overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades.
Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early - before symptoms develop - during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss.

A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they’re estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth’s environment, most proteins don’t last nearly that long. That’s because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment.
Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases.
Cutting proteins
The basic peptide bond isn’t especially interesting-looking—it’s what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.)
Peptide bonds are formed by the removal of a water molecule from parts of an amino group and an acidic group.

Peptide bonds are formed by the removal of a water molecule from parts of an amino group and an acidic group.

Breaking these bonds apart simply reverses the process by breaking apart the peptide bond and a water molecule, and linking their parts. Because both components are chemically stable, the reaction requires an enzyme to occur with any frequency. Without an enzyme, a typical peptide bond would be stable for hundreds of years in water.
Life has evolved a handful of enzyme mechanisms that manage this catalysis. The research at issue here relied on two different ones. One is a zinc protease, where the positive charge of the zinc atom coordinates the peptide bond that’s being broken, key parts of the protease, and a water molecule. The protease partially pulls a proton off the water molecule, activating it to attack and break up the peptide bond.
The second protease the researchers use is called a cysteine protease. In this case, a cysteine (one of the amino acids) in the enzyme is activated to attack the peptide bond, creating a temporary intermediate where part of the protein being cut is chemically linked to the enzyme. A water molecule eventually breaks this intermediate apart, releasing the second part of the cut protein.
Both of these mechanisms require a handful of specific amino acids from the protease to be located in close proximity within the catalytic center of the protease. Other amino acids in the protease help ensure these key catalytic amino acids are brought together in the right place with the right orientation. The rest of the protease may also enforce a degree of specificity on what proteins get cut. Some proteases, like the ones active in our digestive system, can make cuts next to any amino acid. Others are slightly more selective, preferring to cut near positively or negatively charged amino acids. And a few are very highly specific, such as the protease that activates insulin, which only cuts near a very specific series of amino acids.
Designer enzymes
The people behind the new work, primarily from Nobel-winner David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, viewed designing a protease as a challenge. For one, the stability of the peptide bonds means that reactions wouldn’t take place without an effective catalyst. And to get that catalyst requires an extremely precise arrangement of specific amino acids. So it wasn’t obvious that the AI protein design tools the lab developed were up to the task.
Both projects took a similar approach. Just like evolution, they started with an existing protease. One was a zinc protease used in a crayfish’s digestive system. The other was a cysteine protease from yeast. In both cases, the protein structure was known, as were the key amino acids that catalyze cleaving other proteins. The design process started with these amino acids.
The design process started with software called RFdiffusion2, which creates a backbone for the enzyme (the backbone consists of the protein’s repeated peptide bonds). The researchers gave RFdiffusion2 a number of constraints. To start, any backbone it designed had to bring together the key catalytic amino acids needed for a functional protease. They also gave it a target amino acid sequence where the protease would eventually cut. The backbone had to accommodate that target sequence in close proximity to the catalytic center.
With a backbone laid out, the process next moved to ProteinMPNN, a tool that works along the backbone, populating it with specific amino acids. (That tool featured in Google’s efforts to watermark AI-designed proteins.) ProteinMPNN selects each amino acid based on a series of constraints. For starters, the amino acid must be compatible with the backbone folding up into its planned structure. Next, in critical areas, each amino acid chosen needs to be compatible with the formation of the enzyme’s catalytic site. And finally, in nearby areas, it has to be compatible with latching on to the intended target.
The researchers repeated this process dozens of times for both the cysteine and zinc proteases. For the cysteine protease, they made 12 different backbones and populated them with 69 different sets of amino acids. For the zinc project, they tried 135 different protein designs. They used AlphaFold3 to predict the structures of many of these designs and found nothing in the databases that looked much like them, confirming their tools weren’t simply stealing previously identified structures.
Do they work?
The researchers started by making a single, long protein that contained the protease, the sequence it was designed to target, and a fluorescent protein. They then tested to see if the fluorescent protein was cut loose. In the case of the cysteine protease, they got 13 designs that worked, a success rate of 19 percent, although all of them were considerably less active than the yeast enzyme that was used as a model.
The zinc project was a bit more complicated. They tested many designs that didn’t include the water molecule that normally takes part in that reaction. These had a relatively low success rate, with only 14 out of 89 showing weak catalytic activity. When they modeled the ones that didn’t work, they found that the designs often let a water molecule block the site where reactions should take place.
So, they also tried designs where they placed a water molecule in the right location as an additional design constraint. These had a much higher success rate, with 35 out of 38 showing some catalytic activity. Again, however, their activity was considerably lower than the enzyme that was used as the starting point for the designs. (They did get one design with a better level of activity, but it wasn’t specific about where it cut other proteins.)
To find out whether this activity could be improved, the researchers identified amino acids that were in close proximity to the active site of the protease, but not actively involved with the catalysis. And they swapped in every alternative amino acid that wasn’t predicted to disrupt the structure of the design. They found some versions that were considerably more active; the best version they identified accelerated the cleavage of the peptide bond by a factor of 109 while remaining highly specific for the intended target protein sequence.
Similar things happened with the zinc-based protease. Their v2 version of their protease, which incorporated some of the random mutations, was 30 times more active than the original design it was based on. It also accelerated peptide-bond cleavage by a factor of 1010.
As a final demonstration of this approach’s promise, the researchers designed zinc proteases that could target proteins associated with neurological disorders, such as Alzheimer’s and frontotemporal dementia. Attempting to modify their existing design to target a new sequence didn’t work well, so they started the process over from the start and managed to find something that could cut the intended target in cells. For the researchers, this suggests that we might ultimately be able to influence the course of some genetic diseases by targeting the malformed proteins that cause them.
What do the results tell us?
The potential therapeutic use of this is complicated. Proteins are often difficult to deliver to the site where they’re needed, and can often trigger an immune response. Things get even more challenging if the protease target is inside a cell rather than on the exterior. That would likely require the target cells to make the protease, which would involve delivering the gene encoding it to the cells where it’s needed. So, there are considerable hurdles that would need to be cleared before we could potentially start developing therapies using this technology.
The researchers also highlight how the work shows some limitations of the tools. As used, they successfully designed proteins that matched all the physical constraints they were given: They folded up into structures that brought the amino acids needed to catalyze a reaction into roughly the right location, and latched on to specific target amino acid sequences.
But we don’t, at the moment, have the ability to tell these tools we want any specific catalytic activity. So many designs lacked some of the subtle details that make evolved enzymes such great catalysts. In other words, the tools are great at structure, but they’re not necessarily great at activity. And, while structure is essential for function, it isn’t everything. As the researchers saw, introducing random mutation could still make subtle structural tweaks that produced enzymes that were considerably more active.
Of course, this protein design software is only a few years old, and both developers and users might have ideas for incorporating constraints beyond physical location.

- Brittle Ice blocks can be naturally found over crevasses in Ice Caves or generated using Blue Ice and Water.
- A single Blue Ice block can continuously generate Brittle Ice blocks when water is flowing horizontally towards it.
- Brittle Ice cracks and breaks when players or most mobs stand on it.
The Ice Caves in Minecraft are becoming more dangerous with each passing week, as the Brittle Ice block has just made its appearance among the experimental features. Unlike regular Ice, this new block starts cracking when you stand on it and eventually breaks. So, if you thought you knew the Ice Caves biome by heart, here is everything you need to know about the Minecraft Brittle Ice block, how to get it, and more.
Items Required to Make and Mine Brittle Ice in Minecraft
Before you start making Brittle Ice in the upcoming Minecraft 26.4 update, you’ll need a few basic resources. Thankfully, unlike most Minecraft farms that require an entire chest of Redstone components, this one requires a minimal setup. So, here’s all that you need:
| Required Items | Quantity | Where to Get | 
|---|---|---|
| Blue Ice | 1 | Find these at the bottom of Icebergs and underneath frozen ocean biomes | 
| Water Bucket | 1 | Use an empty iron bucket on a body of water to pick it up | 
| Pickaxe with Silk Touch | 1 | Get the Minecraft Silk Touch enchantment on any pickaxe of your choice, preferably Diamond. | 
Note that getting the Silk Touch enchantment on your pickaxe or any other tool is mandatory because it will help break the Brittle Ice block and drop it as an item. Without the enchantment, your tool will simply break the block, and it’ll disappear.
How to Make Brittle Ice with Blue Ice and Water in Minecraft
Now that you have collected the required materials, it is time to create your own Brittle Ice generator. This method eliminates the need to repeatedly explore the Minecraft Ice Caves, allowing you to farm as many blocks as you want from your own base. Follow the steps below to make Brittle Ice:
Step 1: Craft an Iron Bucket and Pick Up Water
- To make a bucket in Minecraft, you need to place 3 Iron Ingots in a V shape on the Crafting Table grid.
- Place one at the top-left cell, one at the top-right cell, and the third one at the center to create the bucket.
- Once made, head to any river or body of water, and interact with the surface with the bucket in your hand to pick up water.
Step 2: Get Blue Ice from Icebergs
- Head to the bottom of the Icebergs or the frozen ocean biomes of Minecraft to find the Blue Ice blocks for your generator.
- Use a Pickaxe enchanted with Silk Touch to break the Blue Ice block and head back to your place where you want to create Brittle Ice.
Step 3: Create a Brittle Ice Generator
- Find a flat area and dig a small channel to control the flow of water.
- Place a single Blue Ice block at one end of your setup.
- Use the water bucket to release water on the other end so that it flows directly against the Blue Ice block.
- A block of Brittle Ice will generate before the Blue Ice.
- You can now use the Silk Touch enchanted pickaxe to break the block and pick it up.
- Since Brittle Ice will keep on generating, you can repeat the process for more such blocks.
Alternate Ways to Find and Get Brittle Ice in Minecraft
If you want to explore the game and find some Brittle Ice blocks yourselves through this risk-reward feature, the best place to look is the new Ice Caves biome. However, beware of the several cave mobs in Minecraft that can spawn here.
Brittle Ice appears over the crevasses, which are narrow openings and fissures carved into the cave floor. These formations can create dangerous sections of terrain that can otherwise seem like any ordinary-looking icy surface. Here are some easy steps to get Brittle Ice from the Ice Caves:
- Explore the underground Cave system, particularly those beneath the colder biomes.
- Look for crevasses covering the slightly transparent ice blocks.
- Carefully approach the formation and identify the Brittle Ice blocks that have small cracks on their surfaces.
- Do not stand on Brittle Ice; instead, stand on a nearby solid block and then use your Silk Touch pickaxe to break it.
- Explore other crevasses to obtain more Brittle Ice while also keeping your eyes open for the Frostbite zombie mobs in Minecraft.
All Uses of Brittle Ice in Minecraft
Brittle Ice isn’t just another decorative block that you would craft and store in your inventory. It has a unique mechanic of breaking when an entity stands on top of it. Map creators and builders already have a ton of ideas for unique setups using Brittle Ice. So, here’s what you can do:
Create Collapsing Floors and Parkour Challenges
Brittle Ice progresses through its cracking stages every second when one stands on it before eventually breaking. Once it breaks, the adjacent Brittle Ice blocks also advance by one cracking stage, creating a chain reaction.
This makes the block perfect for custom parkour maps in Minecraft where the player must keep moving rather than carefully planning their jumps.
Build Traps for Players and Hostile Mobs
Want to give your friends a reason to question every block in your Minecraft base? Brittle Ice blocks are your perfect option.
One way to counter falling into the abyss when there is Brittle Ice all over the area is to use non-entity blocks to traverse. This includes boats, minecarts, cushions, and more. Among them, using a boat in Minecraft is the best choice to slide down the icy blocks and never fall down.
Create Frostbite Exclusive Pathways
One of the coolest interactions involves the new Frostbite mobs that can walk over Brittle Ice without breaking it. This gives them a unique advantage to chase you inside the caves biome.
You could use this behavior to create mob-specific pathways, themed adventure maps, or survival challenges where Frostbite can safely cross areas that collapse upon your touch.
And that completes the guide on how to make Brittle Ice blocks in Minecraft, where to find it, and all of its uses. So, how are you going to use it in the game? Tell us in the comments below.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to India for his second visit in six months, with energy and trade relations on the top of the agenda as he visits Mumbai and Jamnagar, the U.S. Department of State announced on Wednesday (Octobre 14, 2026).
However, Mr. Rubio, who is expected to visit India from October 19 to 22 after travelling to Samarkand in Uzbekistan for a regional conference, will skip Delhi.
“[Mr. Rubio] will meet with senior government officials to strengthen the U.S.-India strategic partnership, exchange views on regional and global dynamics, and discuss prospects for enhanced energy cooperation,” the State department said in the statement, adding that Mr. Rubio will also meet business leaders to “promote investment opportunities”.
Mr. Rubio’s scheduled visit to Jamnagar is important as it hosts the world’s largest single-site refinery, operated by Reliance industries, and is expected to include a major reception hosted by the Ambani family. The Jamnagar refinery is one of the top three companies refining Russian Ural crude oil, although it has reduced its share of the imports. The visit would follow just a day after U.S. President Donald Trump is mandated by the U.S. Congress to propose extra tariffs as sanctions on India and other countries buying Russian oil, under the Sanctions Against Russian and Iran Act (SRIA) passed into law last month.
In March 2026, Mr. Trump announced that Reliance Industries would invest in a refinery in Brownsville, Texas, although details of the exact collaboration have still not been released.
The U.S. Secretary of State is expected to meet External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar during the visit, but the Ministry of External Affairs didn’t confirm the visit or answer questions on why Mr. Rubio is skipping Delhi on this visit.
Asked about the U.S. statement on the trip, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that the government would make the announcement “at the appropriate time as to what will be the issues to be taken up”. He also said that the government would disclose details of the visit “as and when they happen”. To another question, he said that India had already conveyed its concerns over the SRIA to the U.S. government.
Tension in ties
The visit by Mr. Rubio comes at a time of tensions in the India-U.S. economic relationship for a number of other reasons as well. Senior officials and Ministers on both sides have acknowledged there is trouble in the Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA), with Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman saying that the talks last week had “plateaued”.
The U.S.-India ties were dealt another blow last week as the Trump administration suspended permission for five Indian tech outsourcing companies to certify Indian professionals as eligible for green cards or permanent residency. The visit would also come just ahead of the key mid-term elections in the U.S., where Mr. Trump’s Republican Party is expected to face losses.
Mr. Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet nonetheless on December 13, on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Florida, and possibly in November at the ASEAN linked summits in Manila. Both leaders spoke over the telephone on September 30.
In Kolkata on Monday for celebrations of the U.S.’s 250th Independence day anniversary, U.S. Ambassador to India and the region Sergio Gor indicated to journalists that more engagements would be announced soon, saying “stay tuned for what comes next.” Mr. Rubio last visited Delhi in May 2026 to attend the Quad Foreign Ministers’ meeting.

Trump’s DOJ threatens to block California votes in explosive pre-election showdown
The Justice Department on Tuesday gave California officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action

The Department of Justice has given California authorities 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action, according to a letter Reuters reviewed, marking an unprecedented attempt to find evidence of voter fraud ahead of next month's elections.
The letter, authored by acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter and sent to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, says federal officials gave Los Angeles County administrators a "password-protected thumb drive" containing the names of individuals the government "believes are likely noncitizens" who were issued mail-in ballots.
The directive requires the state to withhold ballots from those named on the list until it can verify their citizenship status. Flagged voters who have already received ballots must have their submissions "segregated" once returned, and ballots already submitted should not be counted "until citizenship has been determined," the letter dictates.
Federal authorities "will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," the letter warns, if state officials fail to follow these instructions.
"Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes," McCotter wrote in the communication.
The ultimatum reflects a heightened effort by the Trump administration to pressure states over alleged voting by non-citizens, signaling that the Justice Department may be prepared to challenge ballots in the weeks before the November 3 election, when Republicans will be defending narrow congressional majorities.
Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten Pels confirmed the letter's existence in a statement to Reuters, stating: "The department will take all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure compliance with federal law."
Spokespersons for the White House and the California secretary of state's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Under President Donald Trump, the Justice Department has repeatedly asserted that voting by noncitizens is a widespread problem, despite numerous studies demonstrating that the practice is rare.
A Reuters review in September found that while software glitches and clerical errors may have added more than 30,000 noncitizens to state voter rolls since 2000, it remained unclear how many had actually cast ballots.
Experts emphasized that these figures were far too small relative to the nation's 170 million registered voters to influence election outcomes.
In July, the Justice Department dispatched letters to chief election officials across all 50 states, warning of potential criminal prosecution if they knowingly permitted noncitizens to vote or remain on voter rolls.
The department's Civil Rights Division has requested nonpublic voter information, including birth dates and Social Security numbers, from nearly every state as part of its effort to identify noncitizens. It has filed lawsuits against 30 states led by both Democrats and Republicans that refused to release their rolls, losing 26 of those cases.
Reuters reported last month that the Department of Homeland Security was utilizing a commercial data broker to access sensitive voter details not included in public records, a practice that officials and experts warned could result in eligible citizens being mistakenly identified as illegal voters and potentially detained.
Federal prosecutors have also stepped up prosecutions against noncitizens accused of registering fraudulently or voting in previous elections, announcing 16 new criminal cases on Monday.
Officials in Democratic-led California have clashed for months with the Trump administration over federal efforts to intervene in state voting procedures based on allegations of voter fraud.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin informed California officials on July 16 that federal authorities believed noncitizens were present on the state's voting rolls, according to the letter.
California could play a pivotal role in deciding control of the US House of Representatives, particularly after state voters approved a new congressional map favoring Democrats amid a nationwide redistricting push initiated in Republican-led states.
Voters in Los Angeles will also decide on a local ballot measure that would permit certain noncitizen legal residents to vote in municipal elections.

Kipchoge, 41, breaks course record at Melbourne Marathon
- Published
Two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge says "his body is still peaking" after winning the Melbourne Marathon in a course record time at the age of 41.
The Kenyan crossed the line in two hours nine minutes 10 seconds for his 17th career win over the distance and first since the Berlin Marathon in 2023.
"I believe that my body is still peaking - still able to compete with the next generation," Kipchoge said.
"The oldest athlete is still competing but I am happy to run with the Gen Zs."
The course was partly raced along the Australian Formula One track at Albert Park and finished inside the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG).
"On the course, it was really wonderful, I enjoyed seeing people standing, cheering, and shouting my name," added Kipchoge, who slowed down inside the MCG to wave to the fans.
"It was actually different - running on a beautiful course, but also running on the Formula One track, and above all else, finishing on a cricket ground.
"It makes me proud to run with the younger generation and inspire the running community in Melbourne."
Australian Thomas do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35, with compatriot Reece Edwards third.
New Zealand's Camille French won the women's race in 2:28:25, followed by Australian Sinead Diver and Nichola Sheridan of Ireland.
The Melbourne Marathon was the third leg on Kipchoge's world tour, on which he hopes to complete a marathon on all seven continents, including Antarctica, over two years.
Each marathon will raise funds for the Eliud Kipchoge Foundation, which focuses on education, environmental sustainability and health.
Kipchoge is considered one of the greatest long-distance runners of all time, winning two Olympic marathon golds, plus a silver and bronze over 5000m.
His honours also include a world title, 12 World Marathon Major victories and two official world records.
In 2019 he became the first person to break the two-hour marathon barrier under special conditions in Vienna, clocking an unofficial time of one hour 59 minutes 40 seconds.

Even as the Centre informed the Supreme Court on Monday (October 12, 2026) that it had decided to cap trade margins at 30% for non-scheduled cancer drugs, the court questioned why the benefit of such price regulation should be confined to cancer drugs and not extended to other essential medicines and medical products.
The development comes after a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta expressed concern over stark disparities between the price to retailer (PTR) and the maximum retail price (MRP) of certain medicines, particularly cancer drugs, with mark-ups in some instances soaring to 1,000%. The Bench had flagged that such exorbitant mark-ups constituted “broad daylight dacoity” and placed an enormous financial burden on patients.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, informed the Bench that the proposed 30% trade-margin cap would cover both patented and non-patented cancer medicines, with an expert committee headed by the Director General of Health Services tasked with identifying the drugs to be brought within its ambit. The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) will examine the committee’s recommendations before issuing a price notification to implement the cap.
The Bench, however, said that while the intervention was commendable, it was inadequate, and questioned why other medicines and medical devices could not also be brought within the 16% retailer margin prescribed under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013.
“This is just the tip of the iceberg... this has come around only because of the unduly hard observations we made during earlier hearings. What about other drugs,” the Bench asked.
The top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha seeking stricter enforcement of price controls under the DPCO to curb disproportionate margins across the pharmaceutical supply chain.
Justice Mehta drew attention to steep markups on medical devices and consumables, pointing out that an India-made cardiac stent costing around ₹5,000 was being sold by hospitals for more than ₹25,000. He cited the example of a saline drip line carrying an MRP of ₹11 being sold for ₹270.
“We understand that there are transportation costs, raw material costs, R&D costs and other ancillary costs, but all these are included in the MRP. What is the logic behind allowing them to sell at 400 times the actual cost? How can you allow this? What is the benefit for the patients?” the Bench observed.
‘Balance in pricing’
Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, also appearing for the Centre, cautioned against a uniform cap across medicines, arguing that low-value products often required higher margins to remain commercially viable for retailers. Excessive regulation, she said, could discourage retailers from stocking such medicines and affect their availability, particularly in rural areas.
Ms. Bhati stressed the need to preserve some room for market forces rather than subject the entire pharmaceutical sector to price controls.
“Higher margins in such cases are important for ensuring the availability of such medicines to consumers… Our concern is that there has to be a balance in pricing. There has to be some level of market play available for drugs. We do not want to control the entire ecosystem of drugs. The policy was framed with the outlook that there should be intervention only when necessary,” she submitted.
The Bench, however, was not persuaded, observing that ensuring the availability of price-controlled medicines was the government’s responsibility.
“If the DPCO -approved medicines do not reach customers, then it is the duty of the government to ensure it reaches [sic] the patient. The actual dispute is over which medicines should be on the DPCO-controlled list and which should not,” Justice Mehta observed.
Accordingly, the Bench gave the Centre until October 27 to work out the modalities for capping medicine prices, when the matter will be heard next.
Centre’s affidavit
The Centre, in its 551-page affidavit, said the proposed trade-margin rationalisation (TMR) was expected to reduce the MRP of anti-cancer drugs by 20% to 70%, translating into estimated annual savings of around ₹2,500 crore. It said the measure would reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure and improve the affordability and accessibility of cancer medicines, while retaining a 30% trade margin for the distribution chain.
The Centre cited a similar intervention by the NPPA in 2019, when a 30% trade-margin cap was imposed at the first point of sale on 42 select non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines. The margin was based on an industry-practice assumption of 10% for distributors and 20% for retailers.
The measure, it said, led to a substantial reduction in the MRP of 526 brands and annual savings of around ₹984 crore for patients, based on information furnished by pharmaceutical companies. The Centre said the 2019 exercise provided a policy and operational precedent for extending trade-margin rationalisation to a wider range of non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines.
Detailing the existing price-control mechanism, the Centre said the ceiling price of medicines listed in Schedule I of the DPCO is determined by taking the simple average of the price to retailer of brands and generic versions with a market share of at least 1%, and adding a 16% margin.
“The ceiling price so fixed becomes the MRP, i.e., the price above which the drug cannot be sold in the market. However, the manufacturer is at liberty to give an appropriate margin to the wholesaler and the retailer within the ceiling price,” it said, adding that ceiling prices had so far been fixed for 935 formulations.
For non-scheduled formulations, manufacturers are free to determine the initial launch price, subject to the NPPA’s regulation of subsequent price increases. The Centre said competition in the pharmaceutical market generally acted as a restraint against arbitrary pricing.

For the first time in medical and legal history, a prisoner has “survived a complete execution attempt in the U.S.” According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Christa Pike’s failed execution was “the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era (since 1976). There is no precedent.” This game-changing bioethics case may even end lethal injection.
About 7,000 people were executed in the U.S. between 1900 and 1976, and 1,683 people after 1976. Ultimately, since 1900, only 0.6% (55) have been women. Pike is now the second woman on death row the U.S. Supreme Court declined to rescue from a botched execution.
On June 18, 1953, the controversial case of accused spy Ethel Rosenberg, who had two small children, also came before the Supreme Court. It overturned her stay of execution. The following day, on June 19, 1953, the electric chair execution of Rosenberg failed; the settings were not properly adjusted for a woman of Rosenberg’s size, and she did not die after the first round of electrocution.
A doctor examined her and informed the state she was not dead and that they needed to electrocute her a second time. The report from United Press International and The New York Times described the debacle and the role of two physicians involved who “ordered” more electrocution. According to Rosenberg’s biographer, “she was removed from the electric chair after three charges, only for it to be discovered her heart was still beating, so, gruesomely, she had to be strapped back into it.”
Nineteen years later, in 1972, after five more women were executed without incident in the U.S., the Supreme Court of California ruled the death penalty unconstitutional in People v. Anderson, which led to the commutation of all California death sentences to life sentences. This included three of the women involved in the brutal Manson murders — Susan Atkins, Patricia Krenwinkel, and Leslie Van Houten — all scheduled to be gassed. That same year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that capital punishment violated the Eighth Amendment in Furman v. Georgia.
In response to the Furman ruling, states began to explore more humane methods of execution, which is what led to the current lethal injection protocol, originally pioneered by Oklahoma’s state medical examiner at the time, Jay Chapman in 1977, and later adapted by Jack Kevorkian as a method of “medicide” — an early version of what we now call medical assistance in dying.
In 1976, the U.S. Supreme Court sanctioned state executions again in Gregg v. Georgia because it saw lethal injection as a “sanitized, quasi-clinical procedure” upholding the Eighth Amendment. Lethal injection became the norm when executions restarted in 1977; Ronald Reagan compared it to putting an animal to sleep. On June 11, 2001, Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh was executed using the Chapman protocol. It was even broadcast on a closed-circuit system to survivors and affected families.
But over time, due to a variety of systems issues with obtaining certain medications, the lethal injection protocol has deviated from the standard devised by Chapman.
More importantly, since the lethal injection protocol requires an intravenous line insertion, the person administering it has to be competent in IV infusion. But the people facing execution often have veins that are tricky to access. A disturbing report in 2022 found that more than a third of executions are “botched” because of unskilled personnel.
Since the American Medical Association and the American Nurses Association state that it is unethical for medical providers to participate in any way in executions, state prisons struggle to find skilled personnel to handle lethal injection, resulting in many failed attempts. The case of Lee Hamm, another failed attempt at lethal injection, raised numerous questions about the role of health care providers after a botched procedure.
Just prior to Pike’s planned execution, NPR reported that the opaque Tennessee protocol does involve health care providers, and some are willing to cross ethical lines. Physician Mark Fowler, for instance, was involved in the failed execution case of Tony Carruthers in May.
But the Carruthers case created a bioethics chasm where “dozens of Tennessee medical professionals told the governor that health care professionals shouldn’t help with executions, ever. No matter the method.” Fowler reportedly was involved in Pike’s failed execution as well.
The majority of health care providers maintain either the American Medical Association’s code of ethics or the American Nurses Association’s position. A recent Hastings Center Bioethics Forum essay concludes that lethal injection is unethical, while other bioethicists have suggested that the presence of a health care provider would not only be “lending the prestige of medicine to the execution” but also provide the false impression that lethal injection was being supervised by doctors, and therefore more acceptable.
The Pike case is novel not only because it’s the first time in legal history a prisoner has survived a completed execution procedure resulting in dizzying legal repercussions, but because of the “hot mess” clinical ethics case that has emerged.
When Pike remained alive after the failed procedure, she was rushed to the hospital for lifesaving treatment. What were the “goals of care”? To make her medically stable enough for another attempt at execution? (Tennessee’s Prison Commissioner resigned, and the state has paused executions for the remainder of the year, but not indefinitely.) Per national and local news reports on Oct. 7, Pike initially remained intubated and unconscious as her health care team planned to remove life support in the belief that Pike was progressing to brain death. Pike also remained in restraints (handcuffed and shackled to her bed), which complicated her care.
But then she awoke and spoke, raising new questions about her neurological status. Pike first inquired: “Where am I and who are you?” Her attorneys state: “There is still a lot of cognitive confusion. … She is very aware that the state tried to execute. … She is very aware up to a point.”
Any clinical ethicist would advise at this juncture that Pike may fully regain decision-making capacity and is already showing signs of understanding and appreciation. Patients who are inmates and have decision-making capacity can make all medical decisions, including end of life decisions, but the correctional institution may limit options based on costs. In general, correctional officers should not be involved with inmates’ medical decisions, but health care providers do not have the authority to remove restraints; such decisions reside with the correctional facility.
Bioethicists have been actively debating this case, with consensus that if Pike were deemed to be incapacitated, a court-appointed surrogate decision-maker (someone who makes decisions in the best medical interests of a patient who does not have autonomy) would be necessary since the state — even Tennessee’s Adult Protective Services — would have a conflict of interest. Pike’s biological family has provided insight into her childhood that would also raise questions about authentic surrogacy. Because of Ford v. Wainwright, incapacitated prisoners cannot be executed, so if Pike regains capacity, the legal road is unclear.
As of this writing, it’s impossible to predict Pike’s ultimate prognosis or fate, but the legal and medical issues in the Pike case are on a collision course. Pre-Pike, lethal injection was “passing” as a “death with dignity” medical assistance in dying procedure, which, ironically, is illegal in several death penalty states, including Tennessee. Post-Pike, lethal injection will never be the same. Its procedural flaws have been exposed; it’s the emperor with no clothes because it only “pretends to be medicine.” Of course, there are other forms of execution that actually look like one instead of medicine, as in the case of the planned execution by firing squad of the Fort Hood shooter, which may even be streamed live.
For states that want to continue lethal injection, medical expertise at various points in the process — whether it’s training prison staff, providing medical opinions on “candidacy” for lethal injection, or actually participating — will likely become a requirement that most health care providers will find ethically incompatible with clinical ethics principles of practice. If medical expertise becomes a legal requirement for lethal injection, but no reputable health care provider will participate, then the stigma of participation may effectively end lethal injection as we know it.
M. Sara Rosenthal, Ph.D., is professor and founding director of the University of Kentucky Program for Bioethics and Oncology Ethics Program and chair of the UK HealthCare Ethics Committee.

Afcon move to every four years under review by Caf
- Published
The Africa Cup of Nations could continue to be held every two years, with discussions under way to reverse its proposed switch to a four-year cycle.
Speaking on Friday at a Confederation of African Football (Caf) strategy conference in Cape Verde, president Patrice Motsepe said: "We've discussed it over the last few days.
"We are looking at everything, including having the Afcon coming back every two years. We are very clear, the matter is being reviewed."
The tournament has taken place every two years since 1968, bar a one-year gap between the 2012 and 2013 editions.
However, in December 2025 CAF announced it would shift to being staged every four years after the 2027 Afcon in East Africa and a 2028 edition.
That planned alteration to the schedule had received widespread criticism across the continent.
National associations had raised concerns about the visibility of their teams, the commercial implications and where Africa's biggest competition would sit in the international football calendar.

Discovery+ subscription prices went up today.
Ad-free plans for new subscribers went from $10 per month to $12/month. Ad-based plans went from $6 to $7.
The new prices take effect for new subscribers immediately. Current subscribers to the streaming service, which primarily features unscripted content, like reality shows and documentaries, will receive 30 days’ notice before the new prices take effect, starting with bills issued as of November 12.
The higher prices come a week after Paramount Skydance bought Discovery+ parent company Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), forming Skydance.
However, a Skydance spokesperson told Ars Technica that the pricing changes were in the works before Discovery+ knew about the merger’s closing date and were not planned in anticipation of a merger.
The spokesperson said that Discovery+’s prices are regularly evaluated to ensure that they are in line with the content and experience that the service offers, and the new prices reflect that.
Discovery+ has increased its prices three times since launching in 2012. Before today, the most recent price hike occurred in January 2025, when ad-based monthly subscriptions increased from $5 to $6, and ad-free plans went from $9 to $10.

A “video recording device” was found in the cabin of a Royal Australian Navy ship in Cairns, the defence department has revealed, just hours after senator Jacqui Lambie alleged in parliament that a camera had been found concealed in a women’s shower on the vessel.
The department confirmed on Wednesday afternoon that a device had been found aboard the HMAS Leeuwin three days earlier. In a statement after Guardian Australia had contacted the department for response to Lambie’s allegations, a spokesperson said police were investigating, but did not reveal further details about where the device was located.
“On 11 October 2026, Defence became aware that a video recording device had been located in the cabin of Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin, while alongside in Cairns, Queensland,” they said.
“The incident was referred to the Joint Military Police Unit and Defence is working with civilian authorities. Defence takes this incident extremely seriously and does not tolerate unacceptable behaviour in any form.”
On Wednesday morning, Lambie – an ADF veteran and advocate for defence personnel – told the Senate that she’d been contacted by a former member of the navy with allegations about a camera being found aboard HMAS Leeuwin.
“The sender told me that concealed cameras have recently been found in the female sailors’ showers facilities on the vessel HMAS Leeuwin, based in Cairns,” she said in the Senate.
“I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing. Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered.
“How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask Navy.”
Guardian Australia asked the department if any perpetrator had been identified, if the defence force was aware of hidden cameras being found in other navy facilities, and if any such footage from hidden cameras had been found to have been shared online.
The department did not directly answer those questions. In its statement, it said HMAS Leeuwin had “remained alongside to enable the investigation and ensure immediate support was provided to members of the ship’s crew”.
“The welfare of individuals remains Defence’s priority, and support is ongoing. As the matter is currently under investigation and to protect the privacy of the affected individuals, Defence is unable to provide further comment at this time,” it said.
Asked at a subsequent press conference about the incident, Lambie said she was unhappy with the department’s response.
“Defence needs to know this. Your people had a gutful, and if there was abuse going on, they’re now coming to me. OK, I’m right on their tail. Enough is enough. Get control of what is going on in the defence force,” she said.
“What I want to know is, have they gone around on the rest of those boats, the subs, whatever, and had a look and make sure there’s no other cameras? Because we are not sure whether it’s coming from contractors that go on them, or whether it’s come from defence members.”

Women account for 43% of the workforce in India’s Ayush services sector, with their representation crossing 50% in several organised segments, including hospitals, day-care centres, educational institutions and wellness establishments, according to a new assessment of the sector released by the Central government on Thursday (October 8, 2026).
The Ayush Services Sector Report, prepared by the Research and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) and released on Ayurveda Day 2026, estimates that the sector supports 1.76 million livelihoods across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services.
Women’s representation is highest in spas and wellness resorts, where it exceeds 60%, followed by educational institutions at 58%, day-care centres at 57% and hospitals at 53%, says the report.
The findings come as the Ayush services economy expands beyond traditional clinical practice into wellness, education, preventive health and medical value travel.
16.91% growth
The sector, comprising Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy, was estimated at $36.92 billion in 2024-25. It has registered a compound annual growth rate of 16.91% since 2022-23.
Standalone clinics remain the largest segment, generating an estimated $16.21 billion, or 43.9% of the sector’s revenue. Day-care centres contribute another $10.13 billion. Together, the two segments account for more than 70% of the sector’s revenue.
“More than one million livelihoods are concentrated in local and standalone clinics, underlining the sector’s employment footprint across urban and rural areas,’’ says the report.
The wellness segment has recorded a 21.29% compound annual growth rate, while yoga centres registered about 75% growth in revenue over two years, according to the assessment.
Ayurveda remains the largest individual Ayush system, accounting for $17.73 billion, or about 48% of the total services revenue.
The sector is also gaining a foothold in medical value travel. Ayush-related medical value travel generated an estimated $1.77 billion in 2024-25. Although international patients account for only around 5% of patient volumes, they contribute an estimated 15-25% of hospital-segment revenue, with therapeutic programmes typically involving stays of five to 11 days.
The assessment projects that the Ayush services economy could expand to between $216 billion and $318 billion by 2047.
Job opportunities
Union Minister of State for Ayush Prataprao Jadhav said the sector’s expansion was creating employment opportunities across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services, while also opening avenues for entrepreneurship and women’s participation.
The report projects further employment opportunities in healthcare delivery, wellness, education, medical travel, research, digital health and allied services as the sector expands.

The leak was only detected a week after the exam was conducted, triggering massive protests in Parliament and eventually leading to the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan after millions of young people -- under the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) banner -- hit the streets.

Frederick G. Banting and John J.R. Macleod were awarded the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of insulin, a hormone that regulates blood glucose levels. Their work helped establish insulin as a treatment for diabetes, a disease that, in its severe forms, had often been fatal before insulin therapy became available.
The prize was shared equally. Banting and Macleod were recognised “for the discovery of insulin”. The award acknowledged research conducted at the University of Toronto in the early 1920s, when investigators developed pancreatic extracts that could lower blood sugar in diabetic animals and subsequently demonstrated their therapeutic potential in humans. Charles Best, who worked with Banting, and biochemist James Collip, who helped purify insulin for clinical use, also made important contributions to this work.
Research on pancreas and blood sugar
Diabetes had been linked to the pancreas decades before insulin was isolated. In 1889, researchers Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering demonstrated that removing the pancreas from dogs produced diabetes. Subsequent research established the importance of the islets of Langerhans, clusters of cells within the pancreas, in regulating blood sugar.
The challenge was to identify and extract the substance responsible for this effect. Several researchers attempted to prepare pancreatic extracts, but obtaining a preparation that could be used safely and consistently in patients remained difficult.
Frederick G. Banting was a Canadian physician and surgeon whose interest in diabetes led him to investigate the role of the pancreas in regulating blood glucose. After serving in the First World War, he returned to Canada and worked in medical practice before pursuing research.
John J.R. Macleod was a Scottish-born physician and physiologist who had built his career around teaching and research in physiology, including carbohydrate metabolism. By 1920, he was a professor of physiology at the University of Toronto.
Banting approached Macleod in 1921 with a proposal to isolate a substance from the pancreas that could regulate blood glucose. Macleod provided laboratory facilities, scientific guidance and access to experimental animals. Banting began the work with Charles Best, a medical student who assisted with the experiments. Their collaboration brought together Banting’s research hypothesis and Macleod’s experience in physiology, setting the stage for the experiments that led to the development of insulin as a treatment for diabetes.
The researchers tied off the pancreatic ducts of dogs, allowing the enzyme-producing tissue to degenerate while attempting to preserve the islets. They prepared extracts from the pancreas and tested them in dogs whose pancreases had been removed. The extracts lowered blood sugar and improved the animals’ clinical condition.
These experiments provided evidence that an extract from the pancreas could help compensate for the loss of its normal blood sugar-regulating function. However, the early preparations were not suitable for prolonged use in humans because they contained impurities that caused adverse reactions.
Purifying insulin for treatment
In 1922, biochemist James Collip joined the research team to improve the purity of the pancreatic extract. His work helped produce a preparation suitable for clinical testing.
In January 1922, insulin was administered to Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old boy with severe diabetes, at Toronto General Hospital. The first injection produced limited results, and an abscess developed at the injection site. After the preparation was further purified, a second course of treatment produced a marked improvement in his condition, with a substantial reduction in blood glucose and urinary glucose.
Thompson’s response demonstrated that insulin could be used to treat diabetes in humans. The development of more reliable preparations and the expansion of production subsequently allowed treatment to reach more patients.
Insulin did not cure diabetes, but it changed the outlook for people living with the disease. Before its introduction, severe diabetes was often managed through restrictive diets that could prolong life only for a limited period. Insulin enabled patients to use glucose more effectively and helped prevent the severe metabolic disturbances associated with insulin deficiency.
The role of Best and Collip
The Nobel decision remains a significant part of the history of insulin research. Although Banting and Macleod received the prize, the work involved a larger research team.
Banting was unhappy that Best had not been included among the laureates. He shared half of his prize money with Best. Macleod, in turn, shared half of his prize money with Collip, recognising his contribution to the purification of insulin.
Later historical assessments of the discovery acknowledged the importance of contributions made by researchers who were not included in the award.
Laboratory discovery,modern diabetes care
The introduction of insulin marked a turning point in the treatment of diabetes. It allowed many people living with severe insulin deficiency to survive and helped establish hormone replacement as a major approach to treating endocrine disorders.
Insulin is produced by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy or stored for later use. When the body produces insufficient insulin, or cannot use it effectively, blood glucose levels can rise.
Insulin remains essential for people with type 1 diabetes, in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells that produce the hormone. It is also used by some people with type 2 diabetes when other treatments do not adequately control blood glucose.
The treatment has evolved considerably since the first pancreatic extracts were administered. Modern insulin preparations are manufactured under controlled conditions, with different formulations developed to vary how quickly they begin working and how long their effects last.
The Nobel recognition
Banting and Macleod received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for 1923. Banting delivered his Nobel lecture, titled ‘Diabetes and Insulin’, on September 15, 1925, while Macleod’s lecture, ‘The Physiology of Insulin and Its Source in the Animal Body’, followed on May 26, 1925.
The discovery also has a lasting connection to World Diabetes Day, observed on November 14, the birthday of Banting, who was born in 1891. More than a century later, insulin remains a cornerstone of diabetes treatment, changing a condition that was once often fatal into one that can be managed with sustained treatment.

Why Saudi Arabia has struggled to defend its airport against recent Houthi attacks
The attacks have struck Saudi airports, killed at least 14 people and forced schoolchildren and businesspeople to stay indoors
