Saudi Arabia possesses one of the world’s most costly and sophisticated arsenals, packed with American warplanes, missile defences and other cutting-edge technology.
Yet in recent days, it has appeared helpless in the face of waves of missiles and drones launched by the Houthi rebel group from neighbouring Yemen. The attacks have hit Saudi airports, killed at least 14 people, and forced schoolchildren and businesspeople to remain indoors and work from home.
The Iran-backed Houthis, once regarded as little more than a ragtag militia, have transformed into a formidable fighting force. They have damaged the region’s top oil producer, threatened vital supply routes in the Red Sea, and now risk reigniting a full-scale war on the Arabian Peninsula that displaced millions and killed tens of thousands.
The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports government forces in Yemen the rebels seek to overthrow. As Saudi Arabia investigates how its air defences failed to stop the Houthis' attacks, it must also consider how to respond and what the rebels might do next.
Here’s what we know and don’t know about the Saudi and Houthi conflict:
Saudi Arabia has a vast arsenal of US weapons
Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It says the Saudis received 12 per cent of all U.S. arms exports from 2021-2025.
Over the years, the Saudis have purchased American F-15 warplanes, Patriot air defence systems, as well as advanced radars and offensive missile systems, according to the think tank, which tracks global arms transfers.
Saudi Arabia's annual budget for 2026 listed $83 billion for military expenditures. Earlier this year, it struck a $9 billion deal with Washington for 730 Patriot missiles.
But it has a huge area to defend
The Houthis have been able to exploit Saudi Arabia's large size.
Vulnerable energy, civilian and military assets are scattered across the country's sparsely populated territory roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) through rugged desert areas.
“Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defence can guarantee complete protection,” Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, said in a post online Monday.
At the same time, regional officials say that Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptors and has reached out to allies for help.
Saudi Arabia recently struck a joint defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey. But so far, the two countries appear to be largely staying on the sidelines or limiting their support.
President Donald Trump said this week he is evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. But he has not yet announced a decision.
Houthi weapons and tactics are battle-tested
Like their patron Iran, the Houthis have deployed asymmetric warfare for the 21st century by capitalizing on their strengths — primarily drones and missiles. For the Houthis, success on the battlefield doesn’t require toppling Saudi Arabia; disrupting the Saudi economy and sowing fear within its society may be enough to give the Houthis leverage in any possible negotiations to end the fighting.
The Houthis have a large arsenal capable of striking targets well over 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) away. Some warheads change direction during flight and pose an extra challenge to air defence.
The group has fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Israel since its war in Gaza erupted in October 2023. While most were intercepted, a handful managed to land, in one case killing an Israeli man. Another strike hit an Israeli airport last year.
Andreas Krieg, a professor at King’s College London, said this experience in challenging Israel’s cutting-edge air defenses has given the Houthis confidence and expertise as they now strike Saudi Arabia.
“They’ve learned how to over-saturate the radars,” he said.
The Houthis, working with allied militias in Iraq, have also targeted Saudi oil installations, including a vital pipeline used to export oil through the Red Sea while movement through the Strait of Hormuz is limited. The Houthis have also seized territory in Yemen near the Bab el-Mandeb, a key Red Sea waterway, putting additional pressure on Saudi oil exports.
Saudi Arabia appears to have miscalculated
Michael Ratney, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, says the kingdom assumed the Houthis wouldn’t strike civilian targets like airports. Doing so marked “a paradigm shift,” he said.
Ratney, now an adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the Saudis now find themselves in a position where they have to respond while also trying to prevent the fighting from spinning out of control.
“They can’t not strike back — they were attacked in a very brutal way by their archenemies,” he said. “They need to exert military pressure on the Houthis and then find a way to kind of deescalate.”
Rather than sending troops into Yemen, the Saudis will likely launch airstrikes against the Houthis and ramp up support of nationalist forces, several analysts said.
“It will be surrogate warfare,” Krieg said.
The Houthis are now a formidable force
While the Houthis don't have the firepower of Saudi Arabia, they have grown into a fearsome force controlling roughly one-third of Yemen thanks to help from Iran.
The United Nations estimates that the Houthis by 2024 had recruited up to 350,000 fighters. That's up from just 30,000 in 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in the internationally recognised Yemeni government's civil war against the Houthis and imposed a naval blockade.
Ratney says the Houthis now have a “symbiotic relationship” with Iran and should not be seen as an Iranian puppet.
The strikes on Saudi airports and economic assets symbolise a sharing of lessons in asymmetric warfare between the Houthis and the Iranians: how to not just puncture expensive air defences, but also damage vulnerable energy installations and threaten global maritime routes.
“Over the course of the past few years, the Iranians have been innovating and sharing that with the Houthis and it’s gone both ways. The Houthis have been innovating, and sharing it with the Iranians,” Ratney said. “It’s no coincidence that they’ve ended up with a similar approach.”
Their recent military successes have made the Houthis feel “untouchable,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a fellow at Chatham House focused on Yemen.
“It’s very hard to convince a man he’s going on the wrong side if he just moved forward and he has a gun in his hand,” he said. But the Houthis are now likely to suffer a brutal Saudi counterattack, he said.

Indian stockbrokers’ combined active client base on the NSE rose by about 1.6 Lakh to 4.61 Cr in September, despite benchmark indices recording their steepest monthly decline in six months. Market leader Groww continued to widen its lead in India’s stockbroking market over the previous month, adding 1.01 Lakh active users even as benchmark indices recorded their steepest monthly decline in six months. Meanwhile, Angel One managed to narrow its gap with Zerodha, as the latter saw a marginal decline in its active client base, while Dhan continued to add clients, according to NSE data. Dale Vaz-led Sahi emerged as the fastest-growing broker, with its user base rising about 11% to 2.53 Lakh. The expansion came amid a selloff in Indian equities, driven by foreign investor outflows, elevated crude oil prices, and inflation concerns. Despite the market weakness, domestic investors continued to invest in equity mutual funds. Groww Leads As Zerodha, Upstox Lose Clients Groww’s active client base increased to 1.34 Cr in September from 1.33 Cr in August, taking its market share to 29.16%. However, its net additions slowed to 1.01 Lakh from 2.2 Lakh in August. Second-largest broker Zerodha lost 5,313 active clients during the month, taking its base to 67.92 Lakh. Angel One added 36,956 active clients to reach 67.56 Lakh, narrowing the gap with Zerodha to around 35,830 clients. The two brokers had 67.97 Lakh and 67.19 Lakh active clients, respectively, in August. Zerodha’s market share stood at 14.73%, marginally ahead of Angel One’s 14.65%. The gap between the two brokers has narrowed as Angel One continued to add clients while Zerodha’s base contracted in September. Angel One’s September business update, however, pointed to a mixed picture, with client growth accompanied by weaker activity in some segments. Its client base rose 1.1% MoM to about 4 Cr, while gross client acquisitions fell 19.6% to 4.5 Lakh. The number of orders increased 11.7% to 12.2 Cr, taking average daily orders to 58.2 Lakh from 52.1 Lakh in August. “While cash market share moderated in September 2026, exit trends improved, with sequential growth in average daily orders and turnover market share across overall equities and equity derivatives," the company said in its monthly disclosures earlier. Further, fintech unicorn Dhan, operated by Raise Securities, continued to gain ground. With the addition of 13,624 active clients in the month, Dhan's user base expanded to 11.21 Lakh. Its client base rose from 11.07 lakh in August, when it added 19,818 clients. Despite the slower pace of additions, Dhan maintained its position as the eighth-largest broker by active clients. Among other leading platforms, ICICI Securities added 4,410 active clients to reach 21.61 lakh, while HDFC Securities added 2,532 to reach 13.54 lakh. Upstox lost 10,343 active clients, taking its base to 18.54 lakh from 18.65 lakh in August. The biggest dent in the active user base was incurred by SBI Securities. The retail stockbroking subsidiary of SBI Capital Markets lost 22,525 active users to end September with 10.21 Lakh, compared with 10.44 Lakh a month earlier. Indian Equities Fall Amid FII Outflows The Nifty 50 declined 6.1% in September to close at 22,620.45, while the BSE Sensex fell 5.8% to 72,480.29. This marked the benchmarks’ second consecutive monthly decline and their steepest correction since March. Alongside foreign investor selling, geopolitical uncertainty and elevated crude oil prices weighed on markets. Higher oil prices fuelled concerns about India’s import bill, inflation, and currency stability, while a weaker rupee added to the pressure. According to JM Financial Institutional Securities’ September flow tracker, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) recorded net equity outflows of ₹39,660 Cr ($4.1 Bn), while domestic institutional investors (DIIs) were net buyers of around $8 Bn. FIIs invested a net ₹9,300 Cr in the primary market but withdrew a net ₹49,000 Cr from the secondary market. Their ownership of Indian equities fell to 13.8% in September 2026 from 19.9% in September 2016. Edited by Akshit Pushkarna Creatives by Varshita Srivastava

Community outraged after single dairy farm kills 11,000 fish
Maryland has already sued the farm over alleged repeated discharges of manure and other pollutants into Basin Run

A Maryland community is demanding answers after nearly 11,000 fish died in a local stream, with residents blaming a nearby dairy farm for polluting the water.
The Maryland Department of the Environment traced the mass fish kill, which affected 25 species, to manure runoff from Kilby Farm on Firetower Road in Colora, Cecil County, CBS Baltimore reports.
Now, state officials are asking a judge to hold the farm’s owner and operator, Hartland Holdings LLC, in contempt for allegedly violating a court order to stop polluting the waterway.
“Unfortunately, he's not following the rules, and the stream, and importantly, the community is paying the price,” Adam Ortiz, deputy secretary of MDE, told the outlet.
MDE says the farm’s owners took over the property in 2017 and significantly increased the cattle herd by 2021. The agency alleges the resulting waste was not properly managed, allowing manure to contaminate Basin Run.
The state has already taken the farm to court in a state lawsuit over alleged repeated manure and pollution discharges into Basin Run, with Maryland also asking a judge to hold the dairy in civil contempt for allegedly violating a 2025 settlement.
“These violations are unacceptable. We are taking this issue very seriously and have already obtained a preliminary injunction from the court barring this facility from discharging pollution into the waterway. We are now asking the judge to hold the operator in contempt of that ruling,” MDE told CBS Baltimore in a statement.
“The count is 0-2. You got to get it right this time. Otherwise, more punitive actions can take place,” Ortiz said.
Continued pollution could threaten other waterways, including the Susquehanna River and the Chesapeake Bay, officials warn.
The farm’s owners reportedly declined to comment to CBS Baltimore, which said it had also contacted their attorneys and was awaiting a response.
Longtime residents say the fish deaths reflect years of worsening pollution in Basin Run.
John Woodrow, who has lived beside the waterway for 70 years, told CBS Baltimore that conditions began deteriorating about five years ago.
“Everybody knows why it's happening. Everybody knows, but greed makes it keep on going,” he said.
“Next thing you know, you start seeing increased weeds on the side of the stream, less fish, more algae growing on the rocks, water less clear,” he added.
Nearby resident Ashley Bowley told the outlet that protecting the waterway should matter even to people who do not live along its banks.
“It hurt to see that happen. You shouldn't have to live near Basin Run or be drinking the well water to care about this,” she said.
The case is scheduled for a settlement conference in Cecil County Circuit Court in April 2027.
The Independent has contacted the MDE and Cecil County for comment. A contact for Kilby Farm or Hartland Holdings LLC could not be reached.

India on Wednesday issued a fresh safety advisory for its nationals in Saudi Arabia amid continuing security concerns following missile and drone attacks in the Kingdom. The Indian Embassy in Riyadh has urged citizens to follow local authorities’ instructions, remain indoors during aerial attacks and refrain from circulating videos or news related to ongoing events. The advisory, issued on Wednesday, comes after deadly attacks on civilian infrastructure blamed on Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The embassy also provided updates on Indians injured in the October 10 attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, flight disruptions, alternative travel arrangements and visa overstays. “In view of the current situation, all Indian nationals are advised to continue to follow local authorities’ instructions, stay indoors in case of aerial attack, and refrain from circulating videos or news related to ongoing events,” the embassy said in a post on X. The Best Coffee Grinders for Espresso or Pour-Over
Featured in this article
coffee Is Only as good as the beans you use to make it, and the beans you use are only as good as the grinder you use to render them extractable. Beans fed into a coffee grinder right before you brew them might as well be a whole different substance from the bag of ground beans you get at the supermarket, full of aroma and flavor compounds that quickly dissipate as they oxidize in the air. (It also helps to use fresh beans from excellent roasters: Check out our Best Coffee Subscriptions guide for some of our favorites.)
Grinders have become the most active tech frontier in coffee, and over the past decade coffee geeks have become devoted to the idea that getting the right grind on your beans is every bit as important as the machine you brew with. Uneven grinds can mean uneven extraction and uneven flavor—which is why we use particle size analysis to test the character of each grind from every grinder we review. But, of course, particle size alone does not tell the whole story, which is why I use the grounds from every model for cups of drip coffee, pour-over, Aeropress, and, when applicable, espresso.
Our Reviews team has tested dozens of grinders over the past five years, and I've retested all the top burr-grinder picks this past year. And while super-high-end grinders like the wonderful Mazzer Philos ($1,595) can run into the thousands, our top pick, the Baratza Encore ESP ($200), will keep most people happy for much less. This said, the Fellow Ode Gen 2 ($400), our favorite flat-burr grinder for drip coffee, is able to wring a special sort of poetry from each cup. The five machines below are the coffee grinders we currently recommend to anyone who cares a lot about home coffee.
Be sure to check out WIRED's other coffee coverage, like the Best Drip Coffee Makers, Best Espresso Machines, Best Latte and Cappuccino Machines, and Best Cold Brew Devices.

Best Budget Coffee Grinders
As mentioned above, the best bang for your buck will always be a hand grinder like my favorite, the Kingrinder K6 manual coffee grinder ($109). A precisely machined manual coffee grinder can rival coffee grinders many hundreds of dollars more expensive, both in precision and durability. And so the best manual coffee grinder will also be the budget option that'll lead to the best coffee. I've personally come to love the routine and the control.
But I get it. You'll happily grind your pepper with the best pepper grinder, but you draw the line at grinding coffee. Mornings are hard. Electricity helps. These are the budgetiest of budget electric coffee grinder options for each style of brew, all blessedly hands-off. None of these will lead to the clarity of flavors or sweetness or delicacy of our top picks. But they're the absolute lowest-cost devices we recommend for each category of brew.
Just when you thought Oxo had already cornered the market on affordable conical burr coffee grinders, the company comes in at an even lower price with this compact model. The Oxo Brew is stacked like a wee layer cake. And so the grind cup is housed within the column of the device and can be pulled out when you're done grinding. But while this is quite clever, neither consistency of grind nor ease of use is quite on par with Oxo's $110 basic conical burr, which remains my pick for an entry-level drip coffee grinder. But it's also very easy to move from the cabinet to the counter and back, and $30 less is $30 less. This is the lowest-price electric grinder I could actually recommend for Aeropress, drip, pour-over, French press, or cold brew. I wouldn't attempt espresso, though.
The lowest-cost electric espresso-capable grinder I can recommend with a clean conscience is the Wirsh Geimori T38 Plus for $150. This portable conical-burr grinder is about the size of a Christmas nutcracker and looks alarmingly like Pinocchio's left leg. But it offers surprisingly low coffee retention, stepless grind adjustments, and far better precision than expected for a grinder of its price. It achieves this by grinding at low RPMs—meaning it grinds quite slowly and carefully for an electric grinder. This also means the T38 Plus takes more than 30 seconds to grind enough beans for a double shot of espresso. This is disqualifyingly slow for batches large enough for drip or French press, and the T38 doesn't really have the clarity you want for pour-over. Still, it might be the only electric grinder I've tested south of $150 that can make decent espresso on non-pressurized baskets. It's also wee—great for small kitchens or as a travel coffee grinder. It's the grinder I'd definitely take with me to a hotel room if I didn't feel like grinding coffee by hand.
Look, blade grinders like this KitchenAid won't offer the powdery fineness and full-bodied coffee pleasures of a great conical burr, nor the precision of WIRED's top flat-burr pick. Blade grinders chop the heck out of beans, offering an uneven grind. But this is a very affordable coffee grinder, it's simple as pancakes to use, and blade-ground fresh beans are still a little better than the stuff in the supermarket. That said, they're probably still worse than getting beans fresh-ground at a café and using them within a week. When non-bean-geek friends ask for a grinder that costs less than dinner for two at Arby's, this is the one I offer up—especially if they're using darker grinds, and favor French press or a less expressive drip coffee maker. At the very least, it's enough so you're not crippled when you get whole-bean coffee as a gift. But let's be clear. The Oxo Compact conical burr grinder above is five times as good for about $30 more.
Results of Particle Size Analysis of Coffee Grinders
I of course assessed coffee grinders by tasting the resulting coffee across a number of brew styles and beans. But I also backed up my taste buds with scientific instruments. I analyze the flavor profile and the grind consistency of each of WIRED's top burr coffee grinder picks using particle analysis by a device called the DiFluid Omni. You can read a broader discussion of that particle analysis here.
Specifically, I tested each of WIRED's top burr grinders on multiple grind settings using the same medium-grind coffee beans—at both espresso-fine grinds and medium grinds more suitable for drip or pour-over coffee. Since September 2025, I also test every grinder I review or consider as a top pick, including the Moccamaster KM5, whose results are included here. I tested at least five times for each grind sample, collating the results into a characteristic curve for that bean and grinder.
Expand the discussion below for detailed discussion, bar graphs, and such.
Particle Size Analysis of Top Coffee Grinder Picks
Particle size analysis of coffee grinds is not a cut-and-dried test: It's more a clue as to the probable character of a brew. Patterns begin to emerge that correlate to the experiences I've had tasting coffee from each grinder. Taste is the ultimate test, alongside consistency of finicky espresso pulls. But quantitative analysis helps me (and you) actually trust and maybe understand those sensory test results.
When looking at these bar graph curves below, there are also a few rules of thumb. Big boulders north of a thousand microns will often lead to muddier character. Too many fines below 100 microns might lead to bitterness. A tight particle size distribution is associated with greater clarity of flavor. Look at the standard deviation (SD) for a clue as to overall precision: Smaller numbers indicate likely greater clarity. This said, a broad distribution of coffee ground sizes can also lead to better body and more perceived sweetness.
Our top pick for most people, the Baratza Encore ESP, proved itself to have quite precise results at very fine grinds—with standard deviation below 200 microns on espresso grinds, and 30 percent of particles concentrated within a single range. At its price range, this is admirable precision matched by very few grinders.
The same wasn't as true at pour-over coffee settings for the Baratza Encore ESP (seen above at setting 22), which showed a broader and more heterogeneous particle size distribution—with both small and large particle sizes. In practice, this led to a full-bodied and rounder cup, but with a little bit less of the precise aromatics one can get from our favorite grinder for drip and pour-over, the Fellow Ode Gen 2.
The Ode showed a characteristic bell-curve shape, surrounding a single high peak, which corresponded with the precise aromatics I taste when brewing drip or pour-over coffee using the Ode.
Even greater precision was on display with the Technivorm Moccamaster KM5, a flat burr grinder that showed precise results across the board—rivaling the Encore ESP at fine grinds and the Ode Gen 2 at grinding for drip. It's not as user-friendly as some of the top-pick devices, and the resulting brews can sometimes feel clinically clean, with a thinner body. But my lord it does offer clarity.
The Kingrinder K6 hand grinder, our top manual grinder pick, also showed strong peaks at grind sizes appropriate for pour-over coffee. Shown here are analyses of two medium-fine grinds, at 60 and 70 clicks from zero, respectively. Hand grinders have a secret weapon, which is that they cause you to grind slowly—which works very well at coaxing out more clarity from conical burrs. For pour-over grinds, the Kingrinder showed a higher peak than basically any grinder I tested, meaning grinds are very concentrated in a tight range of sizes: as many as 40 percent of coffee grounds were functionally the same size, and about 70 percent were grouped tightly around this. This leads to quite pronounced, intense flavor notes.
At grind sizes suitable for espresso, the Mazzer Philos bests this precision, with more than 90 percent of coffee grounds huddled in a tight grouping while using the i200D burr set. Nonetheless, while boulders are all but nonexistent, enough coffee fines exist to give each shot an almost syrupy consistency. The result is both body and perceived sweetness, with a surprisingly delicate clarity. While I haven't tested the i189D burrs also available as an option, reports from the world say that the i189Ds lean even harder into clarity of flavors. But note that at bigger grind sizes more suitable for drip coffee, you'll get a quite broad distribution. This will lead to a well-rounded cup, but may not offer the clarity of flavor of the Fellow Ode Gen 2 or the Kingrinder K6 for drip and pour-over brews.
Frequently Asked Questions
How We Test Coffee Grinders
WIRED tests coffee grinders by grinding a lot of beans and making a lot of coffee—testing each grinder to see if it can serve well for espresso, Aeropress, drip, and pour-over coffee, and coarse-ground cold brew and French press. I tend to always grind a drip Stumptown Homestead or Single-Origin Colombia as a baseline, because each is readily available at my local supermarket with stamped roast dates, and because I know the flavor well enough that I can detect variations. But I'll also try out a number of flavors and roasts on each grinder for different brewing methods.
We assess each grinder for decibel level while grinding, ease of cleaning and operation, hopper design, the presence or absence of “popcorning” (where the beans pop around inside the hopper, often leading to more uneven results), messiness and static electrical buildup, grind retention, ease of use, value, and simple aesthetics.
Previous WIRED reviewers assessed grind uniformity visually with the aid of macro lenses or filtered coffee grounds with sieves. In more recent rounds of testing, I reassessed each top coffee grinder pick using particle grind size analysis, with the help of the DiFluid Omni roast color and particle size analyzer, as well as a data analysis app.
I tested both fine and medium grinds on each grinder, using the same beans for each grinder, roasted within a month of testing. I repeated the particle analysis at least five times for each grinder and setting, and collated the results. I assessed the uniformity of the grind and the overall distribution of particle sizes—paying particular attention to the share of coffee fines (the tiniest particles smaller than 100 microns) and boulders (big coffee bits larger than 1000 microns).
Why Grind Whole Beans Instead of Buying Pre-Ground?
The reasons are simple: flavor, freshness, and aroma.
Whenever you open a vacuum-sealed bag of beans, a little invisible clock starts. Oxidation begins to erode the character of your beans, breaking down organic compounds and degrading them, turning your lovely beans to cardboard. Aromatic flavor compounds also escape from the bean, gassing out into the air where they do no particular good.
When you grind your beans, these processes go into overdrive. Freshness for whole beans can be measured in weeks. For ground beans, freshness in the open air is a matter of hours or even minutes. That bag of pre-ground beans you got from the supermarket? It's still coffee, of course, and it'll taste like coffee. But the vibrancy is gone. As far as true freshness is concerned, that coffee's been dead for weeks. (Pre-ground beans can be kept airtight for a week or so and maintain their flavor if you get them ground fresh at a coffee roaster.)
The only reliable way to get truly excellent flavor from your coffee beans, the way you experience it at a café, is to use fresh, whole beans. This is also how you can exercise some control over extraction and dial in your brewer or espresso maker to get perfect results for each bean.
Espresso requires a fine grind, pour-over a little coarser, and electric drip coffee a little coarser than this. Each grinder should have a guide to the best adjustments for each brewing method. Lighter-roast beans will want a finer grind than dark-roast to aid in extraction: Porous dark-roast beans give up their secrets a lot easier.
It's all kinda fun to figure out if you let it be fun. But certainly, when you strike paydirt, you'll know it: Finding the right marriage of grind and bean, on a good grinder, can turn into the best cup you've ever had. It's like the magical first time you seared a perfect steak or baked a perfect layer cake. Effort meets reward. It's marvelous. The grinders in this guide will help you find that moment more often.
What Is a Conical, Flat, or Blade Grinder?
Most coffee grinders fall into three main types: Conical-burr, flat-burr, and blade grinders. Burr grinders are generally higher quality and higher cost.
Conical-burr grinders are the category occupied by our top pick, the Baratza Encore ESP, and pretty much all of the most affordable grinders that still make good coffee. And there's a reason for this: Conical tends to offer the sweet spot at the intersection of high performance, cost, and flexibility. In a conical grinder, coffee beans are crushed and ground between two rings of burrs. They deliver a finer, much more consistent grind than you’d get with a traditional blade grinder, even the nicest blade grinder you've ever met. Conicals do tend to throw off more fines than a flat burr, but many feel this leads to more body and a more rounded flavor character.
Flat-burr grinders are thought to be more precise than conical grinders (though this is by no means universal). They’re also typically more finicky and also more expensive. Burrs are laid on top of each other, and the beans pass through them as they grind. The grinder action pushes the grounds out of one end, instead of relying on gravity like a conical-burr grinder, which means the beans spend more time in contact with the burrs. This often results in a more consistent grind, and therefore more precise flavors. For this reason, flat-burr grinders are often preferred as a way to elicit clarity of tasting notes in single-origin beans for pour-over, drip, and Aeropress.
Blade grinders have a chopping blade that spins around like a food processor. But blades don't produce even results. Some of your coffee will be fine powder at the bottom, and at the top you'll have bits too large for even French press. The result is an inconsistent, unpredictable brew. These grinders are generally quite cheap. But in case you're wondering, using fresh beans in a blade grinder is still probably better than buying stale ground coffee. (You can learn how to shake the beans to even your grind just a little. Pulsing the machine often also works. See world barista champion James Hoffmann's video for some more blade grinder hacks.) Still, if you can afford it, the conical or flat-burr grinders on this list will lead to far better coffee than any blade.
What's the Difference Between a Cheap and Expensive Burr Grinder?
The machinery in a high-quality burr grinder is a bit more complicated, and it's built to withstand greater wear and tear. In cheap burr grinders, the burrs can get blunt from regular use, and flimsier motors may burn out in a matter of months.
But also, coffee grinders have undergone a revolution in technology and design in the past decade. Manufacturers have been experimenting with different shapes of burr even on conical burr grinders—pentagonal, hexagonal, heptagonal. And grinders with more precise cuts will cost more money.
Flat burrs also cost more money to manufacture, and are seen as having more precision. The true geeks are swapping out for new generations of flat burr that offer greater precision in machining, and multistage grinds. Grinder makers are experimenting with larger and smaller burrs and different materials. It's a hive of invention out there. And these precision parts cost money: Some burr sets might cost hundreds all by themselves.
The end result of all this attention is a greater range or finer adjustment of grind sizes, better and more reliable calibration, and often more precision in the resulting coffee grinds—and thus more precision in the flavor of your coffee or the brew of your espresso.
Can I Run Pre-Ground Beans Through My Burr Grinder to Get Better Coffee?
No, please don't do this.
First off, if you're trying to improve the flavor of store-bought beans, the game's already lost. One of the main reasons to use fresh-ground whole beans is to avoid oxidation, and pre-ground beans have already been cardboarded up by evil, stale air.
But also, you'll mostly just muck up your machine. Logically, it might make some sense. Your grind is too coarse, so let's just run them through again at a finer setting, and perfect coffee results! Alas, on burr grinders, pre-ground coffee will get stuck inside the burrs, gum them up, and cause you to have to take the whole thing apart and clean it with your little brush and put it back together.
What Are the Best Coffee Grinders for Espresso?
Quite simply, the best coffee grinders for espresso are the ones that offer the finest calibration at the “fine” end of the spectrum. If you want to get super specific, look for coffee grinders that offer a number of fine calibrations at the fine end of the spectrum.
Dialing in individual espresso beans can require quite fine adjustments—and so even if a grinder is technically able to grind fine enough for espresso, it should also be able to make precise enough adjustments within that range to account for different beans, roasts, and machines. (For a real-world counterexample, witness the wall WIRED reviewer Joe Ray ran into when trying to get the (excellent) Wilfa Uniform Coffee Grinder to work for espresso. Without fine adjustments, chances are you'll fail.)
Otherwise, what you're looking for is excellent build, a motor that can withstand the higher torque you'll need to grind finely even on lighter roasts, and a machine that deals well with static electricity: Finer espresso grinds can turn static into a terrible enemy, sending coffee grounds spraying wildly.
The most vaunted espresso grinders can travel upwards into the high hundreds of dollars (see the Timemore Sculptor 064S flat-burr) or the thousands of dollars (see the Zerno Z1).
The Mazzer Philos Coffee Grinder ($1,595) offered maybe the best shots of espresso I've pulled at home in the past year. This offers delicate flavor and syrupy shots like the ones you'll get from a café, even on lower-cost espresso machines. (See my full review of the Mazzer Philos.)
But in this guide, we focused mostly on the best espresso grinders for the 90-some percent of people who are trying to gain access to good coffee without spending four figures. For most people and most budgets, our top pick, the Baratza Encore ESP ($200), will be the best choice, with sturdy construction and 20 grind adjustments for espresso alone. If you don't mind a little elbow grease, you can tune your grinds even finer by using a manual coffee grinder like the Kingrinder K6 ($109).
And then there's the true budget electric option. The tiny, slow-grinding Wirsh Geimori T38 Plus ($150) is the lowest-cost electric espresso grinder I've tried that can actually make good espresso on non-presurized baskets, though I'd probably limit it to medium roasts or darker, lest you strain the machine. Torque is not a strong suit.
Honorable Mentions and Runners-Up
Baratza Encore for $150: Baratza's original Encore is the Honda of the conical burr grinder world: easy to maintain, runs great, easy to use, lasts forever, replacement parts easy to find. It's been on the market largely unchanged for more than a decade. For not much more money, though, our top-pick Encore ESP offers beautiful adjustment on espresso settings, so I tend to recommend paying an extra $50 for the added versatility. But the original Encore remains a solid entry-level choice.
Baratza Virtuoso+ for $250: The Virtuoso+ uses the same burr set as the ESP, but is not quite as optimized for espresso. The biggest upgrade against the Encore ESP is a timer. Both have similar rock-solid but compact builds (although the Virtuoso is a little more stylish with its fitted grounds bin), 40 grind settings, and burr grinders for consistent grounds. The Virtuoso’s digital timer, however, is great for those wanting consistent coffee ground dosings each morning. You’ll have to dial in on your grind time versus coffee grounds output, but once you figure that out, you can walk away from the grinder and multitask if you please. —Tyler Shane
KitchenAid Burr Grinder for $200: This KitchenAid is stylish and easy to clean, and former WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey likes that the burrs are accessible thanks to their placement directly beneath the hopper. It also features precise dose control, with grind size controlled by a dial. For espresso lovers, one excellent feature is that you can swap the little container that catches the grounds with a holder for a portafilter.
Technivorm Moccamaster KM5 Flat Burr Grinder for $349: The performance on this stepless (read: infinite adjustment) grinder is somewhere between good and damn good. The razor-thin grind size distribution in early testing makes the KM5 a credible rival to the similarly priced Fellow Ode, in fact. And like the Ode, this Moccamaster is made especially for bringing out precise flavors on drip and pour-over. Particle analysis shows this Moccamaster to potentially offer even more precise grinds, leading to an almost clinically clean brew with light body. The KM5 not overly user-friendly, mind you: It cranks at 90 decibels, you have to hold down its analog switch to grind, and its aesthetics are the same sturdy industrial chic as all Moccamasters. Indeed, it's designed to sit alongside the classic drip coffee maker that's been on our buy-it-for-life guide since we've had one. If you prefer clarity to ease of use, this gives the Ode a run for the money, for less money.
Eureka Mignon Filtro for $269: The precision on flat burrs is terrific. But usually, so is the price. This no-frills Filtro from beloved Italian coffee brand Eureka clocks in at more than $100 less than our top-pick flat-burr, and it's an absolute metal-clad tank of a machine, says former WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey. It's as robust as the higher-end models and offers excellent consistency of grind size. Sure, it's a little loud, and you have to hold the button down when you grind. But life is full of trade-offs.
Lardera Wilfa Uniform for $299: This Wilfa has long been on our list as a great flat-burr grinder for pour-overs and drip. It remains such, though the Ode springboarded it as the top pick with its Gen 2 burr update, at about the same price. Like its name suggests, the Wilfa offers a beautifully consistent grind size and will make you a lovely pour-over. That said, it's fussier to adjust and louder than the Ode.
Breville Smart Grinder Pro for $200: WIRED has recommended this Breville in the past for its accessible burrs that make it easy to clean. But it's not really optimized for lighter-roast espresso, and ever since Breville bought Baratza, they've slowly been swapping out the grinders in their top-line semi-automatic espresso machines with those excellent Baratza burrs. For a stand-alone grinder at the same price, we give the same advice to you.
Baratza Vario W+ for $600: The Encore has a bigger, beefier, flat burr cousin, the Baratza Vario-W+ (7/10, WIRED Recommends) with a built-in scale and ridiculously granular adjustment (230 settings!). But like a lot of flat burrs, it struggles on finer grinds, according to WIRED contributor Joe Ray. And static is an issue. With price in play, the Ode Gen 2 comes out on top, but Ray was still a big fan of the Vario.
VSSL Java manual grinder for $165: VSSL specializes in ultra-durable camping tools, and it applied this same durable construction to this hardy campsite-ready hand grinder that WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson attests to be rugged enough to survive the zombie apocalypse. The handle folds out to provide a lot of leverage while you grind, and you can use it as a hook to hang the device up when you're done.
Also Tested
Wirsh Geimori GU38 for $200: The GU38 grinder from Wirsh/Geimori uses an identical burr set to the T38 Plus model I recommend as a budget espresso grinder. It's also bulkier and built a little sturdier. But the angled hopper causes more coffee retention, including some coffee beans that just refuse to feed into the grinder. Performance also seems slightly less reliable than the TU38, perhaps because the GU38 grinds faster. Either way, I'd opt for the lower-cost T38 Plus over this quite similar model.
Aarke Flat-Burr Grinder for $400: This pretty, shiny, stainless steel Aarke grinder contains a unique feature when paired with Aarke's coffee brewer, detecting the water in the brewer's tank and grinding the appropriate amount of beans. But this feature wasn't as calibrated as we'd like, and there have been a lot of online reports of grinder jams. I didn't have the same problem, but at more than $300 for a grinder that hasn't been long on the market, prudence is often rewarded.
Hario Skerton Pro for $55: The Hario Skerton was the gateway hand grinder for many a coffee nerd, but it has since given ground to newer entrants. It's fast and cheap, but it'll give you a heck of a workout and isn't as consistent for coarse grinds, plus the silicone handle has a habit of falling off.
Hario Mini-Slim Plus for $39: This smaller Hario manual grinder is slower than the Skerton, but its plastic construction makes it good to throw in a travel bag. The low price is its main advertisement.
Cuisinart Burr Grinder for $75: At first, it seems like a good deal. It's Cuisinart, a known brand, and a conical burr grinder for less than $100! But former WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey found that the low price came with a cost: These things apparently burn out faster than a rock star in the late ’60s.
Bodum Bistro Electric Blade Grinder for $20: This little blade grinder is quite cheap, and the model has served WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane for years. That said, after some inconsistent reports on reliability, we favor the KitchenAid as our ultra-budget pick.

Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions, had yet to establish itself as a serious contender. Even the latest models coming out of China, impressive as they were, appeared to be playing catch-up.
The AI race is back on
Google and Meta are challenging Anthropic and OpenAI at the AI frontier.
Then, in the space of a few days, everything changed. Google and Meta both unveiled frontier models they claim can go toe to toe with the best from OpenAI and Anthropic. Suddenly, the race is back on — and it’s anyone’s game.
Until this week, Google looked like it had permanently lost its place among the AI front-runners. Since releasing Gemini 3 late last year, the tech giant had delivered little more than incremental improvements. Gemini 3 was formidable when it launched, but its lead was fleeting, and it struggled to keep up with later offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic, or even some of the open-weight models emerging from China.
A series of internal shake-ups only added to the sense that Google was retreating from the AI frontier. Veteran executive Jeff Dean departed the company with a number of other AI researchers to launch a new startup. Demis Hassabis, the Nobel laureate who spent years at the helm of Google’s AI powerhouse DeepMind, stepped back from day-to-day leadership. Other AI-related teams were moved out of DeepMind and into Google proper. Together, the changes signaled a broader shift in Google’s AI center of gravity, moving away from London and toward California, fueling speculation the tech giant was beginning to prioritize commercializing AI over research.
Then, on Tuesday, Google upended that narrative with the release of Gemini 4 Argon, a new frontier model the company claims matches or beats flagship offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic on numerous benchmarks, whatever value benchmarks are still worth. What’s more, Google has priced Argon aggressively: Per token, it’s undercutting its rivals by as much as 80 percent during its introductory period, and is still significantly cheaper once that promotion ends.
Meta’s arrival was arguably even more dramatic. Unlike Google, which had long been the one to beat in AI thanks to its deep pockets and DeepMind, Meta had never really established itself as a serious contender at the frontier. It was not through lack of trying, but its models struggled to make a mark. Last year, the company embarked on an ambitious and expensive overhaul of its AI operations, spending billions on talent and infrastructure, including Scale AI and its cofounder Alexandr Wang. In April, its new Superintelligence Labs released its first major model, Muse Spark. Impressive, but not quite frontier.
That changed on Monday when Meta finally unveiled a model capable of competing with the industry’s very best. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder Full can compete with leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, including GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1, on numerous benchmarks. In other words, Mark Zuckerberg’s company has finally arrived at the AI frontier.
The return of Google — and the arrival of Meta — makes the AI competition considerably more dynamic and shows just how quickly the balance of power can shift in the AI world. Both have extraordinarily deep pockets and vast ecosystems of products used by billions of people, advantages that AI upstarts like OpenAI and Anthropic simply cannot match. The success of Meta’s Muse agent assistant illustrates that advantage. Its popularity in such a short period of time, and despite the growing list of security and privacy concerns, shows the power of having billions of users within ready reach. OpenAI, meanwhile, is having to work harder to establish an ecosystem of its own, positioning itself as an alternative to Meta.
All this comes as the AI race appears to be entering a new phase. The drive to develop ever more powerful models is becoming increasingly fraught. The growing array of safety concerns and rogue AI incidents means calls to slow development are growing louder. Open models are also getting better and better, making it harder for any one company to stay ahead for long.
If raw power and performance are no longer enough to stay ahead, Google and Meta have plenty of advantages not enjoyed by Anthropic and OpenAI. They may have spent a lot of time playing catch-up, but the past week shows it would be incredibly foolish to count either of them out.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

Actor Seth Green—yes, that one—has seen Godzilla Minus Zero and says it’s awesome.
While introducing the New York Comic Con panel for the 39th film in the Godzilla franchise, Green stressed that the filmmakers behind the movie “have created kaiju that feel physically real and, trust me, emotionally terrifying.”
While a lot of that terror came from the work of Oscar-winning visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima, some it came from the shrieking of Godzilla and his three-headed nemesis, King Ghidorah. Those roars were the work of sound designer Natsuko Inoue and her team, who created the monsters’ outsize vocalizations by rolling speakers to the top of an outdoor dam—much to the horror of people nearby.
“There were people having a picnic, maybe people just taking a stroll,” Hisafumi Takeuchi, who also worked on sound for the film, said during the panel. “The person walking their dog, though—they had the worst time, because the dog was freaking out and barking back at us.”
Since the creatures are imaginary, getting their screams to sound realistic is essential to making them seem believable—and genuinely scary—onscreen. At first, Inoue wasn’t sure if the idea of recording at the dam would work. Those fears were quickly put to rest.
“The first time we sent that roar out on the speakers, I could see the relief and confidence in everyone's eyes,” Inoue said. “By using speakers and projecting it into the real world, capturing the reverb, the echo, the reflection of the sound back with the mic, it manifests it in our world.”
For other kaiju sound effects, Inoue’s team took an analog foley approach. To simulate Ghidorah’s dragon-like wings, for example, they flapped a rubber fisherman’s suit and mixed that noise with the sounds of an accordion-like air duct.
Getting two of Toho’s most famous monsters right was a huge undertaking, especially after the success of Zero’s predecessor, Godzilla Minus One, which brought home $114 million worldwide at the box office. Following that 2023 film’s harrowing mix of post–World War II malaise and bracing kaiju destruction will be tough, but a new trailer shown during the film’s panel at NYCC promised a sequel full of aerial dogfights and a punch-’em-up for the ages between Godzilla and Ghidorah.
Like the previous film, Godzilla Minus Zero is directed by Takashi Yamazaki and features visual effects from Tatsuji Nojima, whom Green called “the first Gen Z Oscar-winner” for his work on One.
Nojima began doing visual effects as a hobby while he was still a teenager before joining animation house Shirogumi as a compositor. After Yamazaki noticed a crude animation of waves that Nojima was working on, the director tasked the budding animator with developing the idea. Nojima turned around a fully rendered shot of ocean water over rocks that looked indistinguishable from reality. After that, Nojima recalled, Yamazaki said, “OK, I think you’re ready to animate and do VFX for Godzilla now.”
During the panel, Nojima broke down how he created a shot from the trailer showing Godzilla bursting out of the ocean while chasing a seaplane. “I simulated 200 million particles to get the whitewater effect correct in Godzilla Minus One,” he said. “With this shot in Godzilla Minus Zero, the scale is absolutely different with the new Imax aspect ratio, plus there was no live-action plate, so we're dealing with a lot of CG on screen. We required 2 billion particles.”
Godzilla Minus Zero is set to hit US theaters on November 6 and Japanese theaters on November 3, which has become known as Godzilla’s birthday since it marks the date in 1954 that Ishirō Honda’s original film was released in Japan.

Though this particular image was fake, law enforcement officials did remove an apparent protester wearing a shirt that read "Release the Epstein Files" from the crowd at a Youngstown, Ohio, rally for Republican candidates running in the midterm elections on Oct. 12.
In October 2026, an image (archived) circulated online that social media users claimed authentically showed a protester wearing a shirt that read "Release the Epstein Files" at a Trump rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on Oct. 12.
News footage from the rally showed what appeared to be Republican supporters grappling with a person wearing a black shirt that read "Release the Epstein Files" until law enforcement officers stepped in to remove the apparent protester. Livestreamed footage from the rally showed Trump reacting to the incident, claiming that the person was a paid protester and commenting on their weight.
The image that circulated online shows a crowd of angry people wearing red hats emblazoned with the words "Trump" and "USA" confronting a person wearing a black shirt that reads "Release the Epstein Files." One Threads user who shared the image wrote:
At Ohio Trump rally, I saw a brave woman surrounded by male violence. One bastard punched her, pulled her hair, and dragged her to the ground. When police officers arrived, I thought they would help her and arrest the attacker. I was wrong. She was led away while Trump cheered on the thugs. As a German, this is unbelievable to me. A brave woman among raptors. Trump's followers are chilling and disgusting—just like the man himself. She is my hero today.
(@two_and_a_half_dachshunds, accessed via Threads)
The image also spread on X (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us to ask if the image was real.
The image was fake. A SynthID detector, which looks for invisible watermarks in AI-generated media, concluded Google's AI tools created the image. In a follow-up post, the Threads user above also confirmed the image was AI-generated and suggested they created it.
"I intentionally chose a symbolic graphic over sharing the horrific, raw footage of a woman being dragged and beaten by men at that rally," the user wrote.
A Google reverse image search identified the Threads post as the earliest version of the image. We contacted the Threads user for confirmation they created it and await a reply.
Though this particular image was fake, the incident it was based on did take place on Oct. 12 during a rally for Republican candidates in Youngstown, Ohio.
Footage from the rally showed a scuffle in the audience, with at least four people grappling with and grabbing at one person as they appeared to attempt to pull the person to the ground. Law enforcement officials who appeared to be from the Mahoning County Sheriff's Office arrived at the scene and separated the apparent protester, who was wearing a shirt that read "Release the Epstein Files," from the crowd.
As officers pulled the apparent protester from the crowd, Trump said, "He's a paid protester, they're all paid. They get paid by the lefties in order to destroy our country. They're scum."
The President then appeared to comment on the protester's weight, adding, "Oh, he's got to go on a diet. He's a fat guy. Wow."
Though Trump repeatedly identified the apparent protester as a man, news outlets including The Hill and Fox News reported that the person in question was a woman. Snopes has not independently verified the identity or gender of the person, nor what started the incident at the Youngstown rally.
Trump's claim that the person in question was a paid protester remained unproven as of this writing.
The apparent protester's shirt that read "Release the Epstein Files" was likely intended as criticism of the Trump administration.
Democratic lawmakers have criticized the Trump administration for failing to release all of the documents pertaining to the investigation into late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, while United Nations experts condemned "serious compliance failures and botched redactions that exposed sensitive victim information" as part of the documents the administration did release.
Youngstown Mayor Derrick McDowell said on Facebook (archived) that Youngstown Police Department officers were not involved in the incident at the rally. Snopes contacted the U.S. Secret Service and the Mahoning County Sheriff's Office to ask if either agency carried out arrests at the rally.
The Mahoning County Sheriff's Office had not returned our request for information at the time of this writing. The U.S. Secret Service referred our request to the sheriff's office.

Trump press secretary Katie Zacharia may have violated California law by calling herself an attorney, group says
Nonprofit watchdog files complaint with State Bar of California after she ‘repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practice law without a license to do so’

A watchdog group has accused Donald Trump’s new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia of violating California law by describing herself as a “lawyer” and working as an attorney in California despite never being admitted to practice law in the state.
Campaign for Accountability, a nonprofit group, filed a complaint with the State Bar of California on Wednesday stating that Zacharia has “repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practice law without a license to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime.”
“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie,” according to the group’s executive director Michelle Kuppersmith.
“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” she added. “The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has.”
In a statement to The Independent on Tuesday night, Zacharia said she “practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials” while working for a Chinese firm, but did not answer whether she has ever been admitted to any state bar. The White House only noted that Zacharia has her juris doctorate, an academic degree.
The White House did not immediately respond to The Independent’s request for comment in response to the bar complaint.
Growing scrutiny into Zacharia’s legal experience followed Tuesday morning’s report from news outlet Popular Information, which sought to untangle her public statements and whether she is licensed to practice law in the U.S.
That afternoon, during her first appearance alongside the president, reporters asked Zacharia where she had ever passed a bar exam. She responded, “When I moved to China.”
After graduating from Pepperdine University’s Caruso School of Law in 2011, Zacharia worked for Chinese firm Zhong Lun.
“Published reporting indicates, however, that China does not permit foreign nationals to sit for its national bar examination or to practice Chinese law,” according to Wednesday's complaint from Campaign for Accountability.
“In any event, admission in a foreign jurisdiction would not authorize Ms. Zacharia to practice law in California or to hold herself out as entitled to do so here,” the complaint states.
Her LinkedIn does not list any experience as an attorney except for 15 months as “general counsel” with Fix California, a right-wing nonprofit group founded by Trump ally Richard Grenell.
It’s a misdemeanor in California to consider oneself an attorney entitled to practice law without a license with the State Bar. It’s punishable by up to one year in jail and a $1,000 fine.
The complaint asks the State Bar to determine whether Zacharia’s work for Fix California similarly violated state law — and to refer any allegations to the Ventura County District Attorney for prosecution.
“The rules against unlicensed lawyering exist to protect the public,” Kuppersmith said. “To be meaningful, the rules must apply to people with the biggest megaphones, not just to those with no platform.”
Zacharia does not appear to have worked as a legal professional following her work with Zhong Lun and Fix California. She began working as a commentator for right-wing media outlet Newsmax in 2024 and then as a commentator with Fox News the following year.
According to Campaign for Accountability, Zacharia has been identified as a lawyer in at least 18 appearances on Fox News since March 2025.
She also worked as a deputy assistant secretary for public affairs with the Department of Homeland Security from February to March of this year.
Since June, she has served as a senior communications adviser with the president’s social media platform TruthSocial and its parent company Trump Media & Technology Group — roles that she appears to hold alongside her work at the White House, according to LinkedIn.
In June, Zacharia was also appointed to the advisory board of NovaRed Mining, where she will provide “strategic guidance to the Board of Directors and management team in the areas of public affairs, government relations, communications, capital markets visibility, and corporate development” for a copper and gold mining project and “emerging artificial intelligence initiatives.”
The company, which later rebranded to NRED Intelligent Mining Inc., described her as “an attorney, political strategist, media commentator, and international advisor whose career spans legal affairs, public policy, strategic communications, and business development” in a press release announcing the appointment. CEO Brian Goss also touted her “legal expertise” in the announcement.

Container ship hit by projectile sinks in Strait of Hormuz, Singapore says
- Published
A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities.
All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said.
Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water.
The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula.
Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday.
Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added.
Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization.
The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time.
However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency.
One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping.

Kyiv, Oct 14: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced outrage Wednesday over Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of Ukraine's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of US President Donald Trump's demand for a ceasefire.
Moscow's forces pounded Ukraine's power grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, for the third straight night, Zelenskyy said, after Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” 4.5 years after Moscow's forces invaded.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has agreed to halt Ukraine's monthslong campaign targeting Russian oil refineries that caused fuel shortages for Russians. Ukraine's last reported hit on an oil refinery was last Friday.
The Kremlin has not confirmed that Moscow signed off on the truce, with a spokesman saying only that “contacts on this matter continue.”
Trump's efforts to stop the fighting have made no progress.
Ukraine claims it is pushing Russia back on the battlefield
Ukrainian officials say they are pushing back Russian forces in eastern Ukraine, which Russia's bigger army has been trying to capture for years. Ukraine has liberated 277 square kilometers in the operation that started in the summer, Ukraine's Third Army Corps commander Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi said Wednesday.
It was not possible to independently verify the claim, and Russian officials did not comment.
Ukrainian officials fear US support for the war effort is falling away after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and isolate Putin.
Ukrainian officials said the deal would help Russia continue its invasion, while European leaders fear Moscow's wider ambitions on the continent and accuse Russia of sabotage as part of a hybrid war on the continent.
Zelenskyy was due in London on Wednesday for talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham as Kyiv and its European supporters race to shore up Ukrainian defences. The Ukrainian leader could go to Brussels to attend a European Union summit later this week after his London trip.
“We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond -- and to respond forcefully” to Russia's ongoing aerial barrages, Zelenskyy said in a social media post Wednesday.
“Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation,” he said.
Russia hits three Kyiv power plants in attack, causing outages
The Russian Defence Ministry said in a statement Wednesday that its forces attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure in Kyiv, the wider Kyiv region and the northeastern Kharkiv region overnight, striking a total of six power plants.
Russian forces hit all three of Kyiv's combined heat and power plants overnight into Wednesday, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on Telegram. At least 600,000 people were left without power, Zelenskyy said.
Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and Kharkiv overnight, Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine fears dwindling US support for its war effort
Ukrainian officials are concerned that US support with military intelligence and the use of tech titan Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications system may be in jeopardy. Ukraine uses Starlink for defence against aerial attacks and for long-range drones targeting military sites in Russia.
Musk's SpaceX overnight imposed a speed limit on Ukraine's Starlink terminals mounted on drones, Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, said on Telegram.
Ukraine's drones rely on Starlink for control in flight. The speed restrictions significantly complicate logistics, the work of unmanned systems units and mid-range strike operations, among other things, officials say.
“Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” Beskrestnov said, without elaborating.
SpaceX made no immediate comment.
Ukraine didn't receive the usual advance warning from its partners of Russian missile attacks that hit Kyiv, Zelenskyy said Tuesday. He did not specify which partners he was talking about when referring to the lack of a warning, but the development raised fears that the US may not be providing Kyiv with usual intelligence.
Five people were killed and 36 injured in a Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital that lasted from Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning, Kyiv police said.
Trump has said the US has not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, however, and a lawmaker on Ukraine's parliamentary Defense Committee told The Associated Press that intelligence sharing with international partners has not stopped.
The lawmaker spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to give statements to the press.
Ukraine attacks a Russian data centre with long-range drones
Ukraine is trying to fight back with attacks on other targets on Russian soil.
Russian air defences overnight downed 902 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions, illegally annexed Crimea and the waters of the Azov Sea, the Russian Defence Ministry said in a separate statement Wednesday.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 493 drones flew toward the Moscow region. Most were downed far away, and 180 were intercepted as they approached the Russian capital, he said. He did not report any damage or casualties.
In Russia's Saratov region, one person was killed and several residential buildings were damaged, Governor Roman Busargin said.
Russia's state-backed Sberbank confirmed an attack on its Saratov data centre, once slated to become Europe's biggest data centre.
Russian state news agency Tass quoted Alexander Vedyakhin, Sberbank's first deputy chairman of the board, as saying that Sberbank systems were operating normally.
Zelenskyy visits London for talks on more help in the war
Burnham, the British prime minister, vowed to keep backing Ukraine in the war.
“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe,” he said ahead of Zelenskyy's visit.
Analysts noted that Trump's latest moves girded Europe into standing firm behind Kyiv.
“Ahead of a tough winter for Ukraine, Donald Trump's swing back toward Russia bodes ill,” Rym Momtaz of Carnegie Europe wrote Tuesday. “But instead of panicking, Kyiv's European allies are focusing on action.”
Britain, like the European Union, is also looking to impose more sanctions on Russia. (AP)

Father receives life sentence in New York for murder of Montreal girl
No parole eligibility for 25 years for Luciano Frattolin
A Montreal man has been sentenced to life in prison for killing his nine-year-old daughter and leaving her in a marsh in rural New York.
The sentence comes two months after a jury in Essex County Court convicted Luciano Frattolin of second-degree murder and concealment of a human corpse in the death of Melina Frattolin.
Judge Tatiana Coffinger delivered the sentence after rejecting a motion to set aside the guilty verdict.
Frattolin would not be eligible for parole before 25 years. Coffinger also sentenced Frattolin to one to three years for concealment of a corpse. That sentence will be served consecutively.
The defence issued a notice of appeal following the sentence.
Melina had been living in Montreal with her mother, and had gone on a road trip to the U.S. with her father in July 2025.
On the night they were scheduled to return home, Frattolin called police, reporting that his daughter had been kidnapped after he had stopped the car he was driving on the side of the road.
During the three-week-long trial, the defence argued that local police had not adequately investigated Frattolin's claims that his daughter was kidnapped.
The prosecution called on several police officers and experts, however, who used car location data, cellphone data and surveillance camera footage to recreate Frattolin's movements on the day his daughter died and prove his story was false.
The jury spent an hour deliberating on Aug. 10 at the end of the trial, before concluding that Frattolin had drowned his daughter in a marsh in a rural area of New York.
