A large randomised controlled trial among heart failure patients in India led by the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST) in Kerala, has found that hospitalisation episodes and all-cause mortality among heart failure patients can be significantly reduced if patients are systematically followed-up by a nurse, with the help of a mobile health application.
The two-year Telemonitoring and Integrated Multidisciplinary care for Heart Failure (TIME-HF) trial found that heart failure patients with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) who received nurse-led collaborative care had a 22% lower risk of death than those receiving usual care. They were also more likely to remain alive without hospitalisation during the two-year follow-up.
The trial results were published in the American Heart Association’s Journal, Circulation, on August 30, 2026.
What makes the trial relevant is that it addresses critical gaps in heart failure care: in Keralam, heart failure registries have reported high mortality post-discharge — 82.7% mortality over 10 years, alongside the fact fact that only 25.4% of the patients with heart failure receive guideline-based therapies. It also holds lessons for the rest of the country: with nearly 27% of all deaths in India being due to heart disease, and 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease occurring between the ages of 40 and 69 years, there is an urgent need for quality, post-discharge care.
What the trial did
The TIME-HF trial involved 1,507 adults at 22 government and private hospitals in Keralam and neighbouring States, with 755 patients assigned to the intervention and 752 to usual care. The mean age was 61.9 years; 77.6% were men, 57.3% lived in rural areas and 70% had relatively low educational attainment. Ischaemic heart disease was the predominant cause of heart failure, accounting for 77.4% of cases.
Results indicated that nurse-led intervention substantially improved prescription of the four major components of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure — renin-angiotensin system inhibition/ARNI, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors.
“Our heart failure patients receive sub-optimal care, as most of them do not adhere to therapies or follow up with the doctor on time. There is also the issue of physician inertia. HF Registry evidence indicates that the median survival after diagnosis of heart failure is just 3.7 years. This collaborative care model is proof that survival and quality of life of these patients can be improved if we systematically address the gaps in care so that proven therapies for heart failure become part of routine care,” said lead researcher and additional professor at SCTIMST P. Jeemon.
Centring nursing care
The model put a trained nurse at the centre of the care pathway, who would closely monitor heart failure patients after discharge, educate the patient and family about heart-failure self-care, lifestyle modification and encourage medication adherence.
Nurses reviewed the patients’ medication regimen at discharge to ensure that there was no deviation from the guideline-mediated therapies. This was again reviewed at every follow-up visit with the help of a mobile-health app. The m-health app helped the nurses monitor all physical parameters of the patient real time and to identify warning signs of worsening disease, communicate and connect with patients and physicians so that timely hospitalisation was possible.
All participants underwent scheduled follow-up visits every three months for two years. Adherence to all four guideline-directed medical therapies was only 22.1% in the usual-care group, while it was 37.3% in the intervention group at two years.
“The health system engaging with the patient regularly was the key here. The m-health app gave the patient updates in real time to the nurse. Oxygen saturation levels, weight gain, weight loss, drop in blood pressure or respiratory rate comes as alerts, and then were escalated to the physician,” Dr. Jeemon points out.
The TIME-HF trial thus helped address one of the health system’s persistent weaknesses: that of proper follow-up care of patients with chronic diseases. The model is suited for strengthening chronic disease management and reducing the burden of hospitalisation and mortality in resource-limited settings across the country, experts said.

For as long as Anshita Mehrotra can remember, conversations at her home were all about cosmetic formulations, ingredients, and consumer behaviour. For Mehrotras, beauty wasn’t just another industry but a family business. Her mother, Shailey Malhotra, had built Fixderma into one of India's trusted skincare brands, serving millions of consumers. And the obvious path for Anshita was to step into an already successful business. Instead, she chose a road less trodden. After graduating in Canada and returning to India in 2018, Mehrotra began exploring a gap in the beauty market that’s worth tapping into. And it didn't take long to find one. Like millions of Indians with naturally curly hair, she knew the daily struggle of keeping her textured hair hydrated. The products available in the market largely revolved around oils, which moisturised but often left hair greasy and difficult to manage. There was little available that could hydrate curls, style them, be used daily, and still feel light and smell good. The market was dominated by expensive salon-grade products that were not suitable for daily use. “There was no curl cream or shampoo for hair like mine. The market simply didn't exist, and there was a huge unmet need staring us in the face, and I knew I could build in that space,” Anshita Mehrotra, founder of Fix My Curls, told Inc42. Having grown up around the beauty industry, she understood the product development process, knew the experts she needed to work with, and had access to manufacturing capabilities. After almost eight months working with hair care specialists, she developed what she says was the category's first leave-in curl cream and hair gel specifically for the Indian market. The products were free from sulfates, silicones, parabens, mineral oils, and drying alcohols, and promised an everyday styling routine. In 2019, Mehrotra launched Fix My Curls through its own website, followed by an Amazon listing. But just as the business was finding its footing, the pandemic brought the industry, like much of the world, to a standstill. "It was a difficult year for sales. But with everyone spending more time on their phones, I realised that if I couldn't get the product into their hands, I could at least help them understand why they needed it," Mehrotra said, sharing that within the first lockdown, her educational content led the brand to gain over 12,000 active followers on Instagram. After 2021, Fix My Curls began operating independently of Fixderma and expanded its presence across beauty-focussed marketplaces such as Nykaa, Vanity Wagon, and Sublime Life. According to Mehrotra, that was when the brand found its first real product-market fit. And the next chapter of growth began with a bet on quick commerce. Fix My Curls first entered quick commerce in the second half of 2023 with a limited rollout across a handful of Blinkit pin codes. We were trying to reach out to a new customer base that ordered more frequently. "We were among the first personal care brands to bet on quick commerce. It was challenging because neither Blinkit nor we had a playbook. We were figuring out purchase orders and operations as we went," Mehrotra told Inc42. The breakthrough came in January 2024, when Blinkit expanded the brand's presence nationwide. And by then, Mehrotra's years of educating consumers online had created a loyal audience that was ready to buy. Today, quick commerce is among the largest contributors to Fix My Curls’ total sales. Marketplaces and quick commerce account for nearly 70% of the brand's total sales, while its D2C website contributes around 25%. The remaining 5% comes from exports to markets including Nepal, Switzerland, Malaysia and Romania. While Fix My Curls reported revenue of over ₹21.42 Cr in FY25, it is yet to turn profitable. According to Mehrotra, the company expects to achieve EBITDA profitability of 2-5% in FY27. As it works toward that goal, quick commerce is increasingly emerging as a profitable channel, and during our conversation, Mehrotra shared the lessons she learned over the last three years of building in quick commerce that helped the brand crack the channel. Overcoming Q-Comm Challenges According to Mehrotra, the initial few months in 2023 were challenging. The team was trying to identify the right hero product, determine its pricing, and decide which cities to launch in first. Because the category was new to the platform, Blinkit had no historical data to show which products would sell, how often they would need replenishment, or what consumer behaviour to expect. But now that the company is three years into quick-commerce operations, it has a clear list of dos and don’ts. Building For Q-Comm Cart Behaviour Without a proven framework, Fix My Curls leaned back on its most trusted signal: customer data. Fix My Curls used performance metrics from its hero SKUs on Amazon and its website to decide which products to list first on Blinkit. It also ran self-funded Meta campaigns to spread awareness that they were now available on Q-comm, too. "We would make ads just to tell people that our products were available on Blinkit. Nobody asked us to do it. We did it because we knew we needed to increase awareness," Mehrotra said. But the brand soon realised that the channel was highly price sensitive. Blinkit users weren’t necessarily willing to spend ₹700-₹800 on haircare while ordering groceries. Cart context and purchase intent were fundamentally different. "We realised that if somebody is adding groceries worth ₹1,000 to ₹1,500, our product needs to feel like an easy addition to that cart," Mehrotra explained. In response, Fix My Curls designed smaller trial and travel packs priced between ₹150 and ₹300, which helped the brand sell quickly and maintain smaller but frequent POs. Catching Replenishment Rhythm For Fix My Curls, Q-comm widened execution challenges that didn't exist in traditional ecommerce. Mehrotra noted that, unlike ecommerce channels, where inventory cycles are relatively predictable, quick commerce operates on tight replenishment windows of just four to seven days. "The biggest thing we struggled with was that we just weren't able to fulfil purchase orders fast enough," Mehrotra said. To deal with this, Mehrotra built a dedicated quick commerce function. One team member was assigned exclusively to the channel and is responsible for tracking SKU-level demand daily and maintaining inventory buffers above projected needs. The brand also began closely monitoring daily run rates and planning inventory 15% to 20% above forecasts. However, according to Mehrotra, inventory planning continues to be tested during new product launches, when demand can far exceed projections. She recalled that the quick commerce version of the Milky Leave-In Serum sold out almost immediately after launch, forcing the company to place "three separate purchase orders in quick succession" to keep up with demand. Mehrotra also shared that getting POs delivered on time to fulfilment centres was another critical factor, as larger logistics partners, she found, were often too stretched across clients to handle Fix My Curls’ tight replenishment cycles. Smaller logistics partners, however, proved more responsive and reliable. "The biggest thing is that you cannot miss your purchase order, and to make sure you don't, you have to find the right logistics partner," she added. Building For Q-Comm’s Search Intent Eventually, Mehrotra also realised that quick commerce shoppers were fundamentally different in their shopping habits. Unlike Instagram or a brand website, where consumers often come with a specific intent, quick commerce is driven largely by searching for a specific product. "People were not searching for Fix My Curls. They were searching for products like shampoo, gel or dry shampoo," she said. To accommodate that insight into the product, Fix My Curls worked with quick commerce partners to shape the final form of their dry shampoo. The data showed that customers on the channel wanted travel-friendly haircare, so the brand launched a version that was compact, competitively priced, and under 100 ml. According to the founder, these minor product changes drastically impacted sales, and the company now works closely with quick commerce platforms while developing new products. Fix My Curls’ experience reflects a wider discovery challenge for haircare brands on quick commerce. Being available on a platform is only the first step. How consistently products remain in stock, where they appear in search results, how much shelf visibility they receive and how their prices compare with competitors can also influence their chances of discovery. Future Growth For Fix My Curls’ Q-Comm Journey For Mehrotra, the biggest takeaway from Fix My Curls' quick commerce journey is that the channel is far more than a convenience-led delivery mechanism. It is increasingly becoming a discovery engine. “Quick commerce has helped us reach cities that I genuinely have never targeted. To be honest, I’ve not even heard about some of these cities. Reaching tier-III markets at this scale is remarkable because, in our category, achieving such deep penetration used to be nearly impossible," said Mehrotra. In many ways, quick commerce has helped Fix My Curls solve the same challenge it faced when it first launched in 2019: making an underserved category more accessible. As the company works towards EBITDA profitability and its next phase of product-market fit, Mehrotra believes the opportunity in quick commerce remains significant. However, she is equally convinced that the channel will not be able to accommodate every brand that enters it. "I think the next two years will be a boom, but there's going to be a clean-out after that. In every category, only the players who can move products, replenish inventory and build genuine demand will survive," she said. For Fix My Curls, the focus now is on ensuring it remains one of those players. After spending its early years building a category from scratch and its recent years building a quick commerce playbook, the brand is now entering a new chapter centred on scale, profitability and deeper penetration across India.

Centre invites bids for two offshore mineral blocks in Andaman Sea
The ministry issued the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) to grant operating rights for the Sewell Rise-01 and West Sewell Ridge-01 blocks under a composite licence.
The Union ministry of mines on Tuesday invited prospective bidders to explore two offshore mineral blocks in the Andaman Sea, spanning a combined area of 1,632 square kilometres, as part of efforts to strengthen India’s access to critical minerals used in manufacturing, clean energy and emerging technologies.
At an outreach programme in New Delhi, the ministry officials briefed stakeholders on the geological potential of the blocks, the auction procedures, the regulatory requirements, and the financial assistance available for exploration.
The ministry issued the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) on October 1 to grant operating rights for the Sewell Rise-01 and West Sewell Ridge-01 blocks under a composite licence.
Sewell Rise-01 covers 632 square kilometres, while West Sewell Ridge-01 spans 1,000 square kilometres. Both blocks contain polymetallic nodules and crusts that can contain nickel, cobalt, copper, and manganese.
Officials highlight importance
Ministry of mines Secretary Keshav Chandra underscored the importance of strengthening domestic mineral supply chains to support economic growth, technological advancement, the energy transition and manufacturing competitiveness.
He also highlighted the potential role of a Critical Mineral Processing Park being developed on India’s eastern coast in supporting offshore mineral processing.
Additional secretary Veena Kumari Dermal said the government had undertaken policy reforms to facilitate transparent and responsible development of offshore mineral resources.
“Taking stakeholder feedback into account, the ministry has revised block configurations, including increasing the area of polymetallic nodule and crust blocks to provide greater operational flexibility for exploration,” she said.
She added that the Terms of Reference and guidelines for collecting baseline environmental data and preparing environmental management plans for offshore mineral exploration and exploitation within India’s exclusive economic zone had been circulated to concerned central ministries and departments for comments.
“These will be finalised shortly,” she said.
The Geological Survey of India (GSI) outlined the geological characteristics and mineral potential of the two blocks. SBI Capital Markets Ltd, the transaction adviser, explained the policy framework, tender conditions and bidding requirements, while MSTC demonstrated the process of purchasing tender documents and submitting bids through its electronic auction portal.
The National Mineral Exploration and Development Trust (NMEDT) also explained a scheme providing partial reimbursement of exploration expenses to composite licence holders of offshore mineral blocks.
Auction details
The auction is being conducted under the Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Act, 2002, as amended in 2023, and the Offshore Areas Mineral (Auction) Rules, 2024, as amended. The framework aims to ensure transparent allocation of offshore resources and promote systematic exploration.
Tender documents went on sale on October 1. The pre-bid conference is scheduled for November 4, while the last date for submitting queries is November 13. Prospective bidders can purchase tender documents until December 21, with bids due by December 28.
The government said systematic exploration would be essential to establish the blocks’ mineral potential and assess their prospects for future development.

She joined and applauded hundreds of teenagers who demonstrated boisterously outside school north of Paris

Greta Thunberg on Tuesday threw her high-profile support behind high school protesters rattling the government in France, saying “the whole world is watching with awe”.
She joined and applauded hundreds of teenagers who demonstrated boisterously outside a school north of Paris under the watchful eye of police.
The surprise appearance by the 23-year-old climate activist, along with another day of marches in the French capital and elsewhere, suggested that high school students’ push for more resources for run-down schools is far from running out of steam. That’s despite mass arrests, mounting injuries and fatigue from more than three weeks of blockading schools and demonstrating.
Police used clouds of tear gas, water cannons and repeated charges to disperse protesters Tuesday when violence erupted on the fringes of the Paris marches. The Interior Ministry estimated that 161,500 people marched in demonstrations across the country, including 41,500 in Paris.
Outside the Paul Éluard high school in Saint-Denis, where staff and students have long complained of dilapidated facilities and even rat infestations, Thunberg said French pupils are “fighting back, reclaiming their future that has been taken away from them” and are inspiring young people in other countries.
“The international community sees these students and they’re leading by example,” she said to The Associated Press. “This generation is one that has been growing up with a sense of hopelessness for the future, when we can see our future and our rights taken from us,” she said.
“Of course people are going to fight back,” she added.
The students’ grievances have resonated in neighbouring Belgium, where some schools closed in Liege.
Several Italian cities have also seen student protests, though on a smaller scale than in France and focused on broader complaints. In Germany, high school students are calling for an international youth strike on Nov. 20, in solidarity with the French protests.
Some French pupils say they see parallels between their protests and the “Cockroach” youth movement challenging the government in India and youth-led demonstrations a year ago in Morocco that also demanded better schools and hospitals.
Thunberg also cited protests in Spain, gripped by demonstrations for affordable housing, and in Latin America.
“These movements are connected in one way or another. We are fighting against the same system,” she said.
“Even though these local issues are different and may vary, we have the same enemy and I definitely think that these movements are inspiring each other.”
The government of outgoing president Emmanuel Macron, whose term ends in May, argues that the movement in France is losing momentum. The Education Ministry said fewer schools were closed Tuesday although the number of staff injured since protests began in mid-September has risen to 147. The government says hundreds of police officers have also been wounded but has not detailed the severity of their injuries.
Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. The interior minister suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.
Pupils and university students who blockaded the Maurice Ravel high school in eastern Paris on Tuesday said they feel that their complaints are being heard by supporters in France and abroad but not by the government. Some vowed to keep protesting until that changes.
“We’re certainly making noise and getting people talking, but unfortunately, our message isn’t reaching the people who should be making the changes,” said Ryan, a 20-year-old student who said he didn’t want to give his surname for fear of possible repercussions.
“That’s why the movement needs to keep going and persist.”

People getting voting info from AI an ‘emerging concern’, AEC says

The Australian Electoral Commissioner, Jeff Pope, has said people getting their information about voting in Australia from AI chatbots such as ChatGPT or Claude is an “emerging concern”, and has forced the commission to overhaul its website to attract bots looking for the correct information.
Speaking at a hearing of the joint standing committee on artificial intelligence on Wednesday night, Pope said it was “dangerous” to rely on social media platforms or AI tools as “your only source of research when it comes to forming an opinion around voting” and was something the AEC was working to educate the public on.
He said it may require a legislative response from parliament in terms of what platforms and and cannot do in terms of the content on their platforms around elections.

Victorian Labor pledges to offer free abortion care
Benita Kolovos
The Victorian Labor government will today announce that – if re-elected in November – they will make Victoria the first state to offer free abortion care.
Under the $30m election commitment, the government would pay private providers to deliver medical and surgical abortions up to 16 weeks, removing out-of-pocket costs. This means women would no longer need to pay for GP or specialist consultations, imaging and tests or medications at participating providers.
Medical abortions can cost almost $700 out of pocket for patients with a Medicare card, or more than $1,000 for those without one. Surgical abortions can cost $895 with Medicare, rising to almost $1,500 for those without a card.
The government has also committed to extending the window for medical abortion from nine to 10 weeks’ gestation. If elected, they would direct Safer Care Victoria to lead a clinical review into extending access to the medication up to 12 weeks, which aligns with World Health Organisation guidelines. The review would also cover who should be able to deliver care and where.
Patients who need to travel to access abortion would also be eligible for a subsidy to help with their travel and accommodation costs, community health care providers trained to provide abortion care and 1800 My Options would receive extra funding under the plan.

Abortion care is healthcare and Labor will make it free. Only Labor will protect a woman’s right to choose.

Vaccine skepticism has worked its way from the fringes of the public to the highest levels of the federal government. The Trump administration is reportedly considering changes to a critical policy, the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, that has protected domestic vaccine supply for 40 years, which could further jeopardize vaccine access and even create shortages in the United States. These attacks on vaccines could have much more far-reaching impacts than may appear at first blush: They could effectively blow up a key pillar of the industrial policy that has maintained stable vaccine access in the U.S. for four decades.
This could create a situation where Americans who want vaccines can no longer get them. But as I explain in a new paper, the Trump administration doesn’t have to have the final word. Policymakers at the state level can step in to directly produce vaccines to prevent shortages and harm to the American people.
Vaccine access in the U.S. hasn’t always been guaranteed. In the 1980s, a flood of lawsuits alleged that the vaccines for diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough caused severe seizures in children. While researchers belatedly debunked many of those claims, vaccine makers wound up on the hook for significant payouts to litigants. This led vaccine makers to increase prices, and some exited the market entirely. By 1984, only one company was left producing the whooping cough vaccine in the United States and had raised its price tenfold. This led to shortages and jeopardized supply.
In response, Congress created the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP), a program that provides reasonable compensation to patients injured by vaccines while capping the legal liability for vaccine makers. Because vaccines are exceedingly safe, VICP payouts are rare. According to the government’s own data, between 2006 and 2024, more than 5 billion doses of covered vaccines were distributed in the U.S. During that period, around 10,500 injury claims were awarded compensation under the VICP — or about one individual per 1 million administered doses. The VICP has sustained stable vaccine access while ensuring fair compensation for injured patients for 40 years.
But the Trump administration may be about to upend the VICP, and in doing so, could jeopardize the widespread access to vaccines that most Americans enjoy today.
First, reporting suggests that health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and one of his chief advisers may remove certain vaccines — such as the childhood vaccines it is attempting to render optional under federal recommendations — from the VICP, which would increase legal liability for producers of those vaccines.
Second, based on debunked claims connecting autism to vaccines, the administration may make conditions related to autism compensable “injuries” under VICP. That could quickly bankrupt the program: Such claims could produce $100 billion in awards, far eclipsing the VICP’s $4 billion balance, and approaching 20 times the amount the fund has paid out for all claims to date over its entire existence.
If the VICP is rendered a shell of itself by federal policy, private vaccine makers could retreat from the U.S. market, viewing it as too risky with too much legal exposure to do business. That could lead to vaccine shortages — and a situation where Americans who want vaccines can no longer get them — and ultimately declining immunization rates, more outbreaks of communicable diseases, and more avoidable deaths.
To avoid that outcome, states can step in to create public factories to directly produce vaccines. There is a strong tradition of public factories for vaccines in the United States. For example, in 1894, Massachusetts created a public drug manufacturer and research lab known as MassBiologics, which has produced vaccines for smallpox, tetanus, typhoid, and pertussis, among other biologic products. MassBiologics, now operated by the UMass Chan Medical School, remains the nation’s only nonprofit vaccine manufacturer, and currently produces a vaccine against tetanus and diphtheria that is distributed nationwide.
If the Trump administration persists in jeopardizing the country’s vaccine supply, Massachusetts and other states can mobilize new or existing publicly owned vaccine production facilities to produce those vaccines that would otherwise fall into shortage. Each state could use its health department or university system to establish production facilities to manufacture vaccines jeopardized by federal policy. Those states could license vaccine formulations from the private manufacturers exiting the U.S. market.
Because these production facilities are owned by states, they would be protected by the legal doctrine of sovereign immunity, which insulates states from lawsuits — allowing them to avoid the uncapped risk problem that would otherwise deter production by private manufacturers. To compensate patients with rare but legitimate vaccine-related injuries, each state could create a “mini-VICP” that provides modest, capped payouts for injuries.
These states can serve as a last line of defense against the Trump administration’s anti-vaccine policy. Moreover, states could join forces to create public factories to avoid shortages for critical vaccines.
State vaccine production could face a few conceivable roadblocks.
First, private vaccine makers may be reluctant to share proprietary information involved in vaccine formulation with state governments. States can make these companies more willing to license their vaccines by incorporating strict nondisclosure agreements and restricted use clauses in their licensing agreements.
Second, the Trump administration could try to prevent states from manufacturing vaccines. However, state-run vaccine production may be exempt from Food and Drug Administration regulation, which under the law is permitted to regulate “persons,” not states. This could limit the Trump administration’s ability to obstruct state-run factories.
There is a final impediment states could face: time. Building a new factory, outfitting it for production, and actually producing vaccine doses could require a significant amount of lead time. To expedite production, states should consider using existing facilities, such as purchasing or leasing space from public, nonprofit, or private entities.
Regardless, time is of the essence. There are few institutional barriers standing in the way of the Trump administration doing immense harm to public health by damaging vaccination in the United States. State governments should therefore begin contingency planning now. For more than 100 years, public factories have helped protect Americans’ access to vaccines — and they can meet the moment again now.
Joel Dodge is the director of industrial policy and economic security at Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator.

Rusty or something more? South Africa's concern after Australia loss
- Published
First Test, Durban (day five of five)
Australia 390 & 314-6 dec: Renshaw 82; Nortje 2-56, Maharaj 2-56
South Africa 284 & 206: Markram 75; Hazlewood 6-49
Australia won by 214 runs
South Africa's 12-match unbeaten run came to a shuddering stop with defeat against Australia in Durban, but were they simply rusty or is there more to read into a Test match in which they were outclassed across the five days?
The world champions held on until an hour into the afternoon session on the final day – Aiden Markram fought admirably for 237 deliveries – but Australia, led by Josh Hazlewood with career-best figures of 6-49, eventually broke any lingering resistance to go 1-0 up in the three-match series.
"I would like to see more fight," said Proteas coach Shukri Conrad. "I don't know if it is alarming [but] it is concerning."
So should South Africa be worried at the start of an eye-catching few months which includes the visit of England over Christmas?
Rusty batters or something more?
Much was made of South Africa's run to the 2025 World Test Championship final at Lord's.
They played only 12 Tests – no team played fewer – and qualified after drawing at home against India and losing in New Zealand, before beating West Indies, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Pakistan.
Mitigation for this latest Test also comes from the fact this is their first in almost a year and the majority of their batters played one domestic red-ball match to prepare.
Australia recently came off an eight-month break of their own and lost to Bangladesh in home conditions, as Conrad was keen to point out.
And last summer's famous win over Australia and a 2-0 success in India proves they can beat the world's top teams.
However, this Test only reinforced a worrying trend among South Africa's batters.
Tristan Stubbs and Ryan Rickelton are fine white-ball players, but Stubbs' two Test centuries have come against Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, and Rickelton's against Sri Lanka and Pakistan.
This was an obvious step up.
In the first innings, Stubbs, two overs after Wiaan Mulder had been bounced out, top-edged a pull to fine leg, and in the second he played a loose drive on one.
Opener Rickelton drove and edged at a wide ball late on day two and nicked through a pull in the fourth over on day four.
Similarly, Mulder scored 367 not out against Zimbabwe last year, but Bangladesh are the only other side he averages more than 30 against. His 110-ball stay for 29 on the final day before being strangled down the leg side was at least encouraging.
Wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne, in contrast, lasted only three balls before nudging Matt Renshaw's part-time spin to slip. His Test average of 30.14 drops to 28 against Australia and 15 against both England and India.
Conrad said that "a few of the guys need to step up".
"The real disappointment was the batting in the first dig on a really good wicket," Conrad said.
"Yes, a world-class attack, but quite a few guys getting starts and not kicking on."
Markram & Nortje the positives
Aiden Markram's defiant knock in the fourth innings, in which he batted for almost six hours for 75 runs before edging Mitchell Starc through to Alex Carey in the afternoon session, was one positive for the Proteas.
David Bedingham also looked comfortable in his new position of number three, albeit he was one of those guilty of failing to make the most of starts after reaching 49 and 46.
This defeat was not solely on the batters, either.
Bavuma, who tasted defeat as captain for the first time in this match, allowed the game to drift on day two as Australia extended their score from 124-6 to 390 not out.
Australia's Matt Renshaw played brilliantly for his 190 but was not challenged as he casually farmed the strike and protected Nathan Lyon in their ninth-wicket stand of 134.
And while judging them against Australia's fearsome attack, the most successful quartet Test cricket has seen, is hardly fair, South Africa's bowlers lacked the relentless pressure of their counterparts.
Anrich Nortje was impressive in taking four wickets in his first Test since March 2023. His last spell was quicker than his first as he brought pace and hostility, hitting Steve Smith on the helmet with a bouncer on day four.
But Mulder offered little after his new-ball spells and Marco Jansen was quiet after dismissing Nic Maddinson and Steve Smith on day one.
The return from injury of their premier quick Kagiso Rabada, who was seen bowling at lunch on day five, cannot come soon enough.
Spinners Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj did not escape Conrad's gaze either.
"Anrich's return was phenomenal and really pleasing," Conrad said.
"If we were brutally honest, our spinners were not as sharp as they normally are."
With the second Test starting in only five days' time in Gqeberha, South Africa must hope this Test has removed the rust.
The alternate takeaway would be far more concerning.

A container ship has sunk near the strait of Hormuz and a second cargo vessel was reportedly sinking amid the sharpest uptick in Iranian attacks on shipping since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran.
The surge of attacks suggests Iran is trying to fully close the strategic waterway in a deliberate attempt to frustrate Donald Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The Trump administration has been attempting to deflect attention from the economic impact of the war on Iran by blaming Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries for increased fuel prices.
On Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported at least five incidents including drone strikes in the previous 48 hours targeting tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area.
“There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said.
The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride container ship sank on Wednesday after an attack the previous day while in a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao was also reported to be sinking close to the strait after being previously hit by a projectile on 23 September, maritime security sources said.
Apparently referring to the GFS Pride, Iran said a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine while travelling an unauthorised passage through the strait.
State television quoted a statement from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC) that said the ship was traveling on what it called an “illegal and dangerous route” when it hit the mine.
The unidentified ship, which was shown tilted in the water and spewing a thick plume of smoke, was carrying 2,500 containers, the broadcast said.
However, the UKTMO suggested that both ships had been hit by unidentified projectiles, raising questions over Tehran’s account.
Iran has repeatedly warned ships from trying to transit through the strait without its approval. The US military has been guiding ships through the waterway on a route nearer to Oman’s coast.
The latest attacks come as ships in the area were reporting an intense series of attacks in recent days with six vessels attacked on Sunday alone, according to UKTMO’s monitoring.
Analysis by the Financial Times said 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to 11 October. Of the vessels hit, three were refined energy product tankers while two others were crude oil tankers.
The increased tempo of Iranian attacks appears to have caused a dramatic drop off in oil shipments through the strait, as Tehran appears determined to demonstrate its ability to strike ships before the US midterms that will decide control of Congress.
US fuel prices have surged by almost 70% since Trump launched his war on Iran, and the Republican party is bracing for punishment at the polls.
According to two Iranian officials, Iran has recently begun using new tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions.
The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.
“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials told Reuters.
The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials added.
A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Tehran had changed tactics in one significant way. After the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the IRGC had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including American naval vessels, the official said.
Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.

Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of espionage, Moscow said on Tuesday.
Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services.
Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, saying Imai was accredited with the ministry but was accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.
Japan’s embassy in Moscow told news agency Kyodo that the government was trying to ascertain the journalist’s reported detention.
Russia’s FSB security agency said a Japanese national, who it did not name, was arrested on Sakhalin and alleged he had worked for Japanese intelligence to collect information about Russia’s defences.
The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Moscow and Tokyo have been locked in a territorial dispute for decades over the status of a string of islands in the Pacific Ocean, off the north-east coast of Japan and to the south-west of Russia’s Sakhalin region.
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.
“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”.
The Kuril islands – which Japan calls the Northern Territories – have been under Russia’s control since the end of the second world war, when they were seized by the Soviet Union.
Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an uproar in Japan. Tokyo has said it would continue implementing sanctions against Russia and supporting Ukraine.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

A video of late actor Nana Patekar is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) amid the Cockroach Janata Party’s protest at Jantar Mantar. In the video, Patekar apologises to a man named Abhijeet before speaking in Marathi. The video is being shared with claims that Patekar was apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending an event and was supposed to accompany him to the protest at Jantar Mantar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending the protest at Jantar Mantar.
Fact: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to Marathi film producer Abhijeet Gholap for missing the NAFA Marathi Film Festival. Gholap, who produced the 2011 Marathi film Deool, shared the video on his Instagram account on 8 October 2026, stating that Patekar was unable to attend the festival. The video is unrelated to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke or the protest at Jantar Mantar. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
After reviewing the video with Google’s NotebookLM tool, we found that Nana Patekar speaks in Marathi, apologises to Abhijeet, and regrets not attending an event. Addressing Abhijeet, he says, “It was great working with you in the film Deool.”
Deool is a 2011 Marathi film in which Nana Patekar acted, and Abhijeet Gholap produced it. This suggests that Patekar was referring to Abhijeet Gholap in the video, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke. Patekar also praises Sonali Kulkarni, who acted in the film.
Further search revealed that Abhijeet Gholap had posted the video of Nana Patekar on his Instagram account (archived) on 08 October 2026. In the caption, he wrote, “Nana was unable to attend the NAFA Marathi Film Festival, and he promised he would definitely come this year. We will miss you very much.” In a Facebook post, he wrote, “Nana, you missed your visit. Now we will just keep waiting.”
Abhijeet Gholap is the founder of the North American Film Association (NAFA), which was established to promote Marathi films in North America. According to the organisation’s website, Gholap founded NAFA to bring together actors, directors, choreographers, singers, cinematographers and editors to create Marathi films, web series and documentaries based on local stories and subjects in North America.
To sum up, this viral video shows Nana Patekar apologising to film producer Abhijeet Gholap, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke.

NEW DELHI: What led to a false hijack scare that sent Air India’s longhaul Frankfurt-Delhi flight being diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday has now become the subject of a probe by both aviation and security agencies. The Boeing 787-9 with about 300 people on board had entered Indian airspace via the long route taken these days due to closure of Pakistan skies for Indian carriers when Mumbai air traffic control systems received this aircraft squawking transponder code 7500 which is the aviation code for hijacking or unlawful interference.People in the know say the pilots denied squawking the code and they told ATC that everything was alright. But as per established protocol, the aircraft was diverted to Jaipur where it was parked on a remote bay. Extensive checks were carried out of everyone on board, baggage and the aircraft. Everything was found alright and the plane was cleared to take off for Delhi with the same crew operating this leg of the extended journey.
“After Mumbai ATC received the aircraft squawking the code 7500, they spoke to the pilots who reported that all operations were normal on the flight.
But protocols have to be followed in situations like which was done. Now it is being seen how and why this happened? Was there software on the ATC side?” said people in the know.Senior B787 pilots say there is a “one in a trillion” chance of the code being set to 7500 on the aircraft inadvertently or due to some error. “Each digit has to be physically entered. There is no button that can be inadvertently pressed. So from the pilot or plane side some error to happen is highly remote,” they say.Senior air traffic controllers say Mumbai ATC has a new system and that it’s “unlikely” to be a case of software error. “When a pilot squawks 7500 (hijack), then the colour of this aircraft’s dot on the radar screen turns red and an alarm goes off. Code 7600 is for emergency and 7700 for communication failure,” said an official.In a statement, Air India said: “Air India flight AI2030 operating from Frankfurt to Delhi on Oct 14 was diverted to Jaipur following a perceived security concern. The aircraft landed safely in Jaipur. The relevant security agencies carried out the necessary checks and have cleared the aircraft and crew. All passengers disembarked, underwent security checks, and have since reboarded the aircraft. The flight is expected to continue its journey to Delhi shortly.”“Air India teams worked proactively with authorities to minimise passenger inconvenience. We sincerely regret the inconvenience caused to our passengers due to this unforeseen disruption and appreciate their patience and understanding. The safety and security of our passengers and crew remain Air India's highest priority," AI statement added.After landing, the aircraft was escorted to an isolation bay, where a multi-agency security operation was launched. Teams from the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), local police and the Bomb Detection and Disposal Squad (BDDS) inspected the aircraft, passenger baggage and cargo holds.Police sources said security personnel conducted checks as part of the response. The National Security Guard (NSG) was also placed on standby in New Delhi, according to the information provided.Jaipur airport management said the passengers were taken to the terminal building after security checks. “The passengers have arrived in the terminal building. All are safe, and there is no situation of panic. The passengers are in the terminal building, and the authorities are now working on the plan for their departure to New Delhi,” airport sources told PTI.
Airport authorities said normal flight movements and terminal operations continued during the security response. After the checks were completed, the Aerodrome Committee assessed the situation and concluded that the threat alert had been resolved. The aircraft and crew were then cleared for departure.

) Limiting global warming to around 1.8 degrees Celsius, instead of allowing it to reach 4.4 degrees Celsius, could prevent the loss of 1.89 billion years of healthy life to causes such as extreme heat and air pollution, according to a new LancetCommission.
Researchers said that the true burden could be even greater and that without sharp cuts to emissions, health losses would continue to compound beyond 2100, increasingly intensify other threats, such as migration, in ways not yet reflected in these numbers.
The authors of The Lancet Commission on "21st Century Global Threats to Health", launched at the World Health Summit 2026 in Berlin, Germany, examined hundreds of possible threats.
They identified 17 threats posing the greatest danger to human health and survival between 2025 and 2100. These are also the threats that can be averted through policy changes, funding decisions and innovation, they said.
The 17 interlinked "catastrophic" threats spanning diseases, social and economic conditions, environmental change, technology and conflict will shape the health of the next generation, the team added.
If current trends continue, the 17 catastrophic threats collectively could account for tens of billions of years of lost health, the analysis found.
Every country faces significant risks, even as the scale varied by threat and region. Within each country, people with limited resources and marginalised communities bear the greatest burden, compounded by existing inequalities, it said.
Nuclear conflict and the malicious use of artificial intelligence (AI) were identified as the two threats with a potential for extinction, even as their likelihood of occurring were deemed 'low'.
Accounting for both their potential impact and probability, the commission's assessment found that action to prevent nuclear conflict could avert an estimated 133 million deaths and 9.35 billion years of healthy life lost by 2100, while action to reduce the risk of malicious AI could avert an estimated 10.4 billion years of healthy life lost.
"The estimates highlight how much health loss could be avoided in each area. Some are already imposing substantial health burdens today, while others carry a real danger if they materialise. Crucially, all 17 threats are interconnected, which is why they must be addressed together, not in isolation," commission co-chair Christopher JL Murray, director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington, said.
"The striking finding is not only the scale of these threats, but that humanity still has the agency to act. Across all 17 catastrophic threats, the decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation. But delaying action will only serve to shift and increase the costs into the future," Murray added.
The other catastrophic threats to health are air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, childhood malnutrition, conventional conflict, a declining development assistance for health, high alcohol use, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics, obesity, poor mental health, smoking and unhealthy ageing, the authors said.
The commission also puts forth a framework to inform action before harm becomes embedded -- create and fund threat-ready health systems, increase investment in innovation and reassess threats regularly and independently, they said.

The Delhi Police crackdown on the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protest on October 10 has drawn international scrutiny, with human rights bodies and press-freedom organisations flagging police excesses, and international media outlets reporting on the severity of force used against young protesters.
Police detained over 2,000 protesters and used force to suppress the mobilisation in the national capital. In arguably the most brutal assault on press freedom in India since the Emergency, journalists from both independent and mainstream media outlets were stopped from doing their work and detained in a display of police excess that bordered on madness. Some were dragged by their clothes, pushed and manhandled, some had their phones snatched, and pressured to delete footage of police action.
‘Restrictions Violate India’s Obligations under Int’l Law’
The global human rights non-profit Amnesty International on Friday put out a statement urging Delhi police to ensure that the fundamental right to peacefully protest is guaranteed to Indian citizens. In the statement, titled, ‘Delhi police must facilitate right to peaceful protest amid lockdown-like restrictions in capital’, Amnesty highlighted that “approximately 22,000 armed personnel from across the country have reportedly been brought to Delhi, in addition to more than 10,000 Delhi police officers expected to be deployed.”
Aakar Patel, chair of board, stated: “From denying permission for a peaceful demonstration, halting all Delhi-bound trains, and sealing the city’s borders, to issuing an internet suspension order near the protest site, and pre-emptively arresting activists – India’s authorities are leaving no stone unturned in their bid to prevent this march from happening. The right to protest is protected in India’s constitution. The authorities must immediately lift all these arbitrary restrictions, which violate India’s obligations under international law.”
After reports of rapid mass detentions began to surface on Saturday, the United Nations Human Rights Commission published a press release: ‘Concerns over mass detentions before and during protests’. Spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan called for the unconditional and immediate release of all those arbitrarily detained. “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled. Restrictions on peaceful protests must meet strict tests of necessity and proportionality. The Indian authorities should also ensure law enforcement forces exercise utmost restraint in response to peaceful protesters, consistent with the country’s democratic traditions and human rights obligations,” read the statement.
Similarly, the global media watchdog Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) urged Delhi police to “immediately release all detained journalists and media workers, return their equipment, investigate reports of physical abuse, and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests…and the police response without interference.”
CPJ highlighted the detentions of Newslaundry reporters Ashwine Kumar Singh, Astha Savyasachi, and Anmol Pritam, and Scroll reporter Ayush Tiwari. “Newslaundry has also reported that police seized its reporters’ phones, while other reports indicate that journalists were physically manhandled,” the statement read.

Putting out a list of around 20 journalists detained through out the day on October 10, global journalists’ body Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said, “Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police’s actions against the press are unacceptable.”
BBC Focus on Scale of Government Pushback
The BBC published at least five reports specifically focusing on the heavy security deployment, police crackdown and mass detentions. The BBC published first on Saturday, ‘Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest’. The report highlighted the sheer scale of government pushback — it stated that the BBC saw at least five people being detained near the site as “police and paramilitary personnel [were] stationed behind barricades and ropes, preventing people from entering the protest site…and drones could be seen flying overhead.”
The report stated that 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed and that the “restrictions caused major disruption across central Delhi, with traffic diverted from several key roads.” It also mentioned the “dramatic scenes” involving Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi and other Opposition leaders since October 6, as the police vehemently prevented them from agitating.
In a second report, the BBC reported the detention of Dipke, Das, and Ranka and hundreds of other demonstrators. In ‘‘Cockroach’ group leaders among hundreds detained in Delhi protest’, BBC highlighted the way the three were detained before they could even deboard their flight, prominent protest face, All India Students’ Association (AISA) leader Neha Bora’s detention, and how more protesters were jam packed into buses than on the streets. “The large number of protesters expected to descend on Delhi were unable to get anywhere close to Jantar Mantar due to the heavy security presence and road blocks,” the report stated.
In a third report on October 11 — ‘Delhi sees more protests as freed ‘cockroach’ group’s leaders vow to fight on’ — after the detainees were released, the BBC highlighted the 7,000 protesters who were detained and released on Saturday and hundreds were also detained on Sunday. The report led with Dipke’s promise to continue fighting. BBC also posted live updates on the detentions on its website.
The New York Times also published multiple reports on the wrath the Delhi police unleashed on the protesters on Saturday. All their reportage described the scuffle between the state agents and the demonstrators with headlines reading: ‘Indian Police Round Up Protest Leaders and Lock Down Delhi’, ‘From a Sikh Sanctuary to Chaotic Streets, Protesters Brave Police in Delhi’, and ‘Blocked by Police, India’s Youth Voice Their Fury’.
‘Indian Police Round Up Protest Leaders and Lock Down Delhi’ read the headline of a report published by US-based news outlet NPR. The report described at length how “Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India’s youth…sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.”
Highlighting the elaborate measures taken by Delhi police to curtail the movement on Saturday, the report stated: “The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities’ determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilised thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi.”
The British news outlet The Guardian also extensively covered the police action on Saturday. Alongside Dipke’s video from when he was being arrested inside the aircraft, where he can be heard saying, “You can see where the nation is heading…this is dictatorship,” the outlet published a report ‘‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown’, wherein it describes the police lockdown as “severe”.
‘Modi is in Trouble’
Qatar-based Al Jazeera reported on the mass detentions on Saturday, and published a feature headlined ‘Meet the man helping India’s detained protesters get home’ and an opinion piece ‘Modi is in trouble’ on Sunday.
The former video report featured 25-year-old Rajiv Choudhary who built an AI-powered app to help the detainees get home safely after police drop them off at the city’s outskirts; the latter opined that the protests “exposed India’s hollowed-out democracy.” “These acts further erode the tenuous position Modi is in, prompting more rebuke from critics who now question his fitness to occupy the office of the prime minister. On Friday, the opposition parties, led by Rahul Gandhi, met President Draupadi Murmu and submitted to her that the government had subverted India’s democratic framework…Under Modi’s watch, problems have accumulated like barnacles on the side of the ship. Every time he has been challenged, he has gone farther away from the democratic principles on which this nation was founded,” the article read.
British news agency Reuters published at least six reports on the protest since Friday. The first report, ‘Why India’s tens of millions of voter deletions have led to widespread protests’, discussed the contentious SIR deletion which have led to the mass outrage and protests.
“The BJP and the Commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately impacted by the deletions…They say the deletions have affected the outcome of some recent state elections that the BJP won, and have cast a shadow on the electoral process in the world’s biggest democracy,” explains the report.
On the day of the protest, another report details the preemptive measures and subsequent police action. With the headline, ‘India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest’, the report describes the frequent protests as a “new challenge to Modi”. “The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi…The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027,” it states.
While various other articles report on the CJP leaders’ detention and eventual release, the police excesses faced by thousands, a news feature by the agency spotlights Neha Bora’s rise “as one of the most visible faces of a protest movement in India that has mounted the most serious challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government in years.”
Germany-owned international broadcaster DW published four reports on why the protests were taking place, the dramatic detention of CJP leaders ahead of the protest, the police crackdown on Saturday, and the CJP leaders’ vow to continue protesting despite the heavy police action, respectively.
In the report, ‘Indian authorities crack down on ‘Cockroach’ protest’, which was accompanied by a 24-minute-long video carrying footage of the police excess, DW describes the crackdown as “extraordinary”. “Indian authorities launched an extraordinary security operation in Delhi on Saturday to prevent a major demonstration…Roads across India’s capital were sealed, police checkpoints established and public transport heavily disrupted before demonstrators could gather,” the report read.
UK-based Financial Times published two reports on Saturday and Sunday, ‘Police arrest leader of India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement as protesters take to streets’ and ‘India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement plans more protests after release of leaders’, respectively. Both focused on the police crackdown and the protesters’ predicament.
While the global news hub CNN published multiples features on he CJP movement through May-July, on Sunday, it reported the release of the CJP leaders and the excessive police clampdown. In ‘India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement founder and leaders released from detention after Delhi protest crackdown’, CNN stated that the movement’s “target” this time around is the “62-year-old chief of the Election Commission that holds the keys to India’s democracy – the world’s largest – and who the CJP alleges is responsible for disenfranchising tens of millions of citizens.”
CNN witnessed, the report mentioned, that “despite the capital turning into a fortress to keep out protesters and mobile internet blocked, supporters gathered Saturday — as security moved swiftly to crack down on the unrest with many people at the protest site detained by police.”

Saudi Arabia overturns death sentence for man over Facebook comment, Sri Lanka says
- Published
Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court has set aside the death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan migrant worker over a comment he made on Facebook, Colombo's Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra said.
Anojan Sivarasa, 27, was sentenced to death in September after a Saudi appellate court convicted him of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over his comment.
The case sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, spurring diplomatic efforts to seek clemency.
Saudi Arabia's top court set aside the sentence on Wednesday, Hemachandra said in a post on Facebook, where he thanked the authorities and legal teams of both nations for their efforts.
In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.
During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Sivarasa to respond in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.
Although Sivarasa promptly deleted the comment and posted an apology video, a screenshot of it was brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.
It is not clear if there will be further legal proceedings or whether Sivarasa will remain in detention, and for how long. He was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of three million Saudi riyals ($0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court.
Faizer Mustafa, a Sri Lankan lawmaker who is involved in legal negotiations with Saudi Arabia regarding Sivarasa's case, confirmed to BBC Sinhala that Saudi Arabia had overturned the death sentence, adding that they are reviewing the Supreme Court's latest ruling.
Sivarasa's family had earlier said they have had no direct contact with him since 28 September.
International rights groups had also joined calls for Saudi to spare his life.
"Saudi authorities should end their use of abusive laws to hand out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offenses, especially against migrant workers who are already in a vulnerable position with limited protections," Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch, said on Tuesday.

The rise and fall of a MAGA princess
How Kimberly Guilfoyle lost her ambassadorship.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, is out of a job after serious corruption allegations.
What happened? Guilfoyle resigned on Tuesday after being shown the door earlier in the day by Trump’s brand-new White House press secretary, who announced at a briefing that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign.
Her departure comes just six days after a bombshell Wall Street Journal story, which described Guilfoyle’s efforts to solicit money from a Trump donor, including $100,000 to pay down a credit card bill, in exchange for access to Trump officials and conservative media figures.
Guilfoyle also attempted to conceal those efforts: In one text to the donor, Eric Deters, she wrote, “What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing.”
Who is Guilfoyle? Fallen MAGA royalty. Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality, is also the ex-fiancée of Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. (and, more distantly, the ex-wife of current California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat).
There appears to be little love lost between Guilfoyle and Trump, however. On Tuesday, he told reporters that Guilfoyle “wasn’t a member of my family. She I guess dated my son a long time ago.” (The Don Jr.-Guilfoyle relationship is thought to have ended in 2024.)
Why was she forced out? Corruption allegations are not, generally speaking, dealbreakers in Trumpworld; the president and his children are all innovators when it comes to profiting off the presidency, and there’s plenty of self-dealing going on around them.
That being said, Guilfoyle may have crossed the line in two specific ways: one, her alleged corruption benefited her and not the Trump family. And two, the allegations are embarrassingly unsubtle even by the standards of the second Trump administration. The combination appears to have been too much.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
