Trump says oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is set to begin. It's not that simple
Recent deal offered concessions to U.S., but no new resource rights
U.S. President Donald Trump said "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in "our new and beautiful Greenland" early Wednesday.
It wasn't immediately clear what exploration or developments the U.S. president was referring to in his post, and Greenland is a self-governing territory of Denmark, rather than a part of the United States.
Trump posted on his Truth Social platform following a campaign event Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska, to stump for Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan as he seeks his third term to represent the state in an election against Democratic former U.S. congresswoman Mary Peltola.
Rising energy prices — a direct result of Trump's war in Iran — are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for America's working class ahead of the midterm elections next month. Trump's comments Wednesday are likely aimed at addressing voters' concerns before they head to the polls.
But despite Trump's optimism, resource exploration and extraction in Greenland has stymied companies for decades thanks to the island's harsh climate, lack of key infrastructure and difficult geology. Previous efforts to extract so-called rare earth minerals, as well as oil and gas, have never progressed beyond the exploratory stage.
Recent deal doesn't include exploration rights
Trump's comments about the Arctic island come less than a month after he signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic following months of tensions with NATO allies over the U.S. president's repeated demands to take control of the semiautonomous Danish territory. It does not grant the U.S. any special exploration rights, but does place some limits on investments by non-NATO countries in strategic sectors.
A young boy walks in Nuuk, Greenland on Friday, Feb. 6, 2026. The self-governing Danish territory has consistently rebuffed Trump's calls for the U.S. to annex the island. (Christinne Muschi/CP)
The deal also paved the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eased tensions over Trump's repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States. The agreement would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.
Trump has expressed his desire to acquire Greenland since as long ago as 2019 and, during his second term, issued threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a NATO ally.
Representatives of the leaders of Denmark and Greenland did not immediately return requests for comment Wednesday.
Greenland has valuable resources
Greenland has large deposits of the rare earth minerals that are needed to make everything from computers and smartphones to the batteries, solar and wind technologies that will power the transition away from fossil fuels. China currently dominates the world's supply of these critical minerals and the Trump administration is seeking to break Beijing's chokehold on them.
The U.S. Geological Survey has also identified major potential offshore deposits of oil and natural gas.
But tapping these resources could be prohibitively difficult: the rare earth minerals are encased in rock, and the offshore oil and natural gas deposits are covered by Arctic ice.
Trump boasts about Greenland's strategic location
Trump's Truth Social post also touted Greenland's strategic location, saying that "from a security purpose in the defence and offence of both the United States of America, and Europe," the island is "second to none."
"Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our defence will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived," he wrote. "It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the world!"
The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the U.S. military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO.
Trump said last month that the U.S. would "immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations," including "building two very major military bases."

A skin problem can begin with something familiar. An itch that persists. A rash that returns. A patch that looks different from the rest of the skin. What happens next often depends on where a person lives and whether appropriate care is within reach.
The Global Access to Skin Health Observatory is a landmark global study led by Esther Freeman in collaboration with the International League of Dermatological Societies (ILDS) and L’Oréal Dermatological Beauty. Published in JAMA Dermatology, it brings together data from 158 countries representing 97% of the world’s population.
For India, the findings raise questions about where specialists practise, how patients reach them and what happens when treatment is delayed.
What the numbers miss
The study proposes a benchmark of 5.63 per lakh, derived from countries reporting adequate access to dermatological care. This, however, is a reference point, rather than a universal staffing prescription. Dr. Freeman, who is associate professor of dermatology at Harvard Medical School and director of global health dermatology at Massachusetts General Hospital, places India’s dermatologist density well below the benchmark at around 0.5 to 1 per lakh people.
Ramesh Bhat, the Indian co-author of the study and professor at Father Muller Medical College and head of research at Father Muller Research Centre, Mangalore, cautions against directly comparing India with Europe or the Americas, because their health systems differ. What surprises Prof Bhat is that shortages persist despite the number of postgraduate dermatology training seats. He points to the urban-rural divide, with a concentration of specialists in urban areas, and in many cities in southern India, while rural communities face a different reality, where access even to a doctor may be limited.
The study reports that, globally, 79% of dermatologists practise in urban areas. National averages can therefore conceal substantial local gaps. “Dermatologist density gives us an important starting point, but it does not tell us whether a patient can actually receive care,” Dr. Freeman says.
When care is delayed
For Prof Bhat, the consequences are visible in clinical practice. He identifies “delay in diagnosis, wrong treatment, steroid abuse” among the problems arising when appropriate care is unavailable. He singles out leprosy as a condition where delayed diagnosis has implications beyond the individual patient. His concern brings the discussion back to what happens before someone reaches a specialist and whether the treatment they receive along the way is appropriate.
Dr Freeman emphasises the breadth of skin disease, from common infections to chronic inflammatory conditions and neglected tropical diseases. She argues that skin health must be recognised as an essential part of healthcare, with investment directed towards services that already reach communities.
The question is, how to make those services capable of recognising and managing skin disease safely.
Bringing expertise closer
“We need more dermatologists, but we cannot train our way out of this problem with specialists alone,” Dr Freeman says. Primary-care physicians and health officers already manage substantial amounts of skin disease. She advocates practical training, essential medicines and clear referral pathways, allowing common conditions to be treated locally while complex disease and uncertain diagnoses reach specialists.
Prof Bhat also proposes that medical colleges adopt villages, strengthening their links with surrounding communities. He also sees a role for the district residency programme, which takes residents into district settings, and for health camps in reaching rural and tribal populations.
These approaches sit alongside his call for rural specialist clinics and teledermatology. His emphasis is on extending the reach of existing teaching institutions and services, while giving residents the training needed to work effectively beyond major urban centres.
Making remote advice useful
“Teledermatology can be implemented,” Prof Bhat says. But he cautions that training healthcare workers must not result in unqualified practice or drug misuse. Expanding access requires clarity about who can manage a condition and when specialist assessment is necessary.
Dr. Freeman makes a related point. Teledermatology and Artificial Intelligence use need trained frontline providers, available treatment, and reliable referral arrangements. A patient requiring a biopsy, urgent assessment or specialist therapy must still be able to obtain it. “The goal is not to replace dermatologists, but to make their expertise reach much further,” she says.
A remote consultation needs to connect with treatment and follow-up. Advice alone cannot resolve the practical difficulties of obtaining medicines or reaching a referral centre.
What progress should look like
In 2025, the World Health Assembly recognised skin diseases as a global public-health priority. The next step is translating that recognition into national funding and delivery plans.
Prof Bhat’s priorities include an adequate health budget and insurance coverage for dermatological medicines such as biologics and for procedures. He also calls for better training of dermatology residents and dermatology nursing as a separate speciality within nursing education. These proposals bring together workforce development, treatment affordability and rural services, addressing several barriers to appropriate dermatological care.
Measuring progress will require listening more closely to patients. Dr. Freeman acknowledges that the Observatory relied on national leaders and health-system informants, rather than patients directly. Future work should examine waiting times, travel, affordability and diagnostic delays, alongside outcomes and quality of life.
Her planned next phase will examine selected countries more closely to understand where clinicians choose to train and practise, what retains them in underserved areas and which models improve access in different settings. “Five years from now, success should not simply mean there are more dermatologists,” she says. “It should mean that where someone lives is less predictive of whether they can get appropriate care for their skin disease.”
For India, that would mean earlier recognition, appropriate treatment and dependable referral, with fewer patients left to navigate the gaps themselves.
(Dr. Monisha Madhumita is assistant professor, department of dermatology, Saveetha Medical College and Hospitals, Chennai. mail.monisha.m@gmail.com)

The Indian-origin U.S. Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal on Wednesday (October 14, 2026) voiced concern over reports of the removal of 13 crore voter names from the draft electoral rolls in India.
“I am deeply concerned about the actions of the Indian government to purge 130 million people from the voting rolls,” Jayapal said in a post on X, marking the first such comments by a US lawmaker on the issue.
The Democratic Congresswoman from Washington State said she supported the non-violent protests to counter "anti-democratic efforts in India.”
Ms. Jayapal said the developments in India appear to be a similar playbook to what the Trump Administration is doing in the U.S. to undermine voting rights in a democracy.
She said protecting democracies everywhere is essential work, and the Indian people — like the American people — deserve free and fair elections.
“Non-violent resistance movements are essential in these moments, and I stand with the Indian people who are engaging in non-violent protests to counter anti-democratic efforts in India,” Ms. Jayapal said.
Comparing SIR 2002-04 and 2025-26
According to statistics shared by the Election Commission of India (ECI), around 7.2 crore names were deleted from the draft rolls in the first and second phases when the SIR was held in 13 States and union territories.
During the ongoing third phase, where draft lists of 18 States and Union Territories are published, the number of deleted voters stands at 6.16 crore.
The Commission has said that if a genuine voter’s name was inadvertently left out during the SIR process, the voter could seek inclusion through the claims and objections process and subsequently through Form 6.

After a disaster like a landslide, an earthquake, or a major fire, rescue workers have to locate survivors as soon as possible, and they are increasingly using drones for this critical task—especially ultra-compact drones that can fit into the crevices of a collapsed structure. There are, however, some serious limitations to the technology.
Weighing less than a stick of butter, ultra-compact drones don’t have as much compute or power capacity as larger models, and this restricts the power of their sensors. That means if a building is filled with smoke or the disaster happens at night, the drone’s cameras and lidar will cease to function. Even a clear pane of glass can be an obstacle the drone might not sense.
Now, a research team at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands—drawing inspiration from the whiskers of nocturnal animals—has developed a lightweight, tactile sensor for drones to navigate even when they can’t “see.” Some nocturnal animals, like mice and to some extent cats, can explore their surroundings using just the sensations of the environment around them on their whiskers, enabling them to move without vision. The research team wondered whether drones could do the same.
In the world of drone development, tactile navigation is a novel concept that comes with its own challenges. “For tactile sensing to work on drones, it needs to be lightweight, low-latency, and low-power,” Salwa Hamaza, a professor at Delft University of Technology, explained in a press release. Luckily, nature already did some of that innovating.
The “whiskers” Hamaza and her team crafted for the drone consist of delicate wires made of nickel-titanium, each measuring 0.4 millimeters in diameter—about the thickness of four sheets of paper. The antennae, however, were longer than the drone itself. To a palm-sized drone, the researchers attached two whiskers, each nearly 8 inches long with three small pressure sensors at the base. These can assess the bending of the wires, from which the drone estimates its distance from and position in relation to nearby barriers. All calculations necessary for this navigation are processed by a microcontroller onboard the drone, without relying on an external computer.
It may not sound too complicated, but even determining the angle at which to mount the wires was a challenge. Animals that navigate via whisker generally do not fly. Having a long protrusion, even if very light and delicate, can make the drone unstable. When moving along a wall, the researchers saw that resistance from the whisker could cause the drone to rotate and crash.
The researchers compared a total of 72 flights, testing six different angles at three different speeds. The drone flew without major incident when the whiskers were mounted at 30 degrees, 45 degrees, and 60 degrees. Of these, the 45-degree angle was adopted because it resulted in the least deviation in the drone’s orientation. They also took into account the fact that a 60-degree angle reduces the forward sensing range.
The researchers also encountered several hurdles in processing the information taken in by the whiskers. One was distinguishing between actual contact signals and disturbances caused by the drone itself, such as vibrations from the propellers. Even when filtering this noise out, about 38 percent of the drone’s detections were false positives.
The issue seemed to be drift, a phenomenon where sensor readings gradually shift over time. The research team, therefore, developed a correction algorithm that continuously estimates the trend of drifts over time—based on sensor readings when the drone is not touching anything—while in flight. When combined with the filter, false positives reportedly dropped to 0 percent.
These tests were largely done in an environment with three transparent walls arranged in a row. Whenever the tactile sensor touched a wall surface, the drone flew parallel to the wall, maintaining a distance of 60 to 100 millimeters from the surface until it reached the edge. The drone was even able to navigate when the wall was at an angle to it, something a drone with laser sensors would not be able to do.
However, in a real-world situation—like the rubble of a disaster—obstacles are not so neatly arranged. Even in your average room, a drone following a wall could easily get stuck in a corner or overlook barriers to the side. The researchers, therefore, encoded an exploration method that prioritizes moving through unexplored areas by probabilistically estimating the shape of walls. Using this method, the drone successfully found a 2.5-foot-wide exit in a small room with glass walls in 90 percent of tests.
And there is room for improvement, figuratively and literally, given that this touch system only uses a small fraction of the drone’s 192 KB of memory. “We wanted to show that touch does not have to come at the cost of size or computational power,” Chao-Shan Ye, a doctoral student at Delft University of Technology, added in the press release. “Our entire tactile perception pipeline runs onboard using just 34 KB of memory, allowing a tiny drone to sense and respond to its environment in real time.”

‘She takes better selfies’: Shashi Tharoor praises activist Neha Bora after INDIA bloc’s Delhi march
Congress leader Shashi Tharoor praised AISA president Neha Bora for her courage after meeting her at the INDIA bloc’s March for Democracy in New Delhi.
Senior Congress leader Shashi Tharoor praised student activist Neha Bora for her “manifest courage” after meeting her at the INDIA bloc’s March for Democracy in New Delhi on Monday, sharing a selfie with her on X.
“Enjoyed meeting @neha_aisa at the INDIA bloc’s #MarchForDemocracy on Monday. I have great respect for her manifest courage — the courage of her convictions. She also takes better selfies than most!” Tharoor wrote alongside the photograph.
Bora, the national president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), has emerged as one of the prominent faces of recent anti-CEC demonstrations in the national capital.
The 29-year-old PhD scholar marched alongside Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra during the INDIA bloc’s march to the Supreme Court. The protest targeted Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and opposed the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

Who is Neha Bora?
Bora has become one of the most visible faces of a protest movement challenging Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, following a crackdown on demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) and other groups.
The student activist was among several people detained by police over the weekend as demonstrators attempted to protest against alleged large-scale voter deletions and irregularities in the electoral process.
Bora has said she did not initially set out to become an activist. She traces her political journey to theatre and later to the student-led protests against a citizenship law in 2019 and 2020, Reuters reported.
On Saturday, after police blocked protesters from reaching Jantar Mantar, New Delhi’s designated protest site, Bora urged demonstrators to regroup at Dilli Haat, a crafts market about 10 km away.
“Dilli Haat becomes Jantar Mantar today,” she wrote on X before setting off towards the location, chanting slogans as others followed.
Police detained her along with several other activists. However, while in detention, she called on supporters to continue the demonstration.
“I am in detention. The movement is not,” she said in a video posted online, urging those stopped by police to protest wherever they were. She was released later on Saturday.

Furious judge cites Dr. Seuss’s The Lorax as she stops Trump from tearing down trees at DC golf course
Workers cut down and bulldozed hundreds of trees because the president ‘demands haste,’ according to Judge Ana C Reyes

The Lorax said he speaks for the trees, “for the trees have no tongues.” That job is now for a federal judge in Washington, D.C.
District Judge Ana C. Reyes invoked Dr. Seuss’s environmental fable after ordering Donald Trump’s administration to stop work on a public golf course, where crews and tractors ripped out hundreds of trees over the weekend.
Reyes unloaded on Department of Justice lawyers in a tense hearing this week after the government failed to alert the court and preservation groups about imminent plans to raze the public golf course, where more than 400 trees were knocked down.
“Breakneck speed to clear trees that posed no harm. The reason? Disputed. The budget? Unclear. The environmental impact? Unstudied. The urgency? None,” Reyes wrote Tuesday night. “Next steps: bulldoze hundreds more.”
Without her intervention, the “the ground, landscape and vistas will be irrevocably altered” because “destroyed trees cannot be replaced,” preservationists warned in a lawsuit against the administration.
“Just ask the Lorax,” Reyes added.
In a footnote, Reyes said she recently learned that Dr. Suess worked “late into the night” over his depiction of a “smallish gopher-like creature called the Lorax” for “a full year,” citing an article about the author from 1979.
“But then, while on vacation in Africa, Dr. Seuss — inspired by the sight of a herd of elephants— ‘picked up a laundry pad and wrote the whole book that afternoon,’” she wrote.
“The Court has seen no elephants. And it has certainly had less than a year to write. But it very much appreciates that her clerks know something of late-night work and industrious afternoons,” she added.
Trump’s proposed overhaul of the public golf course — part of his extensive plans to remake the nation’s capital with sweeping changes to the landscape and public monuments — was happening “faster than anticipated,” according to preservation groups who are suing to stop the deconstruction.
The lawsuit from the D.C. Preservation League and two D.C.-area residents calls on the court to halt the Trump administration's Washington National plan, the National Park Service’s proposed efforts to replace the public park with what the president is calling “one of the Greatest Golf Courses anywhere in the World.”
The government had previously stated that it would not take irreversible action without completing a legal and environmental review process as required under the National Environmental Policy Act.
But shortly before 5 p.m. Friday, the administration announced plans to begin clearing hundreds of trees. Tractors and heavy equipment tore down dozens of trees the next day, according to the plaintiffs.
The administration claims that the “Tree Management Plan” is “but one step in the Government’s Washington National Plan, which, as Plaintiffs put it, seeks to ‘destroy East Potomac Golf Course,’” Reyes wrote Tuesday.
“It is a coincidence, the Government seems to suggest, that [the Department of Interior] cut down hundreds of trees at the Course weeks after the President asked [the agency] to cut down trees at the Course, and not, say, any other time in the last seven years,” she added. “That asks rather a lot of coincidence.”
The administration has done “precisely” what the preservations feared, the judge said.
Tree removal plans moved from “removing only hazardous, dead, dying, or invasive trees to removing hundreds of healthy, non-invasive trees” — and did so without providing any “meaningful” notice to the plaintiffs and the court, Reyes wrote.
Administration officials “raced” to tear down the trees, because the president “demands haste on his redesign, and not because of some newfound zeal to implement a small part” of a seven-year-old plan, she added.
Kevin Griess, superintendent of National Mall and Memorial Parks, who was hauled Monday into the courtroom, testified that the trees were removed to return the course to “the original state of a links-style golf course,” which had “very, very, very few trees on it at all.”
But asked by the judge whether there is any urgency whatsoever to continue pulling down the trees, Griess said “not that I’m aware of.”
Rebecca Miller, executive director of the D.C. Preservation League, said in a statement that the government’s short notice of the tree removal “fails to honor previous commitments of timely communication made to the court and the plaintiffs.”
She called the government’s “sudden execution” of the plan “a deliberate effort” by the National Park Service and Department of the Interior to bypass the courts and “jeopardize a protected historic resource.”
“Filing late on a Friday and cutting trees at dawn the next morning sure seems to skirt everything this court asked of the administration,” said Alex Dickson, one of the plaintiffs in the case. “They seem to be moving forward any way they can, and looking for loopholes to get there.”

A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.
The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.
The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe through police operations, transnational investigations and ongoing court cases involving brokers, active members, cells or operational networks. It does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias.
The identified groups include Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation cartel (CJNG); the Clan del Golfo mafia, and the guerrilla organisations ELN and dissident factions of Farc in Colombia; Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command) and Comando Vermelho (CV, or Red Command); Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua; and the US-originated Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs, which are also prevalent in El Salvador, Honduras, Guatemala and, to a lesser degree, in Mexico.
These organisations have built a more prominent presence in Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, while their activities have also been noted in Germany, Romania, Croatia and Slovakia. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (Gi-Toc) also includes Bulgaria.
Daniel Brombacher, a political scientist and director of the Europe Observatory at Gi-Toc, said: “There is something new happening with a presence of Latin American groups in geographies where there’s no pre-existing infrastructure.
“This phenomenon is no longer limited to the traditional gateway countries,” he says. “Recent police operations have uncovered Mexican-run methamphetamine labs in southern France, north-eastern Poland and Brandenburg, south of Berlin. Latin American groups are also appearing in Romania and Bulgaria along the Balkan route.”
Latin American national authorities and experts suggest the list may be even longer. An unpublished report by the São Paulo public prosecutor’s office, partly based on data from the Brazilian intelligence agency (Abin) – which the Guardian reviewed – shows, for example, that the PCC, now Brazil’s biggest criminal group, operates in 16 European countries, including the UK, Ireland, Iceland, Serbia, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.
The suspicion that Latin American cartels and factions are seeking to become established in Europe is not new. Since at least the 1980s, Colombian criminal organisations such as the Cali and Medellín cartels had footholds in regions of Spain such as Galicia. In 2013, a Europol report in 2103 warned of their rise. But what authorities are witnessing now is on an another level.
A Europol report this year states that “Latin American MTCNs [most threatening criminal networks] have also settled in the EU, from where they direct operations that affect the EU. This is particularly the case for mobile criminal networks involved in organised property crime.”
Interpol, led by the Brazilian federal police officer Valdecy Urquiza, has been approached, but has not commented.
The problem has become more visible over the past decade. Drug production in Latin America in that time has increased roughly fourfold to reach a record of about 4,100 tonnes in 2024. This comes after growth of up to 35% at the beginning of the decade. More cocaine is now produced in Colombia than during the era of the notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar. Nearly all the world’s cocaine and many related substances originate from Latin America, particularly Colombia.
Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés, an academic at the Autonomous University of Coahuila in Mexico who is an expert on organised crime, says: “The main ones are the Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco cartel [CJNG] in Mexico; the Comando Vermelho and the PCC of Brazil; the Gulf Clan and different factions of the Colombian Farc; the Lobos and the Choneros of Ecuador; and Tren de Aragua of Venezuela.”
He believes that the Latin American presence in Europe is even more widespread than is generally recognised. “Sinaloa cartel and the CJNG have a presence in more than 20 European countries. Obviously, that does not mean they dominate or have large cells,” he says. “Rather, they are business emissaries.”
The UN Office on Drugs and Crime’s 2026 World Drug Report on illicit crimes states that global cocaine production in 2024 was between 3,800 and 4,700 tonnes – more than four times higher than it was in 2014. South America remains the main production hub, with coca cultivation covering a record 385,000 hectares over the past decade – three times the 2014 figure.
Europe has emerged as a key market because it offers organisations higher profit margins than the US. Since the beginning of the decade, European police have confiscated more drugs than American forces, and data indicates that Europe now represents about a quarter of global consumption.
Europol recently reported that out of 731 MTCNs operating across Europe, 149 are connected to Latin American organisations. Of these, 67 have Latin American members, and 22 mainly consist of Latin Americans.

In 2022, New York fined three Amish schools for not complying with a law mandating schools only accept students with updated vaccines, following the 2019 removal of a religious exemption from that law. The small schools were fined $2,000 for every student without updated vaccines every day, for a total of $118,000 before the schools sued the state.
New York fined the schools, not the children.
The New York Department of Health did not clarify to Snopes whether it had fined any other schools or whether it had continued to fine the three schools since 2022.
In early October, some social media posts claimed the state of New York had "declared war on the Amish" with vaccine requirements enforced by fines. Many Amish communities have lower childhood vaccination rates than the rest of the U.S. population, although vaccination is not universally rejected in these communities.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claimed the state was fining each unvaccinated Amish child $2,000 per day. The post asserted that New York Democrats took away the religious exemption often used by Amish families to opt out of childhood vaccine requirements.
Users shared similar posts claiming New York Democrats were fining unvaccinated Amish children $2,000 each day on Instagram (archived) and X (archived). Snopes readers emailed us asking whether the rumor was true.
It's true that New York fined at least three Amish schools $2,000 for each unvaccinated child it allowed to attend the school each day. New York did not fine the children themselves, and it's unclear whether the state is still actively imposing fines on these schools or any other over their vaccination policies. Therefore, we've rated this claim a mixture of true and false information.
These details are outlined in a lawsuit, Miller v. McDonald.
According to the case, in 2019 New York repealed the religious exemption to its school immunization law — which applies to all public, private and religious schools in the state — after a measles outbreak in 2018 and 2019 centered around communities with clusters of unvaccinated people (PDF Page 3).
Democrats were the majority in both the state Senate and state Assembly in 2019. The governor at the time was Andrew Cuomo, a Democrat.
The immunization law prohibits schools from allowing children who do not have their scheduled vaccinations to attend the school until those vaccination requirements are met. New York audited three Amish schools' compliance with the law in 2021, and in 2022 it fined the schools for allowing children to attend who did not meet the vaccine requirements (PDF Page 7).
A school is fined $2,000 for each violation of the law every day (PDF pages 7-8). Every attending student who does not meet vaccine requirements is considered a violation, which means the school is fined for each noncompliant student every day. Prior to imposing the fines, the state sent a letter to school administrators warning it would impose the fines.
New York applied the fines under the assumption that two schools failed to comply for one day and acted as if there were only one noncompliant student attending for 10 days at the third school. That resulted in fines of $52,000 for 26 students at one school, $46,000 for 23 students at another school and $20,000 for one student at the third school, for a total of $118,000.
Notably, this amount was the total of the fines fines placed on the schools at the time the lawsuit was filed on June 2, 2023, the total fine referenced in the latest court decision on June 30 and the total fine referenced in social media posts as of this writing. A legal organization representing the Amish schools said they racked up $118,000 in total fines when announcing it would appeal the latest ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court on Oct. 2.
Snopes reached out to the New York State Department of Health to ask whether the schools were still racking up fines or whether there have been other schools fined since the beginning of the lawsuit. The department did not elaborate on the fines. A spokesperson told Snopes via email:
The state's responsibility is to protect public health, keep New Yorkers and their families safe and enforce the law fairly and equitably. While we cannot comment on pending litigation, the Department is committed to eliminating serious illness and unnecessary deaths caused by vaccine preventable diseases. The Department continues to provide community outreach and education on the safety of immunizations. New York's school immunization requirements are based in science and protect the health and well-being of all New Yorkers.
The lawsuit challenging this law, which does so on religious freedom grounds, has traveled up and down the court system. In 2025, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a lower court's decision to side with New York over the plaintiffs (PDF Page 5), but the U.S. Supreme Court vacated that decision and told the 2nd Circuit to reconsider the case in light of a different case the Supreme Court recently ruled on.
After considering this other case, the 2nd Circuit did not change its decision in Miller v. McDonald. That was the June 30 decision that representatives for the Amish schools are appealing to the Supreme Court once again.
For further reading, Snopes previously fact-checked the claim that autism rates are nearly nonexistent among Amish children because Amish people allegedly rarely get vaccinated.

Farm Boy, L'Ancêtre and Life Smart organic cheeses recalled for possible Listeria contamination
CFIA says recall was triggered by testing; no reported illnesses connected to affected products
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) is recalling several organic cheese products under the Farm Boy, L'Ancêtre, and Life Smart brands due to possible Listeria contamination.
The agency says the national recall was triggered by testing and there have been no reported illnesses connected to consumption of the products.
The affected products include Farm Boy organic Swiss, medium cheddar, old cheddar, extra sharp and three-year-old cheddar cheeses with a best before date of July 30, 2027.
Life Smart organic part skim mozzarella cheese with a best before date of March 30, 2027, is also being recalled, as are several shredded organic cheeses made by L'Ancêtre with best before dates of this December, next January and next July.
L'Ancetre's organic Swiss cheese with a best before date of July 30, 2027, is also included.
A full list of the recalled products can be found here. They were sold in stores across the country.
The CFIA says people should not consume the product if they have it in their home, and to throw it out or return it to wherever they bought it. It warns that products that look and smell normal can still make someone sick.
Symptoms of Listeria include vomiting, nausea, persistent fever, muscle aches, severe headache and neck stiffness. Pregnant women, the elderly and those with weakened immune systems are at greater risk.

Joni Mitchell has become a US citizen, after first moving to the country in the mid-1960s. The Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posted footage of her citizenship ceremony on her Instagram account, along with a photo of her next to an American flag, accompanied by the caption: “A journey that began 62 years ago.”
It means that Mitchell can now vote in US elections, something that she had complained she wasn’t able to do.
At a concert in 2024, Mitchell said: “Fuck Donald Trump, I love that song,” referring to the rap track by YG. She added: “I wish I could vote ... I’m a Canadian. I’m one of those lousy immigrants.”
Mitchell was born in Fort Macleod, Alberta, in 1943, and eventually settled with her family in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Her earliest gigs were at folk clubs there, followed by Calgary and Toronto, where she met US folk singer Chuck Mitchell. They married in 1965 and Mitchell moved to the US. The marriage didn’t last, ending two years later, but by that time Mitchell had established herself as a mellifluous, original voice on the vibrant US folk music circuit.
She released her debut album in 1968, and soon after, using the album’s royalties, moved to Los Angeles’ Laurel Canyon where she recorded her first gold-selling album, Ladies of the Canyon. She remained based in California and currently lives in Santa Barbara.
Mitchell’s most recent studio album is Shine, from 2007. After that she spent a number of years out of the public eye, suffering a brain aneurysm in 2015 that required extensive recovery. But she returned to live performance in 2022 with an unannounced set at the Newport folk festival, and has since performed a number of all-star “Joni Jam” concerts.
A biopic about her is being prepared by director Cameron Crowe, who began work on it in the early 2020s. Earlier this year, record executive Clive Davis announced at a party that Meryl Streep would play Mitchell in the film.

Netflix is in a slump — and it's not just because you can't find a hot new show to watch.
The streaming titan's shares are down 42% in the last 12 months and have been nearly cut in half from their all-time high last summer. Netflix had its biggest round of layoffs in four years on Wednesday, cutting about 1,000 employees, roughly 6% of the company.
So, what's going wrong?
Netflix's viewership growth has slowed as free competitors like YouTube gain momentum, and initiatives like games and podcasts have yet to become breakout hits. Add in the company's surprise bid for Warner Bros., which it later abandoned, and some investors are feeling on edge.
Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters said in a memo that entertaining the world "requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources" but added that the company is still on track to reach its financial goals this year.
Many of Netflix's struggles aren't unique to the "Stranger Things" maker, which disrupted Hollywood by pioneering paid TV streaming and has a major influence over culture.
"Even the top streaming companies are not immune to stagnation and financial difficulties," said Ross Benes, a media analyst at EMARKETER, Business Insider's sister company.
Other entertainment giants like Disney and NBCUniversal have turned to layoffs recently.
Here are five of the biggest challenges facing Netflix right now.
1. Engagement growth is slowing
Although Netflix is still growing revenue at a healthy pace while generating billions in profits, Wall Street is concerned about its viewership trends.
Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos told Bloomberg at an event last month that "we're not growing as fast as I want us to, and we're working on making that move faster."
Netflix grew global viewing hours by 2% year over year to 97 billion in the first half of 2026. The streaming giant also announced last quarter that it would share its engagement report only once a year, down from twice a year.
When announcing the move, Netflix told investors that "engagement is not just the quantity of view hours, but also refers to the quality and variety of our offering."
Investors are worried that slowing engagement growth could hurt Netflix's ability to retain customers and persuade them to pay more, though the streamer has an industry-low cancellation rate.
Engagement is also "the golden compass for advertisers" since higher usage helps them reach broader audiences, said Brandon Katz, an analyst at Greenlight Analytics. If Netflix keeps growing viewership, it could charge advertisers higher rates.
The lack of a new breakout hit is also troubling for Netflix analysts. "Stranger Things," the platform's biggest show ever, ended last year, and the streamer needs to find new franchises and buzzy hits that can replace it.
"Entertainment is an inherently subjective and streaky industry," Katz said.
2. Competition is heating up from free streamers and social media
While Netflix is still leading its paid peers in viewership and profits, free streaming services like YouTube, Tubi, and The Roku Channel are gaining popularity, especially among younger audiences.
YouTube's viewership share on US TVs was 14.2% in July — nearly double Netflix's 7.8% share, according to Nielsen.
Roku's free streamer and Tubi are also formidable competitors with shares of 2.9% and 2%, respectively. These no-cost services have grown as paid streamers like Netflix have raised their prices.
Netflix is considering starting a free offering in some markets, co-CEO Greg Peters has said.
Then there's the popularity of social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram, which are hoovering up viewership hours.
Netflix is looking to counter social-media foes by investing in video podcasts and creators to increase engagement and connect with younger viewers without breaking the bank.
"With pressure mounting, Netflix will look to turn the tide by getting a boost from low-cost content," Benes said.
3. The Wall Street narrative soured after Netflix's failed bid for Warner Bros.
Netflix spooked some shareholders by making an $82.7 billion bid for the Warner Bros. studio and streaming assets. Paramount Skydance eventually bought the whole company.
Although adding HBO Max and the Warner Bros. studio could have given Netflix a boost, investors worried that its leaders had run out of ideas for growth since Netflix hasn't historically turned to major dealmaking. Besides that narrative, shareholders were concerned about Netflix taking on a massive debt load and going through a complex integration process, Katz said.
Even though Netflix pocketed a $2.8 billion breakup fee when the deal fell apart, the stock never fully recovered.
4. Games and podcasts haven't become runaway hits
Netflix has made major pushes into games and podcasts, though neither has been a game changer so far.
The streamer shut down a pair of game studios this summer and laid off some staffers in October 2024 as well.
Netflix hasn't shared many details about how its games or podcasts are performing. The company said in its July shareholder letter that it had successfully launched games like "FIFA World Cup: Launch Edition" and "Unhinged," and that the kids app Netflix Playground tripled its daily user count, but it didn't specify how much time those games generated.
Neither games nor podcasts were on last quarter's engagement report. If either were a substantial hit, company leadership would likely want to share specific metrics of their success to investors eager to see new growth areas.
Games are "not a bad idea" but likely are "not going to get any subs," said Alan Wolk, a media analyst at research firm TVREV. He added that it "remains to be seen if people will start watching podcasts on Netflix," saying the streamer should adjust its mobile app interface to improve the experience.
Still, podcasts are a cheap way to expand into verticals like news and are also "laundry folding programming" that can form habits, Katz said.
5. Sports rights are expensive and tied up
Another way Netflix is trying to boost engagement is investing in live sports — including NFL games on Christmas Day and the day before Thanksgiving, the MLB Home Run Derby, and one-off events like a boxing match between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua.
While Netflix executives have said these events drive subscriptions at an unusually high rate, sports rights are also increasingly expensive due to bidding wars between TV networks like ESPN and tech giants like Amazon and YouTube.
Live sports are an effective acquisition tool and can help Netflix scale its budding advertising business.
"Sports are the last vestige of the monoculture and where they can reach all the people who never otherwise see ads," Wolk said.
However, sports aren't cheap and offer little to no replay value, making them more of a temporary fix for engagement than a long-term driver of viewership.
Netflix also has to be creative with its sports investments since most of the marquee rights — from the main NFL packages to the NBA, college football, NFL, and international soccer — are tied up for years. The streamer did secure live rights to the Women's World Cup in 2027 and 2031, which it hopes will capture the cultural zeitgeist.

Srinagar, Oct 14: The Directorate of School Education Kashmir (DSEK) has revised school timings across the Kashmir Division, with the new schedule coming into effect from Thursday, October 15.
According to Order No. 410-DSEK of 2026, issued on October 14, all government and recognised private schools across the division will follow the revised timings.

Police in New Delhi detained scores of protesters on Saturday as thousands of officers and paramilitaries patrolled India’s capital, metro stations were shut and mobile internet suspended to guard against a youth protest demanding India’s chief election officer quit.
The protest, called by the “Cockroach” youth movement, hopes to draw thousands of demonstrators who want the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to quit over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party.
Television images showed police in the city’s central business district chasing down a few dozen young protesters, before they were loaded into vehicles and taken away.
About 200 protesters were detained in the area, a police source told Reuters. Those detained outside Delhi included protest supporter Dhruv Rathee, a popular figure on YouTube, a police spokesperson said.
Touted by organisers as a protest to “save democracy”, it aims to be the biggest of the demonstrations that were launched last week after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar’s deputies had questioned and disagreed with him over the revision process that saw about 130 million voter names removed.
Opposition parties have long alleged the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage.
Kumar has not commented. The election commission and the BJP have denied the allegations.
The BJP says Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth are some of the reasons for its electoral dominance and that opposition parties are misleading the country because they are unable to win elections.
Near daily protests by opposition groups pose a new political challenge to Modi, just months after similar demonstrations forced his education minister to quit over exam paper leaks.
It also comes months before a series of important state elections starting in early 2027, including in the BJP-ruled most populous state of Uttar Pradesh.
The protesters, led by the self-named Cockroach Janta party, that began as an online satire, said they would gather at Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning – a site designated for protests by authorities in the heart of New Delhi.
Delhi police said on Friday they had not given permission for the protest because the request did not come on time, adding that CJP had violated undertakings given during previous protests, and that authorities had to enforce the law and maintain peace.
Police said protesters would face the force of the law if they violated the ban.
Tens of thousands of police officers and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the capital, with multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocking roads leading to Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders rejected the police decision and said they would go ahead with the protest.
Authorities have ordered the closure of dozens of metro stations, and cancelled several trains coming to New Delhi. However, the supreme court on Friday said some trains must still run and there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.
“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” the CJP chief, Abhijeet Dipke, said on X.
“Imagine how many lives would be affected because of this shutdown by Modi.”
Mobile internet services in a radius of 4km (2.5 miles) of the protest area were ordered suspended from Friday night to Saturday night, ANI news agency reported citing a government order.
The CJP has said “at least 10,000 people”, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.
Some people detained in the central state of Madhya Pradesh were taken to hotels, The Hindu newspaper reported.
Police have not responded to the party’s broader allegations of mass detentions.
* With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

Gael Monfils apparently retires before planned
Oct 14 (Field Level Media) - Part-tennis standout and part-showman Gael Monfils has apparently retired ahead of schedule.
The 40-year-old Frenchman did the farewell tour this spring and summer, but had received a wild-card entry to the ATP Masters event in Paris in early November. It was presumed he would play his final competitive match in his home country.
But Monfils appeared on the list of retired players list maintained by the International Tennis Integrity Agency and listed as "inactive" as of Oct. 5. Since this body oversees anti-doping protocol in the sport and Monfils would not be subject to those rules, he is ineligible to compete in professional tournaments.
On Wednesday, the Grand Prix Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, an ATP 250 event in Lyon which begins on Oct. 19, announced that Monfils had pulled out of an exhibition match that included countrymen Jo-Wilfried Tsonga, Gilles Simon and Richard Gasquet due to personal reasons.
Monfils has not confirmed his retirement, but, similar to Serena Williams' comeback path, he would have to be available for drug-testing for six months before returning to competition.
Monfils made it clear after his second round loss to Learner Tien at the 2026 U.S. Open - which now appears to be his final profession match -that he plans to enter the business world and announced that he had signed on with a Swiss company to work in wealth management.
Monfils won 13 ATP Tour titles and reached a career-high world ranking of No. 6 in 2016. He reached Grand Slam semifinals at the French Open in 2008 and at the U.S. Open in 2016.
But Monfils was perhaps more well-known for his artistry on the court. Even in his later years, he would run down balls that many younger players would not even attempt and display acrobatic moves on overheads and a deft touch at the net.
Monfils is married to Ukrainian tennis standout Elina Svitolina and the couple has daughter, Skai, who turns 4 on Thursday.

Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted
- Published
What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?
That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.
The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.
The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.
The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.
Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.
With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.
"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.
The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".
Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.
"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.
Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".
Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.
"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.
"But I did wrong."
It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).
Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.
"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.
"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.
"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."
The incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.
In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head".
"To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".
In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.
That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.
Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece.
"You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says.
"And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."
The film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.
When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.
But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships.
"I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."
As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US.
"Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim.
"In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat.
"Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."
The potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.
In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.
At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.
Kim says that began to change as they filmed.
"I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."
Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.
She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.
On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career.
"Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview.
"And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."
Kim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule.
"But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.
The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted.
"It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim.
"I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."
In the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised.
"Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says.
"She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power.
"That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'.
"So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."

Who else besides Danielle Smith is saying 'yes to the nine' in Alberta's referendum?
UCP officials worried premier might lose some immigration and constitutional questions
It’s long appeared that the pro-unity side in Alberta’s referendum would prevail; polling suggests the separatists will lose by a three-to-one margin next week.
Polling is closer on the other nine questions, but Danielle Smith put them to voters, believing she had sure winners.
While she has repeatedly advocated for the “stay” option when asked, she’s focused most of her rhetoric — and the $4 million government advertising campaign — on the referendum’s proverbial undercard, the questions proposing immigration and constitutional reform.
But aside from that taxpayer-funded push, there’s been little public advocacy for Questions 1-9.
Contrast that with the more visible “No to the Nine” campaign that has cropped up alongside maple leafs on many federalist lawns to push against Smith’s questions and the premier herself.
Though Smith designed the questions to be easy wins among her base and the general public alike, they’ve become a target of both the premier’s anti-separatist detractors, as well as prominent separatists, who treat the questions with either scorn or indifference.
Senior officials in Smith’s United Conservative Party privately say they’re concerned that voters could reject at least some of the questions. If it’s a really bad night, they could lose all of them.
Smith announced the nine questions back in February, months before she added the 10th — the referendum to hold a referendum. She’d crafted them based on some of the most popular ideas from her Alberta Next panel in 2025, which was created to suggest future referendum topics that weren’t stay-or-leave.
Opposition to the nine immigration and constitutional questions has become a central part of some pro-Canadian referendum campaigns. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)
In provincially commissioned polls and an online survey last year, the Smith government found wide support for wresting more control over immigration from Ottawa, denying non-permanent residents access to provincial programs, and trying to amend the Constitution to tilt the scales toward the province — and higher opposition to an Alberta-only pension plan, police force or tax collection agency.
“We think we've done that initial culling of the questions to make sure that we found the ones that are likely to get majority support,” Smith told reporters in April.
Translation: the premier crafted these questions because she believed they’d arm her with fresh ammunition against Ottawa, and that voters would rally around her tough-on-immigration stance.
But aside from her own government’s TV ads, billboards and booklets, there have been scant few voices trying to push the nine into the winner’s column. That said, the $4 million spent amounts to more than double the combined $1.8 million raised as of last week by the various pro- and anti-independence groups, according to Elections Alberta disclosures.
Few prominent conservative Albertans, on either side of that stark independence divide, echo Smith’s call to endorse action on immigration and constitutional measures.
The lesser-known group Alberta Women for Independence is one of the few organizations whose blue pro-separation signs also encourage yes votes for the nine questions.
But after its leader Kathy Flett treated a pro-independence town hall in Medicine Hat to a detailed slide presentation on the merits of all nine referendum proposals last week, the more prominent separatist leader Keith Wilson brushed off their importance.
“These other nine questions are — I’m sorry, they’re a political gimmick. They mean nothing,” Wilson said, before later noting he’d vote yes to them, anyhow.
One of the few pro-independence signs that also urges yes votes on the other referendum questions. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)
Some separatists are frustrated because they don’t like the abstract nature of the independence ballot question, or that Smith diluted the referendum with questions that she didn’t have to put directly to voters.
Jeffrey Rath of Alberta Prosperity Project is urging people to “decline the 9” entirely — even as APP itself is trying to educate voters about what those other questions are.
“The nine questions are a deflection from the independence question,” Rath wrote last week on social media. “They are Smith’s built in excuse not to pursue independence!”
Many conservatives have focused exclusively on Question 10, including Alberta’s federal Conservative MPs and former cabinet minister Monte Solberg’s group Vote to Stay.
Former premier Jason Kenney, one of the unity side’s most active conservative voices, has questioned whether the nine questions needed to be referendums, and said some of them even confused him, a former federal immigration minister.
Contrast all that to the array of people pushing against the nine questions, particularly the ones seeking to restrict the social services that non-permanent residents receive.
In a rare show of bipartisan unity, former Progressive Conservative premiers Ed Stelmach and Alison Redford joined NDP counterpart Rachel Notley in a newspaper op-ed Wednesday urging “no” votes on the immigration ballots, warning they’ll harm Alberta’s economy and ability to attract workers.
The Calgary Chamber of Commerce has also been highlighting immigrants’ contributions to society, while its CEO Deborah Yedlin has warned Smith’s suggested $1,900-per-migrant health care fee would be a burdensome “extra cost” for employers.
Christian leaders have taken the unusual step of weighing in, albeit without directly telling parishioners how to vote.
A joint letter from Alberta’s Catholic bishops called on people to “respect human dignity and avoid making any segment of our population the object of resentment or blame," while a letter from Anglican bishops reminded supporters of Scripture’s “call to welcome and care for strangers and sojourners in their midst.”
Labour unions have also argued for “no” votes down the line, including CUPE Alberta’s “no to scapegoating” video that emphasizes how little services for temporary residents cost the provincial treasury.
“It just reinforces that these questions were not wanted by anyone except Danielle Smith,” said Stephen Carter of Alberta’s Voice, the third-party advertising group behind the “No to the Nine” signs.
“She wrote them. She promoted them. And everyone else opposes them.”
Stephen Carter's group Alberta's Voice is behind one of the most visible opposition campaigns against the immigration and constitutional ballot questions. (Sam Martin/CBC)
As much as Smith believed they were winners, the nine questions haven’t been slam dunks in the polls.
Last month’s Janet Brown Opinion Research poll for CBC News said 52 per cent of respondents oppose limiting access to health and education to temporary immigrants, while 45 per cent agree. There was moderately more support for Alberta taking more control over its immigration (54 per cent agree, 42 per cent disagree) and for constitutional changes (49 per cent agree, 45 percent disagree).
A Research Co. survey in late August, meanwhile, found that support for the five immigration questions ranged between 58 and 66 percent, while views on the constitutional questions were more tepid — between 39 and 46 per cent support.
But undermining those numbers is what appears to be widespread confusion and uncertainty about what those wordy questions are asking of Albertans. Brown’s poll suggested that close to half of Albertans didn’t know how they’d vote or weren’t familiar with the referendum ballot’s lesser-known nine.
As if to prove this confusion and lack of familiarity, the United Conservative Party issued its first message last week to its mailing list trying to explain and promote all nine questions. It was 1,708 words long. (It also didn’t tell the party’s backers how to vote on Question 10, perhaps unsurprisingly because of how split UCP ranks are on separation.)
The governing party doesn’t appear to have engaged in any door knocking or get-out-the-vote campaigns on the referendum. The opposition NDP, meanwhile, have been trying to activate pro-unity voters, with flyers that say “Vote to remain. No to the rest.”
The general lack of non-taxpayer-funded, on-the-ground campaigning may have already cost Smith. The Janet Brown poll showed that among Albertans who do know how they’ll vote on the nine, half will follow the “no the nine” mantra, while some will vote no to some and yes to others.
Only about one in 10 planned to fulfil Smith’s request and mark nine yeses.
Given that nearly half of committed voters would choose the UCP, that means a sizable contingent of Smith’s own political backers are not readily following her wishes into the ballot box.

Agentic AI startup RevRag.AI has raised $2.5 Mn (about ₹24 Cr) in a seed funding round led by Accion Ventures to expedite product development and expand to the US market. Cedar Hill Capital, Wyser and Venture Catalysts have also backed the startup. “From the perspective of financial services, the US has a vast number of companies from insurance to credit cards to loans. There is huge penetration there and a large market. And we see that there’s not much competition yet in the category we’re building in,” cofounder and CEO Ashutosh Singh told Inc42 in an interaction. While expanding to the US market appears to be on the top of the list, the startup is also looking to invest further in fine-tuning its own multimodal small language models (SLMs) to bring its tech layers in-house. Important to highlight that all of its platform is built on third-party proprietary models. Singh, with schoolmates Neeraj Gupta and Pankaj Gupta, had founded Revrag in 2023 initially modelled as a savings-oriented fintech platform. The idea of pivoting to a SaaS platform came when the trio realised that, while fintech users have slick interfaces and fast transactions at their disposal, onboarding customers continues to be bogged down by repetitive data entry, multiple verifications and cumbersome documentation. Pivoting early in 2025, RevRag.AI now aims to bridge this gap by streamlining onboarding and sales for banks and fintechs. For this, it offers autonomous AI agents that are capable enough to act as virtual relationship managers embedded within the financial institutions app. Beyond onboarding, the AI agents also automate customer product sales, support functions as well as provide real-time, multilingual assistance. This helps minimise conversion drop-offs, particularly when it comes to users from underserved backgrounds who have limited trust in digital systems and need assistance navigating financial terminology or English interfaces. As per Singh, RevRag’s offerings can save up to 70% of costs when compared to traditional channels while simultaneously helping in revenue generation. Thus, the startup will remain sharply focused on this problem statement rather than expanding into additional use cases. Earlier in 2025, the startup had told Inc42 that it was mulling to launch a no-code flow builder and expand its presence in Indian and American BFSI markets. The startup has shared aspirations to touch an annual recurring revenue of $50 Mn by FY28. It has lined up innovations like AI-led cross-selling, real-time risk scoring, and automated claims handling. As of now, it serves over 45 customers across India including the likes of PhonePe, Razorpay, Bajaj Finance, Motilal Oswal, and IIFL. It earlier raised $1 Mn from Powerhouse Ventures and various angel investors including WhatsApp head Kunal Shah. The fresh round comes at a time when the use of AI in automating fintech business functions is picking up. The global AI in fintech market is pegged to be valued at $45.53 Bn in 2026 and is projected to cross $241 Bn by 2034, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 23.20%.
