30 Great Tech Books to Gift (or Keep for Yourself)
Featured in this article
It is tough to overestimate Big Tech’s influence on the modern world. But how did we get here? The best tech books unravel the rise and, occasionally, fall of some of the dominant companies and characters that created the gadgets and software we spend so much of our lives using.
You’ll find intensely detailed biographies, in-depth company histories, and plenty of drama and enlightenment in these tech tomes, and they also make great gifts for the techy folks in your life. You may also be interested in our Gifts for Book Lovers, Best Cookbooks, and Best Kindles guides.
Updated October 2026: I added five books, including Apple in China, More Everything Forever, Gouged, The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, and The Nerd Reich.
- Chip Chase The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World's Most Coveted Microchip by Stephen Witt Charting Nvidia’s rise to become one of the most valuable companies on earth, this biography of cofounder and CEO Jensen Huang is educational and entertaining. Witt explains how the company spun GPU (graphics processing unit) manufacturing for gaming into parallel processing and a marriage of hardware and software that has powered the rise of AI. It has also made Huang very rich, but he isn’t always painted in a flattering light, which helps to counterbalance the founder worship vibe. For a slightly different view on Nvidia's history, try The Nvidia Way: Jensen Huang and the Making of a Tech Giant, by Tae Kim.
- The Early Days of the Computer The Soul of a New Machine by Tracy Kidder A well-deserved winner of the Pulitzer Prize, this book should be required reading for anyone who works in technology or harbors a curiosity about how it came to dominate our lives. First published in 1981, the book reveals the inner workings of Data General in the 1970s as the company strives to design and release a successful next-generation minicomputer. Kidder captures the struggle between management and creatives and weaves a fascinating tale from an ostensibly dry subject. He explains the intense time pressure on engineers that led to a constant state of crunch, the need for recruits to feel like they are working on something important they have some stake in, and the psychology of leadership intent on realizing ambitious projects. It is positively prescient about the dangers of burnout for the unsung heroes who sacrifice so much to build new machines. Follow this up with WIRED’s article chatting with some of the subjects in the book 20 years after it was published (this article itself is now more than 20 years old).
- Evil Twin Doppelganger: A Trip Into the Mirror World by Naomi Klein This fascinating dive down the rabbit hole of Covid conspiracy is ostensibly about how people confuse Naomi Klein with Naomi Wolf. Klein is a leftist journalist and climate activist; Wolf was a third-wave feminist but is now a rabid anti-vaxxer. If you’re still puzzled over the convergence of wellness and the far-right or wondering why so many ordinary folks are swallowing the kind of misinformation that breeds racism and climate denialism, Klein has some convincing answers. This is challenging and sometimes bleak reading, but it was also the most important book of 2023. It's brutally honest, calling out the absurdities of capitalism and the role social media has played in the rise of narcissism.
- An Icon by Walter Isaacson Released just 19 days after the death of Apple cofounder Steve Jobs, this astonishing biography takes a deep dive into his life and goes some way toward explaining his enduring legacy. Isaacson was picked by Jobs himself, who granted more than 40 interviews to his biographer and reportedly exerted no control over the final edit. Jobs’ intense passion and ambition saw him successfully marry creative ideas with technological innovations and sell them to the general public. This is an accessible book that never gets too technical. It insightfully charts the rise of Apple and Pixar and the development of the Mac, iTunes, the iPhone, and the iPad. While it is flattering at times, Jobs’ ruthlessness is not sugar-coated, and anyone with more than a passing interest in the man must read this book. For a less Jobs-centric exploration of the Mac’s development, read Revolution in The Valley: The Insanely Great Story of How the Mac Was Made, by Andy Hertzfeld.
- Cancel Culture So You've Been Publicly Shamed by Jon Ronson The dark side of the internet’s hive mind is brought into sharp relief by Ronson’s cast of characters—all have been publicly shamed via the internet. From the fascinating tale of Jonah Lehrer’s plagiarism to the vilification of Justine Sacco after an ill-advised joke tweet decried as racist, Ronson digs into the stories behind the scandals and looks at the havoc relentless online shaming can wreak. The book is a fun and fascinating look at how shame, empowered by social media, is a forceful form of social control with real-life consequences. Jon Ronson is my favorite non-fiction writer, and I also highly recommend The Castle: Adventures in a World of Unraveling Men and The Psychopath Test: A Journey Through the Madness Industry.
- Made in China Apple in China: The Capture of the World's Greatest Company by Patrick McGee Who would have thought that maximizing profit at any cost might lead to problems? Apple’s pursuit of every cent led it to outsource virtually all of its gadget production to China, and now it’s grappling with the economic, political, and cultural fallout. McGee has spoken with many former Apple executives and engineers to uncover what happened, why, and what it means for Apple and the US.
- Google’s Machinings In the Plex: How Google Thinks, Works, and Shapes Our Lives by Steven Levy I could have easily included a few entries from WIRED's own Steven Levy on this list, from his hugely influential 1984 debut, Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution, to his most recent release, Facebook: The Inside Story, but I’ve chosen In the Plex. Despite the impact of Google, a company whose name has become a verb, most of us know little about its internal workings. This is the best book to read if you want to change that. Levy secured unprecedented access to serve up a fascinating dive into what makes Google tick, what drove successful expansion into new areas, and how the company and its products have changed the world. If you want more, How Google Works, by Eric Schmidt and Jonathan Rosenberg, offers some insight into management at the company.
- Resisting Big Tech The Internet Con: How to Seize the Means of Computation by Cory Doctorow I remember when the internet was good, before we got trapped in walled gardens and Big Tech put the thumbscrews on us to extract every last cent. Cory Doctorow’s wonderfully evocative “theory of enshittification” is widely accepted now and increasingly common everywhere you look. He reckons that interoperability might just be the antidote, and while his sharp critiques are more fully formed than his suggested solutions, at least he’s trying to offer some hope.
- The Rise and Fall of Theranos Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup by John Carreyrou Noble aims and raw ambition are lauded in the tech world, often attracting praise and investment, but what happens when a project goes wrong? Building on Wall Street Journal reporter Carreyrou’s shocking exposé of Theranos, this book follows charismatic founder Elizabeth Holmes as she tries and fails to build a blood testing machine to sweep away the need for hypodermic needles, with the promise of accurate tests done from a drop or two of blood via a pinprick on the finger. Although the company raised hundreds of millions of dollars, its technology was horribly inaccurate. Rather than admit defeat, it pressed on, which is why Holmes was put on trial for fraud and sentenced to 11 years in prison. The book highlights the dangers of the popular “fake it till you make it” approach. Theranos reached a paper valuation of $9 billion and employed more than 800 people before its spectacular fall.
- Broligarch Bashing More Everything Forever: AI Overlords, Space Empires, and Silicon Valley's Crusade to Control the Fate of Humanity by Adam Becker Silicon Valley ideology and the self-serving narratives of tech billionaires are exposed as delusional rationalizations for the crazed accumulation of wealth and power in this fascinating, reasoned, sometimes depressing, but always well-argued book. Becker does his homework thoroughly to debunk our immoral CEO overlords and the philosophies and movements they espouse.
- Generative AI You Look Like a Thing and I Love You: How Artificial Intelligence Works and Why It's Making the World a Weirder Place by Janelle Shane If you can't help but ponder about artificial intelligence these days, you'll get a kick out of this book. It delves into machine-learning algorithms and their limitations in an accessible, engaging, and often hilarious way. Shane is the research scientist behind the comical AI Weirdness blog, and she does a solid job of demystifying AI, explaining how machine learning really works, and highlighting its strengths and weaknesses. Although you’ll learn about things like generative adversarial networks, the book never gets dull, thanks to witty and moreish writing peppered with practical examples of AI attempts at creativity that are frequently laugh-out-loud funny.
- Power Shifts The New New Thing: A Silicon Valley Story by Michael Lewis Opening on a computerized superyacht, the talented Michael Lewis takes us on an adventure into the mind of billionaire Jim Clark, cofounder of Netscape and Silicon Graphics. The book charts the power shift in Silicon Valley startups from “money men” to “idea men” and engineers. Lewis also attempts to uncover what drives Clark’s endless pursuit of the next thing and his seemingly unquenchable desire for more. This modern captain of industry is restless, constantly dissatisfied, and not very likable. The voyage is an interesting frame, and there are echoes of Kidder’s book in its subject’s idiosyncrasies and the author’s earnest attempt to explore what truly motivates him.
- AI Race Supremacy: AI, ChatGPT, and the Race That Will Change the World by Parmy Olson The race to make AI mainstream is framed as a battle between CEOs, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Demis Hassabis of DeepMind, but Olson does a good job of showing how seeming idealists with good intentions can be swayed by billionaires and end up selling out. If you wonder about the forces fueling the AI arms race, how bloated valuations have led to political power, or the laundry list of ethical and legal concerns AI raises, you’ll find this book enlightening.
- Silicon Valley The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America by Margaret O'Mara If you have ever wondered how such a small suburban area came to dominate the tech world, Margaret O’Mara, a history professor at the University of Washington, has some answers. This concise and comprehensive book weaves together interviews, biographies, and countless other sources to explain how Silicon Valley has driven and dominated technological innovation. O’Mara exposes the foundations that self-mythologizing founders and businesses are built on, and the vital role the government played in their rise. Folks seeking an insider’s view might like Uncanny Valley: A Memoir, by Anna Wiener.

India 'cockroach' leaders detained after entering barricaded protest site
- Published
Leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were detained early on Tuesday after they entered a heavily-guarded protest site and chanted slogans demanding the country's election chief resign over a controversial revision of electoral rolls.
Party founder Abhijeet Dipke shared a video showing Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das being taken away by police from Jantar Mantar, a historic Delhi observatory popular for protests.
Footage showed the two - along with others - climbing over police barricades before chanting slogans while holding the Indian flag.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's opponents allege the voter list revision benefits his party, a charge it and the Election Commission reject.
There have been days of protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
Police have stepped up security across Delhi as demonstrators challenge restrictions on where protests can be held.
Early on Tuesday, Dipke, Das and Ranka all shared videos showing Das and Ranka entering Jantar Mantar.
"You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X.
Das also posted a message declaring that the site had been "reclaimed" and that they were being detained.
It was not immediately clear where police had taken the leaders.
Ranka later appeared on an Instagram live broadcast from a police bus alongside other detainees where they appeared cheerful and said they would not back down.
The detentions came a day after the federal home ministry announced that Jantar Mantar, long associated with public protests in Delhi, would no longer be a designated protest venue. Authorities instead identified three alternative locations where demonstrations can be held with permission.
Before the decision, the CJP had met Delhi Police officials to seek permission for a peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar and had warned that it would announce further demonstrations if it received no response.
"30 mins after we went to Delhi Police asking for a date when we can go to Jantar Mantar, Jantar Mantar was de-notified as a protest site," Ranka had earlier posted on X.
Most of the party's leadership has been in Delhi in recent days. Dipke, however, had travelled to his hometown in Maharashtra after the death of his grandmother. He was among several CJP leaders detained ahead of a planned demonstration on Saturday and was released the next day.
The CJP had called for a protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, but authorities imposed extensive security restrictions across the capital to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site.
Several metro stations were closed, train services were disrupted and thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed.
Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.
Separately, opposition parties held a march in Delhi on Monday from Connaught Place - a major shopping district in the heart of the capital - to the Supreme Court.
The Congress, India's main opposition party, also petitioned the Supreme Court on Monday, challenging the Election Commission's voter revision exercise, which has resulted in tens of millions of names being removed from electoral rolls.
Critics say the exercise risks excluding eligible voters and making it harder for them to prove their eligibility.
Anger over the revision exercise intensified after The Indian Express reported that Kumar had disregarded concerns raised by the two other election commissioners over changes to voter registration. The Election Commission has said its decisions were unanimous.
The current protests follow student-led demonstrations earlier this year over exam irregularities and demands for education reforms.
The CJP led weeks of action that culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group began as online satire after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May. He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people seeking change.
After the summer protests, the CJP evolved into a pressure group, tapping into wider anger over unemployment, exam irregularities and government accountability.

Ukraine's access to Starlink internet service was suddenly disrupted for unknown reasons, interfering with military operations, sources in the country's defense ministry and a top presidential advisor said Wednesday morning.
Serhii Beskrestnov, a top advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said in a social media post that Elon Musk's SpaceX had implemented speed limits for Starlink terminals overnight. Beskrestnov said the restriction throttles the operation of Starshield, the company's dedicated satellite network for military services, at speeds above 100 miles per hour, or roughly 161 kilometers per hour.
Sources in Ukraine's defense ministry confirmed the disruption and told Business Insider that SpaceX had restricted the Starshield operations without warning the military. They said some units have experienced a loss of connection when drones reach speeds as low as 45 mph.
The sources said that the disruption has complicated military operations, particularly drone missions. This includes mid-range strikes, front-line logistics, and air defense intercepts, some of Ukraine's most important drone missions.
Because Starlink does not work inside Russia, the disruption is limited to drone operations within Ukrainian territory and Russian-occupied territory.
Later in the day on Wednesday, the Ukrainian defense ministry reported that SpaceX continues to enforce a speed limit of 161 km/h, though restrictions were significantly tighter earlier in the day. Communication quality has since improved at speeds up to 160 km/h.
Ukraine has said it is in contact with the US, SpaceX, and NATO partners and is working to install backup communication channels.
Amid questions about the Starlink service disruptions, Musk responded to former Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov's concerns and gratitude for partial restoration on social media, saying that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he said.
"Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX," Musk said. "Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
Critical in combat
As the technology has in military and industrial sectors worldwide, SpaceX's Starlink has become critically important to Ukraine's military.
Kyiv has adopted it as a battlefield communications tool and also uses it in drone warfare. Drones equipped with Starlink dishes, which can be controlled remotely by pilots hundreds of miles away and adapted to new targets mid-mission, have become one of the country's most potent weapons in the battle against Russian forces.
Ukraine's dependence on Starlink has made it reliant on Musk and SpaceX, however.
As Business Insider recently reported, Starlink has provided Musk a vital source of influence and soft power that stretches the globe. In 2023, the world's richest man said he refused a request from Ukraine's military to activate Starlink to assist a Ukrainian assault on Crimea, and Reuters reported last year that SpaceX jeopardized a 2022 Ukrainian counteroffensive by cutting Starlink access to front-line troops.
Recently, Musk has proven to be more supportive. In February, SpaceX clamped down on Russian forces' use of Starlink terminals in Ukraine after Ukraine's then-defense minister made a personal appeal to the billionaire CEO, a move that allowed Ukrainian forces to wage a successful counteroffensive.
'It is clear this action is not coincidental'
Musk has not yet addressed reports of Starlink disruptions in Ukraine.
On Saturday, he reignited past criticisms of Zelenskyy with a post on X that the Ukrainian president had "gone too far" with his strikes on Russian refineries.
The Starlink disruption comes after a series of Russian ballistic missile attacks against Kyiv on Monday and Tuesday nights. Ukrainian officials said that in both cases, international partners did not provide an advance warning about their launch, breaking from standard practice.
Asked by reporters before the attack on Tuesday if the US would cut intelligence with Ukraine over its strikes on Russian energy sites, President Donald Trump said that Washington continued to share it.
Zelenskyy's advisor suggested that the Starlink disruption could be linked to tensions between the US and Ukraine.
"It is clear that this action is not coincidental and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram, according to a translation of his statement. The cause, however, remains unclear.

Manitoba
Family of Manitoba woman who died after dental procedure says association has 'conflict of interest' issues
There are only 2 provinces where an association advocates for and regulates dentists
Manitoba is one of the last remaining provinces whose dental associations also regulate the profession and investigate complaints against dentists — a structure the family of a young woman who died after a procedure says raises conflict of interest concerns.
Virginia Blatz, 23, was pronounced dead in hospital after she went to see Dr. Ronald Janz at the Boundary Trails Dental Centre in Morden to have her wisdom teeth removed on Nov. 27, 2024, according to a statement of claim filed by her father, Dulaney Blatz.
In the nearly two years since her daughter's death, Victoria Blatz said the Manitoba Dental Association — which is both the provincial regulator and industry advocacy group — has maintained a "code of silence" about its investigation, and that the family has been "kept in the dark."
The family's former lawyer got a letter from the dental association's legal counsel in September, saying information wasn't being shared with them because the organization's registrar is the official complainant under rules set out in the Dental Association Act.
The family filed a separate formal complaint against Janz this spring. They also filed a lawsuit against the dentist , claiming the care he provided to Virginia led to her death. The lawsuit was filed in Manitoba's Court of King's Bench late last month.
According to the dental association's registry, Janz is restricted in his ability to administer local anesthetic drugs. He is allowed to administer them if he's under supervision.
The family believes the association's two functions — advocating for the interests of dentists and protecting the public — are brushing up against each other.
Blatz's parents say they have been 'kept in the dark' about the Manitoba Dental Association's investigation into her death. (Submitted by Dulaney and Victoria Blatz)
"It's a conflict of interest. You've got too much sympathy for when something like this happens…. It has felt that they have advocated solely almost for the dentist and themselves," Victoria said.
"That whole body really needs to be dismantled, and it needs to be made into a body that reports to the government and to the public, just like they do in other provinces."
Manitoba and New Brunswick are the last remaining Canadian provinces where a single group handles these two roles, Dr. Jack Gerrow, executive director of the Canadian Dental Regulatory Authorities Federation, confirmed in an interview.
- Manitoba family still searching for answers nearly 2 years after daughter died following dental procedure
- Family of Manitoba woman who died after dental procedure files lawsuit
Dulaney said he believes there is a serious "conflict of interest" within this dual-role structure, likening the province's dental association to an "Old Boys club," adding the family's interactions with the group left them feeling frustrated.
"It needs to be shut down, and we need to put something better in place for Manitobans," he said.
"Change should have come a long time ago, before Virginia got into that dentist's chair."
University of Toronto bioethicist Kerry Bowman agrees. He says it's "absolutely an inherent conflict of interest" for associations to act as both a professional industry group and a regulatory body.
Bowman believes the two functions largely have "opposite goals" that could cause friction between each other.
"I think it's very naive to think that these things can be merged," he said.
University of Toronto bioethicist Kerry Bowman says there's an 'inherent conflict of interest' when professional associations also act as regulatory bodies. (Craig Chivers/CBC)
The dental association said in an email to CBC News that "having these two functions within one statutory body does not, in itself, mean an investigation is conflicted or that professional advocacy influences its outcome."
Manitoba's Dental Association Act gives the association regulatory authority in the province, and the group says it "has a duty to protect the public" when it receives complaints. Complaint investigations are "kept separate from the MDA's member services and advocacy activities," the statement said.
The association said dentists are involved in investigations because their clinical expertise is necessary to discern whether standards of practice were followed. However, it says conflicts — whether actual or perceived — are "identified and managed through disclosure, recusal and exclusion from decision-making."
Manitoba association an outlier within Canada
Dental associations across Canada have been shifting away from this dual role for decades.
Ontario has long had a separation between the Ontario Dental Association and the Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario. More recently, Alberta's dental association and regulatory college became two distinct groups in 2022, after the government introduced new rules requiring regulators and industry groups to separate.
Blatz's parents filed a lawsuit regarding her death in Manitoba's Court of King's Bench in late September. (Submitted by Dulaney and Victoria Blatz)
Last year, Manitoba's western neighbour, Saskatchewan, saw the College of Dental Surgeons of Saskatchewan start the process of splitting into two independent organizations.
The Manitoba government has slowly been shifting health professions in the province to regulation under the Regulated Health Professions Act, which was proclaimed in 2014.
The province started talks with the dental association last year to bring industry oversight under the act, a provincial spokesperson said in a statement to CBC News.
The legislation doesn't allow regulatory colleges to also serve as professional advocacy groups, the province said.
The act already governs a handful of health professions in the province, including doctors, nurses, registered psychiatric nurses, audiologists, speech language pathologists and paramedics. All health professions in Manitoba will eventually be regulated under the act.
Process of splitting to start next year: association
Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara told reporters on Oct. 7 that shifting regulation of the dental sector to the act is about "enhancing accountability" and "supporting transparency" among health professions, suggesting it will ultimately make care "better and safer" for Manitobans.
"You separate the regulatory body from the more advocacy arm of the organization. So previously, where lines might seem a little blurry, there's clarity that's created," the minister said, adding the move is "modernizing the way that these organizations function."
The dental association said it has informed the province it plans to start the formal transition to the act in 2027. The association expects the process to take between two to three years.
Manitoba Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara speaks to reporters during a media scrum on Oct. 7. Asagwara says shifting regulation of the dental sector is about 'enhancing accountability.' (Randall McKenzie/CBC)
Once it completes the shift, dental regulation and public protection would become the responsibility of a separate body called the College of Dentists of Manitoba. Meanwhile, the association would keep its name and remain a professional organization representing dentists in the province.
Bowman, the Toronto-based bioethicist, said he believes it's "wise" for governments to step in and encourage more division between these roles, particularly at a time when patient trust in medical professionals has been dwindling.
"Patient trust matters. The vast majority of patients …, when they become aware that these two things are merged — regulatory and professional — they're very concerned that this is not a proper assessment of their circumstances at all, and that it's not objective," he said.
Bowman said divorcing the regulatory and advocacy sides of the association will take time and effort to get it right, but he believes the move will buoy public confidence.
"I'm not going to say it's going to solve all problems, but it's going to increase trust," he said.
"They really have to be separated."
Lengthy investigation a 'denial of justice'
University of Manitoba ethicist Arthur Schafer said the investigation into Virginia Blatz's death is taking so long that it "almost passes the boundary of belief," calling the more than 22-month delay a "denial of justice."
Schafer said the family and the wider public are entitled to know what happened and who is responsible. Without these answers, Manitobans will lose confidence in the association, he said.
"Dentists depend upon public trust — all health-care professionals do. They can't practise their profession unless they're trusted by the public. If the dental association is so lacking in transparency when things go wrong …, then it will soon lose the trust of the public," he said.
"Families are entitled to know, and the public is entitled to know what went wrong, whether anyone was blameworthy, whose responsibility — if anyone's — it is for this tragedy."
University of Manitoba ethics expert Arthur Schafer says the public will lose trust in the dental association if they believe it's not being transparent. (Submitted by Arthur Schafer)
The dental association said in a statement that it "recognizes the profound loss Virginia Blatz's family has experienced" and "continues to carry out its responsibilities under the Dental Association Act."
The organization said it's "bound by legal, privacy, and procedural-fairness obligations that limit what it can say before the process reaches its public stage" in order to "protect the integrity of the investigation and the fairness of the process for all involved."
These obligations are "not a means of avoiding accountability," the association said.
If Virginia's case moves on to a formal inquiry, the hearing will generally be open to the public, unless there's any legally required restrictions, the statement said.
The dental association said it will share more information "as soon as it is legally permitted and procedurally appropriate."

The skincare scheme that led to consumer complaints, lawsuits and a federal investigation
It's a familiar experience for anyone who has walked through an American shopping mall: A friendly salesperson approaches with a free sample of skincare cream, offering the promise of younger-looking skin. As you pass, they launch into a stream of chatter — a compliment on your handbag or a question about what's in your shopping bag. It's the kind of encounter that shoppers often walk away from without a second thought.
But behind this familiar mall ritual, NPR uncovered something far more costly: customers hit with thousands of dollars in charges they never authorized and products they didn't want and can't return.
In Michigan, an elderly man with dementia was charged $42,000 for skincare products and devices. His family didn't realize the situation until his credit score dropped, his son told NPR.
In New Mexico, a spa employee sold a woman a $30,000 red-light therapy device. She alleged in a lawsuit that he also charged $78,000 for what he said was sales tax without her consent.
In Hawaii, a disabled woman was shown to the back room of a spa for a "free" facial. The salesperson took her walker, she wrote in a complaint to the state, and refused to let her leave for hours until she spent $2,600.
These stories share a common thread: The stores they visited have contracts to buy skincare products from Mazal Group, a California-based company managing dozens of brands sold in thousands of stores worldwide. And those brands are all owned by one family.
Over the past year, NPR spoke with more than 50 people impacted by this enterprise, including customers who say they were taken advantage of, their family members and former employees. This investigation draws from state and federal court lawsuits, hundreds of online reviews and nearly 500 consumer complaints that NPR obtained from agencies via Freedom of Information Act requests. NPR staff visited stores selling products from Mazal Group in Virginia, Maryland and California, as well as the company's Chatsworth, Calif., headquarters.
NPR's investigation finds that stores selling skincare products purchased from Mazal Group have routinely pressured shoppers, including older adults and people with disabilities, into buying expensive skincare products and services they did not want, could not afford or tried to refuse. The business model that a decade ago federal agents called a "credit card overcharge scheme" is active today in malls and shopping districts from Honolulu to Annapolis, Maryland.
Some store and kiosk operators have faced more serious legal consequences than consumer complaints. Federal agencies have investigated individual operators for employing young Israelis on tourist visas to sell these products, resulting in more than a dozen guilty pleas for visa fraud and money-laundering schemes. NPR reviewed social media posts and messages indicating that some stores connected to Mazal Group continue to employ salespeople on tourist visas today. The government hasn't brought similar charges for a decade, and Israel's admission to the U.S. Visa Waiver Program in 2023 has removed a key barrier to entry for unauthorized workers.
Though Mazal Group and the family behind it have publicly shifted responsibility for any wrongdoing onto individual store owners, NPR obtained documents that show their brands suggest stores sell products at abnormally high markups while adhering to a strict refund policy set by the group. And a lab test commissioned by NPR raises questions about whether some of the products they sell contain the ingredients their labels promise.
The playbook
Across the hundreds of complaints reviewed by NPR — filed with state attorneys general, the Federal Trade Commission, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Better Business Bureau and other watchdogs — customers describe their experiences in strikingly similar ways.
Their stories start with a young salesperson standing outside a store or mall kiosk offering free samples. Customers say that if they stop, the salesperson quickly escorts — and in some accounts, physically pulls — them into the store and begins a barrage of sales pitches.
In the complaints, customers describe being kept in stores for an hour or more, sometimes isolated in a back room, while salespeople refuse to take no for an answer. The products carry no price tags, they say, which frees the salesperson to negotiate "special sales" and throw in "free gifts" to sweeten the deal on an expensive cream, facial or red-light therapy device.
Shoppers reported to agencies that salespeople did not disclose the amount they charged at the register, which was often much higher than the agreed-upon price. One told authorities that the salesperson added a zero, increasing the sum tenfold from $1,300 to $13,000. In police reports, others allege a store employee told them their card declined when it had not and charged a second card as well.
In court cases, shoppers alleged the salesperson instructed them to sign on a tablet at checkout, not mentioning it was a final-sale policy that could be used against them in credit card disputes. Some said they were signed up for a "payment plan" that salespeople didn't disclose was really a high-interest loan. In some reports, customers said the salesperson instructed them to authorize charges flagged by their bank as potentially fraudulent.
At the bottom of the bag, many said, the salesperson buried a receipt that said, "All sales final. No refunds. No exchanges."
In official reports and NPR interviews, customers said they were left angry, stunned and ashamed at how much they were charged, from several hundred dollars to more than $100,000 in one case. Records show some customers recovered partial or full amounts through their credit card companies, while others remained on the hook for thousands. Police reports show numerous shoppers tried to escalate their complaint to authorities, but arrests were almost never made.
In written reports, customers compared the ordeal to being robbed, held hostage or physically assaulted. NPR spoke to five individuals who hid the experience from their families for months or years. One woman said she went into a period of deep depression: "I just felt like if this is the way people are, I don't want to live in a world like this."
"We usually don't see a business that is this brazen"
In New Mexico, Attorney General Raúl Torrez's office received dozens of complaints about a store called Santa Fe Spa Center by Voupre that, he said, "painted a picture that this was a business that was just brazenly taking advantage of people."
One woman said a salesperson kept her in the store for hours until she agreed to spend $600 on products from the skincare brand Voupre. The salesperson said her credit card was declined, so she provided another. Later that day, she was "mortified" to see two charges totaling $44,280 in her banking app.
"I thought, 'How did they do that?' I really didn't know what had happened," said the 67-year-old woman, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of reprisal from the spa owner.
When the store would not refund her, she successfully disputed a charge for $27,000 with one credit card company. But she was responsible for $17,280 for a shopping experience she called "traumatic."
Torrez filed a lawsuit against the store in 2024, alleging violations of New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act.
"The scale of the price increases, the aggressive tactics, the repeated practice of misquoting prices and then elevating prices while refusing to return a product — we usually don't see a business that is this brazen and this out in the open, in terms of what they're trying to do to take advantage of consumers," said Torrez.
The spa's owner is Sahar Hori, an Israeli national who, according to court records, is also a U.S. citizen. Hori closed the spa and settled his case with New Mexico in 2025, agreeing to pay $350,000 in restitution to customers.
One of those customers is Mary Lee, an artist from Duluth, Minnesota. She said Hori's employees pressured her into spending nearly $19,000 on products while she was visiting Santa Fe for a writer's retreat. She said she tried to get her money back before returning home, but the refund she said a salesman promised her never came through.
The debt weighed on her like "a lead vest, an anchor," she told NPR. Lee is 65 and retired from full-time work. This year, through New Mexico's settlement, she was made whole.
"I feel a ton has been lifted off my shoulders," she said. "I don't feel like Atlas carrying the world anymore."
A small group of customers brought a second case against Hori, which settled in February 2026 for an undisclosed amount. While his customers were complaining to the New Mexico Department of Justice, financial records obtained in that lawsuit show the store's bank account was used to pay a lease to Mercedes-Benz and rent for a downtown Miami high-rise apartment. On his Instagram, Hori posted pictures of beach vacations in Europe and the Caribbean.
"Mr. Hori acknowledges that some customers were unhappy," his lawyers told NPR, "but he disputes any characterizations that his business intentionally deceived anyone."
A pattern around the country
The aggressive tactics documented in Santa Fe are replicated in shopping centers nationwide.
In Ann Arbor, Mich., Michele Anliker said her elderly mother was "preyed upon" at a Briarwood Mall store called Beauty Essentials during a 2024 Christmas trip, ultimately leaving with $5,000 in Voupre skincare products she did not want. When Anliker confronted the employees, she said, they accused her mother of stealing.
Anliker complained to mall management, filed a police report and distributed flyers warning shoppers away from Beauty Essentials. She posted on Facebook and connected with more than 30 people with complaints about the store. It wasn't until she escalated the situation to the mall's owner, Simon Property Group, that she secured a refund.
Cheryle Grounds' 84-year-old father was unable to recover the almost $10,000 he spent at Beauty Essentials on New Year's Day 2025. He has poor hearing and eyesight, and he walks the mall for exercise. Grounds told NPR that her father believed he bought a facial package but was also charged for Voupre items he understood to be gifts with purchase.
Grounds and Anliker declined to identify their parents by name, citing privacy concerns for their elderly parents.
In Manhattan Beach, Calif., 82-year-old retired teacher Mary Ellen Eckhert — who uses a motorized wheelchair — stopped for a free sample outside the store Mia's by Voupre. She would return to the spa for regular facials over the next year, where store employees ultimately charged her $53,500 across four credit cards, including $24,045 on one visit.
"What kind of a spa charges anyone $54,000?" said her son, Marc Eckhert, who discovered the charges after his mother's bank account overdrew. While the family managed to dispute much of the debt, Mary Ellen Eckhert remains out more than $17,000.
"I'm feeling like I have to continue working in order to pay for all this," she said.
NPR reached out to the former owner of Beauty Essentials, Guy Gabay, and did not receive a response. The store closed in 2025. The Briarwood Mall and Simon Property Group did not respond to NPR's request for comment.
NPR visited Mia's by Voupre and reached representative Daniella Vanon by phone, who declined to comment. The Manhattan Village Mall, where the store is located, did not respond to NPR.
The family behind the operation
While Santa Fe Spa Center by Voupre, Beauty Essentials and Mia's by Voupre were independently owned and located thousands of miles apart, the stores all sold customers Voupre products, a brand sold exclusively by Mazal Group in Chatsworth, California.
The company is a family business, owned by Daphna Oded Weingarten, who operates the group alongside her husband, Eli Weingarten; her brother, Avihu Oded; and his ex-wife, Adi Sharvit Oded.
Mazal translates to "luck" or "good fortune" in Hebrew. The Weingartens and Odeds are originally from Israel, as are the majority of corporate employees and licensees (store owners), according to former staff members.
Five former corporate employees agreed to speak with NPR on the condition of anonymity, fearing retaliation from Mazal Group. A small cohort of non-Israelis staffs the design, engineering and marketing departments, they said, as well as the on-site warehouse that fulfills orders.
The Weingartens and Odeds founded their first brand together in 2005 — a line of hair straighteners called HerStyler, under the company HerStyler Inc. A host of sister brands soon followed, and various other companies to house those brands. In 2015, Daphna Weingarten established Mazal Group to centralize operations for the family's growing portfolio.
The family currently holds more than 50 active trademarks for skin and hair care brands. Among the most prominent are Voupre, Avinichi, Introstem, CbGäRDN, Venofye, Lionesse and Orogold Cosmetics, which sell a nearly identical line of products.
Loading...
"The reason why they have so many brands is because they had to keep remaking brands with different names to sell it a different way to the malls so that they could get a lease," one former employee told NPR.
Another said store owners who purchased from Mazal Group distanced themselves from a brand once it started to accumulate bad reviews and complaints.
"People would complain about a line, about a brand being destroyed and having a bad reputation," the former worker said. "So they would constantly come out with something fresh, something new."
A former corporate employee said it's difficult to measure Mazal Group's precise global footprint because stores open and close frequently, but estimated the company contracts with at least 2,000 stores worldwide.
While reporting this story, NPR attempted to reach the Weingartens, Odeds and Mazal Group via phone and email, as well as visiting the Chatsworth headquarters to request an interview. They did not acknowledge this outreach until NPR sent a letter describing its findings, and lawyers for the group provided a brief statement.
"Mazal Group does not own or operate any retail locations that sell cosmetic products or any other products for that matter. Nor does Mazal Group manufacture any products," said Brian Tilker of the firm Cox Fricke in Hawaii.
Mazal Group looms large in the skincare kiosk industry, but it's not the only player in the market. Premier Dead Sea, an Israel-based skincare company, was once widespread in U.S. malls but has scaled back its footprint in recent years. Its subsidiary, Avologi, manufactures many of the red-light therapy devices that customers reported being pressured to buy inside stores contracted with Mazal Group.
Premier Dead Sea and Avologi also did not respond to NPR's requests for comment.
Operation "Salty Winds"
Federal agencies have investigated crimes associated with the Israeli-owned skincare industry in the past, but a lack of sustained and coordinated oversight has allowed it to thrive from coast to coast.
In 2010, the U.S. Embassy in Tel Aviv, Israel, sent a cable to the Department of Homeland Security warning of fraudulent activity linked to the "Dead Sea industry," which had spread to 36 states.
The term refers to the many Israeli-owned stores and kiosks that were marketing the benefits of products made with salt or minerals from the Dead Sea. The Odeds and Weingartens faced competition from companies like Premier Dead Sea, which was also gaining a foothold in the States with its own family of brands.
In the cable, published by WikiLeaks, the embassy said recruiters in Israel were targeting young people finishing mandatory military service and promising large sums to be made working at American malls. The workers were coached to lie to U.S. consular and border officials to obtain a tourist visa and travel to the U.S. without work authorization, the cable reads. In the States, they were paid under the table and store owners failed to withhold or pay required payroll taxes on their wages, it continues.
The embassy also released a series of public service announcements on YouTube in 2011, featuring the cautionary tales of young Israelis who had been caught by U.S. authorities for illegally working on tourist visas and were either deported or later denied reentry to the United States.
Soon after, federal agencies coordinated to investigate two businesses selling products from brands owned by the Weingartens and Odeds for immigration and financial crimes. The combined efforts of the departments of Labor, State and Homeland Security, the FBI and the IRS culminated in raids, international extraditions and more than a dozen guilty pleas.
In a 2013 operation code-named "Salty Winds," a task force of federal agents surveilled stores and apartments leased to Israeli national Shai Cohen in the D.C.-Maryland-Virginia region. Cohen had kiosks selling Vine Vera and Orogold Cosmetics, brands owned by the Weingartens and Odeds, as well as locations selling Premier Dead Sea and its affiliates.
Cohen's enterprise employed an estimated 60 unauthorized workers and brought in nearly $4 million between 2011 and 2013, according to federal records.
Cohen, two managers and at least seven salespeople engaged in fraudulent marriages to stay in the country long term, according to a Department of Labor interview of Cohen's business partner that NPR obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request. One salesman paid an American woman working at another store in the mall $10,000 to marry him.
Special Agent Matt Grimm, then an investigator for the Department of Labor's Office of Inspector General, led the task force. Grimm recently retired from the Army's Criminal Investigation Division.
While agents were pursuing immigration fraud and tax evasion charges, they also documented a "credit card overcharge scheme" used to dupe shoppers at Cohen's stores.
"There's no price tag," said Grimm, who observed sales and made purchases himself. "Whatever the salesperson on the spot thinks that they can charge for a particular thing, they're going to get. The more they sell, the higher their commission is going to be."
In a Christmastime raid, Grimm's team arrested a dozen young Israelis working at Cohen's stores on tourist visas. The store owner was in Israel at the time, triggering a yearslong extradition process.
Cohen pleaded guilty in 2023 in Virginia to conspiracy to launder money and facilitate the illegal entry, harboring and transporting of noncitizens. He served 11 months of a two-year prison sentence. NPR tried to reach Cohen through his real estate business in Israel and did not receive a response.
One of Cohen's contemporaries was another Israeli national, named Omer Gur, owner of a larger group of stores along the East Coast, including Orogold Cosmetics locations.
"Instead of looking at one kiosk or one store in one location, we wanted to cut the head off the snake," FBI Special Agent Sara Shalowitz said of Gur.
Shalowitz led a team that covertly surveilled Gur's stores for three years before apprehending him in Raleigh, N.C., as he attempted to board a one-way international flight.
Gur pleaded guilty in 2016 to a visa fraud and money-laundering conspiracy that included over 140 unauthorized workers and earned more than $14 million, according to the Justice Department. He was sentenced to 6.5 years in prison and served 30 months. A dozen of his associates pleaded guilty on related charges, Shalowitz said.
"I think we set a real deterrence for why this matters," Shalowitz told NPR. "It's not just some administrative thing to come to the U.S. under false pretenses, defraud numerous agencies … for the profit of your business and your business partners, at the expense of violating U.S. law."
NPR reached Gur, who also works in real estate in Israel, by phone. He declined to comment.
The recruitment pipeline
Cohen's and Gur's prison sentences may not have been a lasting deterrent for store owners or prospective salespeople.
On Facebook groups and Instagram pages, recruiters advertise jobs working in mall kiosks, or "agalot" — Hebrew for "carts." They promise young people the opportunity to bring in a high income and live in American cities with others their age. One account posts memes about the highs and lows of working in the agalot: long hours, difficult customers and boatloads of money to be made.
A young Israeli man posted a video to YouTube in November 2025 describing his last three months working at a store that sells Introstem, a brand owned by the Weingartens and Odeds and distributed by Mazal Group. NPR confirmed the store location in a Texas mall through photographs on his social media accounts.
"There is a lot of money in the agalot," he said. "A seller who is good after a few months, you sharpen your skills, and you become an expert. You can make $10,000 a month like it's nothing."
He described having a company vehicle and furnished apartment, with rent deducted from his pay. Workers make a 30% commission on their sales, he said.
"It's hard work, not easy," he said. "But it's a good job considering the fact that you can print money just based on your silver tongue."
NPR reached the 20-year-old to request an interview. He said he wanted payment, which NPR does not do. NPR is not using his name because it would expose him to federal officials for immigration crimes that he admits to in the video.
"It's illegal," he said. "Why is it illegal? Because you are tourists. You are on a tourist visa, and you come to work."
"But immigration authorities aren't looking for us. Immigration is looking for the Mexicans who sell drugs, less for the Israelis who contribute to their economy."
NPR staff also engaged online with recruiters for stores selling the Weingartens and Odeds' products. One, hiring for a store selling their brand Lionesse in South Carolina, told NPR staff to obtain a visa before they could share more details about the job. They "don't help with visas," the recruiter said.
Between the lines is the suggestion to work on a tourist visa, legal experts told NPR. Companies legally employing foreign staff submit mandatory paperwork to the State Department for nonimmigrant work visas.
Travel to the U.S. has also become easier for Israelis since Israel's 2023 admission to the U.S. Visa Waiver Program. Most Israelis can now visit the U.S. for up to 90 days for business or tourism, visa-free, by completing a short online application 72 hours before travel.
"That removes a key step in the recruitment process," said Grimm, who previously served as a diplomatic security special agent with the Department of State. Since most Israelis no longer need to interview with a U.S. consular official before departure, he said, "it's as simple as getting on the airplane and going. But, you're still not authorized to work."
NPR reached out to the departments of Homeland Security, Labor and State, the IRS and the FBI to comment on whether they continue to investigate Israeli-owned skincare stores for federal crimes. They would not say whether oversight or enforcement is ongoing.
NPR contacted dozens of current and former salespeople at stores selling products from Mazal Group to hear their side of the story. None agreed to be interviewed, even on the condition of anonymity. Two asked to be paid, which NPR declined.
NPR also reached out to Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs to ask whether it is taking action to discourage unauthorized work in the U.S. or address recruitment pipelines.
"The State of Israel unequivocally opposes violations of U.S. law, including U.S. immigration law," said Ester Buzgan, deputy spokesperson for the ministry. "Israeli citizens seeking employment in the United States must hold a valid work visa and comply fully with the law."
"Predatory and systematically unfair"
Because the stores it sells products to are independently owned and operated, Mazal Group claims it isn't responsible for the customer experience. But the company recently settled a class action lawsuit that made public reams of evidence showing that Mazal Group is directly involved in store operations and sets top-down policies that impact shoppers.
Attorneys for a class of former customers filed suit in 2022 in the 1st Circuit Court of Hawaii, alleging Mazal Group, the Weingartens and Odeds, and store owners in the state violated consumer protection laws via a "predatory and systematically unfair and deceptive enterprise."
Mazal Group asked the judge, unsuccessfully, to dismiss the case on the grounds that the company is merely a distributor that "drop ships" products for a "third-party" and owns no brands of its own.
The Weingarten and Oded family directly owns brands and manages the operations of those brands through Mazal Group. And the company's website advertises services beyond distribution, including product development, marketing, leasing, customer relations and accounting.
NPR confirmed with former Mazal Group employees that the company helps store owners secure retail space in malls and assists with the design and layout of individual locations. The company's marketing team designs product packaging and manages brand websites and social media accounts, they said.
"The Mazal Group owners and officers are involved in every step of the process, from product design to distribution to store design and development to sales to post-sale concerns," concluded a research firm hired by the plaintiffs' attorneys.
Mazal Group's agreements with stores also reveal a direct link between company policy and customer complaints. The company requires branded stores — e.g., locations with Voupre or Lionesse in the store name — to exclusively sell products purchased from Mazal Group, adopt a refund policy determined by the group and direct all customer service inquiries to its headquarters, court records show. These agreements also establish guidelines for how salespeople should offer samples to passersby.
After four years of pretrial action, the Hawaii class action case was scheduled for a jury trial in July 2026 in Honolulu. In June, the parties announced they had reached a settlement.
Mazal Group, the Weingartens and Odeds, and two licensees in Hawaii agreed to pay $950,000 in restitution, according to a copy of the settlement agreement obtained by NPR. Mazal Group and the family are responsible for $650,000 of the total payout. After legal fees, funds will be distributed proportionately to 110 class members who filed a complaint with the state of Hawaii.
Mazal Group and the Weingartens and Odeds have denied wrongdoing, and the settlement releases them from future liability for the allegations in the case.
"Highly unusual" pricing and missing ingredients
To understand why salespeople can negotiate the price of a product on the fly, NPR looked into what these items actually cost to make and what's inside them.
NPR obtained internal order forms for Voupre and Avinichi — brands owned by the Weingartens and Odeds and distributed via Mazal Group. These documents show the brands set manufacturer-suggested retail prices at up to 130 times the wholesale price they charge to stores. Voupre's Cannabis Caviar Transforming Mask, for example, costs $23 wholesale, with a suggested retail price of $3,000.
"Pricing at that level typically raises red flags," said Joe Rowett, CEO of VELOX, an Idaho-based marketing agency for skincare and beauty brands.
Well-known luxury brands rarely stretch the suggested retail price to even 20 times the wholesale cost, and most skincare brands operate far below that, Rowett said, making Voupre's suggested markups "highly unusual."
Federal investigators and former employees suggested to NPR that this wide margin gives salespeople the flexibility to negotiate the best sales price to earn maximum commission.
NPR sent a single unopened box of a Voupre "best-seller" for chemical testing. The sample — one box of one product — is limited, but the results of the analysis raise questions about what the label promises and what the product contains.
Many shoppers described being lured into a store with a sample of Voupre Anti-Aging Rescue Solution, which Mazal sells to stores for $19.50 per unit with a suggested retail price of $1,300. NPR obtained an unopened box of the solution from Suzann Roberts, a 90-year-old woman in Ann Arbor who bought the product from Beauty Essentials in 2024 and was unable to return it.
NPR sent the sample to Founders Science Group in Taunton, Massachusetts. CEO Robert Munroe has worked as a pharmaceutical scientist for three decades.
By looking at the product's ingredients list, Munroe identified three ingredients for analysis that could support Voupre's anti-aging claims: vitamin A to accelerate skin-cell turnover, vitamin E to fight collagen breakdown and acetyl hexapeptide-8, a powerful peptide that some call "Botox in a bottle."
The lab could not detect any trace of vitamin A or E, which Munroe said was "surprising and definitely suspicious." Vitamin A can degrade in strength over time without proper preservatives, he said, but it's not possible for vitamin E to disappear entirely. If the manufacturer did not include the actives at production and Voupre listed them on the packaging, he said, "that would be misbranding."
Based on what the lab detected, which included a high concentration of the peptide, Munroe said the solution is comparable to The Ordinary's 10% Argireline Solution, which retails for under $10.
"As far as getting peptide on the skin, you don't need to spend $1,300 to do it," he said.
The formula for Voupre's Anti-Aging Rescue Solution is the basis for nearly identical wrinkle creams that the Weingartens and Odeds sell across other brands like Introstem, CbGäRDN, Venofye and Lavelier.
A new company, the same family
New stores selling the Weingartens and Odeds' brands crop up regularly across the U.S. and globally, especially in port cities and tourist destinations.
Complaints haven't slowed them down, one former Mazal Group employee told NPR.
"It wasn't like it was stopping the business. They were still expanding, opening, expanding, opening, expanding, opening."
The Weingartens and Odeds have also closed companies and shuttered numerous brands over the years. Just last month, Mazal Group itself — the hub of operations for the family business — terminated its business license in California.
NPR reporters visited the Chatsworth headquarters weeks before that, in August 2026. The building, which once sported a Mazal Group logo more than 10 feet high and wide, bore a similar sign saying INV Brands.
Innovation Brands Inc. was founded by Daphna and Eli Weingarten in 2024.
"Streamlining the journey from concept to consumer," the company's website reads. "We leverage global expertise to build, manage, and scale exceptional personal care brands."

D2C supplement brand The Stack has raised ₹21.5 Cr ($2.2 Mn) in fresh capital to bolster its R&D and expand its product portfolio. The round was co-led by Sauce.vc, OTP Ventures and Huddle Ventures, and also saw participation from AYRA Ventures. The funding comes months after the startup raised its first institutional round of ₹5.5 Cr. It claims to have grown 5X since then and is now targeting 6-7X growth in FY27 compared with FY26. Founded by Shreya Jain and Kshitij Rihal in 2024, Bengaluru-based The Stack sells supplements to support sleep, recovery and gut health. The formulations of its five supplements that combine magnesium bisglycinate, glycine, prebiotics and probiotics. The startup claims that one in three customers places a second order within six months, while several opt for subscriptions spanning six to twelve months. Its top 10% of customers account for 30% of revenue, with referrals and word of mouth driving new customer acquisition. “We'd rather have five products people keep coming back to than fifty they try once. We're playing a long game, and our customers are rewarding that patience,” said Rihal, cofounder of The Stack. The startup aims to become one of India's most trusted supplements brands over the next three years, with a focus on transparent formulations, clinically studied ingredients and a quality-first approach to product development. The Stack competes with brands such as Wellbeing Nutrition, Supply6 and Trunativ in India's health and wellness supplements market. The funding comes amid growing demand for dietary supplements in India, driven by rising awareness of preventive healthcare, the increasing availability of global brands and the use of supplements to support the management of chronic conditions. India's dietary supplements market was valued at $5.8 Bn in 2025 and is projected to grow to $6.6 Bn in 2026 and $12.4 Bn by 2033, at a CAGR of 9.5% from 2026 to 2033, according to Grand View Research. On Wednesday, a Meerut court sentenced Muskan Rastogi and her lover, Sahil Shukla, to death for the murder of Saurabh Rajput. The body of Saurabh Rajput, who was Muskan's husband, was found dismembered and cemented inside a blue drum, hitting headlines. Saurabh Rajput was a merchant navy officer. He was killed on March 3, 2025, and his body was discovered about two weeks later. On October 14, district Judge Arvind Kumar Mishra pronounced the verdict in the Meerut blue drum murder case after 126 hearings during a 13-month trial. According to PTI, Muskan, who has two daughters, one seven years old and the other 10 months old, and Sahil were produced separately before the court via video conferencing from prison. Reportedly, Muskan and her lover Sahil appeared restless ahead of the sentencing. It is said that both didn't eat or sleep much, added the Senior Jail Superintendent Dr Viresh Raj Sharma. Before pronouncing the death sentence, the judge asked both whether they wished to say anything regarding the punishment. Judge Arvind Kumar Mishra referred to the Mahabharata and called punishment a form of dharma. He said that Muskan Rastogi and Sahil Shukla would be hanged till death. According to a report by Aaj Tak, Judge Mishra, during the session, referred to a verse from the Mahabharata. He said, “Dand bhi dharm hai (Even punishment is dharma)". He added, as per the publication, “Dand ko hi dharm bataya gaya hai, yani apradhi ko dand dena dharm hai (Punishment has been referred to as dharma, meaning punishing a criminal is itself a righteous act)". The usage of the reference seemingly explains the moral reasoning behind the rare punishment in the viral murder case. Saurabh's mother Renu, brother and other family members were present at the court during the sentencing. Muskan and Sahil were convicted on September 30 for the murder and attempt to conceal the body of Saurabh Rajput. The convicts dismembered Rastoi's body and placed the remains inside a blue drum, which they filled with cement to conceal their crime. The case came to light after the remains were discovered at the couple's house in Meerut. During the trial, the prosecution examined 22 witnesses, including people connected with the purchase of the drum, a knife and other materials which were allegedly used to commit the crime. According to PTI, hotel managers and cab drivers were also questioned in connection with the accused in the case. Outstanding sound quality. Premium build materials. Highly customizable EQ. Most comfortable Nothing headphones. Great ANC and transparency.
TIRED
Love-it or hate-it case. ANC is great, but not the best.
Nothing headphones have always stood out from the competition, and the Headphone (1) Pro is no different. It’s the brand’s most premium option yet, putting it up against the best from Sony, Bose, and Apple. After nearly a month of testing, I’d say these headphones belong among those top-tier choices, while bringing a few unique ideas to the table.
Exquisite Materials
Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz
Nothing Headphone (1) Pro Specs
Wireless connectivity
Bluetooth 6.1 with Multipoint, Auracast
Wired connectivity
USB-C (supports lossless up to 24 bit/192 kHz), 3.5-mm aux (supports lossless up to 24 bit/96 kHz)
Battery life
Up to 30 hours (ANC on), up to 68 hours (ANC off)
Weight
327 grams
Codec
LDAC, LC3, SBC, AAC
Water/dust resistance
IP52
Design is the first standout in the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro. On the outside, it follows the same formula as the Nothing Headphone (1) and Headphone (a), with a distinct square shape and two-tone, transparent outer shell.
The Headphone (1) Pro pushes this design to 11, largely by using premium materials instead of plastic. The square cans are made from a solid aluminum block. The arms are made of titanium. The transparent outer window is made of glass. There’s very little (if any) plastic to be found, yet they actually weigh 2 grams less than the Nothing Headphone (1).
The case is … interesting. It’s basically a hard-shell version of the purse-like case for the Apple AirPods Max 2—a near universally loathed case, I might add. The Headphone (1) Pro case offers better ear cup protection, but the headband remains exposed. It’s something you use once, then promptly forget.
All that being said, these are Nothing’s most comfortable headphones yet. The softer, thicker padding, wider headband, and reduced clamping force make these noticeably more comfortable than the Headphone (1).
Mixing It Up
Noise canceling and transparency are also great, thanks to extra microphones and impressive sound isolation. It’s not quite as bulletproof as Sony and Bose, but it was more than enough for any New York City situation I threw at it.
Inside, things get even more interesting. The headphone uses a triple-driver design—a bass dynamic driver, a precision dynamic driver, and a treble xMEMS driver. The idea is that each driver handles a different frequency range, delivering clearer, fuller, less distorted sound. When every other major ANC headphone brand uses a single dynamic driver for the full frequency range, this triple-driver design is a big risk. Fortunately, sound quality is outstanding.
I’m not going to pretend I’m an audio engineer (I’m not). But songs I’ve listened to for years came back to life with the Headphone (1) Pro, with added emphasis, clarity, and energy in the midrange and treble I didn't expect.
I don’t usually make the stank-face to “Staring at the Sun,” by TV on the Radio, but I did pretty consistently with these headphones. Stevie Wonder’s “Another Star,” with its dense mix of vocals, hi-hat, trumpet, and guitar, sounded more spacious on the Nothing headphones than on the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen). Bass is clear, but not as punchy as headphones like the Sony XM6. I didn’t mind, but it was a little less fun with artists like Bad Bunny and Kendrick Lamar, or anything in the EDM genre. A simple EQ adjustment changed this (more on that later).
This focus on engaging mids and highs meant that music on the Nothing headphones commanded my attention more often. I actually had a harder time achieving deep focus at work with these headphones than with more bass-forward mixes on the Sony XM6 and Bose QC Ultra 2nd Gen.
That was a lot of sound talk, and everyone has different ears, different hearing, and different taste. Luckily, you don’t have to settle for one sound profile with these headphones.
The Nothing Headphone (1) Pro has some of the most customizable EQ settings I’ve ever seen in consumer ANC headphones.
First, there’s a physical “FLAT” switch tucked away on the left ear cup. When you turn it on, it changes to a neutral EQ designed for “reviewing music, producing, or mixing,” according to the brand. As someone who does none of those things, I still had a lot of fun using this mode. I even started to prefer Flat with certain songs and certain genres. One quirk: It increases the volume—I consistently had to lower the volume by two steps.
Second, the Nothing X app offers ample EQ settings. There are two EQ modes: simple, with a familiar three-band EQ (bass, mid, and treble), and advanced, where things get a little crazy. In advanced, you can dial in a +6 dB to -6 dB change for individual frequency bands on both the main driver and precision driver. This level of control is rare in consumer over-ear ANC headphones and will frankly overwhelm some people. That’s why I think more people will enjoy the Explore tab, where Nothing has curated five EQ presets to try out.
Add spatial audio modes on top of that, and you’ve got plenty of options to find your ideal EQ. Though I suspect many people will be happy with the sound out of the box.
Playing in the Big Leagues
The $400 price tag puts these headphones squarely in competition with the established, well-regarded $450 Sony WH-1000XM6, $450 Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen), and $550 (but always on sale for $450) Apple AirPods Pro Max 2. Those are three of the best ANC headphones you can buy.
I think the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro fit in that mix nicely. No, they don’t win in ANC or transparency performance (though both are solid). But it stands out with a unique design, tactile on-ear controls, an excellent sound profile, and in-depth EQ customization. It’s a toss-up whether I’ll use these or the Sony XM6 as my daily driver, and that’s high praise for Nothing's first take on premium over-ear headphones.

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
- Published
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.
The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.
