- Rockstar Games says that its next game won't take another eight years.
- The team, tools, and engine Rockstar created for GTA 6 will help them make their next game quickly.
- LA Noire 2 is rumored to be the next major game from Rockstar Games after GTA 6
Rockstar Games has confirmed that its next game won’t take 8 years to release, unlike GTA 6. In an interview with Jason Schreier of Bloomberg, the company’s top executives revealed that GTA 6 has laid a solid foundation for Rockstar to develop and release new content at a faster pace than ever before.
GTA 6 Will Lay the Foundation for Faster Future Releases, Rockstar Says
Even before GTA 6 hit the shelves, everyone had already begun wondering what Rockstar’s next game would be and, more importantly, how long it would take to develop. Several rumors suggest that LA Noire 2 could be Rockstar’s next major game after GTA 6. Even Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick hinted at a potential LA Noire sequel in an interview earlier this year.
The debate and theories surrounding Rockstar’s next game will continue until the company officially announces it. Although Rockstar hasn’t revealed what its next game will be, Phil Hooker and Aaron Garbut, Head of Development at Rockstar North, have revealed in an interview with Jason Schreier that the company’s next release won’t take another eight years.
In addition to the exceptional team Rockstar assembled for GTA 6, the engine and tools developed during this project will help the team create new compelling content faster than before. “The engine, the tools, and the team we’ve built during this project will allow us to do things more quickly. I feel confident that we can build on top of this and go more sideways than upwards to build more compelling content,” Hooker said.
This can be compared to the development cycles of GTA games: Grand Theft Auto III and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. Rockstar didn’t even take a year to develop Vice City, as GTA 3 essentially served as its foundation.
Rockstar’s Aaron Garbut said that the team “foundationally changed a lot of stuff in the GTA 6 project.” Now that the project is done, the developer won’t rip it apart. Instead, it will serve as a foundation for accelerating the development of its next game. The good news is that players won’t have to wait nearly a decade for Rockstar’s next release, as they did for GTA 6.

Hitachi is exploring developing small modular reactors in Japan as high energy costs have started shifting public opinion toward nuclear power, according to the company’s energy business head.
Hitachi Energy is developing SMR technology with partners, Chief Executive Officer Andreas Schierenbeck said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi. Building a new reactor from scratch could take five to 10 years, he said, while playing down concerns that new projects could face opposition rooted in memories of the Fukushima nuclear disaster more than a decade ago.
“The public opinion is changing slightly,” Schierenbeck said in an interview. “High energy prices are changing these positions.”
Japan relies heavily on imported natural gas and coal for electricity and has faced elevated fuel costs from disruptions linked to the Strait of Hormuz and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Nuclear power, when operating, is among the country’s lowest-cost sources of electricity.
Small modular reactors, having capacity of 300 megawatts or less, are increasingly seen as a way to decarbonize energy, especially in hard-to-abate industries. Only three such reactors are currently operating across the world — in the U.S., China and Russia — and about 70 projects are at different stages of progress, according to the World Nuclear Association.
The Japanese government has been pushing to restart reactors idled after the Fukushima disaster and build new units to replace aging plants, seeking to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels. But strict regulation and local opposition have slowed the revival, with only 15 of the country’s 33 operable reactors currently online.

India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.
Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.
A spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.
Police authorities didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.
The CJP said that among those detained was a group of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being taken away in a bus to an unknown location.
The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.
The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.
The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.
The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.
The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.
Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.
“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture student who attended the Bengaluru protest.
There were also protests over police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.
On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of using “brute force” to briefly detain party leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Vadra, and other lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.
Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.
BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.
Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.

In a bankruptcy proceeding that kicked off yesterday, Disney has offered to buy some of the technology that powers the controversy-plagued chatbot Character.AI.

The move may be surprising. In September 2025, Disney joined others in publicly criticizing Character.AI for stealing content and harming kids. “Character.AI’s infringing chatbots are known, in some cases, to be sexually exploitive and otherwise harmful and dangerous to children, offending Disney’s consumers and extraordinarily damaging Disney’s reputation and goodwill,” Disney wrote at the time.
That scandal ended with Character Technologies wiping all Disney-owned characters from its platform, but since then, Disney has hired former Character.AI chief Karandeep Anand as its first chief technology officer, Deadline reported.
Disney did not respond to Ars’ request for comment on whether the company plans to use Character.AI technology in products for kids.
It’s possible that Disney will be outbid and not acquire any Character.AI intellectual property. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Wednesday that she probably spends “three or four more hours” than her male predecessors tackling household duties on top of her already packed daily schedule.
“In the morning, I bathe, fix breakfast and then wash dishes, not to mention apply makeup,” Takaichi, elected last year as Japan’s first female prime minister, told parliament.
“I feel like I’m spending three or four more hours than male prime ministers doing these things.”
A self-described workaholic, Takaichi has previously said she slept just two to four hours a night and sometimes scheduled 3 a.m. staff meetings.
Gender roles are rigid in Japan and women are chronically under-represented in politics, with just 68 female lawmakers elected out of 465 seats up for grabs at the last Lower House election in February.
Discussions about Takaichi’s time management came up when a ruling coalition member asked her about the marathon hours prime ministers customarily spend attending parliamentary sessions.
It is common for Japanese leaders to devote five to seven hours a day being grilled by opposition lawmakers or otherwise just sitting in parliament.
Citing a study, lawmaker Fumitake Fujita of the Japan Innovation Party, also known as Nippon Ishin no Kai, said that, in 2022, Japan’s prime minister attended parliamentary sessions for 72 days, versus 50 days in the United Kingdom and 13 in Germany.
While acknowledging the importance of legislative discussions, Fujita said: “The fact that our leader is confined for such long hours to parliament isn’t in line with the global standards.”
Takaichi said in a post on X in July that she was “getting consumed until dawn with poring over documents brought home from work and those related to parliamentary questioning.”
“I do enjoy reading these piles of documents at midnight that I took home,” she said on Wednesday.
“But it is difficult for me to squeeze out time to buckle down and think with a clear head” about “the future direction of this country or my grand vision for it,” she said.

I travel by train every chance I get.
Over the past five years, I've spent roughly 154 hours crisscrossing the US on Amtrak trains, and each time, I've had a different experience.
I've lounged on a couch in a private bedroom with a full bathroom, transformed two seats into a bunk in a 20-square-foot cabin called a roomette, and received complimentary meals in the dining car on overnight trains.
I've also saved money in coach and upgraded to business and first class on shorter rides.
In total, I've sampled five different booking types on 10 trains from the Northeast to the Southwest. One premium seat offers the best value for the upgrade.
I spent $50 on a four-hour ride in coach, the most basic seating car.
In May 2025, I took the Amtrak Cascades train from Vancouver, British Columbia, to Seattle. For the four-hour ride, I rode in coach, where seating was first-come, first-served.
Coach has the smallest seat of all the classes, but it's still pretty big and comfy, especially compared to a basic economy flight.
Like on a plane, the seats reclined, and the seat backs had tray tables and storage pouches. Each row also had power outlets and overhead reading lights.
I've taken three business-class Amtrak rides.
In 2022, I spent $120 on a two-and-a-half-hour ride in business class on Amtrak's Acela train from Baltimore to New York City.
Unlike regular Amtrak trains with several coach train cars, the Acela fleet has only business and first-class seating.
The Acela is also faster than Amtrak regional trains. My trip from Baltimore to NYC was 20 minutes shorter than it would have been on a regular Amtrak train.
A few months later, I booked a 10-hour ride on an Amtrak Maple Leaf train from NYC to Niagara Falls, New York. I paid $168 for a business-class seat, which was $100 more than a coach booking on the same train.
Three years later, I paid $180 for a business-class seat from NYC to Washington, DC, on the new NextGen Acela train that launched in August 2025.
All of them included a roomy seat and a complimentary drink.
A representative of the train line told Business Insider that business-class perks on all Amtrak trains also include fully refundable rides if they're canceled before departure and a 25% point bonus on Amtrak Guest Rewards.
The business-class seats were wider than the ones in coach, but they weren't significantly more comfortable on the first two rides, in my opinion. The seat on the NextGen Acela was wider and much cozier than the others. None of the tickets included a meal or in-seat service like the higher-tier cars.
Overall, the bookings didn't have as many perks as I expected in a premium cabin.
While I wouldn't upgrade to business class on most Amtrak trains, I would still book a seat on the Amtrak Acela train again. I think it's worth paying a little extra to save time and arrive at my destination sooner than I would on a regional train.
I've booked two first-class seats on Amtrak trains.
The Acela is Amtrak's only train with first-class cars. I first experienced it in 2022 on a two-and-a-half-hour trip from NYC to Baltimore that cost $270.
I rode in first class again on Amtrak's NextGen Acela train in 2025. My ticket cost $450 when the fleet was just weeks into service. More recent pricing shows $275 for the same booking three weeks in advance.
Both included a meal, access to station lounges, and an even larger chair.
As a New Yorker, part of the allure of a first-class ticket for me was having access to Penn Station's Metropolitan Lounge, a quiet waiting area for select Amtrak customers with comfortable seats and free snacks.
First-class passengers and those traveling in roomette and bedroom accommodations get in for free on the day of their trip, while other passengers can pay $50 to access the club.
Anyone traveling from Philadelphia, Boston's South Station, and Washington, DC, also has access to a lounge. But 10 other stops on the Amtrak Acela don't offer this perk.
On both trains, the first-class seats were larger than those in business class, but I didn't find them significantly more comfortable.
First-class tickets also come with a complimentary meal and in-seat service. I found that the food was significantly better on the second ride.
Although first class had more perks than business class, comfort on the ride is the most important thing for me when traveling by train. And while the first-class seats were larger than the business-class seats, they weren't upgraded enough to justify the price, in my opinion.
However, I couldn't help thinking that splitting a private roomette with a friend might be even cheaper (more on that later).
I've taken two overnight rides in Amtrak's roomette accommodation — a private cabin that's around 20 square feet.
In my experience, Amtrak's greatest value is the roomette, which sleeps two and includes a private room with two beds and complimentary meals.
My first roomette experience was a 30-hour ride on an Amtrak Viewliner train from NYC to Miami in 2021. I paid $500 to stay in a roughly 20-square-foot private cabin with two beds, a table, two chairs, a sink, and a toilet.
Then in 2025, I booked another roomette on an Amtrak Superliner. The 15-hour train ride from Denver to Salt Lake City cost $400.
This roomette was similar to the first, except it didn't include a toilet or sink and had been freshly updated with new seat cushions and lining.
Amtrak is also working on interior updates for sleeper cars on the Viewliner fleet, which will be available in 2026, Amtrak spokesman Marc Magliari told Business Insider.
Each had two chairs facing each other that folded out into a bed, and another bed pulled down from the ceiling.
Both rooms also had a small closet and a mirror. All roomette passengers have access to a bathroom and shower in the sleeper car.
The roomettes made great use of a small space, with clever storage features that reminded me of a tiny home.
I was pleasantly surprised that I could control the temperature inside each roomette with a dial and air conditioning vents. On both rides, the bed and sheets were comfortable enough for one night, though the updated cushions on the Superliner ride were cozier.
For a long-haul train ride, I think the roomette's price tag is worth it for the private space, temperature control, and a lie-flat bed.
I've also slept in two Amtrak bedrooms.
In 2021, I paid $1,000 for a bedroom on a 30-hour ride from Miami to NYC on an Amtrak Viewliner. Then in 2026, I booked a $2,200 bedroom on a 53-hour ride from Chicago to Emeryville, California, on an Amtrak Superliner.
Each was about twice the size of a roomette and included a full bathroom.
Amtrak bedrooms are around 45 to 50 square feet, with a pullout couch, a seat, an upper bunk, a sink and vanity, and a toilet and shower behind a closed door. Like the roomette, it sleeps two and includes complimentary meals.
Compared to the roomette on the same route, the Amtrak bedroom was double the price for twice the space. I thought it was nice to have a big sofa where I could stretch out and put my feet up, whereas the roomette only had two single seats.
Having room to lounge in the bedroom and a private bathroom made me feel more relaxed throughout my journeys.
But with such a hefty price tag for the same number of occupants as a roomette, I don't think it offers better value than the small private cabin.
While I'd splurge on a bedroom for long-haul trips if my budget allowed, I think the roomette is the best deal Amtrak offers.
After staying in five Amtrak accommodations, I think the bedroom was the most comfortable, with plenty of space to stretch and move about. I would definitely book it again for trips longer than just one night. Still, I view the roomette as undoubtedly the best value I've ever experienced from Amtrak.
For $500, a roomette is essentially a tiny hotel room where you can sleep in NYC and wake up in Miami — and bring a buddy to split the cost.

Kenya must be 'clean' to be credible, says Wada chief
- Published
Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility as it prepares to stage the 2029 World Athletics Championships, according to Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), .
Banka was speaking at the end of a three-day visit to Nairobi where he held talks with President William Ruto, government and sports officials, the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya (Adak), athletes and representatives of law enforcement.
Wada said the visit was intended to build on recent progress in Kenya's anti-doping programme at a critical time following Nairobi's selection to host the 2029 World Championships.
"Kenya calls itself probably 'home of champions', but every home has to have a good host and has to be clean to be credible," Banka told the BBC.
"We absolutely need to instill the culture of clean sport."
Kenya was awarded the 2029 championships in September, making it the first African country selected to host the event.
The decision has increased scrutiny of its efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem.
More than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit since 2017.
The Polish former sports minister said he had received a clear commitment from Ruto's government to a policy of zero tolerance towards doping, but warned promises would have to be matched by results.
"Wada will monitor this situation and observe the dynamic. Action speaks louder than words," he said.
Banka said his discussions with Ruto also focused on strengthening an independent Adak, and ensuring it has sufficient government support.
- How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships 
  - Published15 September
2029 will be the real test
Nairobi 2029 could provide a global test of Kenya's ability to protect its sporting legacy.
For a country whose distance runners have helped define global athletics for generations, the stakes extend beyond staging a successful championship.
"The problem with anti-doping is not with rules and standards," Banka said. "The problem is with implementation."
Another challenge is testing infrastructure.
Africa currently has no Wada-accredited doping control laboratory following the loss of accreditation of the facility in Bloemfontein, South Africa.
Wada initially suspended the laboratory in March 2024 because of multiple failures to comply with its International Standard for Laboratories.
Its accreditation was formally revoked in May 2025 after those problems were not satisfactorily resolved.
Banka said Kenya has shown political interest in establishing its own facility, but cautioned against expecting a laboratory to be accredited in time for the 2029 championships.
The process, he said, takes years because the consequences of laboratory error can be enormous for an athlete.
That leaves Kenya facing a more immediate priority: strengthening the system around testing rather than relying on a new laboratory as a solution.
'Doping has no colours and flags'
Banka also rejected the idea that doping should be viewed as an exclusively Kenyan, or African, problem.
"Doping has no colours and flags," he said, pointing to cases across established sporting nations including the United States, Germany and his native Poland.
"The problem would be to ignore this issue, not to tackle, or to pretend that there is no doping here."
Wada, he added, can investigate sport but cannot dismantle the criminal networks supplying prohibited substances.
"We are not a superpower. We are not law enforcement," he said.
"They have tools to really go after those who are destroying the credibility of the sport and the country."
He said intelligence indicated performance-enhancing drugs were being produced in Kenya and described Africa as a significant market.
According to him, athletes are often the "weakest points in the ecosystem", arguing that anti-doping authorities need to pursue not only competitors who break the rules but also the coaches, doctors, managers and suppliers who enable doping.
Some athletes, he suggested, are being exploited by people "who have money, who have power" and see them as a route to profit.

Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993
- Published
Rwanda has signed a 10-year deal with Formula 1 to host races in the African country, starting "in the early 2030s".
The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali and next to the city's new international airport. It will be the first F1 race in Africa since 1993.
A statement from F1 said the project came as a result of "years of collaboration to ensure the right foundations, with the best partner, are in place to deliver a successful, sustainable and world-class grand prix for generations to come".
The circuit, designed by the former F1 driver Alex Wurz, has been "designed to work in harmony with the natural landscape, using the area's elevation changes to create a unique and challenging racing experience while delivering exceptional viewing opportunities for fans," the statement added.
F1 hopes the race will provide an opportunity for the sport to expand its profile in Africa, a relatively unexplored market compared to Europe, Asia and the Americas.
It has not yet been established where the race may best fit into the schedule during the year.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
- Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A 
  - Published7 hours ago
The sport is likely to want to avoid holding the race in the main rain season of March to May. There is a shorter, less disruptive rain season from October to November.
F1 is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.
Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: "For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement.
"Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.
"The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."
F1 president Stefano Domenicali said the new contract was "a landmark moment for F1", which would mean the sport was racing "on every inhabited continent".
Domenicali added: "Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."
Sportswashing controversy
The race is likely to lead to opposition from human rights groups accusing Rwanda of sportswashing, as has been the case with its sponsorship of Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa.
Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
A spokesperson for F1 said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."
The track's build process will be overseen by three companies, with long-time F1 track architect Tilke and DAR working alongside WurzDesign as the creator of the circuit.
It is designed to be fast and flowing, with significant elevation change, using the natural contours of Rwanda's hilly landscape.
The first grand prix in Africa was the final round of the World Championship in Morocco in 1958.
South Africa hosted a race during the apartheid era - from 1960-66 in East London, now known as KuGompo City, before the race moved to Kyalami near Johannesburg from 1976-85.
Kyalami returned for two races in 1992 and 1993 as apartheid was coming to an end.
The country has held talks with F1 in recent years about a return at various venues, including Kyalami and Cape Town, but a deal has not proved possible.

There were days when Dr. Koyyala Ruth John Paul struggled to find food. Estranged from her family after coming out as a transgender woman, she spent years trying to make ends meet, searching for jobs while refusing to give up on her dream of becoming a doctor. When the path to postgraduate medical education was blocked by the absence of clear admission procedures for transgender candidates, she turned to the courts.
On Saturday (October 10, 2026) her perseverance culminated in a milestone. Dr. Ruth John Paul cleared all subjects in the recently announced MD/MS examination results, completing her postgraduate degree in Emergency Medicine at the ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar, Hyderabad, where she studied during the 2023-26 academic session. She has become the first transgender person in India to complete a postgraduate medical course. “I am feeling very happy. It is a matter of pride for me and my community. It is a great achievement in my life,” she said.
A childhood marked by loss
The youngest of three siblings, Dr. Ruth John Paul hails from Khammam district and grew up in a family with limited financial means. She lost her father when she was eight years old and was raised by her mother. She completed her schooling and intermediate education in her native district before clearing the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) and pursuing undergraduate medical education. She came out as a transgender woman during her undergraduate years. This led to her family rejecting her, leaving her separated from them for nearly six years.
The period that followed was marked by financial insecurity and the struggle to survive independently. “There were times when I did not even have food. I struggled to survive and looked for jobs,” she said.
In 2021, she found part-time work at Mitr Clinic (now Sabrang Clinic), which is India’s first transgender clinic. She worked there for around two years while continuing to prepare for postgraduate medical entrance examinations.
A legal battle to pursue her dream
Clearing the entrance examination was not the end of her struggle. Dr. Ruth John Paul said she encountered difficulties during postgraduate medical counselling because there were no clear protocols for accommodating transgender candidates.
With the assistance of transgender rights activist Vyjayanti Vasanta Mogli, she approached the Telangana High Court seeking relief. The legal proceedings continued for nearly two years. An interim order from the High Court eventually enabled her to proceed with admission. In 2023, she secured a seat in Emergency Medicine at ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar.
Her admission marked a turning point, but the challenges did not end there. She said she continued to encounter stigma and apprehension from people who were unfamiliar with transgender individuals.
From apprehension to acceptance
Working in a clinical environment brought its own challenges. As an emergency medicine trainee, she had to interact with patients during some of their most vulnerable moments, while also navigating the prejudices that transgender people can face. She recalled how some people were initially hesitant or uncomfortable around her. “Initially, some people were scared and did not know how to respond. But when I interacted with patients and treated them with care, they began to appreciate me. People who were initially apprehensive have now become comfortable with me,” she said.
A doctor with a larger purpose
Now that she has completed her postgraduate course, Dr. Ruth John Paul wants to use her medical training to help people in need, particularly transgender individuals who require emergency and critical care. “I want to serve everyone, especially transgender people who face critical medical emergencies. I want to provide care without discrimination based on gender identity or sexuality,” she said.

Brady Tkachuk recorded a natural hat trick during an 8:03 span of the second period, brother Matthew Tkachuk posted five assists and the visiting Florida Panthers won 7-3 over the Columbus Blue Jackets on Tuesday night.
Matthew assisted on all three of Brady’s goals, making him the first to assist on each of a brother’s natural hat trick, meaning three consecutive goals in a given game. Brady Tkachuk added one assist for four points; the point totals tied a career high for each Tkachuk.
Seth Jones had four assists, Carter Verhaeghe scored twice and Sam Reinhart posted two goals with a helper for Florida, which went 4-for-6 on the power play.
With Jacob Markstrom day-to-day due to tightness, Florida’s Akira Schmid made 24 saves.
Kent Johnson scored early, while Denton Mateychuk and Cole Sillinger each added a late goal for the Blue Jackets. Cam Talbot stopped 17 of 23 shots before being pulled in the third period for Columbus.
Johnson opened the scoring with 5:49 remaining in the first period. Off an own-zone Panthers turnover, Johnson possessed the puck, broke free and went low to beat Schmid.
Florida, though, tied it 2:27 into the second period, when Matthew Tkachuk slid the puck through the slot for Brady to record his first goal as a Panther. Less than four minutes later, and on the power play, a circle-stationed Matthew sent the puck into the slot for Brady to bury.
Tkachuk completed the natural hat trick with 9:30 left in the middle frame. Again on the power play, Brady benefited from a generous bounce off the end- board of Reinhart’s shot for a top-shelf conversion.
With 6:16 to go in the second, Columbus’ Mathieu Olivier was issued a five-minute major penalty and game misconduct for his slash between the legs of Florida’s Uvis Balinskis. And, in the waning moments of that extended power play with 2:10 remaining before the second intermission, the Tkachuk brothers set up Verhaeghe’s successful net-side one-timer.
Matthew Tkachuk’s fifth assist came 1:20 into the third, via Reinhart’s tip-in, power-play score. Verhaeghe’s wrister through traffic with 16:32 remaining in regulation made it 6-1 and ended Talbot’s night.
Columbus’ Jet Greaves stopped all four shots faced in relief.

October has rolled around, and that means only one thing: Spooky season is here! And what better way to celebrate Halloween than with some of the finest fright fests of the last 50 years?
We’re bringing you a more retro-tinged selection of the best films on streaming this month, but the mix of crowd-pleasers and cult classics offers something for horror fans of all tastes. For instance, David Cronenberg’s grotesque revamp of The Fly, buzzing onto Hulu, and Ken Russell’s Altered States materializing on The Criterion Channel, both bring uniquely visceral takes on body horror to your screens, while sleeper hit Under the Skin on Netflix offers slow-burn sci-fi scares, and Midsommar on Prime Video takes to the hills for a sun-drenched approach to folk horror.
If you fancy something a bit newer, fear not. Well, fear lots actually—Zach Cregger’s shockingly original horror debut Barbarian smashes its way onto Hulu, while Netflix brings the final chapter in the sumptuously scary Mononoke trilogy, an anime extravaganza that looks like nothing else. Plus, there’s even one post-credits stinger of an entry that’s too scary to mention here …
Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.
Barbarian
When Tess (Georgina Campbell) finds her Airbnb in a sketchy neighborhood double booked with Keith (Bill Skarsgård), you’ll probably think you know where Barbarian is headed. You don't—and you should brace yourself for everything that follows. Written and directed by Zach Cregger (in a seismic departure from his early comedy background), Barbarian constantly flips the script, regularly subverting viewer expectations of horror movie clichés at every turn.
Smartly written, brilliantly shot, and psychologically disturbing on multiple levels, Barbarian is a genuinely terrifying entry in the modern horror canon. If you’ve discovered Cregger’s work from the Academy Award–winning Weapons or his recent horror-comedy reboot of Resident Evil, this is where he first made his mark on the silver screen.
Under the Skin
Under the Skin almost defies explanation. Scarlett Johansson plays an alien in human form, roaming Glasgow and the Scottish Highlands, luring isolated and lonely men to their doom, drowning them in an inexplicable oily abyss that seems to exist in a null space. All the while, she’s observed by a motorcyclist, trailing her from victim to victim.
No names are given, no purpose explained (not even to the cast; director Jonathan Glazer shot many of the alien’s initial encounters with humans using hidden cameras, only explaining and asking for their involvement afterward), but it’s far better to watch this blind and make your own mind up. Be warned, though—Johansson’s performance is truly unearthly, and in conjunction with Glazer’s bizarre imagery and a soundscape that maddeningly claws at your nerves, this is a deeply unsettling slice of sci-fi.
Midsommar
This acclaimed indie horror movie stars Florence Pugh as Dani, an American student struggling to deal with a family tragedy, who joins her boyfriend Christian (Jack Reynor) and his friends on a trip to Sweden. The vacation sounds like the perfect escape—nine days of communing with nature at a festival held only once every 90 years; a true once-in-a-lifetime experience. The problem? The festival is a front for a pagan cult, and things get rapidly, wildly out of hand.
Midsommar is a deeply effective and distressing folk horror film, with none other than Jordan Peele, director of the smash hit Get Out, declaring it has "the most atrociously disturbing imagery I've ever seen on film." Perfect date night material for Halloween season, then.
Train to Busan
South Korean cinema seems to love combining the end of the world and trains. Bong Joon Ho’s Snowpiercer got things on track in 2013, but director Yeon Sang-ho really left the station with this 2016 zombie horror masterpiece.
Seok-woo (Gong Yoo) starts his journey on the express train from Seoul to Busan just wanting to drop daughter Su-an off with her mother. Unfortunately, the last passenger to board might be a teensy bit infected with the zombie plague that’s kicking off outside, turning the ride into the express train to hell. The tight confines allow for some incredibly inventive action choreography, while genre fans are treated to a revolting twist on the undead themselves, a misshapen, juddering, ravenous horde that moves like a liquid mass of corpses.
Like all the best zombie films, though, it’s the social commentary that really elevates Train to Busan, with its exploration of class and status standing alongside Romero’s work at his peak. A decade on from release, this is still one of the freshest takes on zombies you’re likely to find—look up animated prequel Seoul Station and stand-alone sequel Peninsula if it leaves you wanting another bite.
Altered States
A bit of a deep cut, but director Ken Russell’s 1980 outing will really mess with your head. No, really—this tale of psychological horror and transformational terror is loosely based on real-world tests of the effects of psychoactive drugs and sensory deprivation on the human brain. The film sees researcher Eddie Jessup (William Hurt) subjecting himself to highly questionable experiments with hallucinogenics and isolation in an effort to tap into other states of being. Unfortunately, he’s wildly successful, not only opening his mind to genetic memories and shared consciousnesses, but seeing his physical body horrifyingly warp and devolve beyond recognition with each trip.
And what a trip—Russell masterfully creates a sense of psychedelic overload with a pioneering use of bizarre imagery and sound, the film shifting with each of Jessup’s transformations until you feel you’ve taken mind-altering substances yourself. An uncomfortably weird experience, Altered States will stay on your mind long after the credits roll.
Colossal
Anne Hathaway is literally a monster—at least she is in this darkly comedic crossover between kaiju flick and character study. After her life in New York falls apart, Gloria (Hathaway) moves back home to New Hampshire. At the same time, a giant monster starts rampaging across Seoul, destroying buildings and causing mass panic. Yet these two incompatible events aren't unrelated, as Gloria starts to realize that she can somehow control the beast from half a world away—but her heavy drinking and constant bad decisions may get in the way of saving the world. Director Nacho Vigalondo lovingly pastiches the likes of Godzilla, Gamera, and King Kong in this quirky film festival favorite.
Mononoke The Movie III: The Curse of the Serpent
A nameless Medicine Seller (Hiroshi Kamiya in Japanese, Crispin Freeman in English) traveling Edo period Japan may seem a humble figure, but his strange tinctures and concoctions make him one of the few capable of tackling mononoke—powerful spirits corrupting places and people alike. This trilogy-capping third movie takes the enigmatic traveler back to the cursed Imperial Palace visited in predecessors Phantom in the Rain and Ashes of Rage, seeking to uncover once and for all why it seems to attract so many dangerous monsters.
A master class in tension and otherworldly horror, Mononoke maintains its stunning visual approach of kaleidoscopic watercolors swirling on parchment, making for one of the most sumptuous and visually striking pieces of animation you’ll ever see. It’s worth noting that there is some real-world controversy over a returning voice actor embroiled in a scandal in Japan, so this might be a rare case where the English dub is the better option.
The Fly
Despite being a remake, David Cronenberg’s quintessential slice of 1980s body horror has almost completely supplanted the 1958 original in the public consciousness (although the original stars Vincent Price and is definitely still worth checking out on Prime Video).
This wholesale reimagining twists expectations away from mad science clichés—it almost feels like a superhero origin movie to start, with scientist Seth Brundle (Jeff Goldblum) accidentally splicing his genes with a fly during a teleportation experiment, and emerging with enhanced physical prowess in every respect. But with great power comes great personality shifts, wiry black hairs growing along his back, and the need to vomit acid onto his food before eating. And, as animal instincts take over, the self-proclaimed “Brundlefly” starts looking at science reporter Ronnie Quaife (Geena Davis) very differently.
The groundbreaking effects work that marked Brundle’s slow metamorphosis into a repulsive hybrid monster won the film the Oscar for Best Makeup, but its ability to pack in some genuine emotion alongside the scares make it easy to see why this is the de facto iteration of The Fly.
The Social Network
Oh, you think this isn’t horror? Ask yourself: What could possibly be scarier than the deleterious impact social media has had on the human condition? Director David Fincher and writer Aaron Sorkin’s biopic telling of the rise, and rise, and rise of Facebook, is the kind of film you watch through your fingers, too.
There’s an almost predatory hunger in Jesse Eisenberg’s Mark Zuckerberg, as he goes from a Harvard student whose hotness-ranking website was popular enough to crash the college’s whole network to a Silicon Valley darling attracting unheard-of sums of investment and power. Like most “based on a true story” horror films, it’s not entirely historically accurate and, true to genre norms, there’s a not-as-good sequel, with Sorkin returning to write and direct the newly released The Social Reckoning, but if you’ve been paying attention to reality the past few decades, this will definitely chill you to the bone.

A forest fire on Indonesia’s Sumatra island fuelled by El Niño has razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said on Tuesday as the country battles devastating blazes and haze.
Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province on Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps, said the head of South Bangka regency, Riza Herdavid.
“They thought it was taken care of. But it’s peatland, and there was still a fire smouldering underneath. So, when they assumed it was over, the wind shifted and quickly drove the fire toward the settlement.”
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people had fled the village.
“My house is gone,” said Leni, a 55-year-old woman staying at a shelter with her family.
“There’s nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me ... I panicked and didn’t have the time to grab anything.”
Another survivor, Haryanti, 50, said strong winds had fuelled the flames, which had torn through homes that were made mostly of wood.
“I immediately ran to save myself. None of my belongings survived ... only the clothes on my back,” she said.
Riza said the village had been built on what used to be peatland in a protected area, but which was converted into a housing complex last year.
Indonesia regularly has wildfires during the dry season, but they have been more intense this year because of the El Niño weather phenomenon, which is forecast to be one of the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago.
Experts also point to slash-and-burn land clearances that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo islands.
This year’s fires have created severe haze locally, with tens of thousands of cases of respiratory illnesses, and caused air pollution spikes in Singapore and Malaysia.
Thick smoke in a province of Borneo has also grounded water-bombing aircraft, according to the disaster agency.
Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, ordered the government on Monday to mobilise maximum efforts to extinguish wildfires that have been raging for three months in some places.
The cabinet secretary, Teddy Indra Wijaya, said the government had deployed more than 60,000 personnel on the ground.

I’ll admit it up front: I don’t like procedures. I’m fine doing them to other people. Having one done to me is different. For 10 years I treated my colonoscopy the way some people treat a check-engine light. I knew it was there, I knew what it meant, and I kept driving.
Every birthday there was a reason to wait. I was too busy, I had no symptoms, I’d get to it next year. I’m 55 now, which means I spent a full decade telling patients to do what I wouldn’t.
Two groups finally wore me down. The first was my wife, who is persistent and usually right, a combination I find exhausting. The second was my colleagues, who brought it up in the lounge more often than you’d think. Once a doctor’s wife and his co-workers are on the same side, the argument is over.
Seeking counsel
Before any big decision, I call my senior partner. He’s been my mentor for years, and he has the sharpest wit of anyone I know. He’s also, as I learned that day, almost no help at all.
I told him I’d finally decided to schedule the colonoscopy. He paused, and then said: “It’s a good thing you called. Now I’ll know why you’re walking funny the next day.”
I hung up, wondering why I keep calling him. I also quietly saved the whole speech, word for word, so that I can pass the same useless advice to the younger doctors in our group. Some traditions deserve to continue.
Why we do this at all
Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer worldwide, accounting for approximately 10% of all cancer cases and the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths globally. . In India, it accounts for about 65,000 new cases a year and is rising, especially in cities, and with no national screening programme, too many cases are found late. Nearly 38,000 Indians die of it every year. It is also one of the few cancers we can actually prevent, not just catch early.
Most colon cancers start as polyps, small growths on the lining of the colon. Over roughly 10 years, some become malignant. That long, quiet stretch is the opportunity. If you find a polyp and remove it, the cancer never gets a chanc’e to start. A colonoscopy is one of the few screening tests that also serves as treatment.
A brief history
Colonoscopy is younger than you might guess. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, William Wolff and Hiromi Shinya in New York used new flexible fiberoptic scopes to examine the whole colon. Dr. Shinya also developed the wire-loop snare to remove polyps through the scope, so they no longer had to be removed through open abdominal surgery. That was a revolutionary change.
The landmark evidence came from the National Polyp Study. In 1993, Sidney Winawer and colleagues reported in the New England Journal of Medicine that removing adenomatous polyps sharply cut the rate of colorectal cancer compared with what would otherwise be expected. In 2012, a long-term follow-up in the same journal showed that removing polyps reduced colorectal cancer deaths by about half. Our whole screening approach rests on those two papers.
The recommended starting age in the United States has also come down. Rising rates in younger adults led guidelines to lower it from 50 to 45. That leaves people like me with no excuse.
The alternative
Think about what skipping it looks like. A polyp grows unnoticed for years, and colon cancer often gives no warning until it’s advanced. Then the symptoms come: bleeding, a change in bowel habits, weight loss, fatigue, anaemia. By that point the conversation is about surgery, chemotherapy, and staging scans.
For some patients it means a colostomy, where the bowel is brought out through the abdominal wall and stool goes into a bag, sometimes permanently. For too many, it means dying of a disease that a simple screening test could have prevented.
Put that way, a day of inconvenience looks like a bargain.
The prep and the procedure
Every patient will tell you the procedure is easy and the prep is the hard part. They’re right.
I’ll spare you the details. You either already know, or you’ll find out soon enough. The good news is that the prep has come a long way. The dreaded jug is no longer your only choice, and tablet preps have made the whole thing far more bearable. If your doctor offers them, take them.
The next morning was close to anticlimactic. I checked in at the outpatient centre, changed into a gown that and got an IV. A nurse went through the usual checklist, and we chatted about nothing.
Then came propofol.
If you’ve never had it, here’s what it’s like. A warm flush rises up your arm, a brief awareness that something is about to happen, and then nothing. No dreams and no sense of time passing. One moment you’re listening to the anaesthesiologist, and the next you’re in recovery with a cup of juice, asking whether they’ve started yet.
The verdict
My gastroenterologist is also a friend, and he was completely professional from start to finish. He was calm and thorough, and he put me at ease. He came by recovery to tell me he’d found one polyp and removed it. It will go to pathology, and I’ll come back for surveillance on whatever schedule the results call for.
That polyp had probably been growing for years while I made excuses. Now it’s gone. That’s the point of screening: find it before it becomes cancer.
The bottom line
It really isn’t that bad. The prep is unpleasant for a single night, and easier than it used to be. The procedure takes less time than your commute, and the sedation is the best nap you’ll take all year. It may keep you from getting cancer. That’s a pretty good trade.
If you’re 45 or older and you’ve been putting it off as I did, talk to your doctor about getting screened. Colonoscopy isn’t the only option. You can do stool tests at home, and your doctor can walk you through other options. The best test is the one you’ll actually do. Doing nothing is the only wrong answer.
(Dr. Dinesh Arab is Director, Interventional and Structural Cardiology, AdventHealth Daytona Beach and Clinical Assistant Professor of Medicine, Florida State University dinarab@yahoo.com)

Assam’s Juvenile Justice Board allows 17-year-old rape accused to be tried as an adult
Hailakandi police, in a statement on Tuesday, said the principal magistrate of JJB passed the order after considering the heinous nature of the alleged crime
The Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) in Assam’s Hailakandi district ordered that a 17-year-old accused in the alleged rape and murder of a 16-year-old girl be tried as an adult.
Hailakandi police, in a statement on Tuesday, said the principal magistrate of JJB passed the order after considering the heinous nature of the alleged crime, a psychological assessment report, a preliminary assessment report from Silchar Medical College and Hospital (SMCH), and an offence report submitted by the investigating officer.
“Considering the heinous nature of the crime, the psychological assessment report and the preliminary assessment report of the Silchar Medical College & Hospital and also the Offence Report submitted by the I/O of the case, the Principal Magistrate, Juvenile Justice Board, Hailakandi has passed an order the trial of the Child-in-Conflict with Law (CCL) will be conducted as an adult,” police said.
The order was passed following an assessment of his psychological condition, medical reports and the findings of the police investigation.
The JJB order comes more than two months after the girl was found dead in her home on the night of August 1 in the Aloichora area under Katlicherra police station. According to senior superintendent of police (SSP) Amitab Sinha, the boy was 17 years and five months old when it happened. He was detained by police in the first week of August, police said.
Also Read:Assam rape: Father says traumatised teen victim ‘couldn’t talk’
A case was registered at Katlicherra police station under multiple sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including section 65(1) (rape of a girl under the age of 16) and section 103(1) (murder), along with section 6 (aggravated penetrative sexual assault) of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012.
The incident triggered widespread protests across Assam’s Barak Valley, with residents blocking National Highway-6 and demanding capital punishment for those involved.
Police said that they initially detained five persons following the incident. During the early investigation, officers said one of the accused was a minor and that investigators sought permission to have him tried as an adult.
Sinha told HT in August that the police department approached the court for an adult trial.
A Special Investigation Team (SIT) was formed to investigate the matter. The SSP said that a detailed chargesheet against five accused, including one juvenile, was submitted before the court in September after examining forensic and medico-legal evidence, witness statements, digital records and materials seized from the crime scene.
Also Read:Assam rape accused tries to flee custody, drowns: Police
According to the lawyers, under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, a child aged between 16 and 18 accused of a heinous offence may undergo a preliminary assessment to determine whether an adult trial is necessary. The Children’s Court determines whether the case should proceed as an adult trial.
The latest decision was welcomed by the girl’s family and some legal practitioners, while others have raised concerns about its implications for juvenile justice and child rights.
“If we look at the brutality of the incident, as reported in newspapers and described in police statements, it was extreme. Such an act is difficult even to imagine being committed by a child. We welcome the court’s decision,” senior advocate Gautam Ghose said.
Ghose said that board has set an example by considering the seriousness of the allegations and the circumstances surrounding the incident rather than treating the accused’s age as the only relevant factor.
However, human rights activist and Gauhati high court lawyer Taniya Laskar said, “The accused can undergo trial under the Juvenile Justice Act, and the court can impose the most rigorous punishment available under that framework. But putting him on trial as an adult is, in my view, a violation of human rights, and the decision can be challenged before a higher court.”
Also Read:Assam: Rape and murder accused beaten to death by mob after fleeing custody
She referred to India’s obligations under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, which recognises special protections for persons below 18 years of age.
She acknowledged the seriousness of the allegations but said judicial decisions must be based on statutory safeguards, evidence and established legal principles rather than the public reaction to an incident.
“Sometimes cases involving rape or other serious crimes receive extensive media attention, and there is a danger that public sentiment may influence how the case is viewed. But when the evidence is examined by higher courts, the outcome can be different,” she said.
Referring to a case from Nagaon, Laskar said a death sentence awarded by a district court in 2018 was set aside by the Gauhati high court this year, resulting in the acquittal of the accused.
“The law must follow the existing rules and should not be influenced by the prevailing situation, media trials or any other external factor. An accused remains an accused unless proven guilty. Members of the public may form opinions based on what they see or hear, but the judiciary must stand above such pressures,” she added.
Supreme Court advocate Milan Laskar, however, said the Hailakandi order should not be viewed as an unprecedented departure from Indian law.
“This is not a standalone example. There have been several cases across the country in which accused persons below 18 were considered for trial as adults considering the nature of the offences,” he said.
Family members of the victim said they are thankful to the judiciary for taking the allegations seriously and hoped that none of those responsible would escape appropriate punishment merely because of their age.
“One of the accused in this case was a minor according to the police and we did not want anyone involved in this crime to escape punishment. We want equal accountability, and we thank the court for this decision,” a family member said.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

The Keralam Assembly on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) referred the Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection) Bill, 2026, which aims at ensuring the rights and protection of the elderly, to the Finance Subject Committee for further scrutiny.
The Bill, piloted by Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan, aims at promoting healthy and active ageing, registration and regulation of senior citizen care centres, capacity-building for family and care givers, and protection of rights, dignity, and social security of the elderly.
Opposition alleges Constitutional breach
However, the Opposition alleged that the provision that a copy of a Bill to be tabled in the Assembly should be made available to members at least three days before had not been fully complied with. N.K. Akbar, MLA, in a point of order, alleged Constitutional violation, failure to calculate the financial burden correctly, violation of Supreme Court directives on advanced medical directives with regard to the Bill’s provisions on execution of ‘living will.’
The LDF government had brought out a policy for the elderly, set up a commission for them, and prepared an elderly budget. “So, the Opposition is not against the Bill. But, serious legal issues exist,” he said.
The Chief Minister, who holds the portfolio of the Department of Senior Citizens, contended that special Acts could contain penal provisions. Moreover, the finance memorandum in the Bill clearly specified recurring and non-recurring expenditure. The government would not incur any particular expenditure in setting up senior citizen unit and forums as proposed in the Bill. The Supreme Court guidelines would be incorporated when Rules for the Act were framed, he said.
The Speaker ruled that the Bill was published in the Gazette on October 10 and its copies circulated among members the same day.
During the discussion on the Bill, the Chief Minister reiterated that “the measure of a civilised society was how it treated its senior citizens”. If the Bill were to be passed, the Keralam Assembly would become a model for the world, he addded.
Focus also on silver economy
Referring to demographic changes and migration of children and youth outside Keralam, he said the population of the elderly in the State was expected to be double the national average by 2036. However, the government was focussing not only on the welfare of the elderly, but also “silver economy” so as to transform the challenges posed by the rising elderly population into an opportunity.
The United Democratic Front (UDF) government had set up a dedicated department for the elderly. Government interventions were planned to ensure active and healthy ageing, tapping into the skills and knowledge of the elderly, conducting a survey of all elderly in the State and their health status, setting up a volunteer corps, registration and monitoring of care homes, and training and certification of care-givers, he said.
“No one should feel they are alone. They should be protected and their rights ensured,” the Chief Minister said.
He also explained the rights and principles that informed the drafting of the Bill.

Buying energy drinks in public is embarrassing. Every time I see someone scanning the cooler for their favorite flavor of Monster or Ghost, I guess which accompanying vape flavor they've picked out, and I know others are making the same assumption about me when I’m scoring a can of Celsius to beat back a hangover or get lifted before a 10-hour bartending shift.
The good news is that it’s easier than ever to purchase your favorite cans from Amazon, and the great news is that you don’t need to put on your Crocs and Cookie Monster jammies to do it. Throw in a nice little discount for buying in bulk and setting up auto-delivery, and you’re basically being paid to not leave your house. The future is here, and it is jacked up on B vitamins, red dye, and taurine.
As a devoted coffee drinker, I often feel like the misquoted New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael when I see neon-colored tallboys of high-octane energy drinks usurping shelf space from my favorite Dr. Pepper and Mountain Dew variants at my local Sheetz. Energy drinks are big business—they raked in close to $20 billion in the US in 2023—yet I don’t know a single person who drinks them on a regular basis.
A good cup of coffee is hard to find at odd hours in the middle of nowhere. Energy drinks, on the other hand, are as no-fuss as it gets. At any hour of the day you can pick out an eye-catching can that boldly advertises its caffeine content, plunk down a few bucks, and shoot into space in just a few swigs. Homebodies and deal junkies don’t even need to leave their domiciles to cop excellent deals with lightning-fast shipping on their most beloved brands, provided they’re Amazon Prime members. I love value, convenience, and caffeine, so I finally caved.
Still thirsty? Check out our other drink-related guides, including the Best Mushroom Coffee and Best Coffee Subscriptions.
Updated October 2026: We've added new drinks from Juno Energy and Kirkland Signature and a new flavor from Melting Forest, removed some discontinued products; and updated links, tasting notes, and prices throughout.
1. Celsius Functional Essential Energy Drink
Though it has less carbonation than most energy drinks, Celsius is punchy without a cloying aftertaste and it does wonders in masking the medicinal notes that are present in similarly potent drinks. This is an absolute unit when it comes to the caffeine-to-volume ratio, and not a single flavor I tried was objectively bad.
Celsius is a hot up-and-comer for a reason, and it’s not shocking to see entire fridges stocked with its whole portfolio right next to the checkout counter at a growing number of gas stations. The can has a whole lot of text I will never read, but it’s attractive and not too much in the extreme gaming or health-nut quackery camps to dissuade potential buyers who care about being seen in public with an energy drink. Like the Beatles or In-N-Out, this is a consensus pick everyone agrees on.
Notes: Nice mellow thrust of energy with very few jitters or butterflies in the stomach. This is a solid road trip or preworkout beverage. A slight dip in energy around 2 pm, but a few jumping jacks got me back on track.

2. C4
C4’s marketing materials position its sports fuel as the beverage of choice for the athleisure set. Does C4’s “clinically studied CarnoSyn beta-alanine” compound help you get swole? Do yoga pants increase flexibility? Who knows, and who cares! Halfway through the can I got happy feet and swapped my Aeron chair for the walking pad. Two miles and 35 minutes later I was still zooming, so I took my dog for a 2-mile run and felt like a million bucks at the end. I crushed a gas station salad for lunch and felt like a Healthy Person for one of the first times in my life.
Notes: With flavors like Frozen Bombsicle and Mango Foxtrot in C4’s arsenal, concerns of this “NSF-certified” drink tasting like saccharine gloop are valid, but the Midnight Cherry was a pleasant surprise. An intense cherry flavor—imagine a Dr. Brown’s dialed up to 11—hits on the frontend, and only a mild trace of diet flavor lingers in the aftertaste. Marketing be damned, you could add this to the rotation at a Taco Bell and no one would know (or care) about its alleged postgains powers.

Classic citrus flavor with minimal aftertaste and plenty of carbonation. That first sip brings back memories of all-night drives, marathon Excel sessions for the computer science class I took before I quit business school, and the countless “bomb” shots I consumed during this era. The gold standard for energy drinks. Minimal negative social baggage, maximal uplift.
Notes: The sugar high is sharp and abrasive, and the caffeine hits once the sugar wears off for stable energy well into the afternoon.

4. Naked
The realm of low- or no-calorie energy drinks offers two options for sweeteners: an unwieldy list of chemicals with confusing names, or allegedly “natural” options like stevia and monkfruit. The former camp commands the lion’s share of the market, but the latter is ascendant and willing to pay a premium for an energy drink with as few ingredients as possible. Naked’s entry in the field is our pick for the best of the woo-woo options that align more closely with yoga than gaming or deadlifting, and the few other options in this field aren’t even close as far as taste and firepower are concerned. Naked boasts just six ingredients, principal among them being fermented sugar and monkfruit. While we loved Jocko Go when it initially blazed the trail for monkfruit-based energy drinks, the mellow tang of Naked outclasses the sharp and astringent sweetness of the signature beverage of the wellness world’s favorite ex-Navy Seal/human-sized clenched fist.
Notes: Tastes like homemade lemonade boosted with just a hit of carbonation, with a barely noticeable “diet” finish that’s much easier to grow accustomed to than Jocko Go. It packs more than double the caffeine, making it a no-brainer when A/B-ing the two. The can is simple and devoid of aggro branding as well, which we’ll concede has no bearing on performance but is still a thing to consider if you’re worried about being seen slurping an energy drink in the office or at the gym.

5. Bloom Sparkling Energy
I never thought I would miss the flavor of old-school sugar-free energy drinks until I embarked upon this lifestyle. Monkfruit and Stevia certainly have their fans in the health and wellness space, but there’s something about the trashy delight of a fizzy, citrusy sucralose bomb of a sugar-free Red Bull that hits differently in this day and age. Gen Z’s endearing rebrand of Diet Coke as “fridge cigarettes” leads me to believe the kids love a little danger, and I’m not convinced a little hit of the S-word every now and then will kill me any faster than microplastics or the ambient thrum emitted by the data centers that are popping up all over my home state of Ohio.
Enter Bloom, which has all the aesthetics of a very-online wellness girlie product without any of the questionable flavors or adjuncts. Bloom’s 180 grams of green tea-derived caffeine does work during the early-afternoon doldrums, and the cute and crushable little can is one of the least offensive items one can be seen sipping on during an 8 am Zoom call or while commuting to the office. I still missed my morningly cup of coffee while I was trying this on for a week, but the tandem of caffeine and B vitamins tricked my brain into adopting a healthful effervescence that came in handy when a mountain of repetitive customer outreach tasks hit my inbox first thing on a Monday morning. This is a fun and friendly fizz-bomb that checks just about every box one may have when searching for a low-cal energy option that’s easy to find at just about any large chain store in the US.
Notes: The Juicy Orange flavor is dangerously close to the exaggerated citrusy sweetness of a Mountain Dew Kickstart—my personal favorite for hangovers and morning indulgence—all with none of the high fructose corn syrup and only one-sixth of the calories in a 12-ounce dose. The last few sips yielded a dry, almost prickly sensation against the back of my throat, but the flavor profile of Bloom is otherwise impeccable. Sucralose leads the charge on sweetness, with a modest dose of ginseng, lychee, green tea, and apple cider vinegar bringing up the rear. I did a double-take when I saw vinegar on the ingredients list, since the sip clocks in little to no bitterness to speak of.

7. Yerba Madre Yerba Mate
Due to its branding, lack of carbonation, and overall vibes, Yerba Madre (formerly Guayakí) is a caffeinated beverage that’s somehow exempt from being regarded as a capital-E Energy Drink by polite society. This is the caffeine vehicle of choice for liberal arts grads who spend their weekends wandering farmers markets with a hangover and a New Yorker tote filled with vegan junk food. 8. Juno Energy
In January 2024, White Claw released a nonalcoholic option, which completed the bubble beverage horseshoe started by the seemingly random ascendance of La Croix in the tail end of the Obama era. There’s now a hyper-niche sparkling drink for freaks with all manner of peculiar interests, which brings us to Juno Energy Cherry Sparkling—a drink that answers the question of why people who eat Luden’s cough drops like candy don’t have a sparkly beverage of their own.

16. Liquid Death
Liquid Death burst onto the scene in the late 2010s with a concept so simple you’d kick yourself for not thinking of it first. Canned water for heshers would’ve sounded insane on Shark Tank, yet there you are, baking in the sun at an all-day metal festival in a parking lot, surrounded by ponytailed dudes named Anders and Zug in battle vests, slurping down water from a can that vaguely resembles the poster of a John Carpenter film. It was only a matter of time until the strength of Liquid Death's branding caused its marketing team to boomerang back to non-water products, so the recent drop of Liquid Death Sparkling Energy makes perfect sense.
What does not make much sense at first glance is the brand's embrace of “unextreme caffeine,” which clocks only 100 mg of caffeine per can. One could imagine the logic behind this paltry dose of the good stuff is that similarly positioned rawk-adjacent brands like Monster and Rockstar have the market for sugary 200+ mg caffeine bombs cornered, so a more mellow approach to microdosing caffeine is a more appropriate lane for a brand that makes mildness seems like the new extreme. This line has four flavors in it—Scary Strawberry, Murder Mystery, Tropical Terror, and Orange Horror. This is America, however, and a business that’s as invested in selling culture as it is a consumable product is immune from the perversions of hyper-partisanship and the cheap thrills of owning the libs. Between Black Rifle's pledge to hire 10,000 veterans as a direct response to a similar pledge made by Starbucks to hire just as many refugees; the Blue Lives Matter-adjacent aesthetic of its merch; and its weekly podcast, which serves as a hyper-macho who’s who of conservative politicians, venture capitalists, and manosphere snake oil salesmen, it’s easy to guess which side of the aisle butters BRCC’s bread.

I would reach for this if I were suffering a stomach bug and avoiding things with pronounced flavors, or if Alex Garland’s 2024 film Civil War came to life and a roving gang of right-wing marauders rolled by and threatened to beat my liberal ass unless I proved my fealty to their king. Two hundred milligrams of caffeine is not nothin’, but it’s stretched a bit too far across the can's volume to really pack the wallop I’d need to outrun Landry and his crew of Pantera-loving degenerates without having to stop to pee along the way. Others Tested
Ardor Tropical Mango (12-Pack) for $38: This is the best of all the Ardor flavors we tried, and it still tastes like someone rinsed out a glass that contained a mango White Claw with plain seltzer. It’s 99 percent flavorless. On the bright side, this may be drinkable if you have food poisoning and need to get caffeine in you without throwing up. I copped a bigger buzz watching commercials for Mountain Dew Kickstart on YouTube. This one is a hard no all around.
Key Keytone Energy Drink Pineapple Passionfruit (12-Pack) for $45: Key is an “all natural” energy drink that’s very proud of its vegan and keto-friendly ingredients. It’s made with Avela, which is described as a “ketogenic ingredient intended for adult use” on its incredibly vague fitness-adjacent website. That’s all well and good if chasing ketosis is your hobby. If it’s not, you should run as far away from this beverage as possible. The initial hit of flavor is a muddled medley of faux-sweetness akin to woo-woo sugar replacements like Stevia or monkfruit, but what comes next is nowhere near as merciful. The astringent aftertaste hits somewhere between the final coat of goop your dental hygienist doles out and that last can of Mom Water that’s left in the cooler after a long day at the pool. The impact of so many foreign substances definitely had me feeling a certain kind of way within just a few minutes, but my attention swung wildly between work tasks, domestic minutiae, and creeping dread about our country's unraveling social fabric.
How I Tested
Across the span of a year, I sampled different energy drinks from an amalgamation of readily available gas station staples, brands the Amazon algorithm was pimping extra hard that day, everything in the Whole Foods end cap that advertised its caffeine content, and a couple oddballs from the past you probably don’t remember.
I graded on taste, which is obviously subjective, and the palpable effects of the caffeine after knocking back a can at 8:30 am every day, after my daily 1.5-mile run with my dog. The extra cans were deployed two hours into shifts at my part-time bartending gig. I took one day off from the experiment due to gut-wrenching stomach pain and horrible night sweats. If there’s a Ghost-addled gamer in your basement as you read this, please consider offering them a wellness check, or a refill on their tendies at the very least.
