The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship.
An audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised.
“Successful UK engagement with China must always be framed by an understanding that the PRC (People’s Republic of China) is an inherently hostile authoritarian state that does not share our values,” an underlined sentence in the audit, published on Wednesday, reads.
The inherent power imbalance in the relationship with the world’s second largest economy is “further compounded by muddled policy and weak engagement”, it says.
It cites the example of a visiting Chinese delegation who had noted that no one who engaged with Beijing at a senior level in government was a Mandarin speaker, or had significant experience of living in China.
Although British expertise exists, it is often siloed and “not translated into capability”, Ipac, which counts members from all the UK’s major parties, says.
In an endorsement, the former security minister Tom Tugendhat said the report was “a clear-eyed and realistic take on the defining foreign policy problem of this century, filling a gap left by years of policy neglect”.
While the report accepts that “disengagement was not an option”, it advocates for clearly defined red lines around issues such as critical infrastructure, frontier technologies and human rights.
The document offers several recommendations, including better institutional coordination, the strengthened use of national security tools, and diversification of supply chains.
It identifies emerging technologies such as AI as posing new challenges, in terms of disinformation and surveillance capabilities.
The climate crisis is identified as a low-risk area for cooperation and alignment.
“Climate targets as set will not be met without cooperation with China, and accepting medium-term dependence. This means accepting supply chains tainted by forced labour and unfair trade practices,” the audit says.
The Guardian has contacted the UK government and the Chinese embassy in London for comment.
It was “very welcome” that there was an understanding that better language skills were needed to deal with China, said Kerry Brown, a former diplomat and director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London.
However, he said, “the critical issue now is lived experience” in China.
“Some of the members of Ipac … are really keen on promoting this very security-oriented idea that going to China is in some ways opening you up to exposure,” he said.
“You can’t teach really important things in a classroom; you can only go and learn them through daily life … and that is the thing that is very difficult to do now, and it’s also the thing that doesn’t seem to be supported.”

In Pakistan, the prime minister has the title, the president has the office, but the military chief has the power. Now, field marshal Asim Munir, the country's most powerful man, is reportedly considering a way to redraw Pakistan's political map.
According to The Economist, Munir is considering a radical solution to Pakistan's governance problems: Breaking up the country's four provinces into 12 to 15 smaller provinces, or possibly reorganising administration into as many as 160 smaller units.
Smaller units, according to the argument for restructuring, would be easier to govern. But in a country where the military has long wielded influence over civilian governments, the political question is whether they would also be easier to control.
The proposal has also raised concerns that weakening provincial governments could shift more political influence from Islamabad's civilian leadership towards the military establishment in Rawalpindi.
Smaller provinces, bigger control? The power game behind Asim Munir’s Pakistan plan
However, the plan remains unconfirmed, and its details are unclear. But dividing Punjab and Sindh, strongholds of powerful political dynasties, could weaken established parties.
Restructuring Pakistan's political map could also change who controls the country's mineral wealth and other natural resources.
The Economist has raised the possibility that the proposal could become a 'divide and rule' exercise, weakening regional power centres and making them easier for the military-backed federal government to manage.
Pakistan's population and resources are unevenly distributed, and many regions remain poorly served by their governments.
Smaller administrative units could bring officials closer to citizens, improve public services and give neglected areas a stronger political voice.
The question is whether the changes would make government more accountable to ordinary Pakistanis or concentrate more power in the hands of Munir and the military establishment.
The divide-and-rule calculation
Pakistan's four provinces are Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and Balochistan. Each has its own elected assembly and provincial government, giving regional parties an institutional base from which to challenge decisions taken by the federal government.
Their populations vary sharply. According to the 2023 census, Punjab has around 128 million people, slightly more than half of Pakistan's population, while Balochistan has approximately 15 million, or about 6% of the national total.
Punjab's size makes administration difficult, and residents in remote rural areas can spend hours travelling to government offices to settle land disputes or access basic services.
Would breaking up provinces weaken political dynasties?
But dividing the provinces would have political consequences as well. Large provinces can sustain powerful leaders, substantial bureaucracies and networks of elected representatives with influence beyond individual districts. Breaking them into smaller units could fragment that influence.
The military establishment could then be dealing with a greater number of provincial leaders, each with a smaller political base and potentially fewer resources to challenge decisions made in Islamabad.
The outcome would not necessarily favour the centre in every case. New provinces could give regional leaders and communities that feel excluded from existing political networks a stronger voice. Much would depend on the powers, funding and autonomy granted to the new administrations.
Still, the proposal raises a difficult question: Is Pakistan considering smaller provinces because its existing ones are too large to govern effectively, or because some have become too politically powerful to manage easily?
Punjab and Sindh: The biggest political stakes
Punjab and Sindh are likely to be at the centre of any serious attempt to redraw Pakistan's provincial map. Both are major political strongholds, and dividing them could change the country's balance of power.
Punjab is the main base of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), associated with the Sharif family.
Nawaz Sharif has served as prime minister, his brother 
Shehbaz Sharif
 currently heads the federal government, and Nawaz's daughter Maryam Nawaz is Punjab's chief minister. The family and its party have dominated provincial politics for much of the past four decades.
One longstanding proposal is to create a separate South Punjab province. Supporters argue that the region has not received adequate political representation or public investment compared with more developed parts of Punjab. A separate province could focus more directly on local infrastructure, education, healthcare and employment.
But dividing Punjab could also break up the Sharif family-led PML-N's large electoral and organisational base, creating new political battlegrounds for regional parties and local leaders.
Sindh presents a different challenge. It is the principal stronghold of the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), whose political roots go back to Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. The party has remained under the influence of his family, including his daughter Benazir Bhutto's widower, Asif Ali Zardari, now Pakistan's president, and their son and party chairman Bilawal Bhutto Zardari.
Karachi, the country's commercial capital, is also in Sindh and central to its economic and political importance. For the PPP, dividing the province could weaken its established networks.
For many Sindhi groups, however, the issue goes beyond party politics: Sindh represents a distinct historical, cultural and linguistic identity.
Opposition to the proposal is already clear. On September 4, the Sindh assembly passed a resolution rejecting attempts to divide the province or create administrative units that would alter its boundaries. Chief minister Syed Murad Ali Shah said there would be no compromise on Sindh's geographical unity, Dawn reported.
Resistance continued in October. According to Dawn, a multiparty conference held on October 11, attended by representatives of the PPP, PML-N and other political groups, resolved to oppose attempts to create new provinces or administrative units in Sindh.
Any attempt to divide the province could therefore trigger a wider confrontation over political power, identity and provincial autonomy.
The mineral wealth behind the debate
Pakistan's natural resources add another dimension to the proposed restructuring.
Balochistan has deposits of copper, gold, chromite, coal and iron ore. Sindh has coal, limestone, silica sand and other industrial minerals, while KP has gemstones, marble, granite, gypsum and other deposits. Punjab is known for rock salt, iron ore, limestone and fire clay. PoK's Gilgit-Baltistan and other areas of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir also have deposits of precious and semi-precious stones and other minerals.
From Balochistan to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: Mapping Pakistan’s mineral wealth
These resources have long been at the centre of disputes over mining rights, royalties, investment and the distribution of economic benefits. Provincial governments and local communities have sought a greater say in decisions affecting their land and livelihoods.
The proposed restructuring has also raised concerns that weakening provincial governments could give the military-backed federal establishment greater freedom to pursue mineral extraction projects in resource-rich regions without facing the same level of resistance from local authorities.
These concerns have not been independently established as Munir's motives. Nor has a detailed plan been made public showing how a new provincial structure would change control over minerals or the distribution of revenues.
The concern, however, is clear. A provincial government can negotiate with Islamabad over mining projects, royalties and development spending. A smaller unit with limited revenue and greater dependence on federal funding could find it harder to resist pressure from the centre.
Balochistan illustrates the sensitivity of the issue, with long-running disputes over who benefits from the province's mineral wealth and how much local communities gain from projects in their region.
Mineral extraction and investment are not, by themselves, evidence of a political power grab. The key question is whether decisions would be made transparently, with meaningful local participation, or imposed by a powerful centre with limited accountability.
Why Khyber Pakhtunkhwa could be a test case
Developments in Imran Khan's party stronghold Khyber Pakhtunkhwa have added to concerns about the military's influence over provincial affairs.
On October 11, President Asif Ali Zardari declared a state of emergency in the province, imposing Governor's rule and effectively suspending the elected government led by Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party founded by jailed former prime minister Imran Khan.
The Shehbaz Sharif-led government cited rising militant violence and the provincial administration's alleged failure to control the security situation.
Imran-led PTI rejected the move, calling it an attack on its political stronghold and accusing the federal establishment of undermining an elected government.
Reuters reported that the emergency was accompanied by the appointment of a new governor and the deployment of troops, amid political tensions over a planned march to Islamabad demanding Khan's release. PTI has denied supporting militancy and disputed the Sharif government's account of its handling of the security situation.
KP is a key centre of PTI's political influence. Suspending its government has changed the balance between Khan's party and the Islamabad administration.
Imran Khan's prolonged imprisonment and the imposition of emergency rule in KP could also be viewed in the context of Asim Munir's long-standing tensions with the former prime minister, who also led Pakistan to its Cricket World Cup victory.
However, the emergency does not establish that Munir intends to divide KP or use it as a model for restructuring other provinces. It has nevertheless raised concerns about the federal government's ability to override elected provincial authorities, including in decisions affecting resource-rich regions.
Similar concerns have been raised about the possibility of greater federal intervention in Balochistan and Sindh. But there is no established evidence of a coordinated plan to impose such measures across provinces.
Is Pakistan's provincial system failing?
The argument for smaller provinces has a basis in the governance challenges Pakistan faces. Its population has grown substantially since 1947, while the current four-province structure has remained in place since 1970. Administering a province as populous as Punjab is a major task, particularly when public services remain inadequate in many areas.
Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi has argued that the country's governance system has "collapsed" and that the existing structure cannot adequately manage population growth, debt and other pressures. He has called for smaller administrative units as part of wider reforms.
Pakistan is world's fifth-largest country in population
But new boundaries alone would not solve corruption, weak public services or economic mismanagement. Smaller provinces would need their own institutions, budgets and administrative staff. Without adequate funding and clear powers, creating new units could increase the cost of government without improving people's lives.
The military's own role in Pakistan's governance problems is also part of this debate. The country has spent long periods under direct army rule, and the armed forces continue to wield considerable influence over security and foreign policy, even under civilian governments.
In recent months, Munir has wielded extraordinary power, from visiting Washington and cultivating ties with Donald Trump to earning the US president's "favourite field marshal" label and attempting to broker a deal over the Iran war.
Under his tenure, Pakistan's army chief has expanded his influence well beyond military affairs, playing an increasingly prominent role in the country's foreign policy.
The Economist has argued that the military cannot be separated from Pakistan's governance problems, pointing to its share of public resources, landholdings and commercial interests, as well as its influence over civilian administrations.
Pakistan's economic difficulties have several causes, including debt, inflation, weak investment and structural problems in public finances. But the military's political and economic position remains a central issue in debates over accountability and the allocation of resources.
Munir's authority has grown against this backdrop. Reuters reported on October 8 that the military had taken on a larger role in foreign and defence policy, including a decision to deploy additional troops to Saudi Arabia under a defence arrangement without parliamentary approval.
If provincial governments are weakened while the military's influence grows, critics fear there could be fewer institutions capable of challenging decisions made by the centre. At the same time, smaller provinces could create opportunities for new regional leaders, depending on how much independence they are given.
The key issue is not simply the size of the provinces, but who would control their budgets, appointments and natural resources after any restructuring.
Can Munir get the plan through?
Even if the military and civilian leadership agree on restructuring, Pakistan's Constitution presents a major hurdle.
Article 239 requires a constitutional amendment to secure a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each house of parliament. If an amendment changes a province's boundaries, it must also be approved by the concerned provincial assembly by at least two-thirds of its total membership before it can be presented to the president for assent.
The general vs the dynasties: Who holds the real power in Pakistan?
That makes dividing Punjab or Sindh politically difficult. The PML-N may have reasons to consider a separate South Punjab province, but splitting Punjab could weaken the Sharif family's political base.
The PPP, meanwhile, has repeatedly rejected proposals to divide Sindh, its strongest provincial stronghold.
The Sindh assembly's September resolution and the multiparty conference reported by Dawn in October show that opposition extends beyond a single party. Any attempt to alter the province's boundaries without political consensus could provoke a wider confrontation.
Balochistan remains a major challenge for the Sharif-Munir duo, with separatist sentiment, demands for greater autonomy and sustained militant activity complicating Islamabad's efforts to assert control over the province.
Senator and former Imran Khan ally Faisal Vawda has suggested, in reporting by The Economist, that a referendum could be held in the coming months. But such a proposal raises questions about the legal process and whether a referendum could replace the constitutionally required approvals.
There is also a distinction between creating 12 to 15 provinces and establishing as many as 160 administrative units.
The first would fundamentally change Pakistan's federal structure. The second could involve districts or other administrative divisions, depending on their legal status and powers.
Until a detailed plan is announced, it remains unclear which model is actually being considered.
What happens next?
Pakistan's debate over new provinces brings together several long-running disputes: The balance between civilian and military power, the influence of regional political dynasties, and control over natural resources.
Supporters argue that smaller provinces could improve governance and give neglected regions a stronger voice. Critics fear that dividing established political strongholds would weaken regional parties and leave provincial governments more dependent on Islamabad.
One military chief, powerful political families: The contest shaping Pakistan
The constitutional hurdles are substantial, and opposition in Sindh is already organised. Developments in KP have added to concerns about the centre's willingness to override provincial authority in the name of security.
Pakistan faces serious governance challenges, but whether redrawing its map would address them is another matter. Smaller provinces could help address regional inequalities if they receive adequate resources, meaningful autonomy and accountable institutions.
If the changes instead weaken elected governments while concentrating control over funding and natural resources in the centre, the promised benefits may never reach ordinary citizens.

In 2026, moviegoers came back to cinemas, packing theaters to see blockbusters like “The Odyssey,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “Toy Story 5,” “Michael” and “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” and low-budget films like “Backrooms” and “Obsession.” But all those movies needed skilled artisans to complete the directors’ visions, including those on Variety’s 10 Artisans to Watch list. The honorees will be feted at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, which runs Oct. 24-31.
Past honorees have often gone on to earn Oscar nominations. Last year, “Sinners” DP Autumn Durald Arkapaw, “KPop Demon Hunters” songwriter EJAE and “One Battle After Another” editor Andy Jurgensen all went on to win Oscars.
- Anne Jimkes Supervising sound editor, “The Mosquito Bowl” Jimkes approached the film’s World War II Pacific Theater setting with a focus on authenticity, researching the specific weapons used by the Japanese and American military forces, including the M1 Garand rifle. Its distinctive metallic “ping” served as more than just a historically accurate reference. “It adds a sense of urgency, and it’s a decision-making moment,” Jimkes says, noting the sound signals when a character must reload, switch weapons or resort to hand-to-hand combat. The sounds of the soldiers were a priority. The breaths and physical reactions recorded on set were pushed forward against the chaos of the battle to ground the characters’ humanity. Even in quieter scenes, the jungle location was alive with sound, creating a sense of pressure surrounding the soldiers. Blending these elements together is a process Jimkes refers to as a “parade of sound,” adding, “Your brain can only process so many sounds at the same time. However, it’s very good at processing rapidly successive sounds.” The sound needed to move the story forward. For Jimkes, that meant determining which sound should take priority in each moment while never losing sight of the people at the center of the film’s story. — Tanya Fedak
- Aulo Licinio Animation supervisor, “Project Hail Mary” Despite having no face, eyes or traditional way to convey human emotion, Rocky became the emotional heart of “Project Hail Mary.” Licinio navigated that by developing physical language for the alien rock creature. Licinio oversaw a team of animators who studied the physical puppet used for filming, using its on-set movements as a reference while expanding Rocky’s mannerisms. “[Rocky’s puppeteer and voice] James Ortiz did a good job getting expressions out of this rock,” he says. “How can we enhance it in a way that we can use in reference? How can we tie the loose ends?” Licinio and his team looked to early puppetry and the exaggerated performances from silent film stars like Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton. Without features to convey human emotion, Rocky instead uses his elbows, body and distinctive head movements, sometimes angling himself just five degrees more to express his feelings. When he is shy, for example, he pulls an elbow in front of himself as if hiding. Some of Rocky’s mannerisms originated on set, including a tapping gesture to answer questions from Ortiz that the animators incorporated into the final character. Other movements, such as Rocky’s finger-like computing gestures, were created in CG. “It’s a collaboration at the end,” Licinio says. “That’s what I like to say about the film.” — T.F.
- Landon Lott Art director, “Pluribus” SCAD alum Lott recalls “Pluribus” production designer Denise Pizzini reaching out to help develop a Norwegian ice hotel that would be built entirely on stage. Lott recalls, “The brief was to create a hotel that felt authentic and entirely sculpted from ice, while designing it around the practical limitations of a stage build.” Lott saw it as a great opportunity to bring together his background in illustration, architecture and set design. On his process, Lott says, “The initial scope of the set was actually larger than what ultimately appeared on screen and included a hotel lobby, foyer, bar and the individual hotel rooms. That meant thinking through the hotel as a complete environment from the beginning, establishing how the spaces connected and giving each one its own identity while making sure they all felt like part of the same place.” Lott knew that many details would be handcarved by ice sculptors. “I was essentially designing artwork that also had to function architecturally, work within the realities of a stage build and give the sculptors something tangible they could interpret and bring to life,” he says. So he turned to real ice hotels throughout Scandinavia, particularly the ICEHOTEL in Sweden and hotels in Norway and Finland for inspiration. — Jazz Tangcay
- Blair McClendon Editor, “Clarissa” For McClendon, editing films is a lot like music. It’s all about finding the right rhythm, texture, pace and cutting where the beat falls. Sometimes finding this groove is deliberate and difficult, and other times, like on “Clarissa,” the experience is filled with happy accidents. “It’s like a rooster crows at exactly the right moment to keep the shot interesting and keep it going, and we were like, ‘Oh, that’s great, that guy has to stay,’” McClendon says. It also helped that the actors delivered great performances, McClendon explains. Stars David Oyelowo, Sophie Okonedo and Ayo Edebiri worked with directors Arie Esiri and Chuko Esiri to allow scenes to unfurl naturally and used editing to enhance characters’ emotions. To McClendon, this is the way it’s supposed to be. One of the biggest misconceptions he shares about editing is the idea that it’s a place for fixing as opposed to fine-tuning. To achieve a final cut, McClendon and the directors discussed their wishes and ideas for what the film would be, and McClendon aimed to make as many of them come true as possible. He knew he was done when they had “emotionally exhausted the avenues of what you’re trying to make.” By the end, he could happily accept that “this is the movie this movie is. It’s not the movie that is in my head or Chuko’s head or Arie’s head or the producer’s head or the DP’s head, but you start to recognize, like, no, that is how this movie runs,” McClendon says. — Isabelle Farina
- Adam Newport-Berra Cinematographer, “The Invite”, “Club Kid” Newport-Berra’s range is on display in two films this awards season: “The Invite,” directed by and starring Olivia Wilde, and “Club Kid,” directed by and starring Jordan Firstman. “I tend to enjoy working with actor-directors because we get this dynamic experience on set where they get to direct the film both from outside and from within during the scene, which I think is a special opportunity for a director to be inside the moment,” Newport-Berra says. “The Invite” takes place over one night and follows two dynamic couples inside one apartment. The premise provided Wilde and Newport-Berra with a creative challenge. “We loved the script, but we thought, ‘How do we make this really sing on screen?’ It can’t just feel like a play. It can’t just be about presenting the material. It needs to be dynamic.” Newport-Berra sought ways to liberate his camera within the confines of the space. With no big cranes available, lensing and composition had to tell the story. “Olivia and I looked through a lot of references, took a lot of photos and talked about why certain images make us feel awkward, seduced, anxious or in love,” he explains. “We really used composition and the focal lengths of our lenses to either compress people and make things feel flat and claustrophobic, or we would use a wider lens to make it feel very intimate, gentle, sexy and seductive.” “Club Kid” emphasizes the character dynamics. Firstman’s Peter finds his life turned upside down after years of partying in New York clubs when he learns he has a 10-year-old son, Arlo (Reggie Absolom). Newport-Berra wanted to handle the relationship between Reggie and Jordan’s characters with care. “It was through rehearsals, and every morning, Jordan and I would check in, read through the script together, and feel whatever we were feeling that day,” Newport-Berra says. — J.T.
- Raül Refree Composer, “La Bola Negra” When scoring Netflix’s “La Bola Negra,” Refree knew he wanted to pursue a timeless, orchestral and avant-garde sound. The film recounts the story of three generations of queer men whose lives are connected through love and loss. Refree tied his instrumentation to the characters rather than the eras. “Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) plays the trumpet, so his scenes rely heavily on the brass section. Carlos (Milo Quifes) plays the piano, so his music features the piano alongside the string section. Finally, Alberto’s (Carlos González) story takes place in the present day, and because he is going through a personal crisis, his music relies much more on silence,” Refree says. As the three stories intersect, the music follows suit by blending these different colors and timbres, building toward the final climax. The film contains several songs including “La Nieve,” sung by Sebastián. “Guitarricadelafuente brought the idea for ‘La Nieve’ to Los Javis (the film’s directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo). 
	They loved it and asked me to incorporate it into the score, so I adapted his initial concept to align with the rest of the soundtrack,” Refree says. “Having worked with Guitarricadelafuente frequently over
the last few years, we have a great creative dynamic, which made it easy to co-write the song and develop the right sound.” — J.T.
- Jessica Ronane Casting director, “Elsinore” Casting for “Elsinore” was a particularly nuanced feat for Ronane. She felt a responsibility to the truth. She had to cast a play within a film based on the real-life happenings of London’s National Theatre in 1989. To do so, Ronane and “Elsinore” director Simon Stone worked closely together scouring their web of actors and building a “story map of all the real people and then started to think about instinctively who has the spirit of the character, and how are we going to identify the right actors to put forward,” Ronane says. Ronane’s instincts led her to focus on performers with theater experience. Once Andrew Scott was solidified for the role of Ian Charleson, Ronane quickly thought of David Dawson to play Derek Jarman. She had seen the pair perform together in a play back in 2014 and couldn’t shake their chemistry. “Seeing the two of them on a small stage together like that in a really intimate setting, I could not stop thinking about that when we spoke about David Dawson in this role,” Ronane says. Casting Olivia Colman as Margaret was also instinctual. Her “particular brand of sensitivity and humor and wisdom and sort of spiciness” made her a natural choice to play the part, Ronane says. “What an incredible thing to be able to build on your instincts like that, to be able to really feel that your taste is appreciated by collaborators who want kind of more of that,” Ronane says. — I. F.
- Allie Shehorn Make-up and hair department head/ special makeup effects department head, “Obsession” For “Obsession,” Shehorn was tasked with creating looks that could withstand the film’s practical effects while still telling the characters’ stories. For Sarah’s (Megan Lawless) face-smash sequence, Shehorn crafted multiple versions of the character’s head, including a live cast taken from the actor as she screamed and a prosthetic version that could ultimately be smashed on camera. Shehorn and the team carefully choreographed each transition, switching from the actor’s live-action performance to the prosthetic before revealing Sarah’s final smashed-in face. Working with the blood rigs presented another technical challenge, particularly because the team filmed scenes out of order. “We actually shot the end sequence of the movie before we did the blood rigs to establish the blood looks,” Shehorn says. “We had to predict where the blood was going on Bear (Michael Johnston), even on Nikki (Inde Navarrette).” One of Shehorn’s more elaborate looks was Nikki’s final appearance after murdering Sarah, which reflects her growing obsession with becoming her. Shehorn used the same lipstick and eyeliner shades on Nikki that Sarah wears, while dried blood sits beneath the fresh blood to represent the fact that Nikki never washes it from her face. She also used Sarah’s eyeliner shade to draw Nikki’s tattoos and, by the end of the film, curled Nikki’s hair as another visual connection to Sarah. “That’s why we kept Nikki’s hair straight throughout the film, because we wanted to show the difference in the characters between Sarah and Nikki, so that in the end we can really push those moments of ‘Oh, she’s really trying to be her,’” she says. — T.F.
- Grace Snell Costume designer, “Sense and Sensibility” Snell is a Jane Austen fan, but she tried not to be intimidated by the fact that “Sense and Sensibility” was an Austen adaptation. “I took my role very seriously and did lots of research, but then I was reassured by our director and the producers that they wanted my version of this,” she says. “What I wanted to do was design a film that I could see myself in, see my friends in, see my family in, try and knock down the wall that often is associated with period dramas.” Georgia Oakley’s film isn’t the first “Sense and Sensibility” adaptation, and while Snell loves the 1995 version, she also knew this film was a different take. Part of that was her blend of modern styling and historical accuracy. “As a designer, it was an amazing experience to try and fight those two sides,” she says. With help from a dress historian, Snell created a modern take on costumes from the “tip of Regency” era using historically accurate fabrics and hand-sewing techniques. Snell was also inspired by family portraits. She wanted the Dashwood women to share clothing in the way that sisters do. “The dynamic of those sisters and how they share clothes and how they’re inspired by each other was important,” she says. “We do rework some of the fabrics so that the garments look like they have a life themselves and how garments are loved and shared and borrowed within a family.” — Mya Copeland
- Danny Vermette Production designer, “Backrooms” Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms” web series became a YouTube phenomenon, amassing over 200 million views across its episodes. When Parsons began adapting the series into a feature film, Vermette had already seen the series but wasn’t fully aware of Parsons’ work. “I watched all of Kane’s stuff and came to realize how much is out there, and what a following it had,” Vermette says. He jokingly refers to this experience as attending “Backrooms University.” In conversations with Parsons, Vermette realized there was much more to the concept than just liminal spaces. Bringing the world to life as a period piece — the story is set in the 1990s — required close collaboration with the film’s cinematographer Jeremy Cox and costume designer Micah Cade to determine what would work within “the yellow universe.” One of the challenges was designing the drop ceilings. “My key thought was to keep this original to the series but bring it up to that next level of cinema and make it beautiful,” Vermette explains. The ceilings were customized, which turned into a major undertaking. “There were a lot, a lot of lights — 375 individual lenses and troffers on the set.” Finding multiples of the same furniture became a challenge. Lead buyer Eric Cairns was tasked with finding 32 of the exact same couches in the tone they wanted. Parsons questioned it. Vermette recalls, “Kane said, ‘I don’t think they have to all be the same.’ I said, ‘But what if they were all the same? Wouldn’t it be amazing?’” — J.T.

Rumors that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security allegedly illegally used water from New Mexico in order to aid in construction of its border wall circulated in October.
Specifically, people claimed that DHS had issued a waiver to remove the state's protections and ownership of the water wells despite ongoing disputes with land owners and lawsuits against the federal government's actions regarding its construction plans.
The claim was true.
On Oct. 2, the Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued a directive — available to read on the Federal Register — that it was "necessary to waive certain laws, regulations, and other legal requirements in order to ensure the expeditious construction of barriers and roads in the vicinity of the international land border in the state of New Mexico."
Included in the waiver was the entirety of the New Mexico Water Code.
The directive further described the El Paso Sector, a Customs and Border Protection jurisdiction that includes all of New Mexico, as an "area of high illegal entry" to justify the move.
A spokesperson for CBP, which is part of DHS, told Snopes via email the agency was "coordinating with the State of New Mexico and the U.S. Department of Agriculture to develop a broader groundwater management strategy" and stressed the importance of how "water is required for road construction, concrete production, and dust suppression associated with border wall construction."
They wrote that "CBP recently instructed the barrier construction contractor to pause on the installation of any new groundwater wells in collaboration with the State of New Mexico and as an initial step in minimizing or avoiding impacts to groundwater water resources," adding they were committed to working with local landowners.
A spokesperson for New Mexico's Office of the State Engineer told Snopes via email:
We have informed the CBP that all water used for the project must come from permitted sources, and we have instructed them in how to do that. To date, they have been unwilling to do so, and they continue pumping water from illegal wells. Therefore, while a pause in drilling new wells is a good first step, more must be done to ensure that New Mexicans' water supply is not threatened by this project.
The agenda for a meeting of New Mexico's Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee on Oct. 6 showed that Nathaniel Chakeres, general counsel at the New Mexico's Office of the State Engineer, made a presentation regarding the illegal drilling and resulting waiver, which he called "unconstitutional."
Searchlight New Mexico, an investigative journalism outlet, quoted Chakeres as telling the committee that "the water of New Mexico is owned by the public for appropriation by private parties. That's in our constitution, and the federal government accepted that constitution when we became a state." Snopes attempted to locate video of the committee meeting but was unable to.
The committee's website appeared to host the minutes from its meetings for public review, but none were available for the meeting in question as of this writing.
In Chakeres' presentation, as one local report pointed out, he "shared an image of an open well casing that sat roughly six inches above pooled surface water," which meant "the next rain storm could send oil, gas or construction chemicals into the groundwater."
That report, by Source New Mexico, quoted Chakeres as saying, "It's appalling. We were shocked when we came out and saw this. No New Mexico drillers drill wells like this."
New Mexico's battle for water at the border
The battle between the state and the federal government's attempts at border wall construction first made headlines in June when the government attempted to seize land belonging to a Roman Catholic diocese in New Mexico after the church refused to agree to an acquisition, leading to a lawsuit.
In July, area farmers met to discuss the issue of federal drilling on the border, voicing their concerns over a dwindling water supply and "unmonitored tapping of border aquifers."
In August, the Office of the State Engineer threatened to revoke licenses of the companies contracted by the Trump administration for the border wall project.
One local news report wrote the officials had found multiple "unauthorized" wells in protected water basins, along with possible safety violations, with one that had the "imminent risk of groundwater contamination."
CBP reportedly agreed to stop drilling following the voicing of these concerns, however, by the end of August, the state sued the federal government and the border contractors, citing that no formal effort was made to cease the drilling. The ongoing legal struggles led to the introduction of the waiver on Oct. 2.
When reached for comment, DHS also provided a statement from CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott that was first released in August, discussing an unrelated CBP project in southern Arizona in which the department is cutting through tribal land for construction. The department has not yet responded to a follow-up about what, if anything, the statement about the Arizona project has to do with the situation in New Mexico.

Musk says any limits on Ukraine's Starlink access down to US, not his firm
- Published
Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network.
Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions.
An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a coincidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.
Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".
Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe [a] huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch [it] on."
Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said.
"Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".
About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.
Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".
The US government has not commented.
While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use.
The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
President Zelensky said it was "one of the largest attacks" from Russia, and while "a significant part of the drones were shot down" there were "also hits".
At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit.
"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation, Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.
US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated towards Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities.
Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire, but on Tuesday, Trump denied this.
Speaking during a visit to London on Wednesday, President Zelensky agreed that he had felt betrayed after the US made a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its of diesel.
"Really yes... but it's a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings," Zelensky said, when asked by UK journalist Piers Morgan if he felt betrayed.
During his one-day visit, Zelensky was greeted with a hug by UK PM Andy Burnham at Downing Street and held an audience with King Charles.
Ahead of the president's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones.
"We are behind you and that will not change," Burnham told Zelensky.

Abhijeet Dipke arrived in Delhi a day after his party's co-convenors, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka.
NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke was heckled at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport while returning to the capital after a brief stay in his hometown.As Dipke was leaving the airport, a man in the crowd called him a "CIA agent", while another confronted him, asking, "Kyun desh ko kharab kar raha hai? (Why are you ruining the country?)"
Dipke arrived in Delhi a day after his party's co-convenors, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, sneakingly climbed over a gate to enter the prohibited area at Jantar Mantar to protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the government. The government had denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.
Later, Das and Ranka, who had singed a bond to "maintain peace for a year", were sent to 5-day judicial custody on the order of Delhi's special executive magistrate court.
Reacting to the duo's judicial custody, Dipke dared Prime Minister Narendra Modi to officially declare an Emergency.In a video posted on X, Dipke targeted PM Modi over the duo’s judicial custody, saying Das and Ranka knew they could be jailed when they set out for Jantar Mantar but went ahead with their plan, carrying and unfurling the Tricolour.
“Under Narendra Modi, even hoisting the national flag has become a violation of the law in this country,” he said.Dipke further said, “I want to tell Narendra Modi one thing: If you have the courage, officially declare an Emergency. Stop hiding behind the police like cowards. Impose an official Emergency and say openly that dissent will not be tolerated in this country, that protests will not be allowed. Say that from now on, the only slogan permitted in this country will be ‘Har Har Modi, Ghar Ghar Modi’.”He further alleged that PM Modi did not respect the national flag, the people of the country or the Constitution.“So declare an Emergency, if you have the courage,” Dipke said.
Rajeev Singh is a Digital Content Producer with The Times of India. He covers politics, policies, defence, and conflicts for readers curious to know their implications. He loves digging into legal maxims and political trivia. On off days, when not turning pages or learning русский, he lives in the reverie of “what ifs” and “how abouts.”

The good news for Netflix: It's been here before.
In 2022, after years of breakneck growth and go-go spending, the streamer suddenly lost subscribers. Cue layoffs, a hasty pivot to an ad model it had always criticized, and tons of industry schadenfreude.
But it turned out that Netflix's growth problems were overstated. Or at least, that its growth problems weren't a sign of opportunity for its streaming rivals.
Years later, Netflix's position at the top of paid streaming services remains unchanged. Meanwhile, Wall Street has grown tired of watching would-be competitors like Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery struggle to make headway — which is why both of those companies are now owned by the Ellison family.
The bad news for Netflix: The levers it pulled four years ago no longer seem available. It has already done the ads thing, and the live sports thing — another move they had previously sworn off. A foray into video games doesn't seem to have produced much at all.
Meanwhile there has been a steady series of reports indicating that not only is Netflix's subscriber and revenue growth slowing, but its existing subscribers are finding the service less engaging than in the past.
Netflix responded to that one by arguing that its engagement was just fine, really — and then announced it would make it harder to understand its performance by cutting back on the audience data it provides to the outside world.
Most concerning: Wall Street and the rest of the media industry have started catching up to the fact that Netflix's competition isn't just other paid streamers, but giant platforms — YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok. Those companies may not have the next "Stranger Things," but they don't have to. They have unlimited content that costs them either nothing (Instagram and TikTok) or nothing upfront (YouTube). And they provide it to consumers for free, in a never-ending river of clips.
It's very hard to compete with that, though you can see Netflix trying: YouTube has a lot of video podcasts, so now Netflix is doing that, too.
None of that has convinced Wall Street, which is why Netflix stock is down 43% over the last year. Some of that was a reaction to the company's pursuit of HBO and Warner Bros. — an uncharacteristic mega M&A swing that investors hated. But after Netflix bailed on that one, shareholders remain skeptical.
That may be why Netflix stock isn't moving on Wednesday, after the company announced it is laying off 6% of its workforce. Cutting heads can cut Netflix's costs and improve its margins. But it doesn't help the company grow — or help it compete with ruthless Big Tech platforms.

In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.
Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.
Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).
Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.
The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia.
However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.
Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”
However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with the unexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.
So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.
The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.
“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.
A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.
Russia has bombed two bridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.
The effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.
Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.
“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.
Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.
The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.
As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”
Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy, on a visit to London on Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.

Son of Zambian bishop detained in post-election raid fears for his father's safety
The son of detained Zambian opposition politician Bishop Trevor Mwamba has told the BBC he is concerned for his father's safety after the former Bishop of Botswana was detained along with 10 other opposition figures by authorities.
Eno Mwamba said his father, who is leader of the United National Independence Party, has been charged with treason following President Hakainde Hichilema's disputed election victory.
The opposition politicians have been held since a raid by security forces on 14 August.
Opposition leader Brian Mundubile, head of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), had gone into hiding after disputing the election result, but has since also been detained by the authorities.
The government accuses the opposition of planning an armed insurgency and have charged the detained politicians with treason. They have denied the charges.

Your flu shot can’t wait
Some parts of the country are already seeing case levels typical of late fall or early winter.
Flu season is starting earlier than usual this year, which I know from reviewing federal data. But I also know it because I woke up with body aches and chills last night, mere days before I’d planned to get my flu vaccination (!).
Already, some parts of the country are seeing levels of flu activity typically associated with late fall or early winter. In Washington state, for instance, doctors are reporting seeing as much flu now as they usually would around Christmas.
Flu activity overall is still low, to be clear. But as of October 7, infections were rising in all 50 states. And flu is spreading before many people — like, say, me — have received their annual vaccine.
Epidemiologists don’t yet know why the flu arrived early this year, or why cases first started rising in Western states like Washington, California, and Nevada. It’s possible that a mutation is helping this year’s flu variants evade existing immunity, one virologist told NPR. International travel could play a role, too: Flu cases also spiked early in Japan and other parts of Asia.
We don’t need to know why the flu arrived early to take some basic precautions, though. So today, we’re talking through some practical tips for coping with an early flu season.
Go a little deeper
An early flu season doesn’t necessarily mean a worse season — but even a moderate season can do serious damage. Last year, influenza sent hundreds of thousands of people to the hospital and caused tens of thousands of deaths, including almost 200 among children.
The first and best way to avoid those kinds of harms is by getting the flu shot, which reduces the risk of serious illness by an average of 40 to 60 percent. In the US, people aged 6 months and older are typically told to get the vaccine by October’s end.
In light of the early onset, however (it takes two weeks to build up full immunity), you might instead want to get your shot ASAP.
There are some everyday precautions you can take, too — many of them familiar from the Covid-19 era. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and warm water, for slightly longer than feels appropriate. Mask when you’re sick or might encounter someone else who is.
And don’t neglect the good habits that support your overall health: getting enough sleep, drinking a lot of water, and eating a balanced diet. (There’s very little evidence for trendier interventions, like supplements, saunas, cold plunges, or the infused herbal baths that my kooky former yoga teacher used to recommend.)
If you do get flu symptoms, reach out to your doctor early — especially if you’re older, pregnant, immunocompromised, or otherwise at higher risk for complications. Prescription antiviral medications, like Tamiflu, prevent the flu virus from spreading inside your body so that your immune system can clear it. But they work best within 48 hours of symptom onset.
To be clear, you needn’t take my word on any of this; I’m just another voice in the public health cacophony! Besides, recent polling suggests that my particular voice — that is, the voice of someone who works in media — is not quite as persuasive as it used to be. (Ditto medical websites and government health agencies.)
But if you have doubts or questions about vaccines, there is someone much closer to home you can consult: Ask your doctor (or nurse or pharmacist) about the flu shot’s risks and benefits. They’re best positioned to break the science down and apply it to your health. In hindsight, mine surely would have told me to stop delaying my shot for a more convenient weekend.

‘Unwarranted and unacceptable’: India slams UN human rights office's concerns over Delhi protest
The response followed the United Nations' expression of concern over mass detentions in Delhi amid protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) on Wednesday called the concerns expressed by the United Nations Human Rights Office over the Delhi protests “unwarranted” and “unacceptable”, accusing it of interfering in India's internal affairs.
Responding to the remarks during a media briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) appeared to be following a selective approach in commenting on protests and law enforcement actions around the world.
“... the concerns expressed by OHCHR (Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights) are unwarranted and at the same time unacceptable because it amounts to interference in India's internal affairs,” Jaiswal said.
“It seems that they have an approach of extreme selectivity because they have not reacted in their public positions on protests which are happening or law enforcement actions which are happening in other parts of the world,” he added.
Jaiswal warned that such an approach could undermine confidence in multilateralism and damage the organisation's credibility.
“And if they continue on this path, then obviously it will lead to loss of faith in multilateralism. At the same time, it undermines their credibility as an organisation,” he said.
Also Read: India hits back at UN rights office over remarks on Delhi protests, calls concerns ‘misplaced’
What India said earlier
Earlier, the MEA had rejected the OHCHR's remarks on the events in New Delhi, describing its concerns as “misplaced” and accusing the office of unwarranted interference in India's internal affairs.
In a statement shared by the ministry on X, India said the right to peaceful assembly was guaranteed by the Constitution and safeguarded by the country's institutions, an independent judiciary and a free media.
“We have seen the OHCHR’s remarks about today’s events in New Delhi,” the statement said, adding that citizens exercised their right to peaceful assembly subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order.
The restrictions also came under legal scrutiny, with the Supreme Court intervening over curbs affecting public transport and calling for a balance between the right to protest and the need to prevent disruption to essential services.
Why the UN raised concerns
The response followed the United Nations' expression of concern over mass detentions in Delhi amid protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The demonstrations were accompanied by heightened security measures and restrictions in parts of the national capital.
The protests, called by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) and other groups, were linked to demands for Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
