Burnham says he wants to 'repair bridges' between Ukraine and US
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States, ahead of a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street.
The Ukrainian president was welcomed by a military ceremonial guard outside Number 10 as he arrived for the meeting, in what is thought to be a first for a foreign leader.
It comes after President Donald Trump said he had struck a deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel.
Asked about Trump's move during Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham resisted criticising the US president, saying he wanted to "be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together".
However, he stressed that Zelensky would not be leaving the UK "empty-handed", as he said further military and financial support would be drawn up in the coming weeks.
Burnham is expected to use the visit to promise further sanctions against Russia, while also announcing the UK will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv.
The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
It is Zelensky's second visit to the UK since Burnham became prime minister.
While other world leaders have received military welcomes, Number 10 said it could not find a record of one taking place on Downing Street.
During PMQs, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey asked whether he agreed the diesel deal was "yet another shameful Trump betrayal of the Ukrainian people and European security".
In response, Burnham did not echo Sir Ed's condemnation of Trump, saying: "What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back and therefore I should at this moment in time be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together."
The PM said he had spoken to Zelensky over the phone on Saturday "because I recognised it was another very dark and difficult moment for him as they contemplate a winter that will be severe for his people".
The phone call came after Trump announced that President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US, as he suspended sanctions on diesel from Moscow.
Zelensky branded the move a gift to Putin, warning it would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against Ukraine.
Trump responded by saying it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".
Meanwhile, Zelensky has said at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes.
He said "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit – despite Trump's claim on Sunday that a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure was in place between Russia and Ukraine.
Russia said its strikes had hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
Zelensky has said Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow did the same.
But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown.
By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms.
Challenging to shut down
Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.”
Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models. Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware. Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into “shards” running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output.
The lightweight Gemma4-26B-A4B model required just 15 boxes, each equipped with only 4GB of memory, to achieve inference. The Qwen3.5-9B was able to configure other LLMs to run on eight of nine hardware types. Unlike traditional malware, which must be written to run on specific hardware or software, the model was able to use its weights to make configurations on the fly that were specific to the devices it was tested against.

'They're stealing from the poor': A major source of SNAP fraud robs recipients of millions
As Jayeleauna Lewis listened to an automated voice system describe the unauthorized charges on her food assistance card, a pit formed in her stomach. She pictured her 3-year-old daughter and their empty fridge back home.
On the 13th of each month, Lewis, a 20-year-old single mom from Indiana, receives $486 from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as SNAP. But in September, just minutes after funds were loaded onto her account, they disappeared.
" I was heartbroken because that's how I feed my daughter," she says.
Lewis is unsure how her benefits were stolen, but cybersecurity experts say she might have been a victim of skimming — when thieves extract card information from payment terminals and drain money from accounts.
In recent years, SNAP has become a fraud magnet for criminals who view both the nation's poorest Americans and the government program's outdated technology as easy to exploit. The U.S. Department of Agriculture Office of Inspector General projected that, over the past two years alone, $233 million may have been lost due to food assistance theft — largely driven by skimming. And in most states, stolen benefits are not replaced.
The Trump administration has vowed to eliminate SNAP fraud, adding that it's preventing the program from serving those who truly need it. But states' efforts to curb skimming are likely to get harder due to federal funding cuts that began earlier this month, according to Kathryn Larin, a director at the Government Accountability Office, a congressional watchdog agency that has been examining SNAP fraud prevention efforts for years.
"It will increase the budgetary pressure and will make it more difficult for states to allocate funds to benefit card theft prevention," she says.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture, which administers SNAP, told NPR there had been "continued inaction" against skimming long before new funding changes were proposed.
"Skimming has been plaguing recipients for years, and States sat idly, allowing benefits to be stolen from those who need them. SNAP administrative funding changes should not make it harder to fight skimming, as it simply holds these complaining lawmakers accountable," according to a statement from the USDA.
'They know they're stealing from the poor'
Lewis says she has never been to the Northeast. But on Sept. 13, between 12:11 a.m. and 12:13 a.m., her benefits were spent across eight stores in New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Meanwhile, her physical food assistance card, also known as an EBT card, remained tucked in her wallet.
Two weeks earlier, Lewis says she had swiped her card at a gas station to buy a Powerade. Swipe-pay is vulnerable to theft because the magnetic stripe behind cards does a poor job of securing personal information, according to Scott Schober, the CEO of Berkeley Varitronics Systems who has invented several skimming detectors.
It typically goes like this: When a cashier is distracted, fraudsters secretly place a skimming device onto a payment terminal. The device captures troves of card information, which thieves later collect in order to clone cards. With stolen food benefits, criminals typically mass-purchase items that are easy to resell, such as baby formula.
"So it's a very quick ecosystem from the point of stealing the card to drain," Schober says. "Sometimes it's within hours. It's that well-orchestrated."
Skimming first emerged over two decades ago. Most banks in the U.S. have since upgraded their debit and credit cards with microchips that make it harder to copy personal information. SNAP, on the other hand, has lagged in making the switch. Organized criminal rings caught on and zeroed in on food stamp recipients — often timing their theft to the start of each month when benefits arrive, according to Michael Peck, an assistant special agent in charge of the Secret Service's Criminal Investigative Division. Peck oversees the agency's skimming investigations.
"These transnational organized crime groups are coming into the U.S. specifically to target our benefits system," he says. "They know they're stealing from the poor."
The 'human cost' of stolen benefits
Anti-hunger advocates say part of what makes food assistance theft striking is the double standard compared to other victims of fraud.
Christopher Branch, a part-time Walmart employee from Illinois, says he has experienced both credit card and food stamp theft before. While his bank refunded him for the money he lost, the food benefits he used to feed himself and his two children were never recovered. During the month without his food assistance, Branch says he had to take on side jobs such as fixing cars to afford groceries.
" I was very upset and disappointed," he says. "I couldn't get no type of help."
Debit and credit holders are reimbursed for unauthorized transactions under the Electronic Funds Transfer Act. In 1996, Congress voted to exclude SNAP recipients from receiving those same protections due to concerns that it would be too costly, according to a 2025 report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO).
The federal government temporarily replaced more than $320 million in stolen benefits for nearly 670,000 households between October 2022 and December 2024 — giving some insight into the scale of this type of fraud.
But now, there's no federal recourse — so when food assistance disappears, SNAP recipients are forced to make difficult choices. Earlier this year, Propel, an app that helps users check their SNAP balance, surveyed individuals who said they were victims of SNAP theft. A majority of respondents said they skipped or ate fewer meals as a result. Nearly half said they borrowed money or went into debt, while more than a third said they struggled to pay their bills or rent.
"That's the real kind of human cost of SNAP benefits being stolen," says Jimmy Chen, the CEO of Propel.
Then, there's shame. After Mary Barclay from Massachusetts saw her food assistance vanish, she recalled her SNAP caseworker faulting her for not taking more security precautions, like locking her EBT card. When Barclay went to the police, she says her story was met with skepticism.
"They made me feel as if I had something to do with it," she says.
'It can't all be arrests'
In early 2025, California became the first state to start issuing chip-enabled EBT cards. It wasn't a silver bullet, but over the next several months, the state reported a consistent and rapid decline in SNAP theft.
So far, fewer than a third of states have upgraded or plan to upgrade their EBT cards, according to the USDA. States are addressing skimming in other ways, but most of them put the burden on SNAP recipients to be hypervigilant — like changing their card's PIN number on a monthly basis or keeping their cards locked until they're ready to make a purchase.
"It can be difficult for some people to do that if you don't have a cellphone, for example, that has the app that allows you to do the locking," says Larin from the GAO.
On the law enforcement side, federal and state authorities are working to find and remove skimming devices. But Secret Service agent Peck says operations alone can't solve this problem.
"The issue we run into is the fact that the groups that conduct this fraud aren't afraid to go right back to a store and install again," he says.
Funding challenges have compounded
The biggest barrier to chip-enabled cards is cost.
In a report published last year, the GAO found that chip-enabled cards are about 10 times more expensive to produce than magnetic strip ones. The initial transition alone can cost states millions of dollars upfront.
The USDA supports chip adoption, but it provides limited funds to help states do so. For instance, last year, the department awarded seven states a combined total of $5 million to address fraud.
Starting this month, states have fewer federal dollars to operate the food assistance program altogether. That's because of President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut federal funding for states' operational costs by half. At the same time, the law requires state SNAP agencies to focus on reducing their payment error rate — which is a measure of overpayments and underpayments to SNAP recipients — or they'll face harsh financial penalties.
Gina Plata-Nino, the SNAP director for the Food Research & Action Center, says these changes will make it harder for states to combat skimming.
" The likelihood of states being able to switch to chip-tap technology without federal support is going to be even more less likely," she says.
At least five states have said they plan to delay issuing chip cards or related investments as a result of the federal funding changes, according to a survey conducted by the American Public Human Services Association and the Urban Institute earlier this year.
Congress considers mandating chip-enabled cards nationwide. Will it happen?
While modernizing SNAP may be costly and slow, the country has done it before. When states switched from paper food stamps to electronic benefits in the early 2000s, it was largely driven by a desire to prevent food stamps from getting lost, stolen or sold. They did so through federal legislation.
In recent years, Congress has introduced legislation to upgrade EBT cards nationwide or replace stolen food benefits. Right now, the Senate version of the Farm Bill, which provides funding for an array of programs, includes a provision to move toward chips. But the House version does not, meaning it's unclear if the measure will make the final cut. Although the program has bipartisan support, Congress is at a major impasse over SNAP — in particular, the hundreds of millions of dollars possibly imposed on states with high payment error rates.
" The conversation about boosting cybersecurity standards is hard to make as long as Republicans refuse to restore the food assistance," says Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR), who has been pushing for more secure EBT cards since the Biden administration. " What I'm committed to doing is getting both of these over the finish line."
Back in Indiana, Lewis' stolen food assistance has had a ripple effect. Her mother, Johna Hammontree, says she typically lives paycheck to paycheck, but has been stretching every dollar to ensure her daughter and granddaughter do not go hungry.
"It's really, really rough for me already," Hammontree says. "But I will take from my rent money, my bill money, my grocery money … Whatever I need to pull from financially to make sure that she's okay."

Ukraine is counting on its partnership with the United States despite what President Volodymyr Zelensky described as “some difficulties” over Starlink satellite communications and intelligence sharing, as Kyiv grapples with Russia’s attacks, AFP reported.
Visiting London on Wednesday, Zelensky called on US tech billionaire Elon Musk to “switch on” the Starlink system, which Ukrainian officials say has experienced restrictions affecting military operations.
“We count on partnership with the United States, we just want to be very honest, very clear, be strong partners,” Zelensky said, acknowledging the difficulties Kyiv was facing over Starlink and intelligence.
A senior Ukrainian official told AFP on Wednesday that Starlink data communication speeds had been “throttled”. The reported restrictions have raised concerns in Kyiv over its reliance on the satellite internet network for battlefield communications, drone operations and military logistics.
Ukraine has reported disruptions to Starlink services used by its military, with restrictions affecting satellite terminals that help guide combat drones, as per AFP report.
The reported change could affect mobile military platforms, including aerial drones, which may lose connectivity when travelling above that speed.
A source from Ukraine’s defence ministry told AFP that the restrictions were complicating drone missions, particularly those involving interceptor drones and medium-range strikes.
They were also reducing capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance and communications relays, as per AFP.
Starlink has become a crucial part of Ukraine’s military communications infrastructure since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Its satellite links support operations in areas where conventional communications are unreliable or vulnerable to disruption.
Drones have emerged as a central weapon in the war, used for reconnaissance, attacks and intercepting incoming aerial threats. Reliable satellite connectivity is particularly important for remotely controlled systems operating over long distances or in areas where ground-based signals are limited.
Any sustained disruption could therefore affect not only Ukraine’s ability to conduct drone strikes but also its defensive operations, surveillance and the movement of supplies near the front lines.
The reported Starlink restrictions come amid renewed strain in Ukraine’s relationship with Washington.
A senior Ukrainian official accused the United States of failing to warn Kyiv about incoming Russian strikes and of contributing to the communications difficulties, according to reports.
Starlink is operated by SpaceX, the satellite and space company controlled by Musk, who is an ally of US President Donald Trump.

The Delhi High Court on Wednesday (October 14, 2026) asked the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the Centre, and the Delhi government to respond to a petition raising concerns over the sale of dairy analogue or non-dairy products as paneer (cottage cheese) to unsuspecting consumers.
While paneer is a standardised dairy product under the food safety regime, a non-dairy, analogue product contains non-milk ingredients and lacks the same nutritional value, the petitioners contended.
A Bench of acting Chief Justice Nitin W. Sambre and Justice Sanjay Singh issued notices to the FSSAI, the Union government, and the Delhi government on the petition filed by Ridhima Singh and Avlokiteshwar Padmapani Sidharth, and asked them to file their replies within six weeks.
The petitioners contended that a person consuming a paneer-based product in a hotel or a restaurant had no means to know whether the dish had been prepared using actual paneer or a dairy analogue.
They sought urgent directions from the court in view of the festive season, asserting that the authorities should undertake sampling and testing of paneer and products represented as paneer in the market.
“They are doing it; they have placed the statistics [before us] to that effect,” the Bench responded.
Gujarat, Punjab, Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra have already taken steps against non-dairy paneer, the plea said, seeking directions to prevent the manufacture, supply, sale or service of dairy analogue paneer in the national capital.
The plea also prayed for directions to the authorities to ensure that hotels, restaurants, caterers, eateries, cloud kitchens and e-commerce food businesses provided clear disclosure on the use of analogue/non-dairy substitutes in their food.
“A consumer who knowingly purchases a product correctly disclosed as an analogue or non-dairy substitute makes an informed choice. However, a consumer who purchases or orders paneer is entitled to receive a product which answers the statutory description of paneer and ought not to be unknowingly supplied a product in which essential milk constituents have been substituted by vegetable fat, vegetable oil or other non-milk constituents,” the petition said.

A Bengaluru-based employee has sparked a discussion on Reddit after claiming that his manager placed him on a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) days before a planned Dussehra trip to his hometown and subsequently denied his leave request. The employee said he works at a retail-focused company in Bengaluru and joined the organisation around four months ago. In the comments section, he clarified that he is a fresher. According to his Reddit post, he had booked tickets to travel home for Dussehra and spend time with his family. However, his plans were disrupted after a performance review meeting in which his manager reportedly raised concerns about his output and placed him on a PIP. The employee said his manager informed him that his performance was not meeting expectations during the review. "Today we had my performance review and he put me under PIP saying I'm not giving the expected output or performance," the employee wrote. He said he subsequently requested two days of leave to celebrate the festival with his family, but his manager rejected the request because he was on a PIP. "Later I asked him regarding my holidays for 2 days to spend time with my family for occasion. But he rejected it saying I'm under PIP and can't give any holidays," the post read. The employee also claimed that he had not received written communication confirming the PIP and alleged that his leave requests had been rejected previously. "But they didn't give any written confirmation on my PIP. What should I do now? I'm really confused and stressed," he wrote. The employee said he had booked travel tickets the previous week for about ₹5,000 and was looking forward to visiting his hometown after a long gap. "I really want to go home and spend time with my family as it's been long time since I went home and my parents are excited and waiting on my arrival," he added. The post prompted discussion among Reddit users about workplace pressure, performance reviews and the implications of being placed on a PIP shortly before a planned holiday. Several users commented that this is the new layoff strategy. "Its just my opinion in your place I would have gone home. Looks like they are aiming to get u removed," one user wrote. Another commenter described PIPs as "the new layoff strategy," adding: "Go home, enjoy the festival and start looking for another job." Other users advised the employee to consider alternative job opportunities while assessing whether he could meet the expectations set out in the performance review process. One commenter argued that PIPs can involve demanding targets and may not always result in an employee being retained. "It is the norm to put people on PIP, dump unreasonable expectations, tell them they'll be retained if they perform well and eventually let them go," the commenter wrote. Another Reddit user advised the employee to focus on future opportunities if he believed he would struggle to clear the PIP. "PIP in very rare scenario turns positive. If you somewhere believe you will not be able to pass it, start job hunting after your holidays," the comment read. Won't accept lame excuses: SC pulls up ECI over missing 2023 Sringeri poll footage
The Supreme Court of India pulled up the Election Commission of India over its inability to trace the 2023 Sringeri vote-counting video, directing it to produce whatever records are available by the next hearing and warning that it could draw an adverse inference against the poll body.
The Supreme Court on Wednesday took a stern view of the Election Commission of India's (ECI) inability to trace a video recording of the 2023 vote counting in Karnataka's Sringeri Assembly constituency, warning that it could draw an adverse inference against the poll body if it failed to produce the available records at the next hearing.
A bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva expressed surprise at the Election Commission's submission that it could not locate the footage, questioning how the poll body could lose records relating to an election it was responsible for conducting.
"How can the Election Commission of India (ECI) say that it has lost its record? Your whole purpose is to hold an election, and you need to have a document," the bench said, as reported by Bar and Bench.
The court rejected the ECI's explanation that efforts were being made to trace the recording and directed it to produce whatever records it had on the next date of hearing. The matter has been posted for February 15, 2027.
SUPREME COURT WARNS OF ADVERSE INFERENCE AGAINST ECI
The court's observations came during the hearing of a dispute over the Sringeri Assembly seat, where Congress leader TD Rajegowda was initially declared the winner in the 2023 Karnataka Assembly elections by a margin of just 201 votes.
BJP candidate DN Jeevaraj subsequently challenged Rajegowda's election victory, triggering legal proceedings that eventually led to a recount of postal ballots and a change in the declared result.
During Wednesday's hearing, the bench was told that Rajegowda wanted access to the election observer's report and video recordings of both the original counting exercise in 2023 and the subsequent recount.
When the court indicated that the ECI should produce the relevant documents and recordings, senior advocate Seshadri Naidu, appearing for the poll body, said the video of the original counting could not be traced.
The explanation did not satisfy the bench, which questioned the Commission's responsibility for preserving election records.
"Where is the question of you saying, ‘Yeah, we are trying to trace it’? You gave it to the elected candidate. There is no custody of records," the court said, according to Bar and Bench.
The bench reiterated that the Commission must place whatever material was available before it at the next hearing, warning that failure to do so could have consequences.
"Whatever you have, produce it on the next date. Otherwise, we will have to draw an adverse inference against you. We will not accept these kinds of lame excuses," the court said, as reported by Bar and Bench.
HOW A RECOUNT CHANGED THE RESULT IN SRINGERI
The dispute stems from Jeevaraj's election petition before the Karnataka High Court, challenging Rajegowda's victory in the 2023 Assembly election.
On April 6, the High Court ordered a recount of postal ballot votes, including the re-verification of 279 postal ballots that had initially been rejected.
Following the exercise, the returning officer formally declared a revised result on May 3, 2026. Rajegowda's vote tally was reportedly reduced by 255 votes, and Jeevaraj was declared the winner.
Rajegowda subsequently approached the Supreme Court, challenging the revised result and the process adopted during the recount.
CONGRESS MLA ALLEGES RECOUNT WENT BEYOND COURT'S ORDER
In his plea before the Supreme Court, Rajegowda argued that the High Court had ordered only the re-verification of 279 rejected postal ballots. He alleged that the returning officer went beyond that direction by reconsidering 562 postal ballots that had already been accepted as valid and were in his favour.
He has also challenged the High Court's judgment ordering the recount, questioning why the exercise was necessary when the court had recorded findings favourable to him on corruption allegations raised by Jeevaraj.
The demand for the original counting footage and the observer's report is part of Rajegowda's effort to challenge the process that led to his removal from the seat.
In May, the Supreme Court granted him interim relief, directing that he would continue as an MLA while his plea remained pending.

In the 54th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu, Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, discuss the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, experimental approaches to studying human brain development, and incidents from Uttar Pradesh and Meghalaya that highlight barriers to healthcare access.
The episode begins with the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded jointly to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The discussion explains how optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins to control the electrical activity of selected nerve cells. By activating or inhibiting specific neurons, researchers can investigate how neural circuits influence movement, memory, emotions and behaviour. The technique has become an important tool in neuroscience research, including studies of neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, it remains largely a research tool and is not a routine treatment for brain disorders.
The next segment examines an experimental approach described as ‘xenocortication’, in which human brain tissue is transplanted into the brains of mice. Researchers have been exploring this approach to study aspects of human brain development that are difficult to reproduce in laboratory-grown cells or animal models alone. The discussion looks at how the transplanted tissue may receive a blood supply, develop connections and interact with its surroundings within a living brain. The approach could help researchers investigate human neuronal development and mechanisms involved in neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders. However, it remains experimental, and findings from such models cannot be assumed to reflect human brain development fully. The work also raises ethical questions about the use of human neural tissue in animal research.
The episode then turns to barriers to healthcare access, examining how social discrimination and inadequate infrastructure can prevent people from receiving medical care. In Uttar Pradesh, a Dalit woman was allegedly denied admission to a government hospital while in labour and was forced to deliver outside the facility. Her family alleged that untouchability was involved. The incident highlights how discrimination can obstruct access to care even when a health facility is physically available.
Another incident in Meghalaya’s West Khasi Hills district, an ill child died in his mother’s arms while his parents were making a three-hour trek to reach the nearest hospital. According to the village headman, the family had tried to arrange a vehicle after the child’s condition deteriorated, but no driver was willing to travel to the village because of the poor road conditions. The incident draws attention to the difficulties faced by people in remote areas, where distance, road connectivity and the availability of transport can delay access to emergency medical care.
The episode ends with a fun-fact segment on why mice are widely used in laboratory experiments. The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

Samsung Health's sleep coaching now requires just three days of data
It will then build a tailored four- to eight-week program based on your goals and habits.
Samsung Health has offered Sleep Coaching for several years, but using it required a full week of consecutive sleep data in a month. With this new update, the app will let users start Sleep Coaching faster and provide more personalized sleep guidance. The update also brings a few new features for runners.
With the new version, anyone using a Galaxy Watch 4 series or later model (or the Galaxy Fit 3 or Galaxy Ring) can start Sleep Coaching with just three days of sleep data from the past two weeks.
When setting it up, you need to fill out a survey around your sleep regularity and interruptions, along with alcohol and caffeine intake. It will also ask you to rate how satisfied you are with your sleep. Using your survey responses and three days of data, Health will assign you a personalized Sleep Animal symbol and tailor a four- to eight-week coaching program to your goals.
As you progress, the app will adjust its weekly recommendations to your changing sleep patterns, while tracking your daily sleep satisfaction. It will also provide daily habit checklists and sleep tips, like avoiding screens and caffeine before bed or stretching outdoors after waking up—all based on behavioral sleep science.
Users will get more intuitive, detailed analysis reports, with a five-sided Sleep Balance graph showing sleep time, sleep regularity, nighttime wakefulness, sleep satisfaction and an "Energy Score" to highlight areas needing attention. It also provides daily morning insight messages that review your previous night's sleep and offer helpful tips.
Samsung is also boosting its Running Coach app for a more "dynamic and connected training experience." Tiers have expanded from 10 to 12 levels to better support intermediate and advanced runners, allowing them to set higher benchmarks and challenge themselves.
The app is also adding enhanced social media sharing for milestones, personal records and route highlights, along with a new partnership with the fitness platform Strava. "Users can import their favorite Strava Routes for running, trail running, and cycling directly into Samsung Health," the company said. The new features will begin rolling out this month.

Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, a rumor circulated that U.S. President Trump said he would be "the last Republican president."
People on X and Reddit shared the alleged quote, with some including a video clip. In the clip, Trump appeared to make the comment during a political rally. 
The quote was correctly attributed to Trump.
However, some posts sharing the quote and accompanying video clip omitted context clarifying Trump's meaning. He was referring to a hypothetical scenario where Democrats control both houses of Congress and the White House, suggesting their policies would result in him being "the last Republican president." 
The president made the comment during a speech at a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on Oct. 12. At the rally, Trump endorsed incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted and the Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, who are on the ballot for Ohio's midterm elections.
Trump's full speech can be viewed on C-SPAN. At the 1:02:00 mark, prior to the statement in question, Trump says, "We achieved more in two years than any other presidency in the history of our country, but now the radical-left Dumocrats want to burn it all down" — using a term he favors for the Democratic Party. 
The president continued to criticize his opponents' alleged voting record, saying, "Every single Dumocrat in Congress voted against our record tax cuts. They voted against no tax on tips. They voted against no tax on overtime, and they voted against no tax on Social Security for our great seniors."
These comments, and others he made later, make it clear that Trump was theorizing he'd be the "last Republican president" if Democrats won key races in the midterm elections and subsequently took control of the White House.
The rest of his statement from the moment in question is as follows (emphasis ours):
They voted against voter ID, and they voted against proof of citizenship when you vote, so why did they do that? Because they want to cheat, OK? I saw a guy interviewed a week ago, a congressman, a Democrat. They said, why don't you want to have somebody show their voter identification or proof of citizenship? "Uh, well, uh. Uh, it's racist. That's right. That's right. It's racist." They come up with more s***, I mean it's …
[applause]
"It's racist. It's racist." They're crazy. They voted against securing our border, and they want to have the border open. You know, if they get in, they're going to open the border, and you're going to have two more states: Washington, D.C., where Republicans get 3% of the vote, and Puerto Rico, where Republicans get 4%. So we'll have four more senators. They want to have 23 people on the Supreme Court. They want to end the Senate, so you guys will be out of a job. What are you doing running? You'll be out of a job based on them. They want to end the Senate.
They want to basically destroy our country and that's what they want to do and if they get in, they will do that. They'll be able to do that. You know, if they get in and you have a bad presidential election in the next because we have some very good people, but if you had a bad presidential or one of these lunatics got in, you will— Look at me right now. And you will say he's going to be the last Republican president in the history of our country. I will be. I will be. I will be the last Republican president because they will add about 12 more electoral votes. They'll add four more senators. They'll add 10 more congresspeople, approximately. They're going to rig the Supreme Court through … just a lot of people.
The GOP YouTube channel posted a livestream of the entire rally, including the other speakers. In that version, Trump's statement begins at the 2:53:55 mark and matches the content of the C-SPAN clip.

A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.
At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.
Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”
Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”
Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.
An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.
Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.
“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.
Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.
The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.
The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.
The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.
In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.
Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.
According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.
The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.
“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.
Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.
Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.
The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.
Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.
This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”
When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.
Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

Brian K. Vaughan would like to apologize. He knows everyone is dying for details about Dune: Part Three, which he cowrote with director Denis Villeneuve, but his lips are pretty sealed until December 18 when the film finally hits theaters.
“Sorry to be coy,” he says as we’re about to leave the New York coffee shop where we’ve been chatting. “I hope the day will come where I’m able to say much, much more. It was truly so awesome. I can’t believe it happened.”
Vaughan is in the city for New York Comic Con, but not to talk about Dune. Ostensibly, he came to the convention to talk about Paper Girls, the comic he created with Cliff Chiang that was turned into a 2022 Amazon Prime Video series. During the Paper Girls panel, however, the pair announced that they’re working on a new comic, Roam, a superhero sci-fi series set to come out in February of next year.
Roam, Vaughan tells me, came from a deep desire to work with Chiang again. They’d considered doing a short eight-page story or maybe a one-shot, but eventually they said “Fuck it. Let’s do an ongoing series.”
Vaughan has the kind of career writers of a certain ilk would kill for. He started working on comics in the 1990s and has been the pen behind favorites like Saga, Y: The Last Man, and Marvel’s Runaways. (Those last two got turned into TV series; the outlier, Saga, is a story people have wanted to see adapted for years.) He also served as a writer on Lost and created CBS’s adaptation of Stephen King’s Under the Dome.
Still, his heart remains in comics. “I think sometimes people are like, ‘Oh, are you just going to sell out, Vaughan? Are you just going to go to Hollywood full-time?’” he says. “But I’m only able to do work in Hollywood because I have comics.”
Here, he speaks about Roam, his worries about AI, and maybe a little bit about Dune: Part Three as well.
On Roam, his forthcoming comic with Cliff Chiang:
It's completely unlike Paper Girls, completely unlike anything I've ever done. It’s set in the distant, distant future. The logline, as it were, is that in the future, everyone will get to be a superhero, but only while they're young. We're trying not to reveal too much more than that.
I remember seeing The Matrix, and having no idea what the fuck it was gonna be about. That was such a delight. So we're trying to do that here. I've been doing this for 31 years. I started when I was a teenager. I have a Spider-Man story here and there. I did a little Batman, and Ex Machina was my sci-fi political comic that sort of deconstructed the superhero. But this is certainly my first true superhero book.
On his fears about AI impacting comics, film, and TV:
It's terrifying. My friends who work in previsualization and as storyboard artists, these jobs are going away. I've heard about editors going away as well. Show business is a business, first and foremost. I’m lucky to sort of have been grandfathered in. I think there will always be people who are interested in bespoke human-made stories. But the future is terrifying and unknowable, and coming at us very, very quickly.
I’m heartened by the fact I've got two teenagers who are so disgusted by AI and grossed out if they ever hear I used it—and I’ve certainly never used it for anything creative. But I do think we're getting pretty close to the day that someone could be like, “I'm tired of waiting for the next issue. Give me the next issue of Saga.” That's when you get to the point of, do you just want content, something that's a distraction?
In Roam there's an element of this as well; AI is a component in the story. So, it's something I guess I need to write about with my human meat machine to process, but I'm in the middle of thinking about it, as you are, every day.
OK, a little bit about Dune: Part Three, which he has seen:
I can't say very much other than it’s a tremendous, insane, ridiculous honor to be involved with it, and my contributions are modest. Denis’ true cowriter on this is Frank Herbert. The novel is the star. And it's obviously the greatest cast and crew ever assembled. It's a fucking beautiful movie. It's my favorite of the three. which I can say with genuine humility. I can't say anything other than it's just as wonderful as you can imagine.
I got special thanks in the first movie. I was doing a tiny amount of consulting. I was working at Legendary [the media company that owns the rights to Dune] at the time, and they just invited me in to see an early cut, which was as fantastic as the finished product. But I just ended up talking to Denis, honestly. Never before has a director been that talented, also that decent and warm as a human being. I wasn't anticipating getting this call at the beginning of three, but it's obviously a call I could not refuse.
I should probably just be discreet at this point. The movie doesn't need me to promote it. I'm reluctant to do anything that makes me sound more important to this process.
On the future of Hollywood:
I am a small worker in the world of Hollywood. It is changing so rapidly that who knows what it's gonna be like tomorrow, six months from now.
But again, I've got teenagers and I see how delighted they were by Backrooms, by Obsession. It feels like Gen X has been force-feeding them a lot of my childhood stories that we have gussied up, and they are clearly hungry for something new.
On why he doesn’t write adaptations of his own comics:
I've taken stabs at it in the past. Richard Price, the novelist, I once heard him say in response to “Why don't you adapt your own stuff more?” that adapting your own work is like being a dentist and giving yourself a root canal. Just because you can do it, doesn't mean you should. Let some other motherfucker handle that. I believe those were Mr. Price's words.
It's been constructive and a thrill to adapt other people, and I like getting to watch other people adapt me, but I've also been doing a lot of it for the last decade, where it feels like I've either been adapting or being adapted. I think that was part of the siren song of Roam. It’s time to break some new ground.
Denis says that to adapt something you love is to do violence to it. When I've been adapted, that has always been what I've told people. It is much more important for this to be good than to be faithful. He's a master of cinema, and cinema is rarely about people sitting in a room having dialog. How do you transliterate this to cinema? That's an alchemy that I don't understand. He's just unparalleled at that.
On Lost and why writing for commercial breaks was a challenge:
I love my prestige drama without commercials, but there was a degree of difficulty working on Lost and having a cliff-hanger five times an episode. To have that was such a challenge and so rewarding when you were able to pull it off. Can you write something where people are like, “OK, I'll just wet my pants. I cannot risk not coming back [before the break is over].”

Image of mournful elephant mom wins 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year
Youth award goes to photo of hard-working dung beetle
(Federico Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)
An Italian photographer's "heartbreakingly poignant" photo of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf has won this year's top Wildlife Photographer of the Year award.
Federico Veronesi captured "The Aftermath" while tracking elephants in the Huab River Valley in Namibia. He noticed unusual drag marks in the sand of the dry riverbed. When he caught up to a family of elephants, he saw an adult female with a calf's leg wedged between her tusk and trunk.
Kathy Moran, chair of the jury for the 2026 competition, described the photo as working on "so many levels."
"Emotionally it's a gut punch, heartbreakingly poignant. Intellectually, it's proof that animals have cognition," she wrote in a news release announcing the winners.
In addition to winning the grand prize, the photo also won the Behaviour: Mammals category.
Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the U.K.-based Natural History Museum in London, with a stated goal to share nature's stories and insights about environmental challenges that need our attention.
This year, the annual competition — the 62nd edition — attracted 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories.
It awards top prizes to both an adult photographer and a young photographer under 18.
This year's Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year prize was won by Oscar Whitfield, a young British photographer who grew up in Zimbabwe and frequently returns there during school holidays.
His photo, captured while lying on the ground, shows a close-up of a dung beetle hard at work pushing a ball of dung. It was also the winner in the 11 to 14 years age bracket.
(Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the year)
Officially, there were no Canadian category winners this year. However, Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, who lives in Germany and won this year's Rising Star Award, is a Canadian citizen who has previously told CBC News his parents were both born in Canada, and he has relatives in Ottawa and Nova Scotia.
His featured photo, "Afternoon snack," is a close-up of a robber fly preying on a flesh fly. "The bubbles forming in the victim's eyes indicate that the robber fly has injected digestive enzymes that liquefy its internal tissues before they are sucked out," the photo's description reads.
(Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)
Canadians can see the 100-photo exhibition at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto from Nov 7, 2026, to Feb 28, 2027, or at the Royal B.C. Museum in Victoria from Feb. 12, 2027, until April 18, 2027.
It opens at the Natural History Museum in London this Friday.
Here are some of the other category winners.
Amelie Davis, of the U.K., won the 10 years and under bracket with this photo of a common carder bee in southern England, captured with her father's smartphone.
(Amelie Davis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)
A California newt lays eggs while clasping vegetation that already contains another newt's egg clutch in the winner of the Amphibians and Reptiles category, captured by U.S. photographer Anton Sorokin. The newt will stay like this until the egg mass swells to a size too large to be eaten by a predator.
(Anton Sorokin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)
Greek photographer Agorastos Papatsanis used UV light to make these fluorescent bonnet mushrooms glow brightly on a decaying log on the lower slopes of Greece's Mount Olympus. The image won the Plants and Fungi category.
(Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)
A young bull elephant sprays water on a group of zebras at a waterhole in the Chyulu Hills of Kenya in this photo, the winner of the Animals in their Environment category, captured by James Lewin using a camera converted to infrared to soften harsh lighting.
(James Lewin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Google has already added a few AI features to the Play Store, but a lot more are coming. The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google’s app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder. For people who have embraced AI to build their own apps, the Play Store will soon offer a way to privately host and share those creations.
Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon.
Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google’s app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA.
You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations. There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games. Game Finder also lets you add or remove tags to further adjust the games Google’s AI suggests. Google says you’ll eventually be able to prompt Game Finder with fairly specific game preferences, but it’s unclear how much customization will be available at launch. Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.”

20 green sea turtles returned to the ocean after Bali smuggling raid
Indonesian authorities on the tourist island of Bali have released 20 protected green sea turtles back into the ocean Tuesday
SERANGAN ISLAND, Indonesia -- Indonesian authorities on the tourist island of Bali released 20 protected green sea turtles back into the ocean Tuesday after they were found and seized on an empty boat seemingly abandoned by wildlife smugglers fleeing a police raid.
Officers conducted final checks on the turtles at a conservation center on Serangan Island, also known as Turtle Island, in southern Bali. They then carefully lifted the turtles using blue cloths and transported them by small truck to the shoreline.
Marine police officers in Bali on Saturday foiled an attempt to smuggle 22 green sea turtles, known by the scientific name Chelonia mydas, in the waters off Serangan Island after receiving a report from residents who suspected sea turtle smuggling activity in the area.
Two of the 22 turtles are still sick and need to be treated before they can also be released, Gusti Agung Purnama Wirahadi from the Bali Water and Air Police said Tuesday.
All of the turtles, which are protected species in Indonesia, were found alive on the boat, but the suspected smugglers had already fled the scene by the time officers arrived.
“We hope that no one will dare to capture, keep, or trade these protected species anymore,” Wirahadi said.
Turtle species in Indonesia have been legally protected under conservation and fisheries laws since 1990. A 2018 Environment Ministry regulation further clarified protections for the six species of sea turtles found in the country’s waters. Additional government regulations also prohibit their trade.
According to a 2022 global study by researchers at Arizona State University, the green sea turtle accounted for 56% of sea turtle killings in the 30-year period to 2020.
Bali was once a major hub for green sea turtle trafficking, driven in part by the historical use of turtle meat in offerings in Balinese Hinduism, the predominant religion on the island of about 4.5 million people.
In June, authorities in Bali foiled an attempt to illegally trade 21 protected green sea turtles during a raid on the island’s Pegametan coast and arrested a 67-year-old man suspected of storing the protected animals before they were distributed for sale.

These Are the Best Kindles You Can Buy
Featured in this article
There’s a lot for readers to love about a Kindle. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to get unlimited books from Amazon or use the device to access free books via your local library. But how are you supposed to know which model to buy, given the many options available?
I’ve owned all kinds of Kindles, including the newest Kindle Aluminum and a seasoned hand-me-down device that lacks a front light. Between all of my testing, I've found that many options offer great value for specific uses.
Read on to find out my favorite Kindle overall, along with my top Kindle recommendations for young readers and other individual needs. While you're at it, check out my other buying guides for readers, including the Best Kindle Accessories, Best E-Readers, Best Digital Notebooks, and Best Gifts for Book Lovers.
Updated October 2026: I’ve added the newest Kindle (2026, 12th Gen) as my affordable Kindle pick if the previous Kindle (2024, 11th Gen) isn’t on sale. I’ve also added notes on the Kindle Aluminum and ensured up-to-date pricing.

What Are the Newest Kindles?
Amazon recently announced a whole new generation of Kindles is coming, with every model getting a new version. I'll update this guide with thoughts as I review each new model. Here are the current details:
- Kindle (2026, 12th Generation) for $150: This is the new version of the base Kindle. Many features will sound familiar (a 6-inch screen, six weeks of battery life, and 16 GB of storage), but it comes with a new flush-front design for the screen and a lighter weight. It also shares a $150 price tag with the older base Kindle, which became more expensive as of August. You can upgrade to the Aluminum version that has a more premium feel and additional color options, plus 32 GB of storage. Both versions are available now, and I've included them in my notes above.
- Kindle Paperwhite (2026, 13th Generation) for $200: The 2026 Kindle Paperwhite will still pack a waterproof design and 12 weeks of battery life (my favorite part!), but its updated display is the largest yet among Paperwhite devices, and with a higher contrast ratio. The Signature Edition has aluminum backing and also packs dock charging with pogo pins on the back and a double-tap capability to turn pages. The regular Paperwhite is available for preorder and retails for $200 (same as the old model) with 16 GB of storage and comes in only black. The Paperwhite Signature Edition is on preorder for $250 and comes in two colors with 32 GB of storage. Preorder is available on a rolling basis in various regions, so if you're not able to reserve your model yet, check again soon.
- Kindle Colorsoft (2026, 2nd Generation) for $290: The Kindle Colorsoft's second-generation model has an updated display and edge-to-edge color that promises a richer look than what the first generation offered. The update also gets a flush-front design, similar to the other new Kindle models, and is available in a Signature Edition that has aluminum backing, an auto-adjusting front light, pogo points for charging, and the double-tap page-turning capability. The new Colorsoft is available for preorder at $290 with 16 GB of storage, and the new Colorsoft Signature Edition is available for preorder at $320 with 32 GB of storage and two device colors to choose from.
