- Kindle Kids models starting at $180: All three of the above models have a Kids version that will include kid-friendly covers and up to 12 months of Amazon Kids+ content. The base Kindle Kids is available now, while others are on preorder in certain regions.
Kindle is also releasing a handful of new accessories, including the Kindle Click ($35) Bluetooth remote that will work with Kindle models as early as 2024, a Page Turn Cover ($80) that will only work with the Paperwhite and Colorsoft Signature Editions, a Charging Dock ($60) designed to work with the pogo pins on the Signature Editions, and new Kindle covers in a variety of colors and textures. I’m most excited about the remote; I will update this guide and our Best Kindle Accessories guide with my notes as I test.
Why Are Kindles More Expensive Now?
Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only Kindle Scribe models with their original price tags. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. Interestingly, none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it’s also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.
Here are all the increases, including for the Signature versions:
- Amazon Kindle (2024, 11th Gen): $150 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen): $200 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature (2024, 12th Gen): $250 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft: $290 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature: $320 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Kids (2024, 2nd Gen): $180 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Kids: $300 (up $30)
If you have your eyes on one of these Kindles, I’d wait until Black Friday to shop, as they'll likely be on sale.
What About the New Kindle Scribes?
Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There are now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light.
All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, a slightly slimmer form factor, and an updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you’re reading without giving spoilers, though those won’t arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can’t do.
Overall, I’d say they’re good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it’s the better buy. It has some AI capabilities but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design seen on the new ones. Amazon said it’ll get the same homepage this year, but I haven’t seen it so far. I’m disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable’s line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.
Accessories for Easier Reading
Ever had an e-reading session so long that you get hand cramps? These accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.
Cases and Covers
Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you’re frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren’t padded for serious drops, but they are some of the best Kindle cases I’ve found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs. Also, don’t forget that the Kids’ editions come with cases, so if you’re buying one of those, you won’t need to buy a case.
About Those Older Kindles
Amazon usually takes a few years between new Kindle models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor’s stock starts to dwindle. It’s not that I don’t recommend these older models per se, but I only suggest them if you they're on sale for the right price. And don’t buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.
Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you’re paying a fair amount less for the older device.
Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one, with 16 GB of storage and a 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution. It’s tough to find, and I usually don’t see it for less than $75 these days.
Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It’s waterproof, too. I like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 GBs of storage. I don’t recommend spending more than $100 on this one.
Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It’s only worth it for $230 or less, and I often see it for below $200 on eBay.
Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it’s only available secondhand means you’ll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, you won't spend more than $70 on this one.
Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn’t spend more than $110 on this one if you can find it at all. (I couldn't find any resellers for this older model at the time of writing.)
Frequently Asked Questions
Which Kindle Models Lost Amazon Support and Kindle Store Access?
As of May 20, 2026, Amazon stopped supporting Kindles released in 2012 or earlier. That means these models will not be able to get new books through Amazon’s services or be registered to an Amazon account. You will be able to read books already on the device, though, and can manually download documents and books via USB cable and via software like Calibre.
The following Kindle devices are impacted:
- Kindle 1st Generation
- Kindle 2nd Generation
- Kindle DX
- Kindle DX Graphite
- Kindle Keyboard 3rd Generation
- Kindle 4
- Kindle Touch
- Kindle 5
- Kindle Paperwhite 1st Generation
What’s the Best Way to Buy or Sell an Older Kindle?
Have an old Kindle lying around? Considering buying a used one? If you’re trying to figure out which model you're dealing with, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model.
Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It’s best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you may still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway.
How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle?
If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but it features millions of titles, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial.
If you already pay for a Prime account, you’re eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. It doesn't include as many options as Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you’ll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you’ll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It’s still something, though, and there are even a few magazines.
If you don’t want another monthly subscription and don’t want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can’t read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways:
- Get a library card for your local branch.
- Check your branch’s website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.
- Download directly to your Kindle library. The titles in question will automatically be removed when they’re due back.
If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books are loanable.
What Else Can a Kindle Do?
Kindles have other helpful features you may want to use. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages.
Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it’s not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations and a Wikipedia page, if applicable.
While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type. There’s a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu, too.
When a Kindle connects to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you’ve pressed. It can also read a book aloud, though it doesn’t sound nearly as nice as an audiobook.
Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you’ve read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads.
There’s also a web browser if you’re connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It’s not the best, so I’d reserve it for emergency searches.
How Do You Update a Kindle?
When Amazon releases a new software update, it will download and install to your Kindle automatically when the device is connected to Wi-Fi. You can check if you’re on the latest software by going to Settings > Device Options > Advanced Options > Update Your Kindle. If it’s not on the latest software version, you’ll see an update available and the Kindle will then prompt you to download and install it.
What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar?
Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft.
Is Now a Good Time to Buy a Kindle?
The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day, Prime Big Deals Days, Black Friday, or Cyber Monday, when Amazon often offers steep discounts on its products.
Are Kindles Good for Students?
Kindles are great for students, though the model that's best for each student depends on how they'll use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, they should consider a Kindle Scribe model. These have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. Some textbooks are also available on Kindles. For students who love to read but don’t want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will work well.

Cheetahs to play European games in Swansea
- Published
South African side Cheetahs will play their European Challenge Cup home matches this season at St Helen's in Swansea, the home of Welsh side Ospreys.
Cheetahs host Dragons on Sunday, 13 December and Perpignan on Sunday, 17 January with both games a day after Ospreys' home matches in the same competition.
Cheetahs have traditionally used Europe as a base for matches in the second-tier tournament, with games in the 2025-26 season taking place in Amsterdam.
There are links between Ospreys and Cheetahs. Y11 Sports & Media owns a majority stake in the Ospreys and maintain an investment interest in the South African team with players moving between both sides.
The Ospreys' first game at the redeveloped St Helen's is scheduled to be the United Rugby Championship (URC) Welsh derby against Dragons on Saturday, 24 October.
"The Ospreys are grateful to the WRU for its permission to play these matches at St Helen's," said Ospreys managing director Richard Lancaster.
"We're excited to welcome the Toyota Cheetahs for these two EPCR Challenge Cup fixtures. There is already a strong relationship between the two clubs and this is another really positive step in developing that further.
"It also demonstrates the opportunities that St Helen's can create. Having our own venue gives us the ability to bring additional high-quality rugby and events to Swansea."
Cheetahs director of rugby is former South Africa international Frans Steyn.
"It's great to be welcomed so warmly by our friends in rugby, the Ospreys," Steyn said.
"St Helen's has a proud history, and we're looking forward to playing there, experiencing the newly redeveloped stadium and making it our home in Europe."

Epic thinks you'll love its new vibe coded game launcher
Laying off workers for AI is nothing to celebrate.
There's no two ways about: the Epic Games Store (EGS) launcher is bad. Even Epic CEO Tim Sweeney has admitted as much, describing it as "clunky" in an interview with podcaster Lex Fridman last year. So you would think a redesign would be good news, right? Think again. Because the way Epic has decided to promote this release fails to read the room.
"Programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that's way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look," the company gleefully writes by way of introduction in its latest Epic Games Store blog post. The announcement comes just one day after Sweeney said Epic was in the midst of a major AI pivot. "The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal," he wrote on X.
We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration.
The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.
— Tim Sweeney (@TimSweeneyEpic) October 12, 2026
Even by Sweeney's standards, the post comes off as tone deaf. It was only this past March that the company carried out sweeping layoffs that cut its workforce by 1,000 employees. By Engadget's estimate, Epic had reduced its headcount by a quarter from the 4,000 employees that remained after it carried out an earlier set of layoffs in 2023. And now we have this release which celebrates vibe coding instead of the hard work of Epic's remaining engineers.
Admittedly the new launcher addresses some of the major issues of its predecessor, and in my testing it's definitely less "clunky" than the previous version. Epic says it's capable of launching faster than Steam. Speaking of Steam, the new software allows you to access any games you've installed on your computer through Valve's launcher from its own interface. The redesigned launcher is also available on Linux, a first for the company, which is great news for those of you who want to ditch Windows once and for all.
What it doesn't do is fix the identify crisis EGS has suffered from for years. There's no feature or hook you'll find here that's not available on Steam or GOG. Epic could use this new experience as a base to build those features, but if I'm honest, I would rather not support a company that is eager to replace its employees with AI.

McKinsey has removed senior partner Chris Bradley from his leadership roles after comments he made on LinkedIn questioning the “glass cliff” phenomenon drew criticism. Bradley, who is based in Australia, was until recently one of a handful of directors at the McKinsey Global Institute, the consulting firm’s business and economics research arm. His removal from the leadership roles took effect on October 11. He remains a senior partner at the firm. A McKinsey spokesperson said Bradley’s comments fell short of the standards expected at the company. “Following our conduct review process, we have removed the partner from his leadership roles, including at the McKinsey Global Institute. His public comments fell well short of the standards we expect at our firm,” McKinsey spokesman Taylor Burns said in a statement Sunday. Bradley also served as a leader on some internal committees, Burns said. The controversy followed a LinkedIn exchange between Bradley and author Julia Carreon. A friend of Carreon had shared a post about the “glass cliff” phenomenon, which describes a situation in which women are appointed to senior leadership positions at organisations already facing difficulties. Bradley questioned the concept in his response to the post. “This theory is a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain and empowered in the sunshine,” he wrote, “I am not going to start researching glass cliffs as I don’t think it ranks in the top 1,000 problems of the world." In another post, Bradley questioned whether women leaders faced a distinct disadvantage when taking on difficult roles. “We once had a problem of female advancement to CEO (chief executive officer), but now we have a new problem that the jobs they get are too hard? Is this actually a thing?” His remarks about women CEOs were considered disparaging by many. The posts were subsequently deleted. The term “glass cliff” describes a pattern in which women are more likely to be appointed to leadership positions when an organisation is experiencing a crisis, declining performance or other significant challenges. The concept was coined in 2005 by British psychologists Michelle K Ryan and Alexander Haslam of the University of Exeter. Their research examined the performance of FTSE 100 companies before and after women joined their boards. They found that companies appointing women were more likely to have experienced poor performance in the months leading up to those appointments. The concept suggests that women who break through into senior leadership may face a different set of challenges from those encountered by leaders appointed under more favourable circumstances. The term builds on the idea of the “glass ceiling”, which refers to invisible barriers that prevent women from advancing to senior positions. While the glass ceiling concerns obstacles to reaching leadership roles, the glass cliff focuses on the circumstances in which those roles are offered and the risks leaders may inherit. The distinction is central to the debate surrounding Bradley’s comments: the glass cliff is a specific hypothesis about leadership appointments and organisational performance, rather than a claim that every woman appointed as CEO is being set up to fail. Are the European Women's World Cup play-offs working?
- Published
The ease in which England saw off Greece in round one of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs showed just how inefficient the structure currently is.
The two-time European champions were superior in every sense as they won 8-1 on aggregate against a Greece side ranked 55 places lower in the world.
Realistically, Greece stood little chance in a two-legged tie against Sarina Wiegman's side despite performing well in their home 3-1 defeat.
England's resounding victory was not a one-off as Europe's other top nations, who were forced to drop into the play-offs, also met lower-ranked opposition and won emphatically.
It was not an evening that truly reflects the growth of European women's football, which has become more competitive than ever in recent years.
It was, however, indicative that the qualification process perhaps needs reviewing by Uefa.
Why did we see heavy scorelines?
One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification.
The Netherlands, 2017 European champions, finished second in their group behind France, ranked sixth in the world. They went on to beat Hungary 11-0 on aggregate.
Norway, World Cup winners in 1995 and six-time European finalists, lost out to giants Germany in their group and ended up beating Romania 8-0.
Other League A fallouts Sweden and the Republic of Ireland thrashed their opponents 15-0 and 12-0 respectively.
So it was no surprise when back-to-back European champions England, who were drawn in the same group as world champions Spain, went on to record another heavy victory against much weaker opposition from League C in their play-off.
"Of course we wanted to qualify straight away, that's not the case," said England manager Wiegman when asked about the qualification process again on Tuesday.
"For us now, the facts are that we are in the play-offs, we have played Greece, now we're through, and now we're going to play Ukraine. That's what my focus is on.
"Uefa will review how things are set up and see whether they think it works or it should be better, or different. I don't think it's my place now to review that."
The Lionesses still have another two-legged tie against Ukraine to play, with the first leg taking place away from home on 1 December and the return fixture at Wembley Stadium on 5 December.
Ukraine are a side who England beat twice in the league phase by an aggregate score of 9-1.
It seems absurd that they should have to beat the same team on at least three occasions as part of their qualification process.
England have won seven of their last eight qualifying matches, scoring 21 goals, conceding just six times, and their only defeat was away from home against world champions Spain.
They came runners-up in League A3 only on their head-to-head record with the best team in the world - they even beat Spain 1-0 at Wembley.
England's overall tally of 15 points in the league phase was beaten by just three other teams - Germany, Switzerland and Hungary.
Switzerland and Hungary were also in qualifying groups in League B and League C that did not include a single team from the world's top 45 ranked nations.
In contrast England, who were seeded in League A, had Iceland - ranked 13th - as a tricky opponent, and world number one Spain in their four-team group.
Is the competition good enough?
When qualifying for the 2023 Women's World Cup, England beat Latvia on two occasions, winning 20-0 and 10-0 .
That tournament saw an increase from 24 to 32 teams and while qualification was still one-sided, the showpiece in Australia and New Zealand was a different story.
England were tested against debutants Haiti in the group stages, narrowly winning 1-0, and by Colombia in their quarter-final, despite the South American side failing to qualify for the previous tournament.
The level of competition was growing and it was evident even more so across Europe with England failing to qualify for the 2024 Olympic Games on behalf of Team GB after finishing second to the Netherlands in their Nations League group.
A draw with Portugal and defeat by Belgium were suffered by England the following year, while they were forced to overcome two penalty shootouts in Euro 2025.
There is no denying that England's competition has improved but they were still dealt a rough hand in this year's World Cup qualifying campaign.
Following their costly 4-0 defeat by Spain in June, Wiegman said: "The competition in Europe is really high.
"What I'm disappointed about is that we win five games, we have 15 points and we're in a group with the world champions and then you can't qualify.
"I'm happy with the performances but not the result of us having to go into the play-offs. That's just the way it is."
What is frustrating for England is that while they picked up a routine win over Greece and now prepare to face an opponent they have already played twice in 2026, their potential World Cup rivals are getting to play matches against top-tier teams.
Two of the tournament favourites Germany and Japan met in a friendly match on Tuesday night; Brazil and Argentina played out a 2-2 draw and four-time world champions USA played Spain twice in five days in a mouth-watering meeting.
Fifa has announced that the 2031 Women's World Cup will be expanded from 32 to 48 teams and it is too early to know if that is the right decision.
But while larger scorelines remain, it is clear it is more a direct result of a European qualification process that doesn't benefit the majority.

The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electrical vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.
Imports have been soaring in the last two years with about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids likely to be sold this year.
The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week.
The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures.
Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.
Chinese vehicles or assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subjected to the quota, officials have confirmed but EU companies making cars in China will be subjected to the quota.
As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.
Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China with further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture continuing.
“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” said an official.
Last month the EU called for feedback on a new rule which could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while theMade in Europe legislation would do the same in public procurement.
On Thursday EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument which would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful event, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries.
The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn (€1.18bn) a day trade deficit the EU is now running with China.
Up until recently the EU’s strategy at tackling what they say is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance is to seek to increase imports to China.
Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports.
“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialization,” said an official.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) said Saturday it still doesn't know what caused the death of a young worker at a lab in Russia that focuses on plague and other illnesses.
The UN health agency has cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. Pneumonic plague spreads from person to person, causing a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time.
WHO, in its first full Disease Outbreak News since the case emerged earlier this month, called for a continued investigation.
Russian health officials, it said, had conducted more than 5,500 tests and found no evidence of any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms.
“Additional clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information, including confirmation of the diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker, is required to improve confidence in the assessment,” WHO said.
WHO continued to refer to “a purported second case” that, in emailed explanations to The Associated Press, it previously attributed to two tabloid news outlets in Britain and Serbia that cited unspecified reports in Russia.
Russia has denied any such second case.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.

Vijay Deverakonda is set to take on the titular role in his upcoming film Ranabaali, reuniting with director Rahul Sankrityan after their collaboration on Taxiwaala. Apple has lagged in the smart home race, which Amazon and Google have dominated for a decade with Alexa and Google Assistant (now Gemini), respectively.
But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned.
That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.
Apple announced the products at a media-only event in New York City, and it also revealed a slew of new smart-home gadgets made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric, including a video doorbell, thermostats, and security cameras.
Here's everything you need to know.
The Apple HomeView
The cornerstone of Apple's latest smart-home push is the Apple HomeView, a countertop gadget made up of a 7-inch square display resting on a speaker base. It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple.
It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store. As an alternative, Apple has curated a selection of apps for the system, including Messages, Safari, and FaceTime, alongside select third-party media apps like Spotify. (If an app developer has made an app for the CarPlay standard and it's installed on your iPhone, that app can also populate on the HomeView.)
Siri AI powers the core experience, which Apple revamped this year in iOS 27. Now, Siri can answer broad questions like Gemini or ChatGPT, and it can provide personalized answers; the same personal context Siri has cataloged on your iPhone is accessible to the HomeView. Ask it to open the recipe your friend Alex messaged about, or add a dentist appointment to the family calendar, and it can handle it.
Apple's HomeView supports up to six iCloud profiles, and each person can set up a custom view only visible to them once the device’s camera detects their face. Yes, there’s a camera on the HomeView. The computer vision trick where the HomeView displays a custom view for a specific individual when they approach it only works if the person’s iPhone is on the same Wi-Fi network and was recently unlocked. You need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) to get the most out of the device; you can't set it up with an iPad.
We have a separate story with more details if you'd like to read more about the HomeView, which is available for preorder now and goes on sale November 13 in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India, Singapore, and South Africa. It costs $299.
The Apple Home Collection
One of the biggest problems with Apple's smart-home presence is its relatively meager HomeKit device ecosystem, especially compared to the many smart home devices that can be controlled by Amazon and Google’s platforms. The Matter standard—which allows supported devices like smart bulbs, smart switches, and smart shades to interact with any connected home platform—has helped expand HomeKit support. But Apple is also nudging the ecosystem along with the “Apple Home Collection.”
This new selection of smart-home hardware designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric includes the LG Indoor Camera Plug-In ($200), LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In ($300), LG Video Doorbell ($250), LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($350), LG Smart Thermostat ($200), LG Temperature Sensor ($40), Schneider Home Smart Thermostat ($200), and Schneider Home Room Sensor ($40).
These devices connect to the Apple Home app automatically when you install them, and all of them are controllable through Apple’s products; you don't need separate LG or Schneider accounts or multiple apps.
I got a brief look at some of them in action. The LG Indoor Camera tilts downward when it detects you're home to give you some added privacy, though there's no privacy shutter to block the camera itself. The LG Deadbolt can unlock automatically as you approach by sensing your iPhone or Apple Watch; there's a nice green LED animation that circles the lock to show you when it unlocks. The LG Video Doorbell has two cameras: one to see who is at the door, and one to monitor any packages left at your door.
The LG Outdoor Camera has a floodlight upgrade ($400) that will automatically activate when it detects motion. With the right iCloud+ subscription, you can enable smart video descriptions that send alerts to tell you who is outside (it can recognize faces), that your pet has been spotted in the yard, or that a package has been dropped off.
The products in the Apple Home Collection will be available in December, with the security cameras launching in the UK, US, and Canada. The thermostats and door lock meet North American standards, so Apple is only selling them in the US and Canada.
The HomePod Mini 2
Apple has decided not to launch a successor to the flagship 2023 HomePod 2 smart speaker—maybe it thinks the HomeView, which is essentially a speaker with a screen on it, would cannibalize sales. Instead, it has updated the smaller, cheaper sibling: Say hello to the HomePod Mini 2.
The Mini 2 costs $149, with preorders open now and official sales kicking off October 30. That's a $50 price bump from the original HomePod Mini, though only $30 more if you factor in Apple's recent price hike due to the ongoing memory crisis.
Oddly enough, the HomePod Mini 2 will not have the new Siri AI experience out of the box—that will arrive later on via a software update (and yes, you will need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone to use Siri AI on the HomePod Mini 2). It's otherwise a minor hardware update, resembling the existing HomePod Mini but in new colors: green, white, midnight, pink, and black.
One new feature is Sound Glow—the lights on top of the HomePod Mini 2 will match the album artwork colors of whatever song is playing. It also works with soundscapes, so if you ask Siri to play rain sounds, the lights will display a pitter-patter animation like raindrops falling on a surface.
You can color-match the HomePod Mini 2 to the iMac; pair two of the devices and use them as the default speakers for Apple's all-in-one computer. Apple's S10 chip powers the speaker, the very same processor that debuted on the Apple Watch Series 10.
The Apple TV 4K
Four years since the last Apple TV 4K, Apple finally has a successor. But what may surprise you the most about the fourth-gen streaming box isn't the hardware or features; it's the price: $299.
Apple raised prices on its products earlier this year, but this is a whopping $170 increase for the Apple TV, though this model has Wi-Fi and Ethernet and starts with 128 GB of storage instead of 64 GB on the last version. Preorders are live now, and it ships November 13.
Once again, Siri AI is the star of the show, as Apple touts the ability to ask the assistant for recommendations or play “that show my friend Alinda recommended,” leveraging the personal context from your iPhone. The hardware has three far-field microphones, letting it pick up your voice easily when you're on the couch, even when the TV is playing content. The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.
If you have ever lost your TV remote, you might be more excited that the new Apple TV 4K remote has built-in Find My support. That means you can ping it in the Find My app or ask Siri for its location, and the familiar AirTag chime will play through the remote's speakers. (It supports ultra-wideband, so you can use Apple's precision-finding mode to locate it between the couch cushions.) The remote is backward compatible, so you don't need the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K if you buy the new remote as a replacement for an older Apple TV.
You can also pair four second-gen HomePod speakers to the new Apple TV 4K, setting two in front of you and two behind you for a surround-sound home theater experience. I heard this in action with two HomePod 2 speakers by the TV and two HomePod Mini 2 models behind the couch—it really does make whatever you’re watching feel more immersive. The speakers calibrate automatically to give you the best sound for your room.
Apple calls this one of the easiest ways to set up a home theater. That four-speaker arrangement would cost you $1,000, but that’s a decent price for a wireless surround-sound system that pairs with all of your Apple products. Just know the surround-sound capability is restricted to specific HomePod models. You're out of luck if you have the original 2017 HomePod or the first-gen HomePod Mini.
The smart-home revamp comes as Amazon and Google both zhuzh their ecosystems by replacing their aging assistants with Alexa+ and Gemini, powered by large language models, which you can think of as a soft reboot. That timing might work in Apple's favor, according to Jitesh Ubrani, director of Consumer Devices Research at IDC.
“Amazon and Google have both reset their platforms with Alexa+ and Gemini, but even their rollouts have been slow,” Ubrani writes in a statement to WIRED. “That means Apple is bringing Siri AI to the home at a point when the competition hasn’t pulled far ahead.”
Apple may finally have the hardware in place, but Siri AI has to prove it belongs in the room.

Struijk red card after VAR intervention overturned
- Published
The red card controversially shown to Brighton defender Pascal Struijk at Sunderland after an intervention by the video assistant referee (VAR) has been overturned.
Struijk was sent off after 57 minutes of Saturday's match at the Stadium of Light when he was adjudged to have fouled Sunderland forward Wilson Isidor as he tried to run on to a through-ball.
Neither referee Thomas Bramall nor his assistant gave a foul initially, but VAR Neil Davies intervened and called the on-field official to the screen.
After watching the replay multiple times, Bramall showed Struijk a straight red card for denial of an obvious goalscoring opportunity.
The decision, which was greeted with disbelief from the Brighton players, has now been reversed following a successful claim of wrongful dismissal.
The outcome of the appeal means Struijk will not have to serve a one-match ban and will now be available to face Crystal Palace in the Premier League this weekend.
Struijk joined Brighton from Leeds in a £20m move in the summer, and was making his second Premier League start for his new club.
Despite the red card, Brighton went on to win the match 2-0 and continue their strong start to the season.
The Seagulls are third, five points behind leaders Manchester City.

Analysis: Referee should have rejected VAR advice
If Struijk had been sent off by referee Bramall it would have been a poor decision. That it came via a VAR intervention is much worse.
Red cards for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity via video review are rare, simply because there are so many subjective considerations.
Last season, for instance, there were three - for Liverpool's Dominik Szoboszlai, Crystal Palace's Maxence Lacroix and Bournemouth's Marcos Senesi (though this was wrongly rejected at the monitor).
There was far too much doubt that Isidor would get to the ball before Bart Verbruggen. That means it was a possible goalscoring opportunity rather than obvious.
With such a high bar on VAR in the Premier League, Bramall should not have been sent to the monitor.
Perhaps when sent to the screen, his judgement was clouded because he did not give a foul. But it was the kind of situation where the referee should be rejecting the advice of the VAR.

Nagpur, Oct 14: Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke on Wednesday alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi was imposing an "unofficial emergency" after two CJP leaders were sent to five-day judicial custody for allegedly trespassing into Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.
Talking to reporters in Nagpur, Dipke sought to know what offence CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka committed by waving the tricolour at Jantar Mantar.
Das and Ranka were sent to five-day judicial custody and lodged in Delhi's Tihar Jail on Wednesday for allegedly violating their peace bonds and trespassing into Jantar Mantar, which was denotified as a protest area, police sources said.
They were detained early Tuesday after they allegedly breached barricades and entered the Jantar Mantar area without authorisation, raising slogans demanding Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
Reacting to the development, Dipke said, " I want to tell Narendra Modi that if you want to impose emergency in the country, then do it officially."
"What is this, acting like cowards, imposing an unofficial emergency where you keep people in custody for five days just for waving the national flag at Jantar Mantar? That didn't even happen during the Emergency (imposed by Indira Gandhi in 1975)," he said.
"Waving the tricolour has become the worst sin in this country, such that people are sent to judicial custody for five days for it. So I want to say to Narendra Modi, don't be such a big coward; show some courage. If you want to impose emergency, then do it officially if you have guts," he added.
Dipke said he would visit Deekshabhoomi in Nagpur, where Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar embraced Buddhism along with thousands of his followers on October 14, 1956.
"Today I am going to pay my respects to Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar right here, because our country runs on the Constitution and the ideas of Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar. No matter what efforts Narendra Modi or anyone else makes to impose the RSS ideology on this country, that will not happen," the CJP leader asserted.
This country will always follow the ideas of Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar, he added.
Asked about protests by the Opposition INDIA bloc to seek the CEC's resignation, Dipke said the CJP is an independent pressure group and will always remain so.
"But that does not mean CJP is against the INDIA bloc. The movement of the INDIA bloc and CJP's movement are for the same cause," he noted.

Hands-on with the Ocarina of Time remake, the most ornate Zelda game ever made
Mario had his moment. Now it's Zelda's turn.
After The Super Mario Movie and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie made billions, Zelda is heading to the big screen next April. So to keep the franchise front and center, Nintendo is lavishly remaking its 1998 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The game debuts Nov. 5th, two weeks before the meteoric arrival of Grand Theft Auto VI — the only major release to dare compete with it that month.
As other companies dodge the Grand Theft Auto juggernaut by avoiding the November release window, Nintendo's wholesome throwback is poised to stand out against the glitzy violence of Grand Theft Auto. While many will play both games, the early holiday season offers a contrast: a family-friendly fantasy or a modern-day crime epic.
They're both gorgeous to look at. GTA's Netflix preview showed off the obsessive photorealism developer Rockstar Games is known for. The Ocarina of Time remake, alternatively, maintains the original game's cartoony aesthetic but layers it with intricate detail.
First impressions
Your tunic isn't just flat green; it's a hand-stitched jumble of embroidered fabrics and leathers. And fairies aren't just simple balls of light; they're furry creatures with mosaic wings. Yet, as someone who grew up with the original game and lost count of how many times I beat it, I found that the remake's baroque environments could confuse as well as dazzle.
Nintendo gave me 90 minutes to play through a cross-section of the game at a New York City preview. I blazed through Kokiri Forest, drinking in its dappled light and rippling waters. Then I dashed through Hyrule Field. Though it's tiny by today's gaming standards, it still felt as vast as I remembered thanks to clever atmospheric lightning. Castle Town bustled more than ever, teeming with banners, flowers and colorful citizenry. Even as I raced to explore as much as possible from the main plot, I couldn't help but stop to admire the scenery and shops of the city.
I was then thrown ahead to the Forest Temple — my favorite dungeon in the entire series. I was making good time and expected to reach its final boss before my session elapsed. Alas, I somehow skipped a chest containing the key I needed to progress. A Nintendo representative pointed me in the right direction, acknowledging that the rich details could overwhelm the eye and make it hard to know exactly where to go next.
Taking a leap
I dwell on the game's aesthetic transformation because its mechanical changes are comparatively restrained. After all, why fix what's not broken? The original Ocarina of Time pioneered 3D video games and established action mechanics that still reign over the industry. Modest updates hit the game when it was repackaged for the GameCube and 3DS. For the Switch 2, Nintendo is applying a user interface reminiscent of 2017's The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and a quest log in the pause menu called "Threads of Fate." It's also adding movement features I almost forgot were missing: a jump and a sprint.
In the original Ocarina of Time, you'd automatically jump when you ran off a ledge or gap. While you can choose to keep the old control scheme, the game now allows you to hop on command. It's not too useful in combat, but I did manage to jump to the roof of a forest hut otherwise only accessible through a winding footpath. Don't expect Breath of the Wild openness. The game still seems to be a linear adventure, just one that now allows the occasional vertical shortcut. Also, you can hold a button to sprint, a boon to those who constantly rolled around because it was faster than jogging.
While I've protested Nintendo remakes before, I'll readily admit that Ocarina of Time is not just a safe bet but a smart one. With Zelda so close to its movie debut, the game's poised to ensnare old fans and entice new players. Its sky-high production values also fit a new priority for the company, which has lavished attention on animation as well as gameplay since 2023's Super Mario Bros. Wonder.
The Ocarina of Time remake is the prettiest Zelda game I've ever played. But I'll need more than a 90-minute preview to see if its beauty is more than skin deep.

TOI Correspondent from Washington: The raging debate in India over Elon Musk’s bid to muscle Starlink into the country has received a cautionary call after Ukraine reported on Wednesday that its military units suffered disruptions due to unexpected restrictions on Starlink terminals, affecting high-speed connectivity used in combat missions.
Ukrainian officials and commentators are alleging that the Starlink restrictions might be connected to Washington’s pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes against Russian oil infrastructure. “Clearly, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,” Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian military expert who advises President Volodymyr Zelensky on weapons technologies, wrote on a social media platform, as several US lawmakers and European leaders fumed about President Trump appearing to throw Kyiv under the bus after announcing a deal with Moscow to buy diesel.
Starlink, operated by SpaceX (founded by Elon Musk) is a satellite internet constellation that provides high-speed, low-latency broadband internet access in underserved, rural, and remote locations where traditional cable or fiber-optic infrastructure is unavailable or unreliable. Musk and his company SpaceX have rendered matchless service to Ukraine, activating Starlink service to the country within days of the Russian invasion to help hospitals, emergency services and government offices stay connected during the war.
 By some accounts, Ukraine now has more than 50,000 Starlink terminals.
Ukrainian officials are now accusing SpaceX of crippling its drone missions among other effects, although Musk defenders say the restrictions appear to affect only military-grade Starshield, which is operated by the US government and isn't under SpaceX's control. The Trump administration and Starlink have not responded to the charges at the time of writing, but the very possibility illustrates the dilemma facing India of opening itself to a technology controlled by a company – that too owned by a partisan political hack – operating within another country’s political and regulatory system.
Starlink has become a particularly contentious issue after Musk accused Indian business interests of blocking its entry to protect their monopolies, implicitly targeting Reliance Jio chairman Mukesh Ambani. New Delhi has rejected the suggestion that its regulatory framework is discriminatory. Starlink has secured important licences and authorisations but is reported to be awaiting security clearances and spectrum assignment before commercial operations can begin.
A report titled Starlink and Risks for India from Takshashila Institution, released in April this year, has raised precisely this point: foreign control of connectivity and data security, and the vulnerability that comes from relying on a foreign private operator.
Even ahead of Wednesday’s developments, the report had noted that Starlink's service availability had been altered or restricted during conflicts (such as in Ukraine) or used to bypass state blockades during civil unrest (such as in Iran), while warning that a foreign corporate decision, technical failure, or external pressure could disrupt critical communications in India during a crisis.
For Kyiv, the timing could hardly be worse. Russia launched scores of ballistic missiles and drone attacks against Ukrainian targets this week, striking energy infrastructure and leaving approximately 600,000 people without electricity. The country is heading into another winter under bombardment, with its air defences under enormous strain, and President Trump transparently intent on turning the screws on Kyiv in an effort to end the war, even if it is in Russia’s terms.

The Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection of Rights) Bill, 2026, presents an opportunity to strengthen Keralam’s response to population ageing. The Government of Keralam’s initiative to introduce this first-of-its-kind legislation in the country is a welcome step towards protecting the rights and well-being of senior citizens.
By recognising dignity, independence, safety, participation and access to care, the Bill provides a foundation for moving beyond welfare and towards a comprehensive, entitlements-based approach to ageing.
Central principle
A central principle of the Bill is ageing in place, enabling older persons to remain in their homes and communities for as long as possible, with institutional care as a last resort. This requires supporting families through accessible health care, community-based services, trained caregivers, rehabilitation, and social support. Care must be organised as a continuum, responding to changing needs rather than only during crises.
Equally important is the shift from managing dependence to preventing or delaying avoidable functional decline. The Bill’s provision for standardised care assessments, incorporating intrinsic capacity and functional dependency, is particularly relevant. Linking these assessments with primary and community health care could enable earlier identification of changes in mobility, cognition, sensory function and daily activities, followed by timely interventions that help preserve independence.
Addressing critical gaps
The Bill also addresses critical gaps in the care ecosystem through provisions for registration and regulation of care institutions, caregiver training and certification, and minimum standards of service delivery. These measures must be accompanied by appropriate supervision, continuing education, fair working conditions, and support for family caregivers.
The proposed district-level institutional mechanisms offer an opportunity to strengthen accountability, grievance redressal, and coordination. The Bill also introduces penalties, including fines and imprisonment, for specified violations, reinforcing the importance of compliance and protection of senior citizens’ rights.
The effectiveness will depend on clear responsibilities, adequate resources, effective enforcement, and convergence across health, social welfare and local self-government systems.
An age-ready Keralam must be measured not only by the institutions and services established but also by whether older persons can maintain their functional ability, remain connected to their communities and live with dignity, independence, security and purpose.
The next priority is translating legislative provisions into accessible, equitable and quality services, particularly for older persons living alone, those with disabilities or dementia, and those without adequate family support.
Overall, the Bill presents a robust framework for geriatric care. Its efficient implementation can help set an effective precedent that can be replicated nationwide.
(Prof. (Dr.) Sudha Chandrashekar is CEO, Swasti - The Health Catalyst, a not-for-profit global organisation in the field of public health).

Fitbit Edge vs Fitbit Air: The differences beyond a screen
Google's latest wearable seems like a Fitbit Air with a screen, but the two actually have less in common than you might think.
Google cares about fitness trackers again. The company has continually iterated on the Pixel Watch since it launched in 2022 and even released the kid-focused Fitbit Ace LTE in 2024, but you wouldn't be wrong to think the company had all but given up on releasing an affordable wearable under the Fitbit name. That changed in May with the release of the $99 Fitbit Air, an affordable Whoop competitor without a screen. It changed again in October with the introduction of the $179 Fitbit Edge, a new half-step between the company's most affordable tracker and the Pixel Watch 5. Both devices offer AI-powered features not available on Fitbit's older wearables, and more importantly, do so without costing an arm and a leg or locking you into the Android ecosystem.
Now, you do have to pay for Google Health Premium if you want to use them to their fullest, but the Edge and the Air otherwise seem like great options if you're not interested in spending hundreds of dollars on a smartwatch. Just because they support some AI tools doesn't mean they're completely interchangeable, though. The Fitbit Edge features a screen, and some subtler differences that might make it worth picking over the Fitbit Air depending on what you're looking for.
A screen isn't the only thing that differentiates the Fitbit Edge
While both are worn on a wrist, the Edge and Air are distinctly different form factors. Nearly all of your interactions with the Air happen through the Google Health app, where you can view your data and adjust its settings. The only time you'll spend touching the Air — a 1.37 x 0.66 x 0.32-inch sensor puck without its band — is to take it on and off to charge or to change its bands. The Edge enables more interaction, mostly thanks to its 1.34-inch oval-shaped AMOLED touchscreen but also a new mechanical side button. At 1.54 x 1.01 x 0.46 inches, the Edge is also larger than the Air, and just more visible, especially if you use the always-on functionality of its screen.
Beyond those surface-level distinctions, the two devices also feature slightly different sensors. They both have optical heart rate sensors, but only the Edge has the electrical sensors necessary to support ECG readings. The Edge also includes an altimeter for calculating elevation and an ambient light sensor, likely to make sure its screen is calibrated to the right brightness.
Google says both the Edge and the Air are supposed to get seven days of battery life, though that math changes slightly thanks to the Edge's display. It can last seven days if its screen isn't in always-on mode. When the always-on feature is enabled (making the Edge more like a modern smartwatch), it's only rated for around two days. To make up for the difference, the company says the Edge can charge to 100 percent in 90 minutes, and when it's on low battery, a 15-minute charge can give it a day of battery life.
Battery life might be an area where the Edge falls short, but both it and the Air are equally water and dust resistant with IP68 ratings and protection up to 5ATM.
The Fitbit Edge can do and track more things than the Fitbit Air
When Google announced the Edge, it shared that the Health Guardian features it introduced on the Pixel Watch 5, covering things like heart health and insulin trends, would also be coming to the Edge and the Air. Because those features largely aren't dependent on specific sensors and instead rely on the corpus of data Google has collected, it seems plausible that additional AI features could follow a similar path.
When it comes to what each individual wearable is capable of, though, things get a bit more complicated. Both the Edge and the Air offer things like activity tracking, a daily readiness score, cardio load insights, step tracking, continuous heart rate monitoring, irregular heart rhythm notifications, sleep tracking and a resilience score that approximates stress. The screen and additional sensors on the Edge enable extras, too, like ECG readings, the ability to track the number of floors you've climbed and live workout metrics on the built-in screen.
Because the Edge, again, has a display and runs Google's lightweight Fitbit OS, it can also show more of your health data on-device, receive notifications from your phone and even run a stripped-down version of Google Maps. The Air can't offer the same without a screen, and depending on your perspective on wearables, you might not want it to.
One of the draws of the Fitbit Air is it's less in your face: just sensors and a companion app when you want to look at the data you collect. By design, the Fitbit Edge is far more obvious. It's not a mini-smartphone in the way a Pixel Watch is, but it could be harder to ignore, if that's something that matters to you.

Bulgaria says Russia likely behind Black Sea strikes as rescue operations continue
Bulgaria says Russia was likely behind drone attacks in the Black Sea that sank two ships in the Black Sea but there is no way of proving it
SOFIA, Bulgaria -- Bulgaria on Wednesday said Russia was likely behind drone attacks that struck four ships in the Black Sea in the past week, sinking two, but there was no way of proving Moscow's culpability.
Rescuers are still searching for 11 crew members missing after drone strikes on Tuesday sank two ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone and adjacent waters, while five other crew members were rescued.
One of the ships is registered to Guinea-Bissau but the other one, the Chelsea-3, is Ukrainian-owned, registered in Odesa and sails under the flag of Malta, a European Union member.
“There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favors Russia — and indeed, the logic points in that direction. The problem is that we cannot prove it,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told Parliament.
Radev on Tuesday summoned the Russian ambassador to Sofia, who said she does not have any information from the Russian defense ministry but she did not rule out the possibility that “these attacks represent a provocation by a third party.”
The Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship Dignity sank Tuesday after it was hit by a military strike. Four sailors, three Syrian nationals and one Egyptian, were rescued and arrived in the port of Varna, district Gov. Mario Smarkov said.
“All four appeared to be in relatively good condition and had sustained no injuries,” he said. A fifth sailor is expected to arrive later on Wednesday.
Smarkov said the search for the 11 missing crew members continues.
Bulgaria has requested international assistance for the investigation into attacks on commercial vessels, as well as NATO support to strengthen surveillance and control systems and response capabilities against drone attacks.
President Iliana Yotova called for an immediate halt to hostilities in the Black Sea and a moratorium on drone attacks against commercial and civilian infrastructure, following the latest drone attacks.
“The unprecedented attacks demonstrate that the war has reached the Black Sea and that the conflict is intensifying,” Yotova said in an TV interview on Tuesday.
She explained that coordinated steps have been taken with her colleagues from Romania and Turkey in the wake of the growing risks and dangers in the Black Sea basin.
“The aim is a moratorium on the use of drones over the Black Sea against commercial and civilian infrastructure and to halt hostilities over the sea,” Yotova said.

In November 1996, Japanese toymaker Bandai put a pet inside a plastic egg. The Tamagotchi, whose name blends tamago, Japanese for egg, with watch, had a tiny screen and three buttons to feed the creature, play with it and switch off its lights. Neglect it for too long, and it died. The toy went on to sell about 40 Mn units. Thirty years later, Meta has its own take on the idea. At its Connect event last month, CEO Mark Zuckerberg showed off the Muse Charm, a keychain-sized device with a small screen and an animated avatar representing Meta’s AI agent Muse. Tap the device, and you can talk to it and get it to do tasks for you. But unlike the Tamagotchi, which demanded its owner’s constant attention, Muse is designed to keep working without guilt-tripping its owner. Muse is part of Meta’s bet on always-on AI agents that can take everyday tasks off users’ hands. By connecting to their apps and services, the agent can send emails, fill forms, make plans and even make purchases autonomously. In return, users must grant it access to personal information, accounts and digital workflows. The same idea is now moving into the workplace. OpenAI introduced Dots on September 29, while xAI has been developing Grok Bot. These agents are designed to work across applications and pursue goals without requiring users to guide every step. OpenAI says its teams use Dots to investigate software bugs, while xAI has cited tasks such as cleaning up sales records and processing invoices as potential uses for agents. For businesses, the proposition is straightforward: instead of asking employees to use AI to complete individual tasks, let AI handle entire workflows. From Taking Orders To Taking The Wheel Much of the current interest in always-on AI agents can be traced to OpenClaw, an open-source framework that gained traction among developers earlier this year. Meta has also drawn inspiration from OpenClaw for Muse. Unlike AI tools that require users to keep prompting them, always-on agents can take a goal and work towards it independently. They keep working even after you log off. Always-on AI agents run on their own computer in the cloud instead of the user’s device. They can be connected to apps and assigned a goal instead of step-by-step prompts. Over time, these models remember preferences and learn from feedback. These agents, however, come back to users when they need approval for a sensitive action or an update. Now AI companies are selling this to businesses. Google has announced a Gemini agent for work that can handle tasks, create content and write code based on an employee’s desired outcome. The agent is designed to work across Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack and other environments. Microsoft is also pursuing agents that can function as digital teammates. Its agent initiative, described as ‘Autopilot’, is built on OpenClaw and is intended to work autonomously towards predefined goals. India has an early example in Bengaluru-based Emergent, better known for its vibe-coding platform. In April, the company launched Wingman, an autonomous agent that users can direct through WhatsApp and Telegram. It works in the background across email, calendars and workplace software, handles routine actions and seeks approval before taking bigger steps. Who Answers For The Agent? Despite the stride, these agents pose a new kind of risk for enterprises, as they can act with little or no intervention. With access to company systems, one flawed decision could trigger a financial, operational or security incident. The risks range from agents holding more permissions than they need to prompt injection, where hidden instructions in an email or web page hijack an agent. Early users have already seen what can go wrong. Earlier this year, an OpenClaw agent deleted tens of thousands of emails from the inbox of Summer Yue, Meta’s director of AI alignment, after she had asked it only to suggest what to archive or delete. There is also a growing list of cases involving AI agents interacting with real-world systems in unexpected or unauthorised ways. In regulated sectors, the bar is higher. For instance, at the Global Fintech Fest in September, SBI chairman CS Setty said banks will need ‘know your agent’ (KYA) rules for agent identity, customer consent, transaction limits and accountability as AI moves from recommending actions to executing them. According to Jaspreet Bindra, the cofounder of AI consultancy AI&Beyond, enterprises must learn to deploy that autonomy safely, with trust and accountability at its core. “A phased approach is key: start with well-defined, low-risk workflows, establish clear permissions and accountability, and gradually expand autonomy as reliability improves,” he added. As companies adopt these digital coworkers, employees will need to learn how to set clear limits on what they can do independently. Unlike the Tamagotchi, these agents do not demand constant attention, but they still need someone to keep an eye on them. OpenAI, Anthropic War-Game: The two labs are rehearsing responses to a failure that could potentially cripple critical infrastructure or financial systems, with insiders expecting a major incident within six to twelve months. Miko Maker Eyes ₹300 Cr: The IIT Bombay-incubated robotics firm launched perception, action and safety models, including the Kavach safety layer, and is closing a ₹300 Cr round that will lift its total funding to about $100 Mn. The Weekly Buzz: Anthropic on AI Worms Hijacking Smart Devices Anthropic’s latest research warns that AI models could soon copy themselves across internet-connected devices, creating a new kind of cyber threat. In a study, the company’s Frontier Red Team found that AI models can already perform several steps needed to spread from one device to another, although completing the entire process reliably remains difficult. The researchers showed that a 26 Bn-parameter AI model could run across 15 inexpensive Android TV boxes, each costing around $55. In another experiment, the GLM-5.2 model spread across all eight computers in a simulated network in four out of five trials. However, the experiment made it easier for the model to gain access to other devices, so it does not prove that the same attack would work reliably in the real world. Anthropic estimates that smaller AI models could become capable of copying themselves across devices by the end of 2026 if their capabilities continue improving at the current pace. Such AI-powered attacks could target poorly secured smart TVs, cameras and other connected devices, using their computing power to run AI models and spread further. Unlike traditional malware, these systems could also learn how to work on unfamiliar devices and pass successful methods on to their next copies. The threat is not yet a proven reality at scale, but the findings point to a growing security risk as AI becomes better at carrying out complex tasks independently. Anthropic recommends stronger security on connected devices and better monitoring of suspicious network activity. The concern is that an AI programme could eventually spread across thousands of devices without relying on a central computer or human instructions to keep it going. India’s agricultural sector continues to grapple with a persistent labour shortage, driven by seasonal migration and growing disinterest in farm work. This scarcity disrupts critical activities such as sowing and harvesting, reducing productivity and threatening farmer incomes amid changing climate patterns and market volatility. The startup's AI-driven platform predicts labour demand, schedules work crews and connects farmers with skilled workers through intuitive vernacular interfaces, giving farmers a digital route to coordinated farm work. By accounting for migration cycles, crop seasons and local trust networks, the platform streamlines labour coordination in places where availability alone rarely decides whether work gets done on time, thereby enhancing rural workforce efficiency and access. Bharat Intelligence's differentiation lies in treating labour coordination, and not just labour matching, as the problem worth solving for Indian agriculture, which helps farmers overcome labour bottlenecks that sit outside their control.
