‘If a sibling uses a skin-lightening product, you may be more likely to use one too’. This was among the findings from behavioural research cited by the World Health Organisation (WHO) during a discussion on colourism in Hyderabad on Wednesday (October 7, 2026).
The discussion was part of ‘Complexion of Change: Challenging Colorism Through Policy, Art, and Science’, held at Goethe-Zentrum in Hyderabad. A documentary exploring global skin colour bias and the deep-rooted societal association of fair skin with higher status, beauty and success was also screened as part of the programme.
“Skin-lightening product use was not a single behaviour but was influenced by psychological, cultural and environmental factors,” said Ammaarah Martinus, Behavioural Insights consultant at the WHO.
The psychological dimension includes motivations such as wanting to appear fairer, younger or to fit into society. The cultural dimension includes the influence of families, communities and social networks. Mr. Martinus said research had found that people were more likely to use a skin-lightening product if a sibling used one. She also spoke about access to such products . In India, skin-lightening products could be easily purchased in local markets and supermarkets. “Interventions to address skin-lightening therefore need to work across all three levels rather than focus on only one aspect of the behaviour,” she added.
Psychologist and researcher Bharti Upparu said children begin receiving messages about skin colour at a very young age, often without anyone explicitly telling them that one skin tone is preferable to another. They observe who is complimented, who is bullied and who is teased, and gradually learn which physical characteristics society values. “A person perceived as fair and attractive may unconsciously be associated with other positive characteristics such as competence, goodness and trustworthiness. Such biases can compound into an overall perception of a person’s character and affect how others interact with them,” she said.
The discussion also highlighted that colourism is not restricted to women. Arpit Bhutani, co-founder of Circular Innovation Lab and moderator of the session, pointed to products marketed specifically towards men and noted that the pressure to conform to lighter-skin beauty standards also affects men.
Former Miss America Nina Davuluri recalled an incident involving a friend’s baby, when an older family member cautioned against taking the child into the sun because the child could become darker. “Such comments are not necessarily made with malicious intent but can come from a desire to see children succeed in a society where lighter skin is perceived to offer advantages,” she added.
Mercury in skin-lightening products
In remarks before the documentary screening, Monika Stankiewicz, executive secretary of the Minamata Convention on Mercury, said mercury was among the chemicals of highest public concern according to the WHO and that cosmetics were one pathway through which people could be exposed. “Mercury-containing skin-lightening products can damage the skin and may also contaminate households, potentially exposing other family members,” she added.
Ms. Stankiewicz stressed that the issue was not solely a chemical problem but also a social one linked to beauty standards and the pressure to conform to them. She said meaningful change could not come through regulations alone and that activism, art, culture and storytelling also had important roles to play.

Tens of thousands of students have taken to the streets of Tirana, the Albanian capital, setting alight a government building and two banks and hurling stones at police during a protest over rising education costs and corruption.
Police responded with water cannon and teargas to disperse protesters who started a fire at the ministry of education building, overturned bins and smashed the fronts of local businesses. A branch of Raiffeisen Bank near the education ministry also caught fire.
The protests are the most violent outburst yet against Edi Rama, the prime minister, who won a fourth term in office in May last year but has since faced growing discontent at perceived graft surrounding top officials. Protesters also dismiss opposition figures as unpalatable alternatives.
The unrest caps a summer of peaceful protests against Rama, triggered by the proposed development of a luxury resort along Albania’s pristine southern coast backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, which has been caught up in legal disputes.
“This is a revolution. We are tired of peaceful protests. We will not stop until Rama resigns,” said Lora, a student who declined to give her last name as she threw rocks at the police.
Others chanted “resignation” and “police of crime”.
Student organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, a lack of financial support and employment prospects after graduation.
The unrest is part of a broader wave of student activism sweeping Europe over education and living conditions. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education.
Albanian media reported that Wednesday’s protests had spread to universities at Elbasan and Shkodër.
The government condemned the violence.
Albana Koçiu, the deputy prime minister of Albania, said on Facebook: “Protesting is a legitimate right, but it cannot be used as an excuse for violence, city destruction or ugly fighting in the middle of the road. I call on students and every honest citizen who believes in the right to protest: distance yourself from violence and vandalism!”
The police issued a statement calling for calm. “Any person who uses violence, burns or destroys property, or attacks police officers, bears individual responsibility and will face the law, in accordance with the offences committed,” they said.
Meanwhile, the EU, which the Balkan nation aspires to join, voiced concern over what it called the “violent escalation at the protest in Tirana”.
A statement by the EU delegation in Tirana said: “We take note of the allegations of excessive violence by the police against protesters and journalists,”
Calling for a prompt investigation, the delegation encouraged “all sides to de-escalate the tension”.

US inflation rises more than expected ahead of midterm elections
- Published
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.
The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.
Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have spiked following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.
The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US.
What is inflation?
Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increase over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.
Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).
It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.
The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.
What causes inflation?
There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.
If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.
Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.
Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.
Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.
What is the current rate of inflation?
Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices.
Car fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.
In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau or Labor Statistics.
Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.
Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher.
At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year.
Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.
How have tariffs affected inflation?
Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.
While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.
Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.
In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.
Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.
Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.
- What tariffs has Trump introduced and why? 
  - Published22 August
Has inflation been worse lately?
While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years.
During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.
Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.
Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.
Can inflation ever go down?
It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.
A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.
Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.
Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect prices to fall further. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

South Africa hope to host first African Olympics
- Published
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed South Africa have shown an interest in becoming the first African host of the summer Olympics in 2036.
Hungary, India, Qatar and Turkey are also working towards becoming first-time hosts, while Germany and South Korea are in discussions with the IOC having held previous summer Games.
The IOC stated that the seven countries are engaged in "continuous dialogue" with the governing body and have set a deadline of 31 October for submissions of stated interest.
Virtual presentations will be given by interested parties to the body's future host commission in November, with IOC feasibility assessments to be carried out by March 2027.
After that, the national Olympic committees, all of whom have previously announced an intention to explore hosting bids, will enter strategic dialogue with the IOC.
The South Africa proposal involves hosting between three cities - Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg.
Durban had been set to host the Commonwealth Games in 2022, but withdrew in 2017.
Ahmedabad, which will welcome the Commonwealth Games in 2030 and has bid for the 2038 Asian Games, will be the host city in India's bid.
The city has also staged four of the last five finals in cricket's Indian Premier League at its Narendra Modi stadium, which is reported to have a capacity of 132,000 and is named after the current prime minister of India, who hails from the city.
Budapest and Doha, the capital cities of Hungary and Qatar respectively, are the hosts in their country's bids.
Qatar hosted football's 2022 World Cup, with multiple stadia in the capital, while Budapest has staged the 2022 World Aquatics Championships and 2023 World Athletics Championships.
Istanbul is the nominated city in Turkey's bid, having previously bid unsuccessfully for the 2000, 2008 and 2020 Games.
The largest city in Turkey will host the 2027 European Games.
Germany has hosted the Olympics in 1936 and 1972, in Berlin and Munich respectively, while the latter city is bidding again for 2036.
Meanwhile South Korea capital Seoul, which hosted the Games in 1988, is part of a bid that also involves the province of North Jeolla.
The IOC also confirmed that a number of national Olympic committees are taking part in non-committal talks with the IOC about hosting future Olympic Games beyond 2036.
The UK government said in May that it is in "discussions about supporting potential bids" for the Olympics and Paralympics in the 2040s.
The 2028 Games will be held in Los Angeles, while Australia will host the Olympics for the first time in 32 years when Brisbane stages the event in 2032.

CAPF Act doesn’t override Supreme Court’s 2025 verdict, IPS deputation necessary: Centre
A home ministry officer, who filed the counter affidavit, denied that this was done to nullify the judgment or challenge the court’s authority.
New Delhi: The Centre has defended the Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026, in the Supreme Court, maintaining that it neither seeks to override the apex court’s May 23, 2025 judgment nor declares the ruling erroneous or void, while maintaining that the deputation of IPS officers to senior positions in the CAPFs is necessary for the country’s internal security architecture.
In a counter affidavit filed on Wednesday, a day before a special bench is scheduled to hear petitions by serving CAPF officers challenging the law, the government said the Act did not re-enact any provision struck down by the court. It also said the law came into force on October 8 through a notification and that the cadre review exercise directed by the court was underway. “It is submitted that the 2026 Act came into force on October 8 by virtue of notification,” the joint affidavit filed on behalf of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) and the CRPF stated.
The petition was filed by more than 800 serving CAPF officers, including Shaurya Chakra, Kirti Chakra and other gallantry award winners, who have challenged the law, arguing that it seeks to circumvent the apex court’s ruling. The bill was passed by Parliament in April despite opposition leaders raising concerns that it would undermine the morale of cadre officers.
A home ministry officer, who filed the counter affidavit, denied that this was done to nullify the judgment or challenge the court’s authority.
The Supreme Court’s May 2025 judgment had directed the Centre to progressively reduce IPS deputation to the five CAPFs — the CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP and SSB — up to the inspector general (IG) rank. The ruling followed an almost 16-year legal battle by CAPF cadre officers over promotional stagnation and the deputation of IPS officers to senior posts.
The cadre officers have argued that large-scale deputation has restricted their promotional opportunities and prevented them from reaching leadership positions. They have also contended that while the court directed the government to progressively reduce IPS deputation, the new law prescribes fixed quotas for deputation at senior ranks.
The government, however, said the recruitment rules of each CAPF had, “from their inception”, provided for the appointment of IPS officers on deputation. It rejected the argument that IPS officers lacked the competence to hold senior command positions, saying they served in internal security, counter-insurgency and left-wing extremism theatres, border districts and intelligence organisations.
Denying that IPS officers occupied most senior posts, the government said 47 of the 607 sanctioned deputy inspector general (DIG) posts were held by IPS officers, while 64 of the 140 sanctioned IG posts were allocated to them.
The affidavit said IPS officers brought knowledge of state administrations, police forces and regional security situations to CAPF leadership. They also acted as a key link between the Centre and state governments in policing, law and order, counter-insurgency, militancy, terrorism and border protection.
The government further said the deputation quotas were “neither without any study nor without determining principle”, as alleged by the petitioners.
On cadre review, the Centre said the exercise was underway within the framework of the 2026 Act. It also provided the dates on which proposals for cadre reviews of all five CAPFs were sent to the Department of Personnel and Training.
Retired CAPF officers and their families have announced a peaceful protest against the Act at Jantar Mantar in November.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed extending restrictions on advertisements of prescription medicines to drug retailers, wholesalers and distributors, seeking to close a regulatory gap in the Drugs Rules, 1945.
A draft amendment notified through Gazette notification G.S.R. 861(E) on September 28 proposes inserting a new sub-rule under Rule 65 to prohibit holders of licences to sell, stock, exhibit, offer for sale or distribute drugs listed under Schedules H, H1 and X from advertising these medicines without prior sanction of the Central government.
Under the existing framework, pharmaceutical manufacturers are prohibited from advertising drugs covered under these schedules without prior government approval. However, the corresponding restriction does not explicitly cover entities involved in the retail and wholesale sale and distribution of medicines.
The proposed amendment seeks to extend the requirement across the drug supply chain, strengthening oversight of the promotion of prescription medicines and reducing the risk of inappropriate self-medication.
Misuse of prescription drugs
The medicines covered by these schedules include drugs that require medical supervision, including certain antibiotics and psychotropic medicines. Unauthorised promotion of such medicines can encourage their use without appropriate medical advice, raising concerns over patient safety and the misuse of prescription drugs.
The proposal follows recommendations made at the 93rd meeting of the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) on February 16, 2026, which examined the need for provisions regulating advertisements by holders of drug sale and distribution licences.
The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days of the date on which copies of the Gazette notification containing the draft rules are made available to the public.
The submissions received within the prescribed period will be considered by the Central government before the amendment is finalised.

Trump commercials paid for by the US government continued airing on TV the day after a judge blocked the ads because they likely violate a US law against government-funded publicity or propaganda.
In the most widely aired commercial, Trump railed against his perceived enemies and said he would “liberate America from these villains once and for all.” The campaign also included a commercial praising Trump’s record as president, another in which Trump calls the US the “most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history,” and commercials related to the Iran war and the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
US District Judge Jennifer Rochon issued a temporary restraining order (TRO) blocking the ads on Sunday, October 11, which took effect at 6:45 pm that night. The order said the government must cancel the ads, “including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026.”
The Trump administration had told the court on October 10 that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) advertising purchases were set to expire on October 11 and would not be renewed. Despite that, the ads continued airing the night of October 11 and on part of October 12. This was also a week after Trump’s October 5 statement that he would start paying for the ads “myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”
A US attorney yesterday filed a status report saying that the government is now complying with the order and issued an apology. “As Your Honor is aware, the Court emailed the TRO to the parties yesterday at 6:46 p.m.,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald wrote in a filing. “Counsel for the Government emailed the TRO to agency counsel at 7:58 p.m. Agency counsel did not become aware of Government counsel’s email until this morning. The undersigned apologizes to the Court and the plaintiffs.”
The ads aired as part of a $20 million purchase order that US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) made on September 20 with LMD Agency, an ad firm. The DHS told the court that the ad placements through October 11 cost $19 million.

Vellore Institute of Technology (VIT) will install at least 65 octagonal LED streetlights on the recently opened ₹90-crore Sathuvachari - VIT High Road, off Chennai - Bengaluru National Highway (NH 48), near the Collectorate in Vellore to prevent accidents.

In October 2026, a claim (archived) circulated that the conservative commentator Charlie Kirk, who was fatally shot on Sept. 10, 2025, once said children could watch public executions "at a certain age" as an "initiation."
Claims about his alleged quote circulated as U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said the U.S. military was planning to livestream the Army firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the Fort Hood shooter.
One Facebook user wrote that "Charlie Kirk once argued that children watching public executions 'at a certain age' would be 'an initiation.'"
Snopes readers contacted us asking about the truth of this and other Facebook posts (archived, archived) with similar claims about what Kirk said.
Snopes previously investigated what Kirk said about children watching public executions in September 2025 and found that Kirk did say that he thought children could watch public executions "at a certain age" and that this could serve as an "initiation."
The commentator spoke about children watching executions during an episode of "Thoughtcrime," his panel discussion show, on Feb. 15, 2024. During that show, Kirk said about the death penalty that (at 49:35), "It should be public, it should be quick, it should be televised."
Later in the show, Kirk and his panelists discussed whether children should watch public executions and Kirk said (at 50:17), "I think at a certain age it's an initiation," though the panel did not agree on what that age was. Kirk did acknowledge during the podcast that public executions and the death penalty were (at 51:17) "heavy" topics but supported public access as a way to deter crime.
Given the above, we find social media users correctly attributed the quote about children of "a certain age" viewing public executions as an "initiation" to Kirk.
What Kirk said
Kirk and his co-presenters Jack Posobiec, Tyler Bowyer and Blake Neff were discussing capital punishment in the context of whether they believed convicted pedophiles should receive the death penalty.
About 40 minutes into the show, the discussion about capital punishment moved on to whether it should be public and, if so, who should watch. Kirk said (at 49:35), "It should be public, it should be quick, it should be televised."
He added (at 49:53), "You could have like 'Brought to you by Coca Cola' and no, I'm not kidding. By the way, I would totally tune in to see some pedo get their head chopped off. Convicted by a jury of their peers. I'm talking about a real thing."
The discussion moved on to whether children should watch publicly broadcast executions. Kirk said (at 50:17, emphasis ours):
I think at a certain age it's an initiation. No, but hold on, you see, if all of a sudden, you look at some of these savages like in Indiana, there was this guy that went in and killed a pregnant woman and her three kids. And, you know what, I want to watch that execution, that'll make my day better. I want to see him on a public block and get him be publicly executed, and I think that would be justice. You think children should have … you should see … what is the age? At what age should you start to see public executions?
Bowyer and Neff each suggested 16- and 12-year-olds, respectively, as appropriate viewing ages. Kirk said (at 51:13), "But it should also be taken in a holy way. Now, I don't mean holy in a bad way, I mean that, like, this is heavy."
Kirk did not say that executions should be mandatory viewing for children or give an opinion on what age he thought was appropriate to start. He did, however, express a belief that making executions public would deter future crimes. The hosts said (at 51:42):
KIRK: I want you to imagine everyday, all of a sudden they said: "And today, remember that awful five, you know, the guy that went and shot up a school?" Because, you know, left hates school shooters, and so do we and, but they focus on the gun, I think they're evil. So, you know, you take one of these school shooters and they say, "Today we're going to publicly execute this person." And they read off—
POSOBIEC: How about the Super Bowl?
KIRK: Yeah, or the shooters at the Super Bowl thing, and you read off what they did and you don't celebrate it, you know, you just say, "Look, this is what they did and if you do this, this will be your fate," ready, set, go. Boom, end of life. And say— As a question— Here's a question for anybody that might be, you know, not persuaded. Would crime go up or down?
BOWYER: It would go way down
KIRK: Down. So then why is this even a question?
Six states — Texas, Florida, Alabama, Tennessee, Oklahoma and Arizona — have carried out a total of 30 executions so far in 2026, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit group that provides data and analysis on issues concerning capital punishment.
According to a DPIC report from 2018, of the 17 states that carried out executions by lethal injection between January 2011 and August 2018, 14 "prevented witnesses from seeing at least some part of the execution" and 15 "prevented witnesses from hearing what was happening inside the execution chamber."
For further reading, Snopes has fact-checked a number of quotes attributed to Kirk, including whether he called Martin Luther King Jr. "awful" or said some gun deaths were "worth it" in order to have Second Amendment. We have also investigated whether the U.S. military could legally livestream Hasan's planned Dec. 3 execution.

Mexico President Sheinbaum orders tech giants to protect kids and teens from harmful online content
Sheinbaum added that if technology companies fail to abide by the mandate, her administration will support legislation to levy punishments against non-compliant platforms

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum announced that she will sign a presidential decree on Wednesday requiring digital platforms, including social media networks and streaming services, to shield children and teenagers from violent, sexual, and other harmful content.
Intended to heighten scrutiny of major technology firms operating in Latin America's second-largest economy, the decree follows an early October attack at a high school in the northern state of Coahuila, where two 18-year-old former students left one person dead and three others injured.
Digital platforms will be given a period of one month to come into full compliance with the decree, according to government adviser Luisa Maria Alcalde.
Sheinbaum added that if technology companies fail to abide by the mandate, her administration will support legislation to levy punishments against non-compliant platforms.
Government officials said they have already held meetings with representatives from Meta, Microsoft, Apple, TikTok, Google, X, and Huawei to discuss the upcoming requirements.
Those companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The measure reflects a broader global movement to safeguard minors on the internet, with authorities across Europe and Australia tightening digital platform oversight and US states enacting a variety of child-safety regulations.
Brazil has similarly moved to reinforce online protections for children.
Such regulatory efforts around the world continue to raise questions over how best to protect young users while simultaneously preserving personal privacy and freedom of expression

Federal prosecutors said a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device had a one-way ticket booked to Saudi Arabia.
In newly unsealed court documents, it was revealed that the federal government feared its case against Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national, might be jeopardized if information about it leaked.
"The defendant, his wife, and a third family member have booked one-way tickets from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia (via Istanbul) for Monday, October 12, 2026," the prosecutors, including US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian, wrote in an October 8 court filing.
The prosecutors wrote that Alfozan had "the means—and will have an incentive—to flee the United States sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested."
On October 9, the FBI arrested Alfozan. He made his initial court appearance on Wednesday when the government unveiled its case against him. Alfozan has been charged with "use of an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications," a felony that carries a maximum of five years in prison.
According to the criminal complaint against Alfozan, the company found a USB device surreptitiously placed on the back of a television located in an "executive conference room." The device was concealed in toilet paper, the complaint said.
Alfozan's lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.
OpenAI previously said in a statement that it used "our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier."

A rep for AFI said Daly, who joined the board in April 1981, is stepping down to pass the torch to the next generation.

AI-powered stock funds bet bots can pick stocks faster and better than humans
PROVIDENCE, Rhode Island, Oct 14 : A handful of fund managers are betting that exchange traded funds run by AI stock-picking models can crunch data quicker and make better investment decisions than humans, even as many people remain wary or even fearful of artificial intelligence.
So far, fewer than half-a-dozen ETFs, collectively managing only about $30 million of the ETF industry's nearly $17 trillion in assets, rely solely on AI-powered bots to control everything from research to stock selection.
While that represents a tiny fraction of the industry, AI is making its way slowly and steadily into the investment processes of most asset managers, to some extent, even if that may not yet be visible to investors themselves. Earlier this year, 91 per cent of asset managers surveyed by Mercer reported plans to increase their use of AI-based portfolio management tools this year and said they are trying to figure out what tasks can be safely handed off to AI.
The performance of the handful of funds that rely solely on AI to generate returns shows they are beating the market, even if their track records stretch back only a few months. Their managers argue these returns will attract more investments into the idea over time.
"Until now you've had two choices: be a passive investor and own an index, or be an active investor" with a human picking stocks, said Tal Schwartz, founder and CEO of Ai Funds. "I want to offer a third option: where it's AI that is doing it all for you."
In August, Schwartz launched the High Conviction US Equity AI-Managed ETF, built on a proprietary AI learning algorithm that analyzes decades of market data. So far, it has attracted less than $20 million in assets, according to data from ETF.com, but Schwartz said it is still early days.
AI can crunch more data more rapidly than any human being, he said, and strips human emotions and cognitive biases out of the investment process.
"I know this is a long-term process, that people will only become convinced over time," he added. "I think that what will convince them is performance."
Schwartz's fund is up 2.7 per cent since its August 21 launch, beating the 1.1 per cent gain for the S&P 500 index in the same time frame.
Two funds launched by Israeli asset manager FinQ in February have handily beaten the 11.0 per cent gain by the S&P over that time frame. FinQ's dollar-neutral US Large-Cap AI-managed ETF has soared 25.35 per cent and the version of the ETF not offering a currency hedge is 23.98 per cent higher since inception.
Two other funds, the Pacer S&P 500 3AI Top 100 ETF and the Pacer S&P World 3AI Top 100 ETF, are ahead 10.34 per cent and 10.33 per cent, respectively, since their launches in early May, compared to a gain of 5.8 per cent for the S&P 500.
Nonetheless, advisers and analysts said the funds' short track records and above-average fees may limit investor interest.
"Advisers are comfortable with AI that informs a decision and uneasy with AI that makes it," said Jeff Judge, a financial adviser at Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland, adding his clients are not clamoring for this.
"Proof that this approach works will really come down to who can thoughtfully manage risk and ride out a down market," said Todd Sohn, ETF analyst at Strategas.
AI-ENHANCED ETFS MORE COMMON
Other firms have rolled out "AI-enhanced" ETFs, which use AI to undertake quantitative analysis, analyze stocks or monitor risk. This cautious approach is more common, insiders said.
"We've been training models using AI for seven or eight years now, and using them to run live capital for about four years," said David Wright, head of quantitative investments at Pictet Asset Management in Geneva.
His firm launched the Pictet AI Enhanced US Equity ETF in February. Since its debut, the fund has attracted $163 million in assets and posted gains of 14.8 per cent, compared to 11.4 per cent for the S&P 500.
Wright compares using AI in the investment process to using a plane's autopilot functions. The autopilot may be able to take off, cruise and land with no humans involved, but, he added, "I wouldn't go on a plane that didn't have a pilot."
Other asset managers are taking a similarly cautious approach to integrating AI.
"I'm not losing any sleep over robots ending the world," said Dan Taylor, deputy chief investment officer of systematic within Man Group, referring to recent headlines. "But I still do worry about AI's ability to deal with the most extreme, unlikely events, where all the action happens, both good and bad."

Perhaps the days when auto shows debuted new models aren’t entirely over. The big trade shows for cars were a gateway drug for many, expos where you could see the newest models of today and the concepts of tomorrow. But automakers increasingly got tired of sharing the spotlight with each other. New reveals moved offsite to events the night or even the week before the show itself. One by one, brands pulled out of auto show after auto show until there was little left to see. And then the pandemic hit.
But the news out of Paris, where its auto show held media day yesterday, seems like we stepped back into a time when automakers would debut new cars aplenty. That retro vibe extends to the cars themselves, with plenty of familiar nameplates reimagined.
France’s Renault has a long and glorious history of delightful concept cars, and more on what it brought to Paris later. But the star of the show was arguably Stellantis, with strong work from Citroen, Peugeot, and Fiat, to name but three. But this article is meant to irritate you, because I’m pretty sure none of the stuff you’re seeing here will come to the United States. And it’s doubly irritating considering what Stellantis’ brands do offer us over here, doubling down on the same malign trends I saw back in 2020: did you know they’re about to relaunch a V8 Hellcat-powered Charger?

The European concepts show us that, as those Kneecap chaps have it, there’s a better way to live. Kakatiya Knights and Mighty Marathas stayed clear on top of the standings, both reaching 10 points after beating Rajputana Royals and Chola Chiefs, respectively, in Archery Premier League Season 2 on Wednesday.
Earlier in the day, Prithivraaj Yodhas downed Chero Archers to move into third place on eight points.
In the final match of the day, Chiefs’ woeful run of form continued as they remained rooted to the bottom of the table with just one win in seven matches, suffering a fifth straight defeat. In complete contrast, Marathas, who had started the season with two losses, have now won five on the trot and appear to be the team to beat.
The last time Prithviraaj Yodhas and Chero Archers met, three Sudden Death tiebreakers were needed to decide a winner. But in the reverse fixture, Yodhas made light work of Chero Archers and registered a convincing 5-1. Yodhas were led by some superb shooting by 16-year-old recurve archer Gatha Anandrao Khadake, who shot 58 out of a possible 60, and Asian Games compound medallist Ganesh Thirumuru (59).
With this win, Yodhas arrested their own mini slump while Chero Archers – who had started the season brightly- have now suffered three straight defeats.
Carrying on from where they left off in their previous meeting, it appeared as though there would be very little to separate Yodhas and Chero as they tied the first set 75-75. But the second set would slip away from Chero as Kumkum Mohod was left with little time to shoot the final arrow and she could manage only a 7, while Yodhas finished the set strongly with four 10s.
USA’s Casey Kaufhold then replaced Kumkum ahead of the third set but she started with a 8 that opened up a window for Yodhas, who saw Gatha step up once more with two 10s in that set. Matias Grande calmly closed out the set and match 77-74.
In the second match, not for the first time this season, Royals had two of the best-scoring archers in the match but when it mattered, Knights came up with clutch arrows, led by the impeccable Neeraj Chauhan, who has emerged as one of the stories of the APL season with his consistently high scores while shooting last in each set. While his 8 in the first set could have proved costly, Royals’ Mete Gazoz missed the 10 by the smallest of margins to give Knights the first set.
The second set would turn out to be the best of the night as all eight archers were in sensational form but Neeraj’s final X gave it to the Knights 79-78. The Royals showed a hint of a fightback by taking the third set, but the Knights sealed their win with Neeraj anchoring with another 10. The local franchise also had Jyothi Surekha Vennam in fine form as she shot 78 from her eight arrows.
For Marathas, the strategy since getting off to a slow start has been ‘attack, attack, attack’ and they found a new hero on the night in recurve archer Simranjeet Kaur, who shot a sensational 59 out of 60. With Dhiraj Bommadevara in good form again, Simranjeet’s scores propped up the Marathas even more with compounds Mike Schloesser and Parneet Kaur doing their bit. The Chiefs, who brought back Chikitha Taniparthi into the starting lineup, struggled to get going once again as they lost all three sets.

Defending champions Rajputana Royals will face the red-hot Mighty Marathas in the second match, and the day’s action will conclude with local franchise Kakatiya Knights facing Chero Archers in what could be the match of the day.

Fraud probe over NATO contracts leads to 5 arrests in Norway and searches in Germany and Romania
The European Union’s criminal justice agency says five people have been arrested in Norway in connection with suspected fraud and bribery linked to NATO ship contracts
BRUSSELS -- Five people were arrested in Norway and searches were carried out in Germany and Romania as part of an investigation into suspected fraud and bribery linked to contracts for ships used for NATO missions, the European Union’s criminal justice agency said Wednesday.
Eurojust said the arrests and searches involved a company and subcontractors linked to it which are suspected of submitting fraudulent invoices for shore-based work to support the ships and their crew during visits to ports in northwest Europe.
Eurojust estimated that NATO member countries suffered losses of around one million euros ($1.1 million), although the full amount of the fraud is not yet known.
The company is also accused of using an intermediary to bribe public officials to secure preferable treatment from NATO’s Support and Procurement Agency. or NSPA.
The NSPA helps the 32 members of the world’s biggest security alliance and their partners to buy defense equipment and other security systems and support. NATO as an organization does not own any ships, tanks or weapons.
The company at the center of the probe was not identified, but its premises in Romania and several homes were searched. Searches in Germany focused on two businesses and one home, Eurojust said in a statement.

South Africa's deputy police chief resigns after being charged with sexual offences
- Published
South Africa's deputy police chief has resigned three weeks after he was charged with sexual offences.
A lawyer representing Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya submitted his resignation letter at his disciplinary hearing on Monday, a police spokesperson said.
The charges relate to allegations that he sexually groomed a 16-year-old girl and raped an 18-year-old woman. He is also facing a charge of trafficking.
Sibiya has denied all the charges. He says he did have sex with the 18 year-old but says it was consensual.
He has been in custody since he was arrested three weeks ago after his bail application was denied.
Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said in a post on X that his departure from the police force was regarded as a dishonourable discharge, external.
The case comes as the police service is in the spotlight at a major public inquiry over allegations of corruption and collusion with criminals.
The inquiry, known as the Madlanga Commission, began in September 2025 and has heard accusations that Sibiya received a gift of 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract.
He denied the allegation.

It’s a big year for Apple firsts. The company launched the first MacBook Neo, unveiled its first folding iPhone in September, and installed a new CEO for the first time in 15 years. Now comes the Apple HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.
Rivals like Google and Amazon have made countless screen-enabled smart speakers since voice assistants invaded the home a decade ago. But Apple stuck with a smaller smart home ecosystem centered on its HomePod speakers, even removing the iPad as a hub device a few years ago, which forced users to buy an Apple TV or HomePod to get started. Maybe that’s why it hasn’t found much success in the home.
Announced Tuesday at an event in New York City, the 7-inch smart display arrives alongside several other new smart home devices as part of Apple’s bid to revitalize its lagging ecosystem. The HomeView costs $299 and comes in two versions—a speaker base and a wall-mounted display—both priced the same. Preorders are live, with sales kicking off on November 13.
A Big Apple Watch
The first thing I thought of after seeing the Apple HomeView in action is that it looks like a blown-up Apple Watch. The 7-inch square screen has multiple “faces” you can swipe through, exactly like the smartwatch. You can even customize the face’s colors and add different complications for more glanceable information.
The faces can range from a clock, your favorite photos of friends, family, or pets (you can even use shared albums) to weather updates and, yes, Snoopy animations. Swipe up for the home screen, which is more like an iPhone or iPad, with apps neatly arranged alongside widgets. Except the HomeView doesn’t run iOS or iPadOS—it runs the generically named HomeView software.
It doesn’t have an App Store. Instead, Apple has a curated selection of apps, including FaceTime, Messages, and Safari. A handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps. If your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup. (There are no video streaming apps like YouTube, Netflix, or Disney+, but if those companies choose to make their apps available on the CarPlay framework, they will show up on the HomeView; for now, you'll have to consume videos by using the Safari browser.)
To get the most out of the HomeView, you need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (an iPhone 15 Pro or newer)—you can’t set it up with an iPad.
The aluminum hardware, powered by Apple’s A18 chip, comes in four colors: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray (Apple color-matches the woven cable, too). The standard HomeView has a speaker base with a screen that tilts manually up or down for angled viewing, but you can also buy a wall-mountable version. The latter offers three mounts to choose from, one of which is DIY-friendly and has a visible power cord that needs to run to an outlet. The other two are designed for professional installers, either hardwired or connected via Power over Ethernet (PoE).
Technically, the primary speakers—two full-range drivers—are built into the screen. But the standard HomeView has a base that houses a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators for stronger bass. It sounds pretty good based on a very limited listening experience, and can fill a large room quite well. The wall-mounted variant won’t have that extra oomph but Apple claims it tunes the audio for wall placement.
The 7-inch Liquid Retina display has familiar elements, like True Tone, which adjusts the screen’s color temperature to match the room’s lighting. The ambient light sensor can also reduce display brightness from 500 nits to 0.3 nits, which is the lowest brightness Apple has ever engineered on a screen. That’ll be helpful if you place the HomeView on the nightstand.
That is, if you're comfortable placing a camera-equipped display in the bedroom. A 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and four-microphone array sit on the front, but they aren’t just for FaceTime calls. The camera handles facial recognition, allowing the software to adapt to whoever is looking at the screen. Apple says all of this data stays on device.
“Trust is becoming increasingly important with rising consumer expectations around privacy and security,” writes Anshika Jain, principal analyst at Counterpoint, in an email to WIRED. “In fact, Apple could actually benefit from its privacy-first approach.”
You can add up to six iCloud accounts, and the user interface will adapt to each person, like Google’s Pixel Tablet. That means your wife can tint every app icon green and have no widgets on her home screen, but if you stand in front of the HomeView, it’ll switch to your setup. You won’t be able to view other household members’ sensitive messages and personal information. For this personal content to show up, you don’t just have to stand in front of the HomeView—your iPhone needs to be on the same Wi-Fi network and must have been recently unlocked.
The HomeView can also recognize voices, which helps if Dad asks Siri AI to “Play music.” It will play from Dad’s music library and his preferred music app, rather than another iCloud user’s music. If you have multiple HomePods or HomeViews, you can manage your speaker groups in the HomeView’s interface.
The HomeView also supports Apple’s Handoff tech, so you can bring your iPhone close to send a Safari recipe to the smart display, or have it continue the podcast you were listening to on your commute. In the middle of a FaceTime or phone call? Put your iPhone near the HomeView, and it’ll transfer it over.
Betting on Siri AI
Like any smart display or smart speaker, Siri AI powers the HomeView. It is, after all, the main way to interact with the device (though yes, there’s a keyboard you can pull up to type). Apple spent a great deal of time revamping Siri this year, finally launching a more capable assistant in iOS 27.
Siri AI on the HomeView understands your personal context from your iPhone, so if you ask it to play a song your friend Eric recommended, it’ll know right away what you mean by looking at your Messages history. You can ask when your brother Jeff will likely arrive at your home from the airport on Thursday, then set a schedule for Siri to turn on the coffee maker 15 minutes before his estimated arrival. All of this can be done with natural language, meaning you don’t have to say specific commands for Siri AI to understand you.
One neat trick is the HomeView’s ability to convert recipe pages from Safari into digestible content. Load a recipe, and it will let you view the ingredients or “Start Cooking,” no need to read three paragraphs of the author’s relationship to the stew. It automatically converts the recipe into step-by-step instructions, even auto-populating timers for relevant steps so you can start individual timers as you progress.
Naturally, the HomeView is also designed to control all of your smart home devices, too. You can create a widget for any device you have added in the Home app to quickly control it on the HomeView. And if you swipe to the left from the home screen, you’ll see the “Camera” face, which shows a live stream of connected security cameras (you can view nine feeds at once).
Much like the upcoming iPhone Duo folding phone, Apple is late to market. The company is betting on tight iPhone integration, glanceable Watch-like software, and a more context-aware Siri to make the HomeView feel more like a screen you’ll actually want on your counter. Everything hinges on whether Siri can hold up its end of the bargain—and the voice assistant doesn’t exactly have the best track record.
“The greater challenge is to make AI useful for everyday interactions,” Jain says. “Apple must provide a more capable Siri experience and ensure seamless control across its entire product range in order to stand out from the competition.”

US lawmakers ask FAA to conduct review before allowing Amazon drone hub near Boston
WASHINGTON, Oct 14 : A group of Democratic lawmakers on Wednesday urged the Federal Aviation Administration to conduct a new environmental review before allowing an Amazon Prime Air drone delivery hub to be located about 30 miles (48.28 km) west of Boston.
Massachusetts Democratic US Senators Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren and Representatives Jim McGovern and Lori Trahan wrote to FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford seeking a new review after communities raised concerns about the planned Westborough hub and its impact on the environment and residents’ quality of life, including noise pollution, health and safety, and privacy.
The FAA said it would respond directly to the lawmakers. Amazon did not immediately comment.
Here are more details:
• On September 28, a group of 15 states and a Texas county on Monday sued the FAA over the agency's environmental review of planned commercial drone package delivery rules.
• The agency in July issued a broad environmental review that allows qualifying drone operators to launch fleets without a site-specific environmental analysis.
• The states — including New York, California, Massachusetts, Wisconsin and Michigan — and Harris County, Texas, said the FAA violated the law by failing to adequately analyze the potential environmental impacts of expanded drone package delivery operations.
• Drone delivery operations are already happening in states including California, Texas, Arkansas, Florida and Utah under the waiver process.
• The FAA said last year that eliminating the need for waivers "will significantly expand the use-case for drone technologies in areas like: manufacturing, farming, energy production, filmmaking, and the movement of products including lifesaving medications."
• The FAA environmental review included reviewing the noise impacts of 1,150 average drone deliveries from a single hub. Drones would depart a hub and travel en route at an altitude of less than 400 feet (121 meters).

Delhi braced for a second day of youth protests demanding the resignation of India’s election chief on Sunday, as a court ordered the release of the “cockroach” movement founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and two other senior leaders.
Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), and the other leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday, as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi.
Indian authorities on Saturday deployed a sweeping crackdown across Delhi and detained thousands of protesters as the youth “cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fuelled anger at the prime minister, Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Reuters reported police detained more than 2,000 people to thwart Saturday’s protest. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across the city on Sunday although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up.
Most detained on the first day of protests were released on Saturday night, police said.
Opposition parties and critics of Modi’s government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters.
The UN human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.
UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said: “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled.” He urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.
India’s foreign ministry said the UN’s approach was “selective” and its statement constituted “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.
The protests are calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), which has been in power for more than 12 years.
Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party.
Modi’s BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Election Commission data cited by the party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
The BJP and the commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The “cockroach” movement, which began as an online satire, rapidly evolved into a pressure group, with street protests against exam paper leaks culminating in the resignation of Modi’s education minister.
The CJP has called its protests against Kumar “Season 2” on its social media handles, and said it would not stop until India’s election system was reformed.

Here's what to know if you're unsure about your measles immunity status
Measles is the most contagious disease known. It can rip through a population without immunity like wildfire. Just look at what's happening in Pennsylvania, says Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a public health effort led by the National Infectious Diseases Foundation.
"In January in Pennsylvania, they had 12 cases. Now we're seeing 100 plus cases per week and over 1,000 cases in Pennsylvania," she says. "If Pennsylvania can see it spread that fast, that can happen in any state that has low immunization rates."
As vaccination rates have fallen across the country, many communities have become vulnerable. Nationwide, more than 4,000 measles cases have been reported this year alone — the highest number in 35 years. Pennsylvania has reported five deaths. New York state declared a measles emergency.
Stinchfield says the recent measles surge has got many people wondering if they're at risk.
"It's a very common question for people to ask, 'am I immune? Am I OK? What do I need to do?' And that is exactly the right question everyone should be asking themselves right now," Stinchfield says.
The best defense is vaccination. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is 97% effective — meaning 97% of people will have an immune response.
"The measles vaccine is safe. It's highly effective, and it confers lifelong immunity," says Dr. Adam Ratner, a pediatric infectious disease physician in New York City and author of Booster Shots, a history of measles.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
But what if you don't know your immunization history, or you only got one dose of the measles shot? Should you get another dose? Infectious disease experts say that depends on several factors.
If you were born before 1957
People born before 1957 are presumed to be immune because back then, measles was so common, just about everyone got it in childhood, says Dr. Larry Kociolek, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago and an associate professor of pediatrics at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
"It was thought that pretty much everyone in the U.S. was infected with measles as sort of a rite of passage in childhood," Kocielek says. He says anyone who's ever had measles can be confident they're protected.
That is of course, if you survived. Before vaccines, measles used to kill 400 to 500 people each year in the U.S.
If you were vaccinated before 1968
People who were born after 1957 and vaccinated before 1968 may need an additional dose. That's because a small group of people who were immunized during that time received an early, less effective version of the vaccine that used inactivated or killed virus.
If you're not sure which vaccine you got, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends talking to your doctor about getting one or two doses of the MMR vaccine.
If you only got one dose of the MMR vaccine
At first, children in the U.S. received just one dose of the MMR vaccine. But that changed in 1989, after public health officials determined that a single dose wasn't enough to prevent outbreaks. That year, the official recommendation switched to two doses of MMR vaccine for children, which is still in effect today.
Kids need the higher protection "because they tend to be at higher risk of exposure, since they're oftentimes in group settings like schools and daycares," Kociolek says.
If you're in a higher-risk group
One dose of MMR vaccine is 93% effective, and traditionally, Kociolek says, that was considered enough protection for most adults, unless they were at higher risk of being exposed to measles. Health care workers, people in a college setting and those travelling abroad are all in this group. If you live with or are in close contact with someone who is immunocompromised, you also need two doses of vaccine to protect them.
But given the recent, dramatic rise of measles across the country these days, "if you are living in areas with high measles activity, it does make a whole lot of sense for adults to go ahead and get that second dose," Kociolek says.
Ratner says it's definitely worth asking your doctor if you should get a second dose.
While measles is often considered to be a childhood disease, a large proportion of people sickened this year have been unvaccinated adults — and people over 20 who lack immunity are at higher risk of serious complications.
No matter your age, "measles is a serious disease," Stinchfield says.
She notes that getting two doses of the vaccine can also help others at higher risk who can't get the MMR shot, including people who are pregnant, severely immunocompromised and infants under 6 months of age.
If you really don't know your immunization history
If you're just not sure if you're protected against measles and you can't find records of immunization, you could get a test to check your blood antibody levels. But those tests aren't perfect, says Dr. William Moss, a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
"It's possible that a person could actually be protected and test negative on one of those," Moss says.
Depending on your circumstances, your insurance might not cover the blood test. But most private insurance plans and Medicaid must cover another MMR vaccine at no cost.
Moss says if you can't confirm how many doses of MMR vaccine you've had, "I would say it is easier and less expensive to just get another MMR vaccine, and there is no harm in getting a second MMR vaccine or even a third, additional MMR dose."
After all, it's much better to be protected than infected.

Bandipora, 14 Oct: A pregnant woman from the remote Gurez valley died on her way to District Hospital Bandipora early Wednesday morning, while her baby was stillborn, following allegations by her family that heavy snowfall and official movement restrictions fatally delayed her medical referral.
The deceased, identified as Haseen Begum, wife of Showket Hameed Lone from Mazgund village in Tulail, was initially taken to the primary health centre in Sheikhpora late Tuesday evening.
According to the family, they found no medical staff available at the rural facility, forcing them to shift her to the sub-district hospital in Gurez.
There, doctors diagnosed her with severely low haemoglobin levels and advised an immediate referral to Bandipora for emergency care.
However, the family said they were initially barred from crossing the high-altitude Razdan pass due to heavy snowfall and nighttime movement restrictions imposed in the border area.
"We contacted Project Beacon officials who assured us they would clear the road ahead of the ambulance, but the sub-divisional magistrate in Gurez did not allow us to move," family members alleged.
The family claimed Begum remained in severe pain throughout the night, and that her baby died in the womb at the Gurez hospital around midnight. The grieving relatives also questioned the lack of emergency blood supplies, pointing out that a blood bank had been inaugurated at the local health facility just months earlier.
Speaking to Greater Kashmir, the sub-divisional magistrate of Gurez confirmed the family was initially stopped from moving on Tuesday evening due to the intense snowfall. He said that after the block medical officer informed him the woman needed an urgent referral, efforts were made past midnight to facilitate the travel.
The magistrate acknowledged the process took a long time due to delays in connecting with the officer commanding of Beacon to mobilise snow-clearing machinery.
He said the road was eventually cleared and the ambulance proceeded towards Bandipora, but added that the woman died on the way. He expressed ignorance regarding the circumstances of the baby's stillborn death at the Gurez hospital.
Dr Mukhtar Ahmad, medical superintendent of District Hospital Bandipora, told Greater Kashmir that the woman was declared "brought dead" upon arrival in the early hours of Wednesday.
"The attendants informed us she may have passed away on the way near Razdan Top," Ahmad said. He confirmed she was referred from Gurez due to low haemoglobin levels, adding that the child had already died in the womb at the sub-district hospital.
The health administration has since taken note of the allegations regarding staff absence and medical delays.
Bandipora Chief Medical Officer Bhajan Kour told Greater Kashmir, "We are investigating the incident."

Hyderabad, Oct 14: The Enforcement Directorate (ED), Hyderabad Zonal Office, has successfully completed the registration of seven immovable properties, auctioned for Rs 15.03 crore in favour of the successful bidders in connection with the Heera Group Ponzi case.
The properties comprise six flats at H.S. Royal, Shaikpet Village, Hyderabad, and one house at MLA Colony, Road No. 12, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad.
The ED said in a statement on Wednesday that proceeds realised from the auction of the attached properties shall be transferred to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) for onward disbursement to the genuine victims/claimants of Nowhera Shaik, Heera Group of Companies and others, in accordance with the directions of the Supreme Court.
Investors duped with high-return promises
Nowhera Shaik and her associates duped investors of over Rs 5,978 crore with false promises of 36% annual returns.
The auction was conducted on October 6 pursuant to the directions of the Supreme Court.
Supreme Court permits property auction
In its order dated March 5, 2025, the Supreme Court allowed the application filed by ED seeking permission to auction immovable properties attached in the case of Nowhera Shaik, Heera Group of Companies and others, with a view to maximising realisation from the attached properties for restitution to the genuine claimants/victims.
Subsequently, the Supreme Court directed the Registrar General, Telangana High Court, to depute T. Venkateshwar Rao, Registrar (Protocol), for execution of the sale deeds on behalf of the petitioner-accused. Accordingly, the sale deeds in respect of the seven properties have been duly registered in favour of the successful bidders.

ED investigation was initiated under the provisions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, against Nowhera Shaik, Heera Group of Companies and others on the basis of multiple FIRs registered by police in different states.

‘Won’t accept lame excuses’: SC takes EC to task over missing 2023 counting video
The Supreme Court warned the Election Commission of India of an adverse inference if it failed to produce records of the 2023 Sringeri assembly election vote count.
The Supreme Court on Wednesday took serious exception to the Election Commission of India’s claim that it could not trace the video recording of the 2023 vote count in Karnataka’s Sringeri assembly constituency, warning that it would draw an adverse inference against the poll body if it failed to produce the available records.
“How can the Election Commission of India (ECI) say that it has lost its record? Your whole purpose is to hold an election, and you need to have a document. Where is the question of you saying, ‘Yeah, we are trying to trace it’? You gave it to the elected candidate. There is no custody of records. Whatever you have, produce it on the next date. Otherwise, we will have to draw an adverse inference against you. We will not accept these kinds of lame excuses,” a bench of justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva told the ECI.
The court was hearing a plea by Congress leader TD Rajegowda, who was unseated following a recount of postal ballots in the constituency, where he had defeated BJP candidate DN Jeevaraj by a narrow margin of 201 votes in the 2023 Karnataka assembly elections.
The bench pulled up the ECI over its inability to trace the original counting footage after Rajegowda sought access to the election observer’s report and video recordings of both the original counting in 2023 and the recount conducted in May this year.
When the court proposed directing the poll body to produce these records, senior advocate Seshadri Naidu, appearing for the ECI, said the video recording of the original counting could not be traced. The submission failed to convince the bench, which asked the commission to produce whatever records were available by the next hearing.
The court posted the matter for February 15, 2027.
The missing footage assumes significance because the dispute centres on the treatment of postal ballots and the legality of the exercise that overturned Rajegowda’s electoral victory. The Supreme Court had, in May, directed the ECI to produce the relevant records concerning the recount ordered by the Karnataka high court and kept all consequential steps taken by the returning officer in abeyance pending further examination.
The dispute originated in an election petition filed by Jeevaraj before the Karnataka high court, challenging Rajegowda’s victory. On April 6, 2026, the high court ordered a recount of postal ballots, including the re-verification of 279 ballots that had been rejected during the original counting.
However, Rajegowda subsequently approached the Supreme Court, alleging that the returning officer had exceeded the scope of the high court’s directions by re-examining postal ballots that had already been accepted as valid.
In an order on May 11, the Supreme Court noted that the returning officer had not only re-verified the 279 rejected postal ballots but had also re-examined 1,251 other postal ballots that had previously been declared valid. The court observed that the exercise appeared to have gone beyond the high court’s directions and that the consequential steps taken by the returning officer were, prima facie, without legal foundation.
The recount, completed in early May, resulted in 255 votes previously counted in Rajegowda’s favour being invalidated, while two votes were added to Jeevaraj’s tally. The revised count gave the BJP candidate a victory margin of 52 votes, reversing the original result. Jeevaraj was subsequently declared elected.
The Supreme Court’s intervention in May allowed Rajegowda to continue as the MLA while it examined the legality of the recount and directed that all steps taken pursuant to the exercise remain in abeyance.
Rajegowda has also questioned the high court’s decision to order a recount, arguing that the court’s findings on allegations of corrupt practices against him did not justify the exercise.
The controversy has also led to a criminal case alleging tampering with postal ballots during the recount. Jeevaraj, who has denied wrongdoing, secured an interim order from the Karnataka high court staying further investigation in the case.
