Winning a Nobel Prize is a matter of great prestige. Winning a Nobel Prize also means the award going to a small number of people while a large number are left out, even if they really deserved to win.
This is partly because of the prizes’ rules. Alfred Nobel’s will said nothing about the number of people that can be awarded at one time but the Nobel Foundation’s statutes limit each prize to at most three people at a time, and no one that has died by the time a prize is announced. Also, scientists need to have been nominated by nominators who have their own eligibility criteria.
A big-picture view of the science Nobel Prizes through history brings another pattern into view: a preference for singular breakthroughs rather than lifetime achievements.
Boyden, Bamberg, and beyond
Start with the Nobel Prize this year for physiology/medicine, to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel, for their work on optogenetics. In 2002, Austrian scientist Gero Miessenböck & co. had first sensitised to light some neurons that were not naturally light-sensitive. Miessenböck is now at the University of Oxford, where his profile page describes him as an ‘inventor’ of optogenetics.
Hegemann and Nagel have been feted for identifying and characterising the protein channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2). The next step was to show that it could control neurons. The first author of the paper that did was Edward Boyden, who helped pioneer the application of ChR2 to neuroscience. Boyden is now a professor of neurotechnology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and the Broad Institute.
Another author of this paper, Ernst Bamberg, had supervised Nagel’s PhD and was part of the team that established the importance of ChR2. A page on the website of the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics, Germany, where Bamberg is now an emeritus professor, says he was instrumental in translating the ChR2 finding into practical applications.
Yet another author, Feng Zhang, is also at MIT now, and in 2007, he was a member of one of two teams that adapted another protein, called halorhodopsin, to silence neurons with light instead of activating them. The other team, consisting of Xue Han and Boyden, had demonstrated the same capability.
These contributions together — rather than only those that the laureates led — turned the ability to control neurons with light into a tool of neuroscience with real-world applications, including in medicine.
No lone wolf
Next, the physics prize — which this year demonstrated the brokenness of the Nobel Prizes on a whole other level. Francis Halzen won the prize all by himself “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”. But IceCube is an international collaboration involving around 450 experts from 58 institutions in 14 countries.
Crucially, the prize-giving committee was not constrained to give the prize to one person here. The Nobel Foundation statutes allow the committee to decide whether its prizes can be awarded to associations or organisations. But the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which awards the physics, chemistry, and economics prizes, does not seem to have adopted this option. If it had, the physics prize could have recognised the IceCube collaboration as a whole.
But even if this rule did not exist, it is hard to say why the committee picked Halzen alone. In 1988, Halzen and (today) University of Hawai’i physics and astronomy professor John G. Learned reported the idea of using Antarctica’s ice mass as the target in which neutrinos from outer space could interact with atoms together. Learned then focused on an underwater neutrino experiment called DUMAND while Halzen pursued a project that eventually became IceCube.
Also, in 2012, while searching IceCube data for neutrinos coming from outer space with very high energies, scientists found two candidate events. The data quickly snowballed into evidence proving that neutrinos could be energised significantly by natural phenomena in space — and the prize citation credits this feat to Halzen alone.
But in real-life (as opposed to Nobel-life), the IceCube collaboration had credited Japanese physicist Aya Ishihara with finding those two candidate events, and for which she received an International Union of Pure and Applied Physics award in 2013. This particular oversight is oddly reminiscent of the infamous Jocelyn Bell Burnell story. Ishihara is currently a professor at Chiba University, where she continues to study high-energy neutrinos and develop the next generation of neutrino detectors.
Furthermore, the 2013 Science paper that reported the high-energy neutrinos also named three scientists named Claudio Kopper, Naoko Kurahashi, and Nathan Whitehorn as its corresponding authors.
The physics prize for Halzen is not misplaced. Halzen was very good — but the point is so were very many others. Aside from the scientists named here, it also required engineers and technicians who could build it in one of the most hostile locations on our planet. And all these people had to work together to make the project and its subsequent achievements possible. Halzen alone could never have done it.
Drawing difficult lines
Finally, the chemistry Nobel Prize this year illustrates the problem with the rule that it cannot be given to people who have died by the time the prize is announced. In 1953, the British physicist Frederick Charles Frank came up with a mathematical way to explain how a small chemical imbalance in a specific kind of reaction could force the reaction to make that imbalance the norm. This way required the reaction to have three properties, called autocatalysis, enantioselective catalysis, and mutual inhibition.
Between 1986 and 1995, Henri Kagan in France and Kenso Soai in Japan had reported evidence of all the conditions of Frank’s model, providing experimental evidence that it could work in the real world. However, Frank died in 1998, aged 87.
That said, the 1995 paper by Soai et al. included Takanori Shibata, who made essential contributions to this branch of chemistry (and was second author on the paper). And whereas Kagan and Soai had demonstrated different aspects of Frank’s model, Shibata was the first author of a 1999 paper that extended the work of Soai et al. to demonstrate the reaction Frank had tried to model. Shibata is currently at Waseda University. And again, it is not easy to rationalise the prize-giving committee’s decision to not include him among this year’s chemistry laureates.
On the other hand, the committee’s decision to exclude U.S. chemical engineer Donna Blackmond throws light on one possible line of reasoning. A technical statement accompanying the chemistry prize credited her with extending Kagan’s attempts to use mathematics to understand non-linear effects in chemical reactions. Blackmond and her team later also took big strides in making sense of the mechanism of the so-called Soai reaction.
And yet, the committee elected to reward the discovery of the validity of Frank’s model rather than work that explained and further extended it.
The S.N. Bose example
In the final analysis, the citations for the Nobel Prizes should not be mistaken for the history of science. Scientists build on the work of others and science advances in these slow but steady increments. When Peter Higgs and François Englert were awarded the Nobel Prize for physics in 2013 for predicting the Higgs boson, there was some clamour in India for not recognising the work of Satyendra Nath Bose. The objection was fair to the extent that you can’t have a fruit without the whole tree and yet petty because it is not reasonable to expect one prize to laud the entire history of a field.
This is why each Nobel Prize award can be a chance to reflect on its limitations, and remember that it is not an ultimate recognition. No prize is.
In that vein, we should also not confuse the number of winners every year with the number of people it takes to do excellent science — from grad students who perform simple experiments to senior colleagues to discuss complicated ideas with. In fact, depending on where in the world you are and your socio-economic standing, your ability to be a good scientist may turn on something as deceptively simple as having someone to help with household chores.
Perhaps most of all, while the Nobel Prizes recognise good science, not all good science wins Nobel Prizes.

The scene is familiar. Five days after a caesarean section, a woman in one of our cities is at home with a newborn, a painful surgical wound, and a folder of papers. The papers list the baby’s feeding schedule, immunisation dates, and the paediatrician’s phone number. There is one line about her own care, a follow-up visit in six weeks. She is bleeding more than she expected. She has not slept longer than ninety minutes at a stretch. Her mother tells her this is normal. Her mother-in-law tells her this is normal. It is extremely common. But “common” does not mean harmless.
What’s happening in India
India has done something remarkable in maternal health. The maternal mortality ratio has fallen from 254 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2004–2006 to 87 in 2022–2024, a reduction of nearly two-thirds. The National Family Health Survey-6 (NFHS-6) records institutional births at 90.6%.
But these numbers leave an important question unanswered: What happens to new mothers after birth?
The NFHS-6 reports that 82.8% of mothers received postnatal care within two days of delivery. The postnatal care recorded within 48 hours of an institutional delivery may well be a check that occurs before the mother leaves the hospital. A check before discharge and continuity after it are not the same thing, and the indicator cannot tell them apart.
Why this is important
The World Health Organization’s postnatal care guidance sets a minimum of four contacts. Each is meant to assess the mother as well as the baby. India’s headline statistic largely overlaps with the first of those four contacts. But no headline national indicator shows whether women received the complete schedule, or what those contacts assessed.
This is not merely a question of comfort. A systematic review of 26 studies involving 8.7 million women globally identified 6,142 maternal deaths. Nearly one-quarter of those deaths occurred between postpartum days 8 and 42. That is precisely when an Indian mother is at home, and precisely when what is happening to her is least visible to the system.
Additionally, the caesarean section rate increased from 21.5% at NFHS-5 to 27.2% at NFHS-6. More Indian women are therefore recovering from major abdominal surgery in flats and small houses, with a newborn, some of them without the extended household support that older arrangements assumed.
What is missing
A qualitative systematic review of 51 studies of traditional postpartum practices across more than 20 countries found the same elements recurring: organised support for the mother, a prescribed period of rest, particular foods, and additional help with the baby. Read as medicine rather than ritual, it is a structured plan for recovery. It feeds her at a time when she is depleted and breastfeeding. And it does the thing our health system finds hardest to implement—treating the weeks after birth as a distinct state requiring care, rather than a return to ‘normal’ life.
Home-Based Newborn Care in India schedules an ASHA to visit the house on days 3, 7, 14, 21, 28 and 42. National guidance is explicit that the visits on days 3, 7 and 42 are for the mother as well as the baby. The ASHA’s job is to look for excessive bleeding, high temperature, foul-smelling discharge, cracked nipples, and engorged breasts. The mother, in other words, is written into the design.
What is missing is the rest of her well-being. The maternal component focuses on danger signs, feeding, and breast problems rather than on recovery. The ASHA’s checklist does not include blood-pressure measurement, a systematic mental health screening, or a follow-up glucose test. And the arithmetic of the schedule tells its own story: six visits for the baby, three of which are hers as well.
Across many Indian communities, the period after childbirth, in some up to 42 days, is marked out and protected. Families understand that a woman who has just given birth needs feeding, rest, and helping hands. The routine postnatal care schedule also centres on the first 42 days.
Yet in both settings, attention can still gravitate toward the baby.
Among 403 women in Gujarat, those with low social support had about two-and-a-half times the odds of postnatal depression compared with women who had strong support. The findings suggest that support may be an important factor, and our households have supplied it for generations. What the customs cannot do is examine the mother. They cannot detect persistently high blood pressure or determine whether anaemia is contributing to the exhaustion everyone is calling normal. Some customs and practices are not actual care; indeed, they may actively prevent a woman from being taken to a doctor when she is bleeding heavily or running a fever. A good postnatal system would add an examination to the help that supportive households give.
What is needed
What would it take to consider the mother’s condition as well as the baby’s? The schedule already exists and so do the workers. What is missing is scope, ownership, and measurement. Visits to the mother and baby after discharge should assess the mother’s recovery as well as her danger signs. Responsibility for the mother’s follow-up should rest with a designated healthcare provider or service, which should document her care after the delivery record is closed.
A structured review can begin in minutes. It should ask about bleeding, pain, and her surgical wound. It should include measuring her blood pressure, particularly if she was hypertensive in pregnancy. It should test for anaemia when her tiredness, or her pregnancy, points that way. It should ask if she is experiencing changes in mood or sleep and whether she’s been having frightening or intrusive thoughts. It should ask about feeding difficulty, urinary leakage, prolapse, and whether she’s experiencing pain during sex. It should arrange a follow-up glucose test for the woman who had gestational diabetes and now carries a substantial lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes.
The point is not the panel. The point is that somebody asks.
Making it part of the system
Primary care also belongs here, not in place of the obstetrician or the ASHA but as part of the system that holds on to what the pregnancy revealed. It is often during pregnancy that high blood pressure or high blood sugar first appears. When the delivery record closes, that knowledge should not close with it.
We measure delivery and newborn outcomes in detail. We should give equal attention to maternal recovery after discharge. Until maternal recovery is counted, too much of it will continue to unfold privately at home, with symptoms described as ‘normal’ by everyone, including the mother herself, until enough time passes that she stops mentioning them and lives with ill health instead.
(Dr. Sowmya Josyula is an internist and public health specialist. She writes on women’s health and on traditional practice examined against evidence. sowmya.josyula@kushalahealth.com)

The Union Health Ministry is engaging with youth volunteers to find people with tuberculosis (TB) who may be missing from the health system. JOSH teams of the National Cadet Corps (NCC) and MY Bharat volunteers are deploying for household-level outreach in 55 districts across 11 States and Union Territories.
Health Minister J.P. Nadda launched the JOSH (Joint Squad for Health) teams under the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan on Thursday. The teams will work at block and ward levels to identify people with symptoms, encourage testing, and support patients so they can complete treatment.
Each team will comprise five NCC cadets and five MY Bharat volunteers and will function under a designated Class-I officer. The initiative is being implemented jointly by the Ministries of Health and Family Welfare, Youth Affairs and Sports and Defence.
The government’s emphasis is on active case finding, with the Health Minister stating that people could be living with TB without recognising their symptoms and therefore remain outside the formal healthcare system. “Awareness is important, screening is important, but our responsibility does not end there,” he said, stressing the need to ensure diagnosis and completion of treatment.
The Centre also felicitated 67,933 Panchayats across 697 districts that were declared TB Mukt in 2026. The JOSH initiative is expected to be expanded to other districts after orientation and mobilisation of volunteers.

Saudi man charged with planting 'sophisticated' recording device in OpenAI office
- Published
A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.
Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.
According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.
Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.
On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.
OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".
According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.
Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.
He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".
On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene.
That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said.
Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation.
If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (£187,000).

Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigns after allegations of improper conduct
WASHINGTON — The White House publicly asked for U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle's resignation on Tuesday as she faced mounting accusations of improper conduct, and she announced within two hours that she was quitting, ending days of talk and speculation about her professional fate. Guilfoyle insisted that she would "vigorously defend" herself.
President Donald Trump's administration had said earlier Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
That revelation came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle "has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."
"She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said just after Guilfoyle's resignation, which was posted on her X account. He said he had not spoken to her but "she will not be there."
Guilfoyle's departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle's reported conduct.
Guilfoyle denies the accusations and cites her 'decades of public service'
In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle addressed the accusations directly in her resignation post on X, saying, "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity."
"I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional," she said. "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."
In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers denied that she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.
The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations."
They did not immediately return calls Tuesday.
The allegations began surfacing weeks ago
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."
But after another report appeared later, Rubio — speaking Thursday before leaving Athens — berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn't know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.
"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
A second U.S. official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department's inspector general was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
There was no immediate response to Zacharia's statement from the Greek government or Cabinet members.
Ahead of Tuesday's announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. "This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity," Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated "the same way as every other ambassador" and argued that an official summons had not been necessary.
Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president's daughter-in-law, accompanied by Dua Lipa's "Dance the Night," from the 2023 soundtrack of the movie "Barbie."
Greece has taken on an increasingly important and influential role because of its geographic location in Southeastern Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly on energy issues as the war with Iran has spiked global oil prices. Besides the vast number of Greek-registered oil tankers that regularly ply the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, Greece is well positioned to be a pipeline conduit for liquefied natural gas imports into the Balkans and beyond.
As the U.S. ambassador to Greece, Guilfoyle had put an emphasis on energy issues, although her close association with executives in that sector was part of what got her into trouble.
Democrats call for an investigation
The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the United States could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.
Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was married to Democrat Gavin Newsom when he was San Francisco's mayor, before he became California's governor. She later was engaged to Trump's son Donald Trump Jr.

In September 2026, a black-and-white photo spread widely purportedly showing Adolf Hitler and other Nazi Party officials inspecting a model of a triumphal arch they hoped to build in Berlin.
Beneath one Reddit post (archived), commenters compared the arch, which was never constructed, to U.S. President Donald Trump's plan to construct a massive triumphal arch of his own in Washington, D.C., just outside the grounds of Arlington National Cemetery.
Snopes readers contacted us to determine whether the picture is real.
In short, the photograph is authentic.
Among the many unfinished projects of Nazi Germany was a plan to redevelop the capital, Berlin, and rename it "Germania." Nazi Party chief architect Albert Speer was put in charge of the design and built a model of the planned city.
Among the buildings was a massive, triumphal arch. The black-and-white photo authentically shows Hitler inspecting the model, presumably designed by Speer.
A reverse image search revealed the picture is on stock image website Alamy, which credits the photograph to the archives of the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung.
Though the "Date taken" information reads Jan. 1, 1939, Alamy also says the picture is "undated." Berlin is noted as the location. The "More information" caption reads:
Adolf Hitler inspects a modell of a planned triumphal arch. Adolf Hitler and other party functionaries inspect the modell of the triumphal arch, which was planned to be built after the end of the war in Berlin. Undated picture. Date created: 01/01/1939-31/12/1945
Snopes contacted Süddeutsche Zeitung to learn more about the photo's history. A spokesperson for the paper said in a statement that it licenses images from its historical archives through Alamy. Therefore, the picture came from the archives of a reputable news publication.
Running the photograph through several tools that detect content generated using artificial intelligence software uncovered no signs that it was AI-generated.
A history of triumphal arches
Historians trace the history of triumphal arches back to ancient Rome. During the Roman Republic, the "triumph" was an extravagant parade the Roman Senate granted to a Roman general (and his army) following a particularly remarkable conquest. Three triumphal arches were built during this period, according to Britannica, but none survive.
During the imperial period, however, Roman emperors frequently declared triumphs for themselves (regardless of their military accomplishments), often building arches as a commemoration. There are three — the Arches of Titus, Septimus Severus and Constantine — still standing in Rome.
The Arc de Triomphe in Paris, built to commemorate the conquests of Napoleon Bonaparte, is one of many arches still extant around the world that pay architectural homage to the Roman triumphal arch. They are built for many reasons —  New York City's Washington Square Arch commemorated 100 years since George Washington's inauguration, for instance, while New Delhi's India Gate is a war memorial.
Trump first mentioned the idea of a triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., in October 2025. When CBS News asked who the arch was for, Trump pointed at himself and said "me." The arch — which has been the subject of multiple lawsuits claiming its construction was not approved in the proper manner or could pose risks to aviation safety and emergency services — would stand 250 feet tall, commemorating the 250th anniversary of the United States.
The Nazis, art and architecture
The ideology of the Nazi Party, beyond the genocidal antisemitism, homophobia, racism, xenophobia and other assorted discriminatory practices, was built on a vision of completely remaking the nation of Germany. This remaking — or a "rebirth" — aimed to turn the state itself into a sort of religion, warping and twisting every aspect of society along the way.
Attendance at this metaphorical "church," of course, was mandatory. "Disagreement is a sign of diversity," Italian writer and philosopher Umberto Eco wrote in his 1995 essay, "Ur-Fascism." Diversity, therefore, would not be tolerated under Nazism.
Part of this "spiritual" rebirth involved attempting to influence the nation's arts and culture. In 1937, the Nazis ordered the confiscation of thousands of modern art pieces the party felt "insult[ed] German feeling."
The Nazis then had the confiscated works exhibited for the public to see in Munich. The exhibition was called "Degenerate Art."
The crusade against "degenerate art" also impacted architecture. The influential Bauhaus art school, pioneers in modern architecture, closed in 1933 on the orders of the Nazi regime. Speer, the architect (and Nazi Party member), quickly rose up the party's ranks and found himself in Hitler's inner circle.
While most of Speer's designs for Germania were never constructed, at least one part of the vision remains. The "Schwerbelastungskorper," German for "heavy load-bearing body," is a massive concrete cylinder located in the Tempelhof neighborhood at the corner of General Pape Strasse and Loewenhardtdamm. 
According to the structure's Information Center website and The Guardian newspaper, it was built as a test for the planned triumphal arch's northeast pillar, because engineers were concerned that Berlin's swampy soil would not be able to hold the weight of the monumental structures. The cylinder was built in 1941, at least partially by prisoners of war.

Food, from the moment it’s in the mouth until it’s excreted as poop, goes through digestion—and this process is a wild journey. Food containing carbohydrates, proteins, or lipids is chewed into a mush in the mouth, where some degree of starch and lipid digestion occurs before it is swallowed. In the stomach, the swallowed ‘ball’ of chewed food is continuously ground and churned until the food particles are small enough to enter the small intestine. Simultaneously, hydrochloric acid (HCl) and pepsin (an enzyme) in the stomach break down complex proteins in the food.
The food, now in a semi-liquid form, reaches the digestive enzyme-rich small intestine, where its fate is sealed for major chemical digestion before being converted into absorbable nutrients. Enzymes in the small intestine break down the partially digested macronutrients—carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids—into smaller molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream, along with vitamins and minerals.
What remains is indigestible food, along with leftover digestive fluids and cellular waste, which enters the colon (large intestine), where digestive enzymes are lacking. However, the gut microbiota—the body’s dynamic ‘organ’—in the colon compensates for this dearth by fermenting indigestible food, including dietary fibres and indigestible proteins. Enzymes produced by the gut microbiota break this indigestible food into useful metabolites and gases before the remainder is expelled as poop.
What are intestinal gases?
In humans, intestinal gases include nitrogen (N2), oxygen (O2), carbon dioxide (CO2), hydrogen (H2), methane (CH4), and trace amounts of hydrogen sulphide (H2S)—the gas with the rotten egg smell. While N2 and O2 mostly reflect swallowed air, H2 and CH4 are odourless gases produced by gut microbiota. It is H2S that is primarily responsible for the smell of gas.
The colon—which hosts the highest microbial densities—harbours microbes that prefer indigestible carbohydrates as food, or as an energy source. These indigestible-carbohydrate-loving microbes (carbohydrate-fermenting) flourish in the colon region close to the small intestine (proximal colon), where their energy source availability is higher. Microbes including Bacteroides scavenge (ferment) human-indigestible carbohydrates such as dietary fibres and resistant starch, producing substantial quantities of hydrogenas a major by-product.
Also thriving in this oxygen-poor, hydrogen-rich ecosystem are microbes that compete for, and convert hydrogento methane, like methanogenic archaea. Likewise, sulphate-reducing bacteria (SRB) in these regions of the colon convert hydrogeninto hydrogen sulphide in small amounts. As the food passes through the colon, the availability of indigestible carbohydrates decreases over time. Microbes like SRB in regions of the colon close to the rectum (distal colon) also ferment human-indigestible proteins for energy, producing hydrogen sulphide in the process.
Studies so far suggest that host cells (through distinct mechanisms) and microbial cells utilise intestinal gases. Excess gases are eliminated as exhaled gas (from the lungs) and flatulence.
What do intestinal gases do?
Recent studies suggest intestinal gases are more than just gas. They can, in fact, serve as markers of gastrointestinal (GI) health, and can regulate gut motility and transit time. Gut motility refers to the muscle contractions in the digestive tract that move the food, and gut transit time is the time it takes for food to move through the gastrointestinal tract before being excreted.
Advancing research reveals that hydrogencan influence gut motility and, in experimental models, shorten transit time. Methane, by contrast, has been shown to slow gut motility and increase transit time. However, findings on the effect of hydrogen sulphide on gut motility and transit time have been mixed.
Microbiota research has also pointed to links between imbalances in gut microbiota and intestinal gas levels and gastrointestinal(GI) diseases/symptoms.
A real-world study measured hydrogen, methane, and hydrogen sulphide levels using breath testing in 3,004 participants with GI symptoms, especially excessive bloating and flatulence, from the United States. The study found associations between intestinal gas levels and GI symptoms: higher hydrogen levels (≥20 ppm above baseline) with diarrhoea; higher methane levels (≥10 ppm) with constipation; and higher hydrogen sulphide levels (≥2 ppm) with severe diarrhoea and abdominal pain. The study also suggested dysregulated hydrogen sulphide production was associated with greater diarrhoea, urgency, bloating, and symptom severity.
Animal models and clinical studies have reported similar associations between intestinal gases and GI symptoms. However, these studies lack identical methodologies and comparison with healthy participants as controls.
Monitoring gases for diagnosis
The most commonly adopted method for measuring intestinal gases is breath testing—measuring gases in exhaled breath. Microbial fermentation activity and gut motility are also assessed indirectly with this method.
However, new techniques are being devised for non-invasive, real-time continuous monitoring of intestinal gases. To capture eliminated intestinal gases (exhaled gas and flatus), researchers have designed respiration/fermentation chambers (airtight rooms with gas sensors and continuous air supply) to explore microbial fermentation activity, track intestinal gases, and monitor the effects of therapeutic interventions.
Alternatively, as flatus has relatively higher concentrations of intestinal gases, researchers at the University of Maryland have developed a device that can be attached to underwear. The device, designed to objectively measure hydrogenin flatus, monitors real-time gas profiles and gas-release patterns, providing insights into gut microbial activity and digestive health.
Why this is important
Measuring and monitoring real-time gas profiles could enable researchers to expand gut microbiota research: define ‘normal’ and ‘abnormal’ levels in intestinal gases, establish mechanisms behind gas effects, and study diverse populations, involving both healthy people and people with GI diseases, over long periods. Doctors could also potentially tailor a treatment plan—diet or gas-targeted medication—to rebalance the gut microbial ecosystem and modulate gas production and track GI health progress.
Therefore, the next time someone lets one rip, remember that intestinal gases have uses beyond popular humour or emptying out a room. These gases are part of a dynamic system that shapes the gut microbiota and influences digestive health, including how one poops, and can serve as markers of GI health.
(Smruthi Prabhu is an independent science writer from Mangalore. smruthigp@gmail.com)

Nasdaq-listed SaaS major Freshworks has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Torii, a SaaS management platform, to extend its IT service management tool, Freshservice, into AI and software spend governance. The transaction is expected to close in the quarter ending December 2026. Founded in 2017 by Uri Haramati, Uri Nativ and Tal Bereznitskey in New York, Torii helps enterprises track AI consumption at the token level, attribute usage to specific internal teams, forecast spend trajectories, and set operational budget limits. By integrating its SaaS management capabilities into Freshservice, Freshworks aims to enable organisations to have better visibility of their AI usage. The system provides IT and finance departments with continuous oversight, replacing manual spreadsheet reconciliation with real-time analytics. “Modern IT teams are being asked to govern more of the business than ever, with less visibility into what it costs. Freshservice already gives IT one place to see everything they run. With Torii, that same view now extends to software and AI spend — what’s running, who's using it, and what it costs, so finance and IT stop reconciling spreadsheets and start making decisions together,” said Freshworks CEO and President Dennis Woodside. Founded in 2010 by Girish Mathrubootham and Shanmugam Krishnasamy, Freshworks offers a suite of cloud-based software to help companies manage customer engagement, sales, IT service management and marketing. After Mathrubootham exited the company in 2024, it has sought to reinvent itself as an AI-native enterprise platform under Woodside’s leadership. Apart from introducing AI-led offerings like vertical AI agents and workflow automation tools, it also underwent a major restructuring earlier this year, trimming 11% of its workforce or around 500 employees, citing automation of work. Growing adoption of its AI products helped Freshworks get back into the black in the quarter ended June 2026. The company reported a net profit of $3.2 Mn as against a net loss of $1.7 Mn in the year-ago period and a net loss of $4.8 Mn in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, its revenue grew 16% YoY to $237.4 Mn.

For patients with advanced cancer and other life-limiting illnesses, palliative care often needs to extend beyond hospital wards to their homes, where families grapple with pain, emotional distress, and the demands of long-term caregiving.
At the State-run Kidwai Memorial Institute of Oncology (KMIO), the Department of Palliative Medicine has made home-based care a key part of its services, reporting more than 750 home-care visits, over 12,000 km travelled and more than 3,000 beneficiaries, including patients and caregivers.
These services were highlighted while observing World Hospice and Palliative Care Day on October 10, which this year carried the theme ‘Pain management: An essential part of palliative care’.
“With the help of volunteers and NGOs, we also extend financial support for children’s education. We provide waterbed and airbed, ration kits, and nebuliser machines for use at home. It is not just about treating the patient,” M.K. Yadhuraj Gowda, Head of the Department of Palliative Medicine at KMIO, told The Hindu.
The home-care service is intended for patients who find it difficult to travel to the hospital because of advanced illness, reduced mobility, or other challenges. Multidisciplinary teams provide medical assessment, symptom management, nursing care, and support in familiar surroundings, helping reduce the burden of repeated hospital visits.
The department’s approach also recognises that serious illness affects entire families. Caregivers may need help managing the practical demands of looking after a patient, as well as support in coping with emotional and financial pressures, Dr. Gowda said.
Beyond death
Palliative care also includes bereavement support for families after the death of a loved one. KMIO’s department provides guidance to help family members cope with grief, manage emotional distress and access support during the grieving process.
The service reflects the broader role of palliative care, which addresses not only physical pain and other symptoms but also the psychological, emotional, social and spiritual needs of patients and their families. Volunteer services add another layer of support for families navigating serious illness and loss.
Pain relief and care for children
Institute director R. Krishnappa said the department provides inpatient palliative care for patients who require specialised management of pain and other distressing symptoms, with capacity for more than 30 patients. Its services include medication and interventional procedures such as nerve blocks and neurolysis for selected patients with severe cancer-related pain that remains inadequately controlled with conventional treatment.
It also provides paediatric palliative care, with age-appropriate pain and symptom management, emotional support and guidance for families caring for children with cancer and other serious illnesses, he said.
Music and sound therapy sessions are conducted for inpatients on Wednesdays, while yoga therapy sessions are held on Thursdays to promote relaxation and emotional well-being alongside medical treatment.
Teleconsultations extend specialist support
The department has relaunched its ‘Call for Care - Neravina Kare’ service to connect patients living outside Bengaluru and in distant locations with specialist palliative care. Through telephone and video consultations, a team comprising a palliative care physician, nurse and clinical psycho-oncologist offers guidance on symptom management and emotional support. Patients and caregivers can contact the service on 9008441708.

The Department of Cardiology at the Government Medical College Hospital (MCH), Kozhikode, which is visited by hundreds of patients from across north Keralam every day, is facing a serious shortage of doctors.
Though the sanctioned permanent staff strength is 14, only eight are on the rolls, and one of the doctors has been sent on a working arrangement basis to the Government Medical College Hospital, Wayanad, too.
According to sources, instead of filling up the posts of Assistant Professors, the authorities have been deploying Doctorate of Medicine (DM) trainees, who work at the hospital to complete their one-year bond period and then leave the job.
Senior doctors say that this stop-gap arrangement does not have any practical use. They claim that at least 10 years of continuous experience in the echocardiogram test room is required for a doctor to deliver an expert opinion. “The DM trainees can be deployed for outpatient department duty, primary angioplasty surgeries for heart attack, and basic echocardiogram procedures, that’s fine. But, if someone gets a doubt in a complex case in the echocardiogram test room, the senior doctors even on operation theatre duty may have to be called in to clear it. There are three such echo rooms here where tests are done simultaneously,” says a doctor.
The department has the posts of one Professor, three Associate Professors, and 10 Assistant Professors. The doctors say that even this staff pattern was set long ago and the number of patients has seen a drastic rise in recent years. Though there were two more posts of Professors earlier, they were reportedly shifted to other medical college hospitals. The present crisis is set to aggravate in the next three to four years when some of the senior doctors will retire from service, they point out.
For the record, around 600 patients seek treatment every day at the cardiology OP section. Over 5,500 procedures, including 980 primary angioplasty surgeries, were performed last year. The patients admitted with heart attack are directly shifted from the casualty to the cardiology intensive care unit (ICU). Up to 10 patients are reportedly shifted to the ICU every day and the primary angioplasty surgeries are done round the clock. There are two cath labs here.
Though the authorities have repeatedly intimated the government about the situation and applications were invited for the posts of Assistant Professors, many junior doctors are not keen on joining duty reportedly because of the unattractive entry-level pay.

In a bid to make cancer treatment more affordable and reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure, the Union government has decided to cap trade margins at 30% of the maximum retail price (MRP) for all non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs.
Also read | Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
The measure will cover branded and generic drugs, domestically manufactured and imported medicines, and patented and non-patented products. An expert committee under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) will finalise the list of medicines to be brought under the measure.
Current mark-ups up to 700%
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), which analysed market data, found that the average trade mark-up on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines was around 170%, with mark-ups reaching up to 700% in some cases. It also found substantial differences between prices charged through retail, hospital, and online pharmacies.
The government said the decision was prompted by the high financial burden of cancer treatment. Around 75% of cancer treatment expenditure is estimated to be borne out of pocket.
The anti-cancer medicines market comprises around 225 drugs and 500 formulations, with an annual turnover of approximately ₹12,500 crore. Scheduled cancer medicines account for about ₹2,250 crore.
Massive savings
A senior official said that the government is drawing on the experience of a similar intervention in 2019, when the NPPA capped trade margins on 42 selected non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs by invoking its extraordinary powers under Paragraph 19 of the Drug Price Control Order, 2013. The exercise had reportedly resulted in price reductions of up to 91%, with annual savings of ₹984 crore across 526 brands.
The latest intervention is expected to result in price reductions of up to 70% of MRP and annual savings of around ₹2,500 crore, the government said.
‘Production must be maintained’
Under the new framework, the trade margin will be capped at 30% of MRP, equivalent to 42.86% of the price to stockist.
“To ensure availability, manufacturers will be required to maintain their existing production level,” said the official.
The government said the measure would regulate trade margins rather than manufacturers’ selling prices or revenue, with the intervention aimed at reducing the margins retained across the distribution chain.

In late September, Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna of California introduced the Free Child Care for America Act, an $80 billion-a-year proposal to make childcare free for nearly every family with kids under six. The bill would let families choose between sending their child to a daycare center, having a relative, friend, or neighbor paid a living wage to care for them, or taking a $1,000 monthly stipend to keep the child home for the first three years. It comes from a lawmaker who openly says he’s considering a run for president. “I want 2028 to be a big-ideas primary,” Khanna told ABC. “A contest on who’s going to have ideas of the future that meet the moment.”
Universal childcare is set to be a 2028 presidential test
Democrats are already rolling out big plans.
If you buy something from a Vox link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Khanna’s is not the only big Democratic childcare proposal released in the last few months. In July, Project 2029 — a group of liberal policy experts developing an agenda for the next Democratic administration — proposed something similar to Khanna’s plan: giving families a choice between free daycare and $1,000 a month to provide care at home or pay a trusted caregiver. The group estimates that would cost about $200 billion annually. Third Way, a centrist Democratic think tank, unveiled its own universal childcare pitch, guaranteeing every family at least three affordable options within a 15-minute drive of home or work by expanding home-based, infant, and after-hours care, and leveraging employers as partners.
Key takeaways
- Childcare is emerging as a major 2028 issue, with big new proposals from Rep. Ro Khanna, Project 2029, and Third Way.
- “Universal childcare” means different things to different people — free for all, affordable for most, or simply enough slots to go around.
- Polls show broad, bipartisan appetite for government action on childcare, with debate over how much families should chip in.
Early childhood policy is quickly becoming a defining issue for 2028 hopefuls. On the right, Vice President JD Vance has staked out an early and controversial position, to pay married stay-at-home parents roughly $9,000 per child annually using existing federal childcare funds. On the left, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is spearheading a new House working group to develop a federal childcare plan. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has been pushing free pre-K for all 4-year-olds, something California Gov. Gavin Newsom has already enacted in his state. And New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who can’t run for president but is widely seen as an influential voice in the party’s future, has made universal childcare one of the top goals of his administration.
Michelle Lujan Grisham, the Democratic governor of New Mexico, recently told Semafor that any politician seeking to run for president in 2028 “absolutely should” run on universal childcare proposals. Last year New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to families regardless of income. Her advice echoed David Plouffe, a Democratic strategist who managed Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign, who said that universal childcare should be in the Democrats’ 2028 party platform.
This new wave of enthusiasm marks a pivot for an idea that has long been seen as a distant pipe dream in American politics. It wasn’t always that way: When women filled factories during World War II, the federal government funded thousands of daycare centers to watch their kids. In 1971, Congress actually passed a bipartisan childcare bill, though President Richard Nixon vetoed it, saying it would weaken the family. In the 50 years since, Washington lawmakers have focused their energies on other big battles, offering little on childcare beyond subsidies for some low-income families. Over that time, the US has fallen out of step with nearly all its peer nations around the world, which help parents pay for childcare, on top of offering paid parental leave after birth.
It’s not hard to understand why the idea is finally getting a serious look in the US. With voters citing affordability as a top concern, politicians are looking for ways they can bring down costs facing families. After paying rent or a mortgage, childcare often stands as many parents’ biggest monthly expense. Businesses have started to care too, as access to reliable care affects both people’s ability to hold down jobs and businesses’ ability to attract and retain workers. It’s why organizations like the Chamber of Commerce have taken up the issue and why red, blue, and purple states alike have been elevating childcare in recent years.
In Congress and in the Democratic campaign world, there’s a strong sense that childcare, long overshadowed by climate, infrastructure, voting rights, and health care, is now at the front of the line should Democrats regain power. Insiders credit both donor influence and a feeling that childcare advocates have duly waited their turn.
But as Democrats begin jockeying for 2028 and universal childcare becomes a rallying cry, it’s also become clear that there’s a big unanswered question at the heart of the politicking: No one yet agrees on what “universal childcare” actually means. Does it refer to care that’s totally free, or just affordable? Is it for everyone, like public school, or targeted at families below an income line? Does it start at birth, and include parents who stay home? Are employers involved, or neighbors and grandparents?
The answers will determine who benefits, how much it costs, and whether the party’s next big promise to families is one it can actually keep.
What is universal childcare?
When I asked Rep. Khanna how he defines universal childcare, he said that it means “childcare should be free” and that families should have flexibility and choice of how to get that care. Workers, he added, should also be paid a living wage in a universal childcare system.
Later, he described the vision for universal childcare as a public good, akin to public school. “From the time a child is born to the time they’re finished college,” he argued, America has the wealth to provide for kids’ education and development.
Others, however, are defining the idea differently. Linda Smith, who leads Child Care Trust, a national policy think tank, helped design the military’s well-regarded childcare system and oversaw federal early childhood programs under Obama. Earlier this summer, she released a framework for universal childcare that emphasized it does not inherently mean free care.
Smith says she wrote it after realizing that even the legislative staffers drafting childcare bills didn’t mean the same thing by the term. “After some candid conversations with congressional staff this summer working on child care policy, it became clear that there are many interpretations of ‘universal child care,’” she wrote on LinkedIn. “If we can’t agree on what the term means, we can’t build durable policy around it.”
She argues the “universal childcare” slogan tends to blur three separate goals: universal access, universal affordability, and universal free care. To Smith, the urgent priority is access. Her vision for universal childcare policy would be a system where all families have access to “affordable, high-quality options” that reflect their needs. Her organization estimates that about 4.2 million children under six with all available parents in the workforce lack a childcare slot within a reasonable distance of home, and she warns that cutting costs without adding new supply could worsen shortages and leave families without available options.
Her answer is a mix of building more supply and sharing the cost. She recommends families paying what they can and employers and government covering the rest. Spreading the cost across several payers, she argues, is likelier to sustain the full mix of care families actually use — including home-based care — than leaning on government or parents alone.
Chris Herbst, a childcare policy expert and professor at Arizona State University, told me he agrees with Smith that there’s no consensus regarding what universal childcare means today. Even in New Mexico, he pointed out, which is regularly touted as an example of universal childcare, a light work requirement exists for families to be eligible. “These are fluid definitions, and as such they are a bit up for grabs at the moment,” Herbst said.
His own view is that a universal childcare system should make the subsidy easy to get and be guaranteed by law, so eligible families get it automatically instead of landing on waitlists when funding runs short.
Another childcare expert, Elliot Haspel, has embraced a definition closer to Khanna and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, arguing that universal childcare means all families can easily secure the type of care they want, and pay no fees to do so. He acknowledged, though, that many things can be called “universal” and be technically correct. “The ambiguity of the term is both what lends it rhetorical power and what can present a major weakness,” he writes.
Some states are adding benefits — but avoiding “universal”
With federal childcare legislation stalled, many states have spent the past few years trying to patch the system themselves. Some states are investing in making care cheaper for families, others in paying childcare workers more, and most in trying to get more providers to open their doors.
The National Conference of State Legislatures has also aimed to get involved. Over the course of a year and a half, state lawmakers across 13 states worked together to hash out a bipartisan policy framework for strengthening childcare systems, a rare cross-party effort on the issue. The NCSL report, released this past summer, steers clear of the term “universal childcare,” but does describe state systems under strain and concludes that incremental fixes alone are unlikely to solve it. The lawmakers stressed there is no one-size-fits-all solution and offered a menu of options organized around seven priorities, from expanding access to investing in the childcare workforce.
In interviews with the working group’s two co-chairs, I asked why their cohort stayed away from the “universal” language. Jim Burgin, a Republican state senator from North Carolina, told me he doesn’t find it to be a helpful term because it could conjure up the image of public schools, which are mandatory and government-run. “I don’t like the term,” he said. “I think we ought to have safe, affordable childcare available to everybody and I don’t want everybody to immediately think we’re setting up government indoctrinated childcare…a lot of people would just push back from that.”
The Democratic co-chair, Washington state Sen. Claire Wilson, said her hesitation was more about precision. “When you say ‘universal’, I think that alone is a question about what do we mean by universal?” she said. In Washington, she explained, it means care open to all families regardless of income, employment status, or immigration status, “but for other states, universal may mean something different.”
Where the public stands
Polling suggests Americans do want to see lawmakers take action on childcare, even if it’s not voters’ top priority when asked to rank among different issue areas. An AP-NORC poll from last year found about three-quarters of Americans say childcare is a “major problem,” and majorities across both parties backed federally funded “free or low-cost” daycare. More recently, YouGov and the 19th News found 52 percent of Americans think the federal government should increase its spending on childcare.
The evidence that most Americans want childcare to be free rather than affordable is less clear. The recent YouGov/19th News found about 40 percent of Americans think parents and government should share in the cost of daycare, compared to 21 percent who thought the government should pay the full cost, and 26 percent who thought parents should cover it all.
A recent New America survey found similar results. When asked if K–12 public education should be a free, taxpayer-funded right, 60 percent of respondents agreed. But only 38 percent said the same of childcare. And among those who “somewhat” or “strongly agree” that childcare should be offered to families for free, paid by taxes, and considered a right, only 31 percent of independents agreed, and just 23 percent of Republicans.
Lena Bilik, a childcare researcher at the Roosevelt Institute, a progressive think tank, told me she thinks public opinion will shift more in favor of free universal childcare when public programs can demonstrate a track record of success, as the country saw with Social Security and more recently the Affordable Care Act. “If we build high-quality public goods that work, I think that with time that problem solves itself,” she said. “But they have to be well-resourced.”
The politics ahead
While states like New Mexico, Vermont, and Connecticut have taken major steps in recent years to expand access to affordable childcare, Bilik of the Roosevelt Institute said even those places vary in how explicitly they pursue the goal of universal childcare, or define it.
The last time Democrats went big on childcare, via the Build Back Better Act, they failed. The bill packaged much of the Democratic agenda into one piece of legislation — climate, healthcare, housing — with childcare bundled alongside paid family leave, elder care, universal preschool, and an expanded child tax credit. It collapsed in late 2021 after talks with West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin fell apart.
When I interviewed lawmakers, advocates, funders, congressional aides, and policy experts in 2024 about what lessons they drew from that experience, I found the field divided over strategy. Childcare never got a vote of its own, and the argument ever since has been whether it should have been pulled out and pursued separately. Some argued activists should have narrowed their focus to one or two care priorities. Others saw that critique as premature capitulation, a sign of a limiting “scarcity mentality.” Many of those advocates emphasized that they had come very close to passing everything, losing in the Senate by a single vote, and pointed to the climate movement, which took decades of sustained organizing and spending to win major federal legislation. Care advocates, they said, just needed to keep pushing.
Two years later, the consensus view among Congressional Democrats and national childcare advocates has shifted, with far more now saying what’s needed first and foremost are “big and bold” solutions that the party can run on — even bigger than the ideas laid out in the Build Back Better Act.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren argued this year that childcare failed in Build Back Better because not enough Democrats were “willing to fight for it” and because the $400 billion proposed spending package for childcare and universal pre-K wasn’t nearly big enough. It was “an exercise in how weak and ineffective we could make the childcare program and still call it childcare,” she said.
Bilik has watched the same change from the research side. The coalition she works with, she told me, has moved away from programs that help only families below a certain income. “What I’m excited about is that we’ve gotten more ambitious with our proposals across the board since Build Back Better,” she said. “We’re finally having conversations about whether implementing something halfway will cause more problems than solutions, so I think the field has moved really far towards being open to a true public program.”
These sentiments are reflected in the recently released Khanna bill, the Project 2029 proposal, and comments over the summer from Democratic Rep. Sara Jacobs, who said free childcare for all should be at the top of the House’s legislative agenda if Democrats take control after the midterms.
How that vision translates into legislation remains an open question. Some advocates I talked to for this story, who spoke off the record to describe private coalition conversations candidly, said they worried their allies were going to make the same mistake of over-promising and then failing to prioritize goals when faced with tough budget realities. Should Democrats take power, leaders will also face pressure to restore Medicaid and SNAP funding, expand ACA subsidies, and address housing costs, all while large federal deficits make new spending harder to finance.
Khanna told me his proposals could be funded by shifting priorities away from increased military spending, particularly the $200 billion increase in the Pentagon budget and the war with Iran. The Project 2029 proposal suggests financing through raising the corporate tax rate, repealing the pass-through business tax deduction, and reforming estate taxes and the “stepped-up basis” tax break on inherited assets. Third Way would also fund its plan partly through a corporate tax increase. But those same dollars could be claimed by other Democratic priorities, which means childcare advocates may end up competing for them.
“Everyone is excited to put out the biggest idea, but there’s no real conversation about how to get there, and I feel like that’s the frustration, where ‘how to get there’ just means electing Democrats and demonizing any incremental progress,” one advocate told me. “That is not a strategy.”
For now, think tanks, presidential hopefuls, and congressional working groups are testing the waters, floating ideas that meet families where they are and, in some cases, go further than what voters say they want. The practical details are unlikely to get settled once the 2028 race is fully underway. If a Democrat wins, the window will narrow further, with unresolved details colliding with other priorities in the first months of a new administration.
“Universal childcare” may remain an amorphous term, meaning free care to one politician, shared costs to another, and a menu of state options to lawmakers who avoid the word altogether. But all of us voters should expect to hear much more of it.

United Nations, Oct 14: India has urged UN human rights mechanisms to avoid “politicisation" and respect cultural and historical contexts, asserting that New Delhi is committed to advancing human rights for all without selectivity and double standards.
First Secretary at the Permanent Mission of India, Anuj Swarup, delivered India’s statement at the 81st Session of the UNGA Third Committee on Agenda Item ‘Report of the Human Rights Council’ on Monday.
Swarup said India will continue to work with the UN Human Rights High Commissioner and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in a “spirit of trust and partnership, as we remain committed to advancing human rights for all without selectivity and double standards”.
“We hope that the UN human rights mechanisms will rise above politicisation and selectivity, respecting cultural and historical context, so that these bodies remain an impartial moral compass for the world,” he said.
India’s remarks came days after it termed the Office of the High Commissioner’s remarks on protests in the national capital “unwarranted” and “unacceptable interference” in the country’s internal affairs.
Last week, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights had expressed concern over “reports of mass detentions of demonstrators, protest leaders, members of civil society organisations, lawyers and journalists, before and during today’s large-scale demonstrations in Delhi.”
Swarup said India's approach to human rights is rooted in its civilizational ethos of pluralism and peaceful coexistence.
“As a member of the Human Rights Council, India has engaged constructively in a spirit of dialogue and cooperation,” he said, adding that as the world's largest democracy, India is committed to ensuring dignity for every citizen.
He highlighted that over 250 million people have been lifted out of multidimensional poverty in the last decade, with the country's social protection system reaching over one billion people, with free food grains for 800 million citizens, free health cover for 600 million citizens, and 320 million bank accounts for women, reflecting India’s people-centric development model.
“India remains committed to promotion and protection of human rights for all, and working with all members to make the Council an effective, objective, and credible body,” he said.
The UN General Assembly on Tuesday elected Brazil, Burundi, Dominican Republic, Germany, Ghana, Ireland, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Nepal, Nigeria, Republic of Moldova, Ukraine, Uruguay and Zambia to the Human Rights Council (HRC) for the 2027-2029 term.
India also expressed its strong objection to a reference made to it in a UN report on the rights of indigenous peoples focused on demarcation, registration and titling of lands, territories and resources.
The report of the Special Rapporteur on the rights of Indigenous Peoples, Albert Barume, on demarcation, registration and titling of indigenous peoples’ lands, territories and resources notes that “in India, although millions of claims have been submitted under the Forest Rights Act, a substantial number remain unresolved, particularly community claims.”
Swarup, delivering India’s statement at the 81st Session of the UNGA Third Committee on Agenda Item ‘Rights of Indigenous Peoples’, strongly rejected the reference in the Special Rapporteur’s report.
“While the report acknowledges that the Forest Rights Act recognises individual and collective rights, my delegation takes strong exception to the unsubstantiated reference to India in paragraph 42 of the report. The assertion that a substantial number of claims under the Forest Rights Act remain unresolved rests on a single submission by an individual. It is not supported by any official data. Such selective reliance on unverified input calls into question the rigour and objectivity of the report,” he said.
Outlining facts from official data, Swarup said that over 5.4 million claims have been filed under the Forest Rights Act, of which more than 80 per cent have been decided, and over 2.5 million titles have been distributed.
India offered to provide updated data to the Special Rapporteur “so that such anomalies based on unverified submissions can be rectified.”
He stressed that India remains committed to the sustainable and holistic development that leaves no community behind, adding that India has consistently supported the promotion and protection of the rights of indigenous peoples.

Paris Saint-Germain coach Luis Enrique came to Manchester City’s defence on Tuesday, saying he hopes the club won’t be stripped of titles after being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules.
Back-to-back Champions League winner PSG plays City at the Etihad Stadium on Wednesday.
City could face sanctions including a huge fine, points deductions or even expulsion from England’s top flight. There have also been calls for it to be stripped of trophies it won during a nine-year period in which it was found to have artificially inflated its revenue by more than USD 1 billion.
“I hope everything works out well for Man City because I think what they have done on the pitch has been incredible over the last few years and they certainly deserved to win all the trophies they have won,” Luis Enrique said ahead of the Champions League game. “The trophies you win on the pitch remain on the pitch. They deserved to win that and I hope they can avoid the sanction.

New Delhi: The government has no plans to cut import duties on pulses for now, Nidhi Khare, secretary, consumer affairs ministry, said on Wednesday, as it banks on domestic crop prospects and adequate global supplies to contain prices despite rising retail costs. The decision comes as prices of major pulses climb and uneven monsoon rainfall raises concerns about domestic production. Rather than lowering duties to encourage cheaper imports, the government is relying on the kharif crop and existing buffer stocks to manage price pressures. “We have a very clear and robust import strategy, and we are following it. Exporting countries are also aware of the Indian government’s policy framework. So, there is no concern about a price rise,” Khare told Mint on the sidelines of an event organized by the Bureau of Indian Standards to mark World Standards Day. India levies a 10% import duty on lentils and chickpeas (chana), while yellow peas attract a 30% duty. Imports of pigeon pea (tur) and black gram (urad) are allowed under the free category until 31 March 2027. The country imported 5.96 million tonnes of pulses in fiscal year 2026 (FY26), nearly 18% less than a year earlier. Imports subsequently rose 62% year-on-year to 1.71 million tonnes in April-July FY27. India’s retail inflation accelerated to 5.54% in September from 4.83% in August, while food inflation rose to 7.74% from 5.97%, according to data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation on Monday. Pulses are adding to household food costs. The Economic Survey 2024-25 said vegetables and pulses together accounted for 32.3% of overall retail inflation during April-December FY25. The figure covers both categories and does not isolate the contribution of pulses. Retail prices of major pulses, meanwhile, have risen by as much as 12.7% over the past year, according to government data. As of 14 October, chana dal cost ₹91.64 a kg, up 5% from ₹87.24 a year earlier. Tur was priced at ₹129.96 a kg, up 12.7% from ₹115.31, while urad rose 9.3% to ₹124.54 from ₹113.99. Moong prices increased 2.8% to ₹113.66 a kg from ₹110.61 a year earlier, while masoor rose 1.6% to ₹90.93 from ₹89.50. The government is counting on higher sowing and buffer stocks to ease supply pressures. The area under kharif pulses reached 12.24 million hectares as of 2 October, up from 11.98 million hectares a year earlier, according to agriculture ministry data. The increase was led by urad, whose acreage expanded by 296,000 hectares to 2.66 million hectares. Arhar (tur) sowing rose by 149,000hectares to 4.79 million hectares, while moong acreage fell 117,000 hectares to 3.37 million hectares. Total pulse acreage was close to the normal area of 12.36 million hectares, although the final harvest will depend on yields and weather conditions.
