What triggered Martinez's outburst?
Martinez said he felt it was important to speak out the way he did. Many United fans are delighted he went down that path, and the defender was highlighting inadequacies in the club's leadership structure.
However, there are a couple of other basic realities.
The first is that Martinez's contract expires at the end of the season. United have the option to extend it by another year.
By being so outspoken against senior figures at the club, was he trying to ensure that option is not triggered, which would allow him to leave for nothing in the summer, or, potentially, for a lower fee in January?
Martinez is good friends with Atletico Madrid defender Cristian Romero and the international colleagues spoke after last night's game. Romero was similarly forceful against the Tottenham hierarchy last season.
Also, while the vast majority of United fans may agree with Martinez, internally his comments create a problem.
Most obviously, Carrick, having deflected questions about the defender's outburst in the immediate aftermath of the game, will face more probing on the matter when he speaks to the media before Sunday's trip to Leeds.
Any players lined up to talk around the Elland Road trip will be similarly quizzed. When Tielemans was asked about it by Amazon Prime on Tuesday night, he replied with a "no comment". Given the comments about recruitment, he would clearly be within his rights to ask Martinez outright "did you mean me?"
Carrick has to manage the delicate dressing room dynamic at a point when he needs a collective focus on trying to win enough matches to keep him in a job.
Sources who know the United boss well are adamant there is no better person to handle the turmoil, and it is at times of crisis like this that his innate calmness is a major strength.
However, after five games without a win, it is a problem Carrick could do without.
Is Wilcox in trouble?
Firstly, it must be pointed out Wilcox is going nowhere.
United sources say the 55-year-old is not in any danger of losing his job.
The club's recruitment department is working on potential targets for January given it is accepted the strategy of not signing left-back competition for Luke Shaw and striking support for Benjamin Sesko was flawed.
Both players have missed matches already this term, with Sesko sidelined for an indefinite period after suffering a recurrence of the shin issue that flared up in May and prevented him from playing any part in United's pre-season matches.
Unlike other major footballing countries on the continent, there is no expectation for sporting or technical directors to speak to the media.
Former United sporting director Dan Ashworth did it once during his five months at the club and was sitting alongside chief executive Omar Berrada.
Wilcox's only extensive interview since he was appointed in April 2024 has been with United's in-house media, when a couple of answers stood out.
"I am a coach at heart," said the former Blackburn Rovers and Leeds United winger, who spent several years working in coaching at Manchester City's academy.
"I am a coach inside, even though I know I have a different job now. That is a strength in my role, but it also causes me a bit of a problem because I always want to interfere in what the managers are doing."
Regarding his strategy for dealing with stress, Wilcox said: "My wife will know when I am bogged down with frustration. When I re-energise, I do it on my own. Me and the dog, walking."
Wilcox has only spoken briefly to the media after matches on a couple of occasions: after the 2-1 win at Crystal Palace last November, when he told journalists to "trust the process"; then again in Gothenburg after the pre-season encounter with Paris St-Germain when he enthused about the potential pairing of Tielemans and skipper Bruno Fernandes.
Recruitment was praised in summer 2025, when Senne Lammens was signed ahead of Emi Martinez, who was Amorim's preference, and Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo, plus Sesko, reinvigorated United's attack.
But the jury is out on the players acquired in the £155m summer outlay this year: Baleba, who missed the first six weeks of the season with injury; Santos, who has been an unused substitute in the last three Premier League games; and Tielemans, whose form has been patchy.
Sources have questioned the overall strategy, and specifically why Tielemans, who has a similar profile to England international Kobbie Mainoo, was signed, even for £35m, and if the £50m committed to Santos would have been better spent on someone who would be a first choice.
What about Ineos in all this?
Trust is eroding among United fans over the minority ownership, agreed on Christmas Eve in 2023.
They might look at the other clubs where Ineos have an influence.
Nice are ninth in the French league and Lausanne-Sport are bottom in Switzerland. This doesn't generate a sense of a wider footballing vision that is paying dividends.
At Old Trafford, questions are being asked for the third season in a row over managers who were backed by the hierarchy in the summer. Erik ten Hag was sacked after nine Premier League games in 2024. Amorim went after 20 matches last season.
Minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe has also been blamed by fans for increasing ticket prices and launching what the club said was a ticket touting investigation among season ticket holders, but which supporters felt was an attempt to drive them out in favour of 'tourist' supporters.
In their latest set of accounts, United's overall debt stood at £1.1bn, with some fans criticising the decision to spend £63.5m on land for a new 100,000-capacity stadium - which is set to cost in excess of £2bn - rather than use the money to strengthen Carrick's squad.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”, has brought renewed attention to using light to investigate fundamental biological processes. These include memory formation, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders, as well as processes involved in infectious disease.
Editorial | Let there be light: On the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology/Medicine
For Nishith Gupta, professor of Biological Sciences at BITS Pilani, Hyderabad, and founder of the Intracellular Parasite Education and Research Labs (iPEARL), the recognition has a personal significance in his own scientific journey.
Mr. Gupta’s decades-long collaboration with Hegemann at Humboldt University of Berlin, where Hegemanna is Hertie Senior Professor of Neuroscience, helped extend optogenetic approaches beyond neuroscience into his study of Toxoplasma gondii, an intracellular parasite that infects humans, mammals, and birds.
Interactive Guide | Nobel Prize 2026
Optogenetics enables scientists to control selected cells or biological processes using light-sensitive proteins.
The Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine stated: “It all began with Peter Hegemann’s curiosity. He wondered how Chlamydomonas, a single-celled alga, is able to swim towards a light source. In the early 2000s, he and Georg Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, an algal protein with unique properties, found on the surface of the cell. When it is illuminated by blue light, a channel opens through the protein. Charged ions then flow into the cell, creating an electrical impulse. They found that regardless of which cell they put the protein in, those cells became light sensitive.” In 2005, Deisseroth showed that introducing channelrhodopsin into rat neurons allowed blue light to trigger nerve signals. In 2007, he showed light-based control in mice.
In contrast, Mr. Gupta, Mr. Hegemann and others used light-regulated enzyme adenylate cyclase, which converts adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the primary energy of a living cell, to produce cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate (cAMP). This molecule acts as messengers, helping transmit signals within cells.
Put simply, the researchers showed that light controls the enzyme, the enzyme produces cAMP, and cAMP helps regulate what happens inside the parasite (Toxoplasma gondii): how it enters cells, moves, and exits cells. This landmark study was published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry in 2013.
While Mr. Deisseroth, Mr. Hegemann, and Mr. Nagel’s optogenetics “solves one of humanity’s great mysteries, how our incredible brain works”, Mr. Gupta, Mr. Hegemann and others’ found light-regulated signalling to investigate parasite’s lifestyle, and infection.
Mr. Gupta says that working alongside Hegemann in Berlin, with their laboratories in neighbouring departments, was an important part of this scientific journey. Joint funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG) supported their collaboration.
After Mr. Gupta relocated to India, Mr. Hegemann continued to support his research through Mr. Gupta’s Wellcome Trust–DBT Senior Fellowship project at BITS Pilani. Researchers from his team continued to visit Hegemann’s group in Berlin.
For Mr. Gupta, the Nobel Prize awarded to Mr. Hegemann and his fellow laureates underscores the far-reaching consequences of fundamental research. A protein that evolved to help an alga sense light has become a tool for probing the brain, investigating infection and understanding how cells function. He says the broader lesson is that technologies developed to answer one biological question can open entirely new avenues of research.
“Light has become more than a means of observation; it is a way to intervene, test, and uncover cause-and-effect relationships,” Mr. Gupta says.

On September 21, 2026, students of King George’s Medical University (KGMU), Lucknow, protested over the death of Divyanshi Yadav, a 2025-batch B.Sc. Nursing student who died of dengue. A student at the protest site told PTI that though Divyanshi was suffering from the disease, she still had to attend college. “Despite being on the deathbed, she was tense about her attendance. Students are forced to come to the college daily to mark attendance, ignoring their medical conditions. We get messages from teachers telling us to come to the college after taking medicine,” he said.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
In September 2025, Subhangini, 23, another nursing student who was in her first year at Bhopal Memorial Hospital and Research Centre (BMHRC), died due to jaundice. A current student, on condition of anonymity, told The Hindu, “There was poor quality of food and water on campus, and the case was mishandled by BMHRC Hospital; her medical leave was not approved, and she had to perform her duty even in an ailing condition.” However, the university denied the allegations.
In most institutions, medical leave requires medical documentation and is granted for serious illness or when a student is severely injured in an accident. The older University Grants Commission (UGC) 2003 regulations required universities to prescribe a minimum attendance of 75% for students to be eligible for examinations, but the 2025 regulations no longer set a universal 75% threshold. Instead, they leave minimum attendance requirements to individual higher education institutions (HEIs) through their statutory bodies.
In most HEIs, the minimum attendance requirement is 75-80%, with a 10% accommodation for medical emergencies. This minimum attendance criterion is higher in medical and engineering institutes, as per their regulatory bodies. For nursing students like Divyanshi, the Nursing Council of India’s guidelines mandate 80% attendance in theory and 100% attendance in practical areas. This framework leaves medical-leave protection largely to institutional rules, producing significant variation in what happens to students when illness interrupts their education.
Problems for students with chronic illnesses
Alex is a third-year B.A. Visual Communication student at a university in Hyderabad. Having transverse myelitis, he became paralysed from the chest down at the age of 10, and the organs on the right side of his body stopped working. Doctors said he would never walk. Defying this, he has regained his ability to walk, but this is accompanied by chronic pain below the chest, subluxations, partial dysplasias, fatigue, and muscle spasms.
Alex holds a 100% merit-based scholarship, and in order to keep it, he must maintain a CGPA of 8 and above and 75% attendance. After he dislocated his kneecap in college in September 2024, doctors recommended a month of complete rest. However, he said, “I was told by the college authorities to either come to college regularly and maintain the 75% attendance or take a year's break and come back to college next year.” His medical leave was denied, stating, “Medical exemption only applies in case of hospitalisations.”
“However, my scholarship would not hold the following year. So I would have to write my exam again and apply for a scholarship again, which was not something I was able to do because of my financial situation. So I had to continue coming to college without taking the recommended one month’s leave. I took one day off, and I continued going back to college every single day,” Alex added.
Alex had to navigate a campus that had minimal accessibility, a long commute to the university, and he was not given leniency for assignments or for showing up to class a few minutes late. This affected his social life on campus and his health. “If I did take that one month’s rest, there was a chance I would have recovered fully. But since I was not able to do it, I still have not recovered. It’s been three years, and I keep dislocating my knee and wear braces to this day.”
A student of Interior Design with an autoimmune condition at a private university in Noida said, “I provided all medical documents explaining my condition; however, the department head asked me to take amla and attend classes.” The student described the process of applying for a leave as frustrating: “I was made to feel like my condition was not important; it came from my own laziness and was something that could be managed with willpower... I was an out-of-station student and had to navigate my illness alone, which was both mentally and financially demanding.”
Attendance adds to evaluation, and the student saw a marked dip in grades. Support, such as make-up assignments, was also not extended by administration or faculty. The student said, “As practical classes are a day long, missing one day amounts to six to eight hours of class time, dipping the attendance to 70-80 % even if two or three classes are missed.”
Cases of unconventional medical proof
Jay was a B.A. English major at a university in Delhi NCR, and months before he joined the university, he had developed chronic pain due to a genetic condition. He had to maintain 75% attendance in every subject, with an 80% requirement and 5% provision for medical leave.
Jay missed many morning classes due to his pain flaring up. As his teachers were accommodating, he was able to sit for his first-year exams. “I had to drop out as my situation worsened in second year. I didn’t have a proper diagnosis; a lot of reports and tests indicated inconclusive results. This couldn’t be taken as enough evidence at that time, and due to considerably low accessibility on campus as well as inflexible leave criteria, I dropped out.”
Tejasdeep Sehgal, a fourth-year student, has had a hearing impairment since the age of 12 and uses a hearing aid. The office of learning support at his university in Haryana provided him with a shaker alarm clock and transcription services that he says are helpful.
Last year, Tejasdeep’s hearing aid stopped working, and he could not listen properly. He then went to Delhi to have it fixed. “It took me two days to get it fixed, and it was a technician who fixed it; therefore, I didn’t have a prescription for it. I had unexcused absences for the classes I missed. However, it could have escalated into a situation where I would not be able to produce documentary proof of my condition to get medical leave.”
A student of Jawaharlal Nehru University’s Japanese department had a viral fever with body pain and had to take leave for two weeks. The student had informed the professor about it over email. When she rejoined class, she was told she was not sick and was asked to write an application to the centre and produce medical documentation. This dismissal by the professor caused the student severe anxiety and panic attacks. The university administration later asked the professor to write an apology letter to the student.
Another student said, “We are constantly told by our seniors not to fall in the bad books of some professor, as they have access to grant scholarships and fellowships and influence your career outside college.”
Describing a similar incident, a Delhi University student said they were made to stand in class. “I was told I was a good student, but irregular in classes. The philosophy professor quoted a scholar on resilience, which made the experience of my sickness seem like laziness. I left the class crying. I felt my hard work would not amount to anything because I was a sick person.”
A fifth-semester student of Humanities, who had been seeking college counselling sessions, upon needing further assistance, had to seek a psychiatrist outside college. The student later missed an exam due to an anxiety attack and was denied approval of medical leave. “I had all the documentation from a fully accredited clinical psychiatrist, and I was told it would have been easier to vouch for me if I was seeking help from college counsellors, who were not psychiatrists and could not have helped me at that time.” The student was made to do multiple rounds to the college healthcare centre, and their leave was still not approved. They had to take the paper again next semester. “The process was bureaucratic and draining.”
Sensitising institutions
Sayan Chaudhuri, a scholar of critical pedagogy and higher education, says, “Teachers and administration need to be sensitised to how chronic illnesses or other conditions might be playing out. I think without that understanding, you can’t have a meaningful intervention. What administrations really need to think about is the kinds of bureaucratic hurdles that are there. Often, administration stands at a huge distance, and you feel a sense of fear about approaching. So there is a need for a culture where it is established that you can get leave, and it shouldn’t feel like it’s a difficult task or it needs certain kinds of skills to be able to ask for a leave.”
He says the problem also lies in the hurdles students face when seeking medical leave. “A documentation-heavy policy is going to run into a contradiction, because the assumption will be that the document can be provided well in advance to the requisite authorities who can go through it, understand it, and approve it. And we know that’s not how it’s always going to work. There will be many things that will fall out of this system. We have to really think of developing a more local understanding of things where teachers can play a proactive role at times, mediate between the administration and the student, because otherwise that contextual understanding may not be there. Medical resource centres and health centres are often very depleted. Counsellors are not always working in a very empowered way, where they can stage interventions in a collaborative and meaningful manner,” he said.
Debaditya Battacharya, Assistant Professor in the Department of English at Jamia Millia Islamia, a researcher of Indian higher education and university histories, says, “National Education Policy 2020 lumps questions of mental health, ability, and disability together under this socioeconomically disadvantaged groups (SEDG); this rubric is indicative of the myopia of policy. Ability is treated as meritocratic given; it is not at stake anymore; it is either the basic minimum you take for granted or simply reduced to an ability enhancement course. But university life has to account for different capacities for ability and disability”
“There is no objective parameter that can justify any figure, whether it be 75 or 65,” Dr. Battacharya said, because students come to university with radically different circumstances. For some, meeting a particular threshold may be relatively easy; for others, especially students from marginalised backgrounds, it may involve negotiating pressures outside the classroom as well.
He says, “It’s teachers who are expected to come with that space of understanding what a student’s real-life circumstances are, as they deal with students in the flesh”. He suggests student-faculty committees hear cases that merit genuine attention on a case-by-case basis, in a consultative and democratic fashion. He says the system should retain the purpose of attendance, maintaining the integrity and spirit of the teaching-learning process without reducing individual students and their circumstances to a single percentage.
(Zain Younis is a Master’s student at Jamia Millia Islamia)

Vissel Kobe maintained a perfect start to the eastern league phase of the Asian Champions League Elite on Wednesday with a 2-0 victory over South Korea’s Jeonbuk Motors to register the team’s second win in a row.
Yuya Osako gave the home side the lead in the 12th minute when he peeled away from his marker to convert from Katsuya Nagato’s corner and Yuya Kuwasaki hit the second midway through the second half.
“I think it’s extremely important to earn three points at home,” said Osako, whose goal was his first in this season’s competition.
“I’m happy we were able to get off to a good start and begin our home campaign on a positive note.”
Kobe had dominated the opening exchanges and deserved to take the lead when Osako struck but as proceedings wore on Jeonbuk’s threat increased.
Brazilian winger Italo cut the home defense open repeatedly after the interval, setting up Bruno Mota to hit the woodwork before substitute Lee Seung-woo headed inches wide of the Kobe goal.
Choi Woo-jin then struck the crossbar from distance before Kobe pounced on the counterattack, with Yoshinori Muto setting up Kuwasaki to sweep his 68th minute shot past Song Bum-keun.
The win moved Kobe level with compatriots Kashima Antlers and Gamba Osaka as well as China’s Beijing Guoan on six points.
Kashiwa Reysol picked up its first win of the campaign with a 5-1 thrashing of Thailand’s Port FC as the Japanese host took a five-goal lead inside the opening half hour.
Tojiro Kubo put Kashiwa in front in the third minute before goals from Yuki Kakita, Riki Harakawa, Koya Yuriki and Hinata Yamauchi gave the home side an unassailable advantage by the 28th minute.
The first eight finishers in the 16-team league phase in both east and west Asia will qualify for the last 16 with the quarterfinals, semifinals and final due to be played in Saudi Arabia in April and May.

Engineering and management graduates have diverse career opportunities across traditional industries, emerging technologies, research and business leadership, said Dr. Mitrabarun Ghosh, Assistant Professor at Paari School of Business, SRM University-A.P.
He was delivering a career guidance session titled “Career Directions: Engineering & Management” for final-year B.Tech students at Tirumala Engineering College, Narasaraopet, on Wednesday. The seminar on “Careers in Management & Sciences” was organised by The Hindu Future India Club in association with Paari School of Business, SRM A.P., in collaboration with Tirumala Engineering College. R. Satyanarayana, Secretary and Correspondent of Tirumala Engineering College, Dr. Y.V. Narayana, Principal, and V.V.S. Pradeep of SRM University were present at the programme.
Dr. Ghosh explained the opportunities available through technical careers and management education, emphasising that neither path was inherently superior and that students should choose according to their interests, skills and long-term aspirations.
While engineering offers opportunities in technology, research, design and innovation, management opens avenues in leadership, strategy, marketing, finance and business operations. Combining engineering experience with an MBA can help graduates pursue careers in product management, consulting and leadership roles, he said.
He highlighted employment opportunities in information technology, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, semiconductors, manufacturing and global capability centres. Government career options through GATE, UPSC Engineering Services, ISRO, DRDO, Indian Railways and public sector undertakings were also discussed.
The speaker drew attention to emerging sectors, including electric vehicles, green energy, space technology, defence startups and chip design. Alternative career options such as technical writing, patent analysis, research, public policy and entrepreneurship were also explained.
Dr. Ghosh guided students on higher education opportunities in India and abroad through examinations such as GATE, CAT, GRE and GMAT. He advised them to consider institutional rankings, accreditation, placement records, faculty expertise, industry connections and return on investment while selecting colleges.
He encouraged students to identify a primary career path and a backup option, prepare strategically for competitive examinations, and strengthen their profiles through projects, internships and certifications.

An engineer at OpenAI allegedly concealed an audio recording device in a piece of toilet paper and attached it behind a monitor inside an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices, according to a criminal complaint unsealed on Tuesday.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who federal prosecutors describe as a 35-year-old Saudi Arabian national and US permanent resident, allegedly spent several weeks querying an unspecified “productivity agent” and an “AI chatbot” to plan his alleged surveillance operation. He used an internal OpenAI tool to ask about meetings scheduled in the targeted conference room.
He also appears to have used a chatbot account associated with his spouse to ask various technical questions about setting up a covert audio recording device, according to prosecutors and the court filing.
OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device that had not been installed in Alfozan’s bag at the office.
Alfozan couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. He made an initial appearance in US district court in San Francisco on Tuesday on one charge of “use of an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison. He joined OpenAI in July 2025 and was fired last Friday to coincide with his arrest.
Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan aimed “to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” but prosecutors nor OpenAI have offered any information so far about a potential motive.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a statement on X. “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.”
OpenAI discovered the bug—which was allegedly “concealed in toilet paper” and “inserted into a USB port on the back of a television” in the conference room—on September 30 during a countersurveillance sweep.
Alfozan previously worked at a cargo logistics startup and at Meta, according to a purported LinkedIn profile for him. In a recent podcast interview, Alfozan said he was also part of a group of Saudi engineers in Silicon Valley who offered consulting services to Saudi organizations.
The LinkedIn profile lists Alfozan as a part-time “venture partner” at RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm based in Saudi Arabia. Neither RAED Ventures nor Meta immediately responded to WIRED’s request for comment.
Last year, the Trump administration signed a pact with Saudi Arabia granting the kingdom access to advanced chips and AI technologies that might otherwise be restricted over national security concerns. Saudi investment firms remain a major source of capital for US tech companies.
Executives Only
According to the complaint, Alfozan allegedly planted the listening device “no later than on or about September 28, 2026.”
The conference room Alfozan targeted “can be reserved only by executives and executive assistants,” and is typically used “for internal leadership meetings,” “technical and product sessions,” and “external briefings” with business partners and government officials, according to the complaint. It is frequently used for discussions involving “highly confidential” information, including about research, products, business strategy, and government relationships, the complaint stated.
OpenAI’s statement called the recording device “sophisticated.” Authorities allege that the device Alfozan planted was called Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, “a thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage.” It currently retails on Seeed’s website for $13.99. OpenAI’s security team tried to export the data stored on the microSD card, but were unable to review it because it was encrypted.
After discovering the device, OpenAI says it notified the FBI and was able to connect it to Alfozan after reviewing chat logs and surveillance footage, and searching a bag he left unattended at the office. The company then gradually disabled his access to company systems as the investigation was ongoing.
According to the complaint, OpenAI security personnel discovered the bag that Alfozan left unattended in a printer room on October 5. The security team went through the bag, which contained a second encrypted Seeed listening device and other personal items connected to Alfozan, including his wallet. Prosecutors say Alfozan later reported the bag as missing to OpenAI and subsequently recovered it from the company’s lost and found.
He followed up with unnamed personnel at OpenAI to say that some of the items that were supposed to be in the bag were still missing—including a credit card, about $500 in cash, and two AirPods—but neglected to mention the second listening device, which had been removed from the bag by OpenAI security.

Pre-owned goods marketplace Circle has raised ₹25 Cr (about $2.6 Mn) in a seed funding round led by Nexus Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors Titan Capital and Myntra cofounder Raveen Sastry. Delhivery COO Ajith Pai also joined the round as an angel investor. The startup will use the fresh capital to expand beyond Bengaluru and strengthen its AI-powered pricing, product discovery, and verification tools. It also plans to expand its logistics network and Trust Hubs, which handle product verification and fulfillment. Founded in 2025 by Chirag Kataruka and Ankit Misra, Circle operates a managed marketplace for pre-owned goods, handling product verification, payments and logistics for transactions between individual buyers and sellers without owning inventory. Its platform combines AI-powered tools with human verification, with products ranging from smartphones, gaming consoles, and cameras to furniture, watches, handbags, and sneakers. Circle handles listing, pickup, and seller payouts, while offering buyers product verification and a three-day guarantee. The Bengaluru-based startup claims to have facilitated around ₹25 Cr in pre-owned goods sales within a year of launch, attracting over 1 Mn visitors and generating 1 Lakh listings in the city. It said sellers typically find buyers within three days, compared with weeks or months on classifieds platforms. The startup previously raised ₹3.4 Cr in a pre-seed round led by Titan Capital in November last year, with participation from Sastry. Circle operates in a pre-owned goods market that includes classifieds platforms OLX India and Quikr, electronics-focused Cashify, and community resale platform FreeUp. These players overlap with Circle across different categories and services, rather than following an identical operating model. Circle’s approach centres on managing transactions to address the verification, payment, and logistics challenges associated with buying and selling used goods. According to ResearchAndMarkets, India’s recommerce market is projected to reach $5.91 Bn in 2026 and $8.61 Bn by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 9.8% over 2026-2030.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

Rahul, Priyanka join Ankita Bhandari's family's protest against ‘VIP’ Sikkim governor's appointment
Ankita Bhandari, a resident of Uttarakhand, worked as a receptionist at Vanantra Resort in Yamkeshwar, near Rishikesh. She was murdered in 2022.
Congress leaders Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra met the parents of Ankita Bhandari in New Delhi on Wednesday evening. Together, they staged a sit-in near India Gate against the appointment of former Uttarakhand BJP in-charge Dushyant Kumar Gautam as the Governor of Sikkim.
The parents of the 19-year-old receptionist, who was murdered in Uttarakhand’s Pauri Garhwal district in September 2022, have demanded that Gautam’s appointment be put on hold until the ongoing Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) probe into the alleged VIP angle in the case was completed.
Activist Yogita Bhayana also joined the protest, during which Ankita’s parents requested President Droupadi Murmu to intervene and ensure that the investigation examined all allegations related to the case.
Gautam served as the BJP’s Uttarakhand in-charge from November 2020 to August 2026, a period during which the party recorded several electoral victories in the state. He was appointed Sikkim governor on Monday.
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi voiced support for Ankita Bhandari’s parents and accused the BJP of protecting a “VIP” accused in the case. On X, Rahul said the family had been waiting for justice for four years, alleging that the accused had instead received protection and a constitutional position. “I and the Congress Party stand with them — in their grief as well as in this fight for justice,” he said.
Ankita’s parents demand investigation into alleged VIP role
Speaking to the media during the protest, Ankita’s father demanded action against Gautam and called for the statements of actress Urmila Sanawar and former BJP MLA Suresh Rathore to be included in the investigation.
“Dushyant Kumar should go to jail...because of the VIP my daughter was murdered,” he told HT.
He questioned the progress of the CBI investigation, alleging that it relied on statements made by witnesses in the lower court. He also claimed that the call details of the accused had not been examined.
“I request the President not to appoint Dushyant Kumar as governor until the CBI investigation is complete,” he said. “Even though the CBI probe is underway, it is depending on the statements of witnesses in lower court. Statements of Urmila Sanawar and Suresh Rathore should be included in the investigation. The call details of the accused were not examined.”
Ankita’s mother also appealed to the President to reconsider the appointment.
“We were hurt by the appointment of Kumar as governor. I request the President, who is a woman and will understand my sentiments, to halt the appointment of Kumar as governor,” she said.
The family has sought a thorough investigation into the alleged involvement of a VIP in Ankita’s murder. Gautam has not been named as an accused in the cases related to the crime, and the allegations against him remain unproven.
Audio clip triggered demands for CBI probe
The demand for a fresh investigation into the alleged VIP angle gained momentum after actress Urmila Sanawar, who claims to be the wife of former BJP MLA Suresh Rathore, released an audio clip purportedly containing a telephone conversation between the two.
In the recording, Rathore allegedly referred to the involvement of a BJP leader in the case. The clip triggered protests across Uttarakhand, with demonstrators demanding a CBI investigation into the alleged role of the unidentified VIP.
Following the protests, the Uttarakhand government ordered a CBI probe in January.
Gautam has denied allegations linking him to the murder and filed a case against Rathore, Sanawar, the Uttarakhand unit of the Congress, Uttarakhand Kranti Dal, the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and other unidentified individuals over claims connecting him to the case.
The Delhi High Court has also directed the removal of social media posts linking Gautam to the murder, observing that the allegations appeared prima facie defamatory, HT reported earlier.
Congress protests Gautam’s appointment
The protest at India Gate came a day after the Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee (UKPCC), led by its president Ganesh Godiyal, held a silent demonstration in Dehradun against Gautam’s appointment as Sikkim governor.
The Congress has questioned the decision to appoint Gautam while demands for an investigation into the alleged VIP angle remain unresolved. The party has called for accountability and further scrutiny of the allegations.
The Congress accused the BJP-led Centre of protecting Gautam following his appointment as Sikkim governor, alleging that the decision undermined the demand for justice in the 2022 Ankita Bhandari murder case.
On X, the party said Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra met Ankita’s family at India Gate in New Delhi.
“The allegation was that pressure was put on Ankita to provide services to Dushyant Gautam. When Ankita refused, she was murdered,” the Congress alleged. It accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi of rewarding Gautam with the gubernatorial appointment despite the allegations against him.
“The daughters and women of the country are watching how Narendra Modi and his government are protecting Dushyant Gautam. Instead of delivering justice to Ankita Bhandari, the entire BJP government is bent on silencing the voice of the victim's family,” the Congress wrote.
What happened to Ankita Bhandari?
Ankita, a resident of Uttarakhand’s Pauri Garhwal district, worked as a receptionist at Vanantra Resort in Yamkeshwar, near Rishikesh.
She was murdered on September 18, 2022. The resort’s owner, Pulkit Arya, son of expelled BJP leader Vinod Arya, and his two employees, Saurabh Bhaskar and Ankit Gupta, were convicted in the case. The three men allegedly pushed Ankita into the Chilla canal following a dispute.
A court in Kotdwar, Pauri Garhwal district, sentenced all three accused to life imprisonment in May 2025.
The alleged involvement of an unidentified VIP remains a contentious issue.

Manufacturing company Zetwerk has raised ₹2,251.2 Cr from anchor investors ahead of the opening of its initial public offering (IPO) for public subscription on October 15. The company allotted 14.91 Cr equity shares to anchor investors at ₹151 apiece, the upper end of its IPO price band. Domestic mutual funds accounted for around 46% of the anchor book, picking up 6.80 Cr shares through 61 schemes across 22 fund houses. Notably, 40% of the anchor investor portion was reserved for domestic mutual funds, life insurance companies and pension funds. SBI Mutual Fund emerged as the largest among these investors, acquiring 1.02 Cr shares through two schemes. ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund also accounted for around 7% of the anchor allocation. Other participating fund houses included Bajaj Finserv, Abakkus, Baroda BNP Paribas, Motilal Oswal and Edelweiss. Global institutional investors accounted for a significant part of Zetwerk's anchor book. Capital Group's Smallcap World Fund Inc received the largest individual allocation, worth ₹288 Cr, accounting for 12.79% of the total anchor portion. Government Pension Fund Global and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority's Monsoon fund were each allocated shares worth about ₹75 Cr, while Nomura India Investment Mother Fund received an allocation worth ₹50 Cr. Among international investors, the anchor book featured the likes of Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, First Sentier Investors and Societe Generale. Zetwerk’s ₹5,012 Cr IPO will open for public subscription on October 15 and close on October 17. At the upper end of the price band of ₹143-₹151 per share, the offering values the company at a post-issue market capitalisation of around ₹25,583 Cr, or approximately $2.7 Bn. The IPO comprises a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 14.45 Cr shares, amounting to ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end of the price band. The company has increased the fresh issue from ₹2,600 Cr proposed in its updated draft red herring prospectus (UDRHP). The OFS component has also expanded by 49.2% from approximately 9.7 Cr shares. Zetwerk’s promoters and cofounders, Amrit Pratik Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan, will each sell up to 1.42 Cr shares. Other shareholders offloading their stakes include promoter group entity Creovate Innovation and funds associated with Peak XV Partners, Accel India, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Kae Capital. The company plans to deploy ₹2,160 Cr from the fresh issue towards repaying or prepaying borrowings of Zetwerk and certain subsidiaries. The remaining proceeds will be used for acquisitions and general corporate purposes. On the financial front, Zetwerk’s operating revenue rose to ₹15,739.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹11,331.9 Cr in FY25. However, its consolidated net loss widened to ₹1,606.2 Cr from ₹370.7 Cr in FY25 due to discontinued operations over the past fiscal. The FY26 loss included an exceptional charge of ₹796.4 Cr linked to changes in share conversion ratios and an impairment charge of ₹453 Cr related to its discontinued civil infrastructure business. In Q1 FY27, operating revenue grew 55.4% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹4,117.9 Cr from ₹2,649.4 Cr. Its total net loss narrowed 46.4% to ₹733 Cr from ₹1,368.5 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. Of the latest quarterly loss, ₹668.9 Cr was attributable to discontinued operations, while continuing operations accounted for ₹64.1 Cr. The year-ago quarter included exceptional charges of ₹803.2 Cr from continuing operations and the ₹453 Cr impairment charge in the discontinued business.

Group of men cheered as woman was sexually assaulted at a University of Chicago frat house party: report
Friend of alleged victim reported hearing crowd of men outside basement bathroom saying 'When’s it my turn?’ and ‘I want to go in there'

A group of men cheered as a 21-year-old woman was sexually assaulted in the bathroom of a University of Chicago frat house this past weekend while her two friends frantically tried to pick the lock to rescue her, according to reports.
The woman, 21, reported that she was sexually assaulted by a man at the Alpha Epsilon Pi house at 5625 S. University Ave., around 2 a.m. Sunday, the Chicago Police Department confirmed to The Independent.
Two of her friends told police that a group tried to stop them from entering the bathroom after the men were seen “cheering and appearing to encourage the activity inside,” according to a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times.
University of Chicago, one of the U.S.’s top colleges, told The Independent that “a person of interest has been identified.” No arrests have been reported, and the individual has not been publicly identified.
There has been a nationwide reckoning over sexual assault on college campuses after a civil lawsuit was filed last month by a Jane Doe alleging that she had been gang-raped by seven fraternity members at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, in October 2024.
According to the new Chicago police report, the woman and two friends attended a party at Alpha Epsilon Pi after seeing the event advertised on Instagram, the New York Times reported.
The three women were dancing in the frat’s basement when the alleged victim began kissing a man. One of the friends, who spoke with the Times, lost track of them briefly but then found a small group of men cheering outside a locked bathroom in the basement.
“They were saying things like, ‘When’s it my turn?’ and ‘I want to go in there,’” she said. According to the police report, the group told her it wasn’t her friend inside.
However, when she forced her way in by picking the door lock, she found her friend partially undressed and slumped on the floor. The man had his hands on the alleged victim’s wrists, and she began to say “make it stop” and “get me out of here,” the friend told the newspaper.
The police report said that when one of the women’s friend told the man to get off her, he “responded that everything was ‘cool,’ as though nothing had occurred.”
The woman and her friends later confronted the man outside the frat house and he said they “had identified the wrong person.” He pointed them in another direction and ran off, per the report.
One of the friends tried to chase him, but ran into a police officer and reported the alleged assault, according to the report. The 21-year-old was then hospitalized, police confirmed to The Independent.
The woman is not a student at the University of Chicago, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. She did not return the newspaper’s request for comment, but one of her friends told the paper she was “obviously shaken up” and worried about her name getting out.
The Chicago Maroon, the university’s student newspaper, published an article Tuesday describing a video shared to TikTok that appears to show the alleged perpetrator.
“He f****** assaulted my friend in the bathroom of the f****** frat party. You record all the s*** you want,” an individual who refers to themselves as the alleged victim’s friend, says in the video, which has been shared online. “I walked in there, you f****** took her clothes off.”
On the video, the man can be heard responding, “she wanted to."
Police said the man is 5 feet 7 inches tall with curly hair. He was wearing a black, short-sleeve shirt with black pants at the time of the alleged assault, according to the police report.
An alert from the University of Chicago said the suspect is not affiliated with the school. He was not named in the alert because he has not been charged with a crime.
“This identification has been corroborated by key witness statements and video evidence from University cameras and license plate readers, all of which has been shared with [the Chicago Police Department] by the Department of Safety & Security,” the university alert said.
The university’s chapter of Alpha Epsilon Pi said in a statement on Instagram that no one affiliated with the fraternity was “involved or complicit with this incident.” The chapter says it is working with authorities.
The fraternity’s national chapter told The Independent in a statement, “There is no evidence at all that any AEPi members participated in this asault or were aware of it while it was transpiring.”
The spokesperson noted that they do not believe the men “cheering on” the attack were part of the fraternity. They said the fraternity members are fully cooperating with authorities.
Cornell’s Jane Doe lawsuit alleges she was drugged and gang-raped by seven members of the now-defunct Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York, in October 2024. None of the men have been criminally charged. All have denied wrongdoing.
Cornell announced this week that it has banned fraternity parties for the rest of the year.
Earlier this month, the Ivy League school appointed former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent investigation into how the school handles sexual assault cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has also assigned state Attorney General Letita James to the case as special prosecutor in a criminal investigation.
After Doe reported the alleged rape in 2024, Cornell began an investigation, which involved multiple hearings and resulted in the suspensions and expulsions of some of the students involved. The Chi Phi fraternity was also shut down.
“Any suggestion that the University did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” the university said in a previous statement. “A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault.”

The Trump administration is delaying by 90 days a federal rule that could prevent Americans from obtaining prescription drugs from licensed international pharmacies.
The move follows growing criticism that the rule, which was initially slated to go into effect on Oct. 22, could drastically reduce the flow of medicines from Canada and other countries. In recent weeks, patient advocacy groups and dozens of congressional lawmakers urged the administration to rethink its approach.
The administration is trying to crack down on illegal goods — particularly opioids — that it says enter the U.S. through low-value foreign shipments and for which shippers generally do not pay tariffs or submit data for tracking. The rule targets the de minimis exemption, which previously allowed shipments valued under $800 to pass through customs more easily.

A ground report from Delhi examines the Delhi Development Authority's CBD Ground near Karkardooma, designated by Delhi Police as an alternative site for holding protests alongside Ramlila Ground and Burari. Over 59,000 metric tonnes of silt dumped at Singhola site in last one year: MCD report
In an earlier hearing, the green tribunal directed the MCD to disclose the quantity of waste dumped at the site again
In a report submitted to the National Green Tribunal (NGT) regarding the silt dumping site in north Delhi’s Singhola, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) informed the tribunal that although the site was cleared, 59,173.4 metric tonnes of silt was dumped there again over the past year.
The civic body said it initiated the process of establishing a 700-tonnes-per-day (TPD) facility to process fresh waste and silt to prevent the formation of new mounds. The accumulated silt will be removed once the facility becomes operational in November 2026, according to the MCD affidavit.
The NGT took suo motu cognisance of a Hindustan Times report, New waste mounds creep up on capital, published on November 4, 2024, which highlighted poor waste management practices leading to the growth of two waste mounds at Singhola and Narela.
Also Read:Delhi: NGT asks MCD about waste quantity at Singhola dumpsite
These sites are in addition to the Ghazipur, Bhalswa and Okhla landfill sites.
In an earlier hearing, the green tribunal directed the MCD to disclose the quantity of waste dumped at the site again.
In an affidavit filed on October 13, 2026, the MCD said that “owing to the urgency of pre-monsoon desilting operations, MCD had to resume the deposition of silt at the Singhola site.”
However, it added that “only the silt extracted from drains during annual drain desilting operations has been dumped at the Singhola site.”
Since July 2025, approximately 59,173.9 metric tonnes of silt was dumped there, the affidavit said.
Also Read:‘Had to resume dumping on cleared Singhola waste mound’: MCD to NGT
Silt dumping at the 7.2-acre Singhola site began on a temporary basis for two years following the collapse of a section of the Ghazipur landfill in 2017.
The site, near Singhola Khampur village, was used to divert and dispose of silt extracted from drains.
By July 2022, approximately nine lakh metric tonnes of silt had accumulated at the site.
MCD officials said the Public Works Department (PWD) and the Irrigation and Flood Control Department of the Delhi government also deposited drain silt there. The MCD subsequently awarded work for the bio-mining and disposal of processed material, and the site was cleared last year. However, silt dumping operations resumed thereafter.
To put this fresh silt dump quantity in perspective, the silt dumped at Singhola is only a fraction of the accumulated waste at Delhi’s legacy landfill sites, which have been in operation for decades.
For instance, approximately 1.5 million metric tonnes (15.06 lakh tonnes) of newer and remaining waste was still left at the Okhla landfill site in August, following the clearance of historical legacy waste accumulated up to 2025.

The Coimbatore Medical College Hospital (CMCH) administration on Tuesday replaced the brown paper covers used to dispense medicines to patients with fresh ones after instructions printed in Hindi on the former triggered a row, with many criticising it as contradicting the two-language policy of Tamil Nadu.
DMK leader and former Minister for Industries T.R.B. Raja was among those who criticised the inclusion of Hindi instructions on the covers.
“(It) seems like the three-language policy is being implemented in Tamil Nadu hospitals too! First Karur... Now the same situation in Coimbatore as well”, he posted on X, along with a photo of a pharmacy cover purportedly issued by CMCH, with instruction in Tamil, English and Hindi. He had posted earlier that similar covers with instructions in three languages were being used in Karur.
A senior official from CMCH said the covers with instructions in three languages were printed and supplied by Chinthamani Cooperative Society and no one had flagged any issue with the instruction in Hindi.
“We replaced these covers with new ones on Tuesday evening,” said the official, adding that such covers had been in use for a long time.
A source from the pharmacy section of the hospital claimed that similar covers with instructions in three languages had been in use during the previous regime as well. Meanwhile, pharmacists were instructed not to use the covers with instructions in three languages and use the new ones, containing Tamil and English.
According to CMCH authorities, the hospital handles around 3,000 to 4,500 outpatients a day, and a large number of migrant workers working in the city and nearby areas seek treatment at the hospital.

A Meerut court on Wednesday (October 14, 2026) sentenced Muskan Rastogi and her partner Sahil Shukla to death for the murder of Saurabh Rajput, Rastogi’s husband, whose dismembered remains were recovered from a cement-filled blue plastic drum in March 2025.
District and Sessions Judge Arvind Kumar Mishra pronounced the sentence after convicting the duo of murder and destruction of evidence.
Also read | Meerut murder case: Deceased’s kin allege involvement of ‘occult practices’
The case, which drew widespread attention because of the brutality of the crime, saw more than 100 hearings and the examination of 22 prosecution witnesses.
Prosecution lawyer K.K. Chaubey told reporters that the Judge referred to the Mahabharata while explaining the punishment, observing that justice required punishment proportionate to the gravity of the offence.
Apart from the death sentence, the court imposed fines totalling ₹70,000 on each convict for murder and the offence related to the disappearance of evidence, Mr Chaubey said.
The two accused, who attended the proceedings through video conferencing, reportedly broke down after the verdict was announced. Lawyers present in the courtroom distributed sweets following the pronouncement.
The detailed court order is awaited.
Rajput, 35, a merchant navy officer, had returned to Meerut from London in late February 2025. His family approached the police after failing to trace him for several days.
According to the investigation, the police recovered his remains from a drum at the house where he lived with Rastogi. It was alleged that the couple’s six-year-old daughter pointed towards the container when asked about her father’s whereabouts.
Police claimed that Rastogi and Shukla drugged Rajput before stabbing him to death and dismembering his body. The remains were placed inside the drum and sealed with cement and sand. The accused allegedly left for a vacation in Himachal Pradesh after the killing.
Police used industrial equipment to break through the hardened cement and recover the remains.
In May 2025, a chargesheet running to nearly 1,000 pages, containing forensic reports, call records, CCTV footage and witness statements was filed in the court accusing the duo for the crime.
Rastogi later gave birth to a girl while in jail. She had been pregnant at the time of the crime.

OpenAI is escalating its trade-secrets fight with Apple on the heels of Apple announcing a family of smart home-focused devices.
The AI company alleged in a new legal filing that an unnamed former employee sent themselves "a hundred highly confidential files" on their last day with OpenAI in June. The files contained information about at least one unreleased device OpenAI is developing, the filing said. The AI company said the former employee worked at Apple for six months before joining OpenAI, and he is now back at Apple.
OpenAI said it's the company's understanding that the unnamed employee later briefed "Apple's senior leadership, including Apple's vice president of operations in Asia" about the AI company's product plans.
"That presentation appears to have happened months ago—and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products," OpenAI's lawyers wrote in the filing.
In a statement, Apple said it has found nothing to support OpenAI's claims. It said the filing on Wednesday is an attempt to distract from its own claims about own former OpenAI employees have stolen Apple's trade secrets.
The files, OpenAI said, contained "highly confidential engineering and manufacturing data about the device(s)" and "supplier information and project files, standards for cosmetic finishes, and reports regarding coating and sealing of hardware components."
In July, Apple sued OpenAI, alleging that the AI company engaged in "a coordinated pattern of misconduct at an institutional level" to steal its trade secrets. OpenAI has denied wrongdoing and said it is not interested in Apple's trade secrets.
In an August blog post, OpenAI blasted the "careless, aggressive and oddly personal lawsuit sadly doesn't live up to that reputation." In a legal filing, OpenAI poked at Apple's perceived struggles amid the AI talent war.
On Tuesday, Apple announced HomeView, a $299 display and the company's first smart home device, which is powered by Siri AI.
Apple also announced a host of smart home products it developed alongside LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple's announcement highlighted how its AI systems could add to the devices, allowing a user to do everything from summarizing what's happening in footage captured by an outdoor camera to automatically adjusting a thermostat when they enter a room.
OpenAI said it is worried that the information the employee took could be used by Apple.
"OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple," the company's lawyers wrote, "where Apple engineers can shape Apple's upcoming products based on OpenAI's confidential and innovative work."
In referencing Apple's ambitions, OpenAI's lawyers linked in a footnote to the tech giant's collection of new devices, including HomeView.

'I reduced my running because of urine leaks' – Commonwealth finalist Korir
- Published
Naomi Korir's career on the track reached a high point in August when she finished fifth in the final of the mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
But things could have been very different for the Kenyan middle-distance runner.
The 28-year-old was born with fistula, a medical condition in which abnormal openings develop between organs and can lead to uncontrolled leakage of urine or faeces.
While Korir loved athletics as a child, it initially forced her to rethink any plans to be a runner.
"I played most of the sports activities: football, netball, athletics, even rugby," she said.
"But it was difficult because [of] the training, and the urine is flowing continuously. It's bad.
"I reduced my running to shorter distances to reduce the leaking.
"I began doing 100m hurdles."
Despite the challenges, Korir's love of sport also offered a form of escape and belonging.
"I could do it because I loved it," she explained.
"Because most of the people could avoid me, I did a lot of activities just to pass time and not to feel that I'm excluded."
Three surgeries and a second chance
The charity Doctors Without Borders estimates that 500,000 women live with fistula globally.
Some develop a fistula after childbirth while for others, like Korir, it is congenital.
Access to good obstetrics, or to simple surgery, means that the condition has all but disappeared in some countries, but it remains a problem in sub-Saharan Africa, where high quality medical care can be hard to access.
Korir was born with genitourinary tract fistula - an opening between bladder and vagina which caused her urine leakage.
Surgery was required, but her first two operations failed to solve the problem.
In August 2013, a third operation finally brought relief for the then 13-year-old.
The procedure was carried out in her home town Eldoret by the Gynocare Hospital, which specialises in fistula, obstetrics and reproductive health.
"It's a difficult condition to live with every day," Gynocare director Caroline Mabeya told BBC Sport Africa when discussing the stigma and isolation women with the condition suffer.
"They are ostracised in the society. That's the psychological torture that they face with the fistula."
The hospital has treated patients from across East Africa since opening its doors in 2011. Its work extends beyond surgery, with a post-operation programme designed to help women rebuild their confidence.
"We offer free treatment for these women at Gynocare because most of them are very poor," Mabeya explained.
"When they come into the facility, they are crushed, they have low esteem. So, there's a huge amount of effort that is put in to make them at least be strong enough to be reintegrated and get back into the community."
'A champion in sport'
For Korir, successful surgery offered a second chance, both on the track and in the classroom.
As well as allowing her to run properly again, she continued her education through Gynocare's Beyond Fistula programme.
"I have a family in GynoCare, a fistula home," she said.
"That is where I schooled after my surgery until I finished my secondary level."
In 2019, Korir began competing professionally and two years later was part of the Kenyan duo which claimed a silver medal in the 2x2x400m mixed relay alongside her partner Ferguson Rotich at the World Relays in Poland.
A year later she went one better, bagging gold as part of Kenya's 4x400m relay team at the African Championships in Mauritius.
The mile at this year's Commonwealth Games was her first appearance in major global final.
"I'm giving hope to young women maybe who have lost hope," she said of her achievements.
"They need to come back again in living and enjoying life."
Mabeya says Korir's transformation makes her a powerful example to the women currently receiving support at Gynocare.
"She makes them realise that you can actually pull yourself out of these struggles and still make it in life and succeed.
"Naomi actually is one of those patients that inspires us to continue working very hard, because we struggle with this condition and these women. The work is not easy."
As a young girl, Korir sang in church and played the keyboard, convinced that music was a more likely career than athletics.
"But now I'm in different career and I'm so happy," she beamed.
And with the World Championships in Beijing next year and the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Korir believes there is another chapter to write.
"I know I'm a champion in life, because conquering fistula alone is being a champion.
"Now I'm looking forward to be a champion in sport."

Sandeepa Dhar believes that education has played an important role in shaping her personality and outlook on life. Reflecting on her journey, she credited her parents, teachers and educational institutions for influencing the person she has become. The actress also spoke about the response to her comedy series Chumbak and admitted that she was initially surprised when directors Aatish Kapadia and JD placed their faith in her for a comic role.
Sandeepa Dhar reacts to the memes and online conversations around Chumbak: “It’s always wonderful when something you’ve put so much effort into works out”
Talking about how education has influenced her life, Sandeepa said, “I think a lot of who I am today is thanks to education. My parents always made sure I received a good education. Even when I wanted to become an actor, they told me to complete my master’s degree first and then pursue whatever I wanted to do. I think that’s a very typical parental response!”
The actress also acknowledged the role her teachers and academic institutions played in shaping her perspective and personality. Recalling her time at St. Xavier’s and Jamnalal Bajaj, she spoke about the opportunity to learn from talented professors and interact with educated minds. According to Sandeepa, these experiences left a lasting impression on her and contributed to her personal growth.
Meanwhile, the actress has been receiving a positive response for her performance as Kiran Kejriwal in Chumbak. Having previously taken on emotionally intense roles, Sandeepa said the appreciation for her comic performance came as a pleasant surprise.
“I’ve done emotionally intense roles in the past, and people have given so much love to Chumbak and my character, Kiran Kejriwal. I don’t know whether the surname had something to do with it, or whether it was the character itself! It’s always wonderful when something you’ve put so much effort into works out,” she said.
Sandeepa revealed that she had initially wondered why she was being considered for a comedy, given that she had not explored the genre before. However, Aatish Kapadia and JD recognised her potential and trusted her to portray Kiran. The actress expressed gratitude for their confidence in her and the audience’s response to the series. She also shared her happiness at seeing memes and discussions about the show circulating online.
For Sandeepa, the appreciation for Chumbak has made the experience particularly rewarding. The response has also highlighted the value of stepping beyond familiar roles and exploring different aspects of her craft.

Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court on Tuesday overturned the death sentence handed to Anojan Sivarasa, a 24-year-old Sri Lankan Hindu migrant worker, over a Facebook comment deemed insulting to Islam and Prophet Muhammad, following sustained diplomatic and legal efforts by Colombo. Sri Lanka’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism confirmed the development in a statement on Wednesday, October 14, saying the Supreme Court set aside the death sentence on October 13, according to Sri Lankan news outlet Newswire. The ruling marks a significant development in Sivarasa’s case, which triggered appeals for clemency from Sri Lankan lawmakers and religious leaders, alongside diplomatic intervention by the country’s government. Sivarasa’s ordeal began after an incident during a Hindu pilgrimage in Sri Lanka in late June, when footage showing a young man kicking a dog accompanying Hindu pilgrims circulated on social media, triggering heated online exchanges. During the ensuing argument, a user allegedly posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity. Sivarasa responded in Tamil with a comment about Prophet Muhammad, which was subsequently deemed blasphemous. Although Sivarasa deleted the comment soon afterwards and posted an apology video, screenshots of the exchange continued to circulate online. His brother, Hamsidan, told the BBC that individuals in Sri Lanka emailed Sivarasa’s employer in Saudi Arabia, alerting authorities to the post. His electronic devices were seized, and his social media accounts were deleted, according to media reports. Sivarasa was subsequently arrested and faced legal proceedings in Saudi Arabia. On July 15, the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court sentenced Sivarasa to five years in prison and imposed a fine of three million Saudi riyals, equivalent to approximately $800,000, over the Facebook comment. However, the case took a more serious turn after the Saudi Court of Appeal overturned the original sentence on September 17 and sentenced him to death for blasphemy under Sharia law, according to Newswire. An appeal was subsequently filed before the Saudi Supreme Court on October 11, paving the way for the latest ruling overturning the death sentence. The Supreme Court’s decision followed weeks of diplomatic engagement and appeals from political representatives and religious leaders in Sri Lanka seeking clemency for the migrant worker. Efforts to secure relief for Sivarasa involved lawmakers from different communities in Sri Lanka, who appealed to Saudi authorities to reconsider the sentence. According to the Tamil Guardian, six Tamil and Muslim MPs — Rauff Hakeem, Rishad Bathiudeen, V. Radhakrishnan, Jeevan Thondaman, Selvam Adaikalanathan and Shanakiyan Rasamanickam — wrote to the Saudi foreign minister on September 24 seeking mercy for Sivarasa. Senior Buddhist leaders, including the Mahanayake Theros of the Ramanna Maha Nikaya and Amarapura Maha Nikaya, also submitted memoranda to Sri Lanka’s president urging immediate intervention, the publication reported. Hindu religious leaders similarly called for action. Sri Lanka’s diplomatic mission in Saudi Arabia also intervened. The Independent reported that Sri Lankan Ambassador Omar Lebbe Ameer Ajwad visited Sivarasa at Dammam Central Prison on October 8 to enquire about his well-being after he was reportedly assaulted by a cellmate the previous week.
