Don't be scared: Being afraid is outright fun, and maybe useful
It's October and that can only mean one thing – the spooky season is in full swing.
Americans are expected to spend more than $13 billion dollars on celebrating this season, whether that's on horror films, costumes, candy or attractions, according to the National Retail Federation.
As much as $300 - $500 million of that spending comes from attending a haunt, where people willingly give up their hard-earned cash to be frightened. And tens of millions of people take part in this kind of activity every year.
But why do people like getting scared? The search for that answer starts with one of the largest haunted attractions in the country, Markoff's Haunted Forest in Dickerson, Maryland. Markoff's has more than a mile of haunted trails and dozens of themed haunted houses. It employs hundreds of engineers, retail attendants, makeup artists and actors.
Open since 1992, the attraction starts with towering skull-emblazoned wooden gates reminiscent of folk horror movies like "The Wicker Man."
Just inside, director of operations Paul Brubacher stands in between two huge bonfires.
"Some of our designers, including myself, have done some music festivals before. So yeah, that's the inspiration… from kind-of [a] Van Helsing vampire village aspect of things," Brubacher says.
There is hardly a thing that happens in this haunt without him knowing.
"This is an emergency radio that we have in each one of our scenes. In case an actor has a problem or somebody falls down and needs to be evacuated," Brubacher says. Before hitting the trail, he takes us behind the scenes to a barn where scare-actors are getting finishing touches of makeup.
Art director and makeup manager Chris Knowles and his team are using a bevy of pressurized airbrushes to quickly creep-ify all kinds of ghouls, vampires and aliens.
"It's great because you can get color on really finely or cover areas. [It] swaps colors really quickly as well, which is essential because we've only got like about seven minutes to do the makeup because we got like 100 odd people and two hours to do it," Knowles says.
Robert Doyle, 38, is in Knowles' chair at the moment.
"I love Halloween. I love going out and interacting with people, entertaining them, making them laugh. Giving them a good scare, you know, giving them a good dopamine rush," Doyle says.
Doyle has played all kinds of frightening characters in his five years at Markoff's. He's been a killer clown, a demon and tonight he's a Nosferatu-style vampire with sharp fangs, a bloody mouth and pupils as dark as coal.
Doyle thinks people keep coming back to places like Markoff's to face down their fears safely.
"People want to challenge themselves and they can say they accomplished something," Doyle says.
Another scare-actor, wearing a black top hat and looking like a cross between a straw and hair covered zombie, and hoodoo shaman is ready for his opening night.
His day-walker name is Jermaine Hoes.
"I am something that you see when you wake up at 3 o'clock in the morning," Hoes says.
Hoes has been a scare actor at different haunts around Maryland for years, and he says his reason for moonlighting as a horrific beast is pretty simple.
"I like scaring people. I like to make you run and scream and holler everywhere," Hoes says.
Leaving the actors so they can get into character, it's time to take to the trail, which begins with an ominous, steady heartbeat pumping through hidden speakers.
The trail is dark, foggy and winding. It's constructed in such a way that you can't escape the scares. Even trying to escape signals to the actors that you're ripe for a fright.
There are snakes, zombified pumpkin heads, ghosts, vampires, ghouls, aliens and even cannibals.
The trail is barely a mile, but between the terrain and its twists, it can take more than an hour to get through.
Voices cry out in pain and shriek in fear. Many seem menacing.
"You can join us," one voice in the shadows snickers.
"Don't you want your face on one of these pumpkins?," another cackles. "It just takes a little bit of a beating!"
Anything that could scare you is here, and it didn't take much in this secluded, murky environment.
The science of screams
"Fear is extremely fast," says Harvard Medical School associate professor of radiology Nouchine Hadjikhani.
For much of her career, Hadjikhani has studied what happens in the brain when someone is afraid. She uses computer screens and brain monitoring equipment to show subjects frightening images and measure their brain's reaction.
"If I show you very briefly, so for, you know, 30 milliseconds or something, snakes and spiders, I will see that your amygdala gets activated," Hadjikhani says.
She says it's this activation that makes a jump scare so effective.
"Your heart goes faster. You go a little further back and you start sweating. Your pupils get high for a stupid image on the screen," she says.
According to Hadjikhani, we get scared when something – usually visual – sets off the fear center of the brain. And she says she can elicit that same brain reaction in people just by showing them pictures of other folks who are scared. But she says it's difficult to know why some people derive pleasure from fear.
You have to talk to them.
Fear is fun
For that we need the scientists at the Recreational Fear Lab at Aarhaus University in Denmark.
Co-directors Matthias Clausen and Marc Andersen have created all kinds of studies into what keeps people coming back for frights.
Over the years, what they've found is that there is more than one type of recreational fear.
"We did an early study where we tried to see if we could identify the personality profile of the horror fan and what we found was a god-forsaken mess," Clausen says.
A rollercoaster enthusiast, for example, may detest horror films. And a scary movie scream queen might lose her lunch at a theme park.
But Clausen says survey after survey at the Fear Lab shows fear-for-fun is surprisingly universal.
"When you engage in recreational activities, you're essentially administering a fear vaccine," Clausen says. Seeking out fear is our way of preparing our bodies for the sometimes scary real world.
And this vaccine is actually fun for most people. "It doesn't hurt," Clausen says.
The duo has called this a "fear inoculation."
Co-director Marc Anderssen has also interviewed subjects who say they treat their own psychological disorders using fear.
"We have a ton of anecdotal stories about horror fans that we meet that tell us that they deal with their clinical anxiety by popping in a horror movie," Andersen says.
"The first time we heard it, we almost fell off of our chairs because it sounds so counterintuitive."
Playing with fear is also incredibly social, says Matthias Clausen. After going through a haunt for example, groups have told him they've experienced a sense of bonding.
"That's something that characterizes in fact most kinds of recreational experiences," Clausen says.
Back at Markoff's Haunted Forest, scare-actor Jermaine Hoes says his coworkers and the people he's scaring are like a family.
"The people, man. The vibes are great. You know, you meet a lot of people here. They have a ball. You get to mix and mingle with them," Hoes says.
Nothing brings people together like a good scare. Next week, find out how monsters, ghouls and slashers can also mean big bucks.

Update | October 13, 20:00 IST Adani Group’s flagship business Adani Enterprises and US-based manufacturing company Jabil Inc have signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding (MoU) to establish a 50:50 joint venture for manufacturing and assembling AI and data centre equipment in India. The proposed partnership aims to produce AI racks, servers, storage, networking equipment, and power and cooling systems to cater to India’s rapidly growing data centre capacity. How many ways can the Trump administration clamp down on international researchers?
In the span of two days last week, the Trump administration issued two sweeping announcements meant to crack down on international students and scholars, who make up a sizable portion of the nation’s biomedical research workforce. On Wednesday, the Department of Homeland Security announced a proposed $70,000 fee for a work authorization program that many foreign students use to gain professional experience. The next day, the Labor Department revealed that it is investigating nine universities — including Harvard, Stanford, and Yale — for alleged fraud related to visas awarded to postdoctoral researchers.
This is all playing out while DHS is fighting in court to impose a four-year cap on stays in the U.S. by graduate students and postdocs. The department is also attempting to revive administration plans to impose $100,000 fees for h2-B visas, which are used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as biotech.
None of these changes have taken effect, but experts warn that the administration’s repeated attempts are already deterring students. A survey by the Association of American Universities found that, while domestic student applications for U.S. Ph.D. programs went up by 3% this year, international applications dipped 21%.
“This is an incredible series of self-owns,” said Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney based in Boston. “The government also knows that none of this will stand up in court. They just want to send a message: Don’t come here.” — Jonathan Wosen
What $250 million in free lunches buys you
You know the saying, “there’s no such thing as a free lunch?” Turns out, that applies to doctors too. Except in this case, the cost of the free lunch is being borne by patients and the health care system, according to a new study.
A new Cochrane review of dozens of previous studies found that gifts (including meals) and payments doctors receive from drugmakers increase inappropriate prescribing, which in turn increases health care costs. One of my favorite details from STAT’s Ed Silverman: “The research found a clear relationship between meals and inappropriate prescriptions. The more meals a doctor received from a company, the more of the company’s drug they prescribed.” Another: pharmaceutical companies spent upwards of $250 million on meals alone in 2022.
Read more about the pernicious influence of lobbying on medicine. And please — if you’ve received particularly lavish or unusual gifts from drug companies, let me know. I’d love to hear more about what this experience looks like on the ground.
DEA suggests new limits for two kratom derivatives
Proponents of natural kratom leaf products have notched another win after the DEA made changes Friday to its proposed temporary order that would place some kratom derivatives — but not natural leaf products — in Schedule I, the federal category for drugs that carry the most risk without any medical benefit.
Originally, federal agencies had planned to temporarily designate 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) above a certain potency threshold as Schedule I, in addition to three synthetic kratom derivatives at any level, including mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI). But a notice of intent issued Friday laid out new thresholds that apply to both 7-OH and MGPI individually or in combination. The new threshold focuses more on the concentration of these compounds within a product rather than the total amount.
The American Kratom Association, which lobbies for natural leaf products, celebrated the change as a resolution to its lawsuit against the original MGPI scheduling, which it argues could have inadvertently criminalized natural leaf products found to contain trace amounts of the compound. But some drug policy advocates and lawmakers want more limits around all kratom products, including natural ones.
It’s unclear when exactly the scheduling will be finalized. Experts agree that some sort of regulation needs to be enacted around kratom-related products, but they aren’t all sure that scheduling is the best approach long-term. Meanwhile, it’s worth remembering that a government watchdog report recently concluded that both DEA and HHS lack adequate policies and procedures on drug scheduling. — Theresa Gaffney
How Americans feel about science, as told in charts
It can sometimes seem like Americans’ relationship to science is uniquely fraught, weighed down by the Trump administration’s deep cuts to research funds, the ever-present battle over vaccines, and our byzantine health care system.
Given all that, new data from the Wellcome Global Monitor surprised me. Those pollsters found that 52 percent of Americans report having “a lot” of trust in science. Across the globe, that number is 26 percent. Americans, in aggregate, are also more eager to get vaccines compared to peer nations; 45 percent of Americans say they would want to get vaccines recommended by a nurse or doctor “right away.” In Germany only 28 percent say the same.
To unpack what these numbers might mean, check out Nick Florko’s story.
Doctors are trained to be deferential. That follows them their whole careers
By the time doctors reach their residency programs, they have completed college and medical school, passing several rigorous exams. Many will be nearing 30, or older. And yet residents often have to ask permission to even use the restroom.
This infantilizing treatment is creating “something plaguing medicine: learned helplessness, a psychological state wherein a person stops trying to change an unfavorable or unsavory situation because they believe that they have no control over the outcome,” writes Frances Mei Hardin, a former ear, nose, and throat surgeon, in the debut of her new column Chief Complaint.
Hardin writes that today’s doctors inherit a sense of powerlessness that’s reinforced by “increasing layers of bureaucracy, hierarchy, metrics, and threats of retaliation or lawsuits that leave physicians with less and less control. And we don’t question it.” Read more about the problems that’s creating — and the possible solutions — here.

Late last month, the state of Tennessee attempted to execute Christa Pike, a woman who has been on death row for decades after killing a classmate as a teenager.
Florida’s uniquely horrifying death penalty system
Can the death penalty ever be fair?
The execution failed: Pike survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital, making her the first person ever to do so.
The botched execution comes at a strange moment for capital punishment in America. Support for the death penalty has been declining for decades. And for a long time, the number of executions was falling, too. But since 2021, executions have been increasing again. The recent surge has been driven largely by one state: Florida.
According to Pamela Colloff, who covers the criminal justice system for ProPublica and wrote about Florida’s use of the death penalty for New York Times Magazine this summer, 40 percent of the executions conducted in the US last year were in Florida.
“There are so many things that make the administration of the death penalty interesting and unique in Florida,” Colloff explained on a recent episode of Vox’s The Gray Area podcast. “Among active death penalty states right now, Florida is unique in that one person determines, from the hundreds of men on death row, who will receive an execution date, and what that execution date is.”
I spoke with Colloff earlier this month following Pike’s failed execution about what happened in Tennessee, what’s driving Florida’s recent zeal for executions, and why victims’ families are often unsatisfied by the death penalty process.
Below is an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to The Gray Area wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify. (This interview also appeared more recently on Vox’s Today, Explained podcast.)
We’re taping shortly after news came out that a woman in Tennessee who was on death row, authorities attempted to put her to death. They gave her two doses of lethal injection medication, and she survived.
How much of the decline in the use of the death penalty has to do with, in your estimation, people feeling like there’s no way to do it that’s humane?
This is the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, just to give you a sense of things. This is more common there than in other states. They’ve changed their drug protocols and we don’t know a lot about what went wrong with Christa Pike. In May, it was an issue with accessing veins, which can be an issue with lethal injection.
I think it’s also important for people to remember that we had the electric chair as the method of execution through the ’80s and into the ’90s in some places. While [lethal injection] is considered a far more humane, quote-unquote, way to do this, we can see that nothing is perfect.
I will say that while the issues of botched executions are very important, and I think there are some other ones coming up to be concerned about, I am more interested in how it is that other errors are made, that other people end up with the ultimate punishment when that perhaps was not the right punishment for what occurred.
You’ve also written that death penalty convictions are just expensive, right? And on top of that, DNA evidence has made it clear that many of the people who were being convicted were not guilty, or there wasn’t strong enough evidence to convict them. How do you think about that mix of factors?
Florida, which I’ve spent a lot of time writing about, is the leading place in America by a mile in terms of the number of executions, and has a very large death row. Florida’s also the leader in wrongful death row convictions. Just to give you a sense of things, Florida holds the distinction of 30 death row exonerations.
What that means is in the modern era — the past roughly 50 years — there have been 30 men who were given dates of execution who now walk free. And for anyone who pays any attention to how the criminal justice system works and how incredibly difficult it is to overturn a wrongful conviction, if we have 30 people in Florida who have that distinction, we know that there are many more.
What’s going on in Florida? When did you realize that something was different there?
It really ramped up last year. Last year, Florida executed 40 percent of the people who were executed in the US in the last calendar year. In this year, there have been 16 men who’ve been executed in Florida so far.
Just to give you a comparison, Texas is the next state with the highest number of executions, and they’ve executed six men in that time. We already have outlier states, primarily southern states, and then we have Florida being the ultimate outlier.
There are so many things that make the administration of the death penalty interesting and unique in Florida. The thing that fascinated me the most is, among active death penalty states right now, Florida is unique in that one person determines, from the hundreds of men on death row, who will receive an execution date, and what that execution date is.
Who is it?
Gov. Ron DeSantis. I went back and looked at what were the patterns here, what were the things guiding Gov. DeSantis’s thinking in setting these dates, and was fascinated to see and very troubled to see that there are a number of men who’ve been there so long.
They’ve been there since the 1970s. These are men who were convicted when Gerald Ford was president, just to make this real to people. But the dates are not being set among the men who are what are called death-eligible, meaning that they’ve gone through all their appeals. They aren’t being done chronologically.
There’s no rhyme or reason to the process. And so there’s this speculation game among victims’ families, prisoners, their advocates about who will be next. And men can sit there on death row for decades with that hanging over them, and that is a Florida phenomenon.
You wrote about Florida’s death row turning from something like a purgatory where people stay for a long time into something closer to an assembly line, right?
I was so struck by the fact that in Florida, in order to have this pace of executions, there were people who were receiving their dates 30 days, sometimes fewer, from their execution dates.
Just to give people a sense of why that is unusual, there are so many things that kick into gear when a death warrant is written. There are numerous legal maneuvers and next steps that happen in the courts. To give you a quick example, there was one defendant in Florida this spring who, five days before he was scheduled to be executed, was finally granted the ability to test DNA evidence in his case that had gone untested.
He had great lawyers who didn’t sleep to make that happen, but that it came as close as five days to his execution date. I think that should give us all pause about how fast this is moving.
You have multiple people in the queue at the same time. There’s a place — a different unit than Florida’s death row — that you’re taken to once you get your date, called death watch.
Tell me about death watch. What does it look like and what does it feel like?
Death watch is roughly 30 feet from the execution chamber. There are three cells. When you receive your date, you are taken from death row to death watch where you’re put — I don’t want to say solitary because if there are one or two other men who are held there — but you’re in a far different situation than you would be on death row where there are guards and other people you know.
From that point forward, there are roughly 30 days where you are held within steps of where this will take place. To me, it was chilling that when I was doing my reporting in the spring on the story that I published this summer, all three cells were filled, and as soon as one person was executed, the pattern was that often the next day a new death warrant would be signed, and there would be a new person in place.
Why do they do that? Why do they put these people next to the place where they’ll die?
That’s one of the many questions I had about that. We talk about not wanting to have cruel and unusual punishment. Our Constitution does not uphold that. But it’s such a unique kind of mental torture, I think, to be 30 feet from where you’ll be put to death.
The other thing I was struck by was the waiting aspect. If you’re on death row, again, you always have this hanging over you. I talked about the way in which, when you’re in that kind of sensory deprivation, you become highly attuned to sounds and smells and things like that.
I interviewed someone who’s not on death row anymore, whose sentence was commuted, who talked to me about recognizing that jangle of keys and the steps that this group of people who come to deliver the death warrant take, and knowing that someone is about to be served with a death warrant, but not knowing, “Is it me? Is it the guy next to me? Is it someone down the hall?”
I just want to say, I understand that there’s a counterargument to all of this, which is that these are people who most often committed terrible crimes. Their victims did not know when they were going to be killed.
I do think, however, as a state that administers this thing, there has to be a rhyme or reason to this. Otherwise, you have total chaos, including for victims’ families, who never know. Are they going to wait one month? Are they going to wait 15 years? They don’t know.

China’s trade surplus hits $938 billion for Jan-Sep as pressure ramps up to rebalance trade
China’s customs agency says the country's exports surged 36.3% in September from a year earlier
HONG KONG -- China’s exports surged 36.3% in September from a year earlier, its customs agency said Wednesday, bringing it on track to exceed last year's record trade surplus as pressure ramped up from its trading partners, including the European Union, to rebalance trade.
The exports data, which was better than what economists had expected, accelerated from the 25% growth in August. High-tech goods such as semiconductors and autos have helped fuel its rising shipments overseas.
Imports climbed 31% in September year-on-year, also accelerating from August’s 28.2% rise.
That resulted in a $133.5 billion trade surplus for China last month, widening from $119.1 billion in August.
For the first nine months, China’s trade surplus reached $938 billion, with expectations growing that it could surpass last year’s full-year $1.2 trillion record.
Strong exports have helped drive China’s overall economic growth this year, at a time when domestic consumption and investment remained sluggish, weighed on by a yearslong real estate sector downturn.
However, China’s export resilience is now faced with mounting challenges, said Ecaterina Bigos, a senior market strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management.
“While U.S.-China trade tensions have eased somewhat, the EU’s push to rebalance directly targets high-value exports,” she said.
The U.S. has launched an ongoing probe against China and other trading partners this year on their excess industrial capacity, although Washington and Beijing last month reached an agreement to extend their trade truce and cut tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods.
The 27-nation EU has particularly been struggling to rebalance a trade deficit exceeding $1.1 billion a day with China. EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič, following his visit to Beijing where he met his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao last week, said a deal has been reached with Beijing, including halving Chinese hybrid car imports into the EU over the next few years.
Many of China’s trading partners are facing weak growth prospects and are fearful of their manufacturing industries being overrun by exports from China, said Eswar Prasad, a professor of economics and trade policy at Cornell University.
Policymakers have also pointed to a weakened yuan, China’s currency, versus the U.S. dollar and other currencies contributing to Chinese exports being cheaper overseas when compared with goods from other countries, adding to trade imbalances.
China has said it has “no need or intent” to gain competitive advantages through currency devaluation and that its trade growth has been driven by its industrial competitiveness in the global market.
China’s trade surplus and its high-tech export model depend on open markets, Bigos said, and while diversifying its exports into markets such as Southeast Asia and Latin America can help, it cannot fully substitute for Western demand.
The country’s reliance on high-tech exports, meanwhile, could face challenges as some U.S. technology industry leaders called for a global slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence over safety reasons.
“A slowdown in the global AI investment cycle could pose a greater threat to China’s export growth than trade restrictions imposed by other countries,” said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board.
Chinese leaders have set an annual economic expansion target of 4.5%-5% for 2026. It is set to release its July-September quarterly economic growth figures next week.
This week, the International Monetary Fund lowered its forecast for China’s 2026 economic growth to 4.5%, down 0.1 percentage point from its previous projection, as it warned that the country's robust exports were unable to fully offset domestic weaknesses.
While Chinese officials have highlighted the need to bolster domestic demand, analysts believe that has yet to become a priority for this year even after authorities recently rolled out new measures to help lift its economy, including subsidies for homebuyers’ mortgage interest payments.

Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence. Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI.
As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.
“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.
Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun, a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.
Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.
The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry.
Last month, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes, which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU— who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress.
OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI, warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer.
As with math, Thompson says we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way.
Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science, and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound.
“We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.”

Petite, lightweight, and kind of kicky for a cargo bike. Can fit in a car’s back seat. Fat tires provide stability. Cushy bike seat is comfortable for long rides. So many accessories. Surprising 500-pound payload.
TIRED
Fast braking requires a firm hand. Range is middling. Battery indicator sneaks up on you. Not as petite as other JackRabbits. Technically a scooter, not an ebike.
I am not an obvious target customer for a cargo ebike, as I neither have kids to tote nor a large space for bike parking. But the new JackRabbit MG Cargo is so tiny, it doesn't conjure the dully utilitarian, heedlessly bulky nature that's common to other cargo ebike models. In fact, when I tested the wee, plucky ebike, I found its fat tires and tiny wheelbase make it feel more like a speedy urban dirt bike than anything else.
But despite being a relative lightweight (55 pounds) and petite enough to fit in the back seat of my old Montero, the MG sports a 750-watt motor that can haul nine times the bike's weight uphill. I even threw a grill onto a bike trailer to test this claim, which held up.
Note that likeall JackRabbits WIRED testers have reviewed, the MG is less an ebike than a scooter that looks and acts like an ebike: Instead of pedals, you get pedal-like footrests, plus a throttle. This means when the battery runs out, the bike stops moving. Also, the listed 48-mile range drops considerably when you ride at top speed or haul a large load. Nonetheless, the MG may have converted me to the pannier class.
After testing this MG for a couple of months, I no longer use my car when I need groceries, even when I'm taking a longer trek to the Grocery Outlet for discount steaks or salmon. The same is true when I want to haul a slushie machine across Portland’s steep mid-city ridge to a friend's house for cheeky weekday margaritas. By not acting like a cargo bike, the MG has convinced me to haul cargo on a bike.
Zippy Little Devil
Photograph: Matthew Korfhage
“How exactly is this a cargo bike?” my editor asked when I showed her a photo of the MG Cargo after it arrived. She wasn't asking out of wonderment. As mentioned, the MG flat-out looks less like a bike you'd use to haul stuff and more like a dirt bike.
JackRabbit is known for making lightweight, zippy, fun little scooter hybrids that physically resemble BMX trick bikes. I loved the easy mobility and high-speed capability of JackRabbit's equally powerful XG Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends) when I tested that model last year. I'd worried that the MG Cargo—18 pounds heavier and nearly a foot longer than the XG—would compromise too much on these virtues. I needn't have worried. As I quickly learned, the pleasantly peppy MG rides like an off-road bike when you're not hauling a big load.
Its three throttle speeds max out at about 20 mph, 15 mph, and 7 mph, respectively. The lowest speed is manageable for a sidewalk, while the fastest hits top speed within about 50 feet on flat ground, unless you've got some weight behind (or on) you. The MG advertises a range of 48 miles, though I'll assume this requires being a lighter rider who is gentle on the throttle. As a 200-pound man with an admittedly heavy throttle thumb, I only made it to about 25 miles, even with minimal cargo. Because the bike's battery indicator shows up as at least half-full for the vast majority of this range, you'll need to test and learn your personal range when doing so is not mission-critical.
Note that because JackRabbits don't have working pedals, the bikes exist in an interesting technical gray area in some states in terms of their classification. Specifically, one could debate whether they're really a Class 2 ebike that can ride on bike lanes and trails. Given the MG's maximum speed of 20 mph—aside from an honor-system 24-mph jailbreak speed you can unlock for off-road riding—it mostly looks and quacks like a Class 2 ebike. In my experience, it's also treated as such.
The MG also offers nice customization options for accessorizing. It's easy to add a couple of rear pannier bags to the rear mounting rack or side racks ($75) on each side, offering enough capacity for most small grocery trips or beach excursions without adding much bulk. You could also opt for a rear basket.
Photograph: Matthew Korfhage
While I can't quite stow the MG as easily as other JackRabbit models, it's still small enough that I can slide it into my back seat—as long as I uncork the front handlebars and turn its front wheel backward. (Some sources refer to the MG as “foldable,” but this isn't strictly true: it just has a quick-release wheel and an easily removed handlebar.)
Which is to say, even without the cargo component, I could like the MG just as a fun little commuter, especially with the welcome addition of a cushy Kinekt active-suspension seat post that provides some added give for longer rides.
The Little Cargo Ebike That Could
Despite its petite size, the MG performs well as a true cargo hauler that you could use to move trailers full of groceries or the more precious cargo of your own children. I didn't borrow any kids to test rear child trailers or JackRabbit's mini-me rear seat and handlebar set ($175). But I did use the MG's preinstalled Burley trailer hitch to haul a box containing a 150-pound grill up a hill with a 7 percent grade. While the MG didn't get to full speed on the ascent, it pulled the grill and my 200-plus-pound self surprisingly well.
The MG's stability and cornering capabilities also fared better than I expected, given its short base. Cargo bikes tend to lengthen their frame to add stability and make room for riders to pedal comfortably while carrying loads on the front or the back. The MG Cargo's stability mostly comes from its cushy fat tires, largely thanks to the clever design of the larger front tire, which both adds stability up front on rugged terrain and lowers the center of gravity where cargo hangs. The lack of pedaling also naturally removes some wobble.
You will make compromises, though: Cornering while hauling a large load can yield a jumpy ride, leading to the occasional overcorrection. The range also drops considerably with heavy carries, given that you can't add your own pedal power. Braking is fast but does require a good grip, especially with larger loads downhill.
For the Occasional Hauler
The MG Cargo lives in an interesting middle ground between commuter and cargo ebike. If I were primarily using it to transport children or work gear, I'd probably opt for a bulkier hauler or the Specialized Global Haul ST, WIRED's top-pick electric cargo bike that offers a more reliable long range.
The best use cases for the MG Cargo are as a fun recreational ebike that stows easily into your back seat or as a multipurpose commuter with built-in storage that saves its rider from needing to wear a backpack. In either case, the cargo capabilities function as bonus features as opposed to being the main draw.
It's less a workhorse than a hobby pony: I've slipped books and a blanket into a pannier so I can read at the park, and I've spontaneously brought home six-packs from the brewery a couple of miles down the road. When I grocery shop using the MG Cargo, I'm spared the bother of tightly packed parking lots that make me angry before I reach the aisles. I zip in, I unlock the panniers, pop in my groceries, and zip right back out. In this way, the MG Cargo also doubles as the cheapest therapist I know.

Pope Leo XIV's surgeon confirmed that he has lung cancer, and he had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, the Vatican said Tuesday (October 13, 2026).
The tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.
The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about 3 hours, the statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said.
Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli Hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localised nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
The Vatican on Monday cancelled all Leo's audiences through Oct 20.
But the decision to have the operation clearly came as a surprise: While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.

Briton Kartal upsets Bencic at Wuhan Open
- Published
Britain's Sonay Kartal upset ninth seed Belinda Bencic as she continued to build post-injury momentum at the Wuhan Open.
Kartal reached a career-high ranking of 44 last year but has slipped to 170th in the world after a six-month injury absence.
Having returned to action for Great Britain at last month's Billie Jean King Cup Finals, the 24-year-old reached the third round at the Beijing Open last week before beating Ukraine's Anhelina Kalinina in her opening match in Wuhan.
The impressive 6-0 7-5 victory over Swiss world number 12 Bencic, a Wimbledon semi-finalist last year, was the second biggest win of Kartal's career by ranking.
"I trusted that I would be able to get my level back, I just didn't know how quickly," Kartal said.
"I did a lot of things right today but I still think there's a long way to go.
"I can produce the level, but can I sustain it? I think that's going to be the hardest challenge. I'm happy to be back, I'm feeling good."
Kartal will face Italian 15th seed Jasmine Paolini or 20-year-old Czech Nikola Bartunkova for a quarter-final place.
Kartal suffered a stress fracture in her back in March, which meant she missed three of this year's four Grand Slams - including Wimbledon.
The Briton, who reached the fourth round at her home Slam last year, was in good form before that enforced break.
That included victories over American top-20 seeds Emma Navarro and Madison Keys at Indian Wells, before she retired against Elena Rybakina in the third round with the back issue.
Kartal has made a positive return, beating Chinese 31st seed Wang Xinyu as she reached the third round in Beijing, and has now won four of her five matches on her return to the WTA Tour.
Former world number one Iga Swiatek also progressed, recording her 40th win of the season with a 6-2 6-1 victory over fellow Pole Magdalena Frech.

the worst person you know probably writes in all lowercase.
they’ll tell you it’s an aesthetic choice, a testament to informality. they’re likely a twentysomething brooklyn resident like myself, bullish on being not the voice of their generation but a voice of a generation, and definitely guilty of posting performative notes-app screenshots and pseudointellectual, stream-of-consciousness “musings” that compare charli xcx to the pope.
what are they really up to, and do they know they’re participating in a long, exclusive, exclusionary tradition? the stylistic choice to write in lowercase is a dead horse that’s been beaten, flogged, and beaten again—what my generation calls ran through. and yet, it’s having a moment. i had to investigate.
for one side of the internet, lowercase writing is feminine.
it’s a “formal feature of how girls engage online,” says rayne fisher-quann, who’s 25 and lives (where else?) in brooklyn. known to the web for the all-lowercase personal essays she writes for her blog internet princess, fisher-quann insists that the offhandedness of lowercase “neutralizes” the self-importance of writing about oneself. it’s a way, fisher-quann says, “to avoid criticism.”
her feelings trace back to the digital spaces she occupied in her adolescence. “i got a lot of intellectual enrichment and influence from early 2010s feminist tumblr,” fisher-quann tells me. a decade-plus ago, incisive microblogs were on the rise on the platform, alongside the now-canonical page justgirlythings. justgirlythings pioneered the art of superimposing an all-lowercase serif-font sentence on a desaturated image (usually of a young woman wearing an oversized jumper and a messy bun sitting by a fireplace). it mostly covered cozy clichés such as “rainy days” and “lazy sundays.” becky campos, the blog’s author, says she wrote justgirlythings “because it almost felt like you were reading more of my diary instead of some polished copy. it showed that i’m more of a real person than some corporation making the posts.”
then there was rupi kaur, the instapoet of my generation. kaur’s work investigated the less manicured parts of the female experience, also through a lack of capitalization, except her words weren’t accompanied by stock imagery—they were the image. this performance of accessible vulnerability, akin to a live-laugh-love pillow, was kryptonite for millennial women: in 2016, kaur’s debut collection, milk and honey, sold more copies than the next-best-selling work of poetry, the odyssey, by a factor of 10. in homer’s defense, he didn’t have instagram.
while kaur describes her fixation on lowercase as an “ode to my identity as a diasporic punjabi sikh woman” (gurmukhi script only has one case) and a way to channel “equalness,” the virality of her work cemented the supple curves of the lowercase alphabet as an expression of femininity during the early days of social media. and the story might end there, if the internet were only populated by women.
but, to burst my own algorithmic bubble: behind every justgirlythings fan is a 4chan power user.
“i’m willing to believe that [using lowercase] is more deliberately aestheticized among young women on tumblr,” says adam aleksic, an internet linguist who goes by etymologynerd, “but none of the mega online communities use regular punctuation.” he and i are talking at a swanky coffee shop in soho, where he’s finishing up research on why the r-word is making a comeback.
to make his point, etymologynerd pulls up 4chan on his phone and starts scrolling. among the rancid all-lowercase musings, i notice a plethora of greater-than signs, angle brackets, and asterisks. because 4chan doesn’t support—has never supported—rich text (italicization, bolding, etc.), users also employ text-markup conventions: *yes* for yes, /i/hell no/i/ as hell no, etc.
while many may contend that writing in lowercase is a callback to one’s youth, sites like 4chan remind us that, at least within the digital sphere, the callback goes back much further and is part of a larger tradition. “lower case? it started with single-case tty model 33. now, it is habit,” ken thompson writes, in lowercase, in an email where he politely declines my request for an interview. (notice how thompson spells lower case as two words instead of one. before lowercase was a cornerstone of identity politics, it was just a lower case of the alphabet.)
ken thompson is 83 years old and, of course, one of the computer scientists to whom we owe the existence of the internet. he’s referring, in his email, to the teletype model 33, a popular terminal used for telecommunications that debuted in 1963. back in the ’50s, computers functioned on terminals that could support only 64 unique characters that—counting numbers, punctuation, and special characters—left no room for lowercase letters. this meant that most early programming languages (fortran, pascal, lisp) were written exclusively in uppercase. it was only between the ’60s and ’70s, when hardware manufacturing started to mature and memory costs started to plummet, that more characters became possible.
in early 1969, thompson got pulled from a project at bell labs, leaving him with nothing but time. so he decided to try to port a video game he had developed on company-owned equipment, space travel, to a more accessible pdp-7 computer he found unused in a neighboring department. he ended up reconfiguring the pdp-7’s operating system entirely and, alongside his colleagues dennis ritchie, douglas mcilroy, and bob morris, kickstarted the development of unix. unix made programming more ergonomic. with it, programmers no longer had to work with obscure machine code; there was no need to rewrite programs from scratch for every new computer model; and, perhaps most notably, it supported two cases.
soon, all the leading research institutions and corporations running on unix had to standardize how they capitalized in code: upper and lower case helped distinguish variables from constants (e.g., snake_case for variables, SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for constants). these naming conventions, coupled with the increasingly collaborative culture of coding that unix established, evolved into a form of etiquette. capitalizing your code correctly was critical to how legible it was to other programmers, and excess capitalization was considered a faux pax. by the time this etiquette trickled down to the threaded text posts on usenet—the global network system created in 1979—the jargon file (better known as the hacker’s dictionary) had consecrated uppercase as SHOUTING.
point is, the internet used to be nerd country, reserved for those with technical expertise and written mostly in their idiom of programmatic lowercase shorthands. but everything changed in september 1993, when aol made usenet access a sign-on service, opening the floodgates to what the original usenet (then later irc and world wide web) users would call noobs. all of a sudden, an influx of digital non-natives started using proper grammar and correct capitalization, blissfully unaware of the rules that maintained the ecosystem they had just besieged. eventually, because there were just so many of them, the lowercase hacker vernacular became a marginalized quirk, and proper capitalization took over as the new norm.
i’m not saying the tumblr girlies stole from early-internet nerds destined for 4chan. but i am saying lowercase wasn’t invented by them, and perhaps has always been the hallmark of the outsider.
of course, maybe none of this matters. according to gretchen mcculloch, author of because internet: understanding the new rules of language, lowercase is a classic case of “resemanticization.” just look at something like “lol.” mcculloch’s theory is simple: first, a phrase is coined for a specific function (L.O.L. as laugh out loud). then, as more people use the phrase in different contexts (lol as an expression of nonchalance), its secondary meaning takes over. in just this way, the meaning of lowercase now bears no connection to its hacker associations, or even to its feminist co-optation.
today, lowercase can be clickbait—gong.io, an ai company that sells marketing data, analyzed over 85 million cold emails and concluded that those with lowercase subject lines get twice as many opens as properly capitalized ones do. i’ve heard of people my age who “become lowercase” because capital letters in texts and dating apps read as “too intense.” lowercase can also be a status symbol—when jack dorsey laid off 40 percent of his staff in february, he did so in an all-lowercase tweet. “the more senior you get, the less formal your emails are,” michelle liang, a tech growth investor, tells me. rarely were any of jeffrey epstein’s emails properly capitalized.
and yet, pockets of the internet still maintain that typing in lowercase is somehow antiestablishment, evident in the twitter trend of posting the phrase “i type in lowercase because i’m anticapitalist.” this could, perhaps, be a nod to the way writers like bell hooks used lowercase writing to “decenter” themselves from their writing; or to every college student’s favorite poet, e e cummings; or to the german bauhaus artists who deemed two cases aesthetically “inharmonic.”
aleksic, the etymologynerd, offers an alternative, more modern explanation: “people might be doing lowercase to signal that they’re not ai,” he says. obviously ai can write in lowercase, but you at least have to prompt it to do so, so there’s some inherent “friction,” etymologynerd says. after all, it’s not exactly easy to read an essay written entirely in lowercase.
the writer and self-diagnosed contrarian sam kriss sees beauty in how this tired, self-contradicting trope splits hairs: “writing enormous block paragraphs entirely in lowercase is the highest form of ‘respect’ i can render you,” he wrote recently on his substack. “reading my posts should be like scrubbing your eyeballs with sandpaper. i will keep attacking you until you are free.” etymologynerd goes so far as to insist that lowercase is the new normal.
or not. when i check back in on internet princess, fisher-quann’s substack, i notice she’s made a big change: she now writes with proper capitalization.
what say you?

After facing backlash and legal inquiries from the Indian government over the presence of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on its platforms, Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta said it was using AI to improve how it detects such illegal content.
These strategies include new large language model (LLM) detection of CSAM, greater ad transparency, AI sweeps of ad content, a red-teaming AI agent to detect vulnerabilities, and detecting bad actors who make new accounts after being removed the first time.
Media reports had observed that CSAM was present in the ads on social media platforms Instagram and Facebook.
The Indian Union government and the National Commission For Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) had met with Meta over the issue.
A few weeks ago, Meta said it would share CSAM reports with the Indian law enforcement authorities. This was in addition to reporting to the U.S.-based National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC).
“Between January and June 2026, Meta actioned 5.3 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content on Facebook and Instagram in India, with over 98% found and proactively addressed before anyone reported it,” said the company in a press release.

'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
- Published
"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV."
Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia.
"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer."
Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner.
Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact".
There are many causes of isolation in China. Like when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country.
But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives.
Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that.
"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs.
"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine."
"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added.
Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver.
The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible.
His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows.
There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles.
Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile.
"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC.
She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult.
But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood.
"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him.
Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits.
Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic.
"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards."
She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves.
"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious."
At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection.
Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee.
"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect."
Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province.
"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said.
The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month.
He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said.
"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her."
After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude.
"The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback."
Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity.
Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly.
"It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said.
"I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy.
"I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

Early voting in the U.S. midterm elections is underway. Voters are deciding which party will control Congress, as well as numerous state legislatures and governors' offices. Snopes' fact-checkers are flagging rumors surrounding the election, debunking false statements by candidates and suspicious voter fraud claims with nonpartisan research and expert sources. Join our effort to keep this election fact-focused by becoming a Snopes member.
Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, some social media users are warning that any election ballot marked by a poll worker could be disqualified, whether it is "a letter, a checkmark, a star, an R or a D any writing of any kind."
The rumor has spread on numerous occasions. Snopes addressed the claim before both the 2020 and 2024 elections. Posts typically feature the same copypasta, shown below (emphasis ours):
A very reliable good friend of mine just finished the pollworker training, and she texted this to me ....."Just finished Poll Manager training! I passed all the classes. I want you all to know something...when you are checking in at the polls and they happen to write anything on your ballot before they give it to you to put in the voting machine...a letter, a checkmark, a letter star, an R or a D any writing of any kind...please request a new ballot. Your ballot will be disqualified if it is written on. Please be on the look out. Make sure poll workers do not write on your ballot. It will cause your ballot to be disqualified."
Please forward this to everyone you know. Make sure poll workers do not write on your ballot. It will cause your ballot to be disqualified.
(Facebook)
The rumor is not true. Many election officials have clarified that a poll worker marking a ballot does not disqualify it. It was not possible to find any evidence of a U.S. state disqualifying ballots containing markings, unless it renders the voter's selections unreadable. Several states (such as North Carolina) actually require poll workers to mark ballots as part of the verification process.
In 2024, Commissioner Ben Hovland, chairman of the U.S. Election Assistance Commission, reportedly told Reuters some marks that poll workers add are acceptable and that rules regarding markings usually have to do with the voter's identity. Snopes contacted the EAC seeking comment. We will update this article if we receive a response.
When addressing the rumor ahead of previous elections, we spoke to several officials who confirmed the rumor is false.
Spokespeople for the Maryland State Board of Elections and Maine's Bureau of Corporations, Elections and Commissions said the claim is misleading. Laws governing elections in Minnesota, Missouri (PDF page 108, Section 2 of "Counting of Votes") and Texas (PDF Page 7) also require poll workers to mark ballots.
Debra O'Malley, communications director for the Office of the Secretary of the Commonwealth in Massachusetts, told Snopes in 2020 (detail in brackets ours):
There is no reason any poll worker [in Massachusetts] would ever mark anything on a ballot, with the very rare exception of a challenged ballot. If a ballot is challenged for legal cause, the voter's name and address, as well as the challenger's, are written on the ballot to be reviewed only in the case of a recount or court order. Again, this is very rare.
She continued: "Ballots are not disqualified at the polling place. If a tabulator cannot read a ballot, the voter is offered a new ballot. If they do not want to spoil their ballot, it is set aside to be counted by hand at the end of the night."
We reached out to O'Malley for an updated comment. We will add her response if she replies.

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.
- This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

Loneliness among parents whose adult children have migrated abroad is associated with higher psychological distress, difficulties in regulating emotions and problematic series watching, an exploratory study by researchers from NIMHANS has found.
The findings assume relevance on World Mental Health Day, observed on October 10, which draws attention to mental health and the need to address psychological well-being. The study highlights the emotional challenges that parents may experience when their children settle abroad and everyday family interactions become less frequent.
64 ‘empty-nest’ parents
Published in BMC Research Notes, the study examined 64 ‘empty-nest’ parents aged between 45 and 65, whose adult children had emigrated and lived away from home for at least two years. The sample comprised 30 fathers and 34 mothers from different families in Karnataka, Haryana and Punjab. Most belonged to middle socioeconomic backgrounds and nuclear families, and more than half had been in the empty-nest phase for over five years.
Rajesh Kumar, associate professor in the department of clinical psychology at NIMHANS and the corresponding author of the study, said the findings highlighted the relationship between loneliness and emotional well-being among parents adjusting to life without their children at home.
“We found a significant association between loneliness and psychological distress. Loneliness was also associated with difficulties in emotion regulation and problematic series watching, which refers to excessive or difficult-to-control viewing that interferes with everyday functioning. This also resulted in the risk of developing non-communicable diseases (NCDs),” he said.
Loneliness significantly predicted psychological distress even after accounting for age and gender. Of the 64 participants, 22 (34.3%) were classified as having higher levels of loneliness, while 42 (65.7%) fell into the lower-loneliness group. Those reporting higher loneliness also reported greater psychological distress, more difficulties in regulating emotions and higher levels of problematic series watching, Mr. Kumar said.
Social changes
Manoj Kumar Sharma, professor in the department of clinical psychology at NIMHANS and head of its SHUT Clinic, said the findings needed to be understood in the context of the emotional and social changes that parents may experience when their children settle abroad.
Dr. Sharma, who is one of the authors, cautioned that the study did not establish that loneliness causes psychological distress or excessive series watching. As it was cross-sectional, it could identify associations but not determine the direction of the relationships, he said.
Mothers reported greater loneliness
Women in the study reported significantly higher levels of loneliness and psychological distress than men.
The researchers said that this was consistent with earlier research suggesting that mothers may experience greater emotional difficulties during the empty-nest phase, potentially reflecting their involvement in caregiving and emotional relationships with their children.
Possible coping mechanism
The researchers said digital media and streaming services could provide an easily accessible form of solitary leisure for parents experiencing less day-to-day interaction with their children.
However, the study did not examine why participants watched series or whether they used viewing deliberately to cope with loneliness or negative emotions. The researchers cautioned against assuming that excessive viewing was necessarily a coping response.
Other factors that could influence media use include social support, physical mobility, retirement, living arrangements, marital relationships, the frequency and quality of communication with adult children, and access to technology.
Social and psychological support
The findings underline the need to pay greater attention to the emotional well-being of parents whose children migrate abroad, as changing family structures and international migration can reduce opportunities for regular face-to-face interaction, Dr. Sharma said.
The authors said interventions to strengthen social connectedness, promote adaptive emotion-regulation strategies and encourage healthier technology use could potentially help parents navigate the empty-nest transition.
