Everstone Capital-backed EV startup GreenCell Mobility has raised ₹330 Cr ($34.6 Mn) in an equity funding round led by Impact Fund Denmark to support the rollout of about 4,500 electric buses currently under deployment. The Mumbai-based startup is eyeing expanding its fleet to more than 5,000 e-buses across 105 cities across India. “Our focus is on executing our order book with rigour, strengthening service delivery and ensuring that the organisation keeps pace with the size and complexity of our operations. This equity investment gives us greater headroom to accelerate our plans while maintaining the standards of reliability, efficiency and customer experience that are fundamental to our business,” GreenCell Mobility managing director and chief executive Devndra Chawla said. Founded in 2019, GreenCell Mobility focuses on deploying and operating electric buses for public transportation. It acquires electric buses via contract manufacturing arrangements with vendors and then deploys them for both intercity and intracity travel. Backed by Eversource Capital, a joint venture between Everstone Capital and Lightsource, GreenCell primarily operates under the brand NueGo. It claims to operate more than 1,200 electric buses in India, including 900 on intra-city routes, 300 under its NueGo brand for inter-city travel, and 50 for MSRTC. The startup also runs over 270 charging stations to support its fleet. The startup previously raised $37 Mn from World Bank’s International Finance Corporation and also counts Eversource Capital, British International Investment and Tata Capital among its backers. India’s electric bus segment has so far drawn strong interest from development finance institutions and lenders backing vehicle deployments under long-term public transport contracts. GreenCell’s latest round suggested that investors are also beginning to back the operating platform layer in the category, not just asset financing. The investment highlights the role of institutional capital in expanding electric public transportation infrastructure in India. Large-scale electric bus deployments require funding not only for vehicles but also for the operational capabilities and charging infrastructure needed to support them. Earlier in March, electric bus manufacturer PMI Electro Mobility, along with its electric bus platform Allfleet, has signed a definitive agreement with private equity giant KKR for an investment commitment of up to $310 Mn, to help scale the electric bus platform and focus on expanding its presence across India. PMI subsequently filed for an IPO via the confidential route last month.

Delhi University’s Executive Council has approved hostel projects worth ₹5,889 crore, proposing new residential facilities and the reconstruction of two existing hostels to expand accommodation for students amid a persistent shortage of affordable housing. The approvals, cleared at an emergency meeting on Tuesday, include ₹4,027 crore for new hostels expected to accommodate 15,758 students and ₹1,862 crore for reconstructing two existing hostels, with a proposed capacity of 6,137 students, Hindustan Times reported. The university said the projects would collectively provide accommodation for 21,895 students. However, the proposals will need approval from the Union Ministry of Education for grant-in-aid before they can move forward. The fresh approvals come as several previously announced hostel projects remain delayed due to funding constraints and construction challenges, raising questions about how quickly the proposed capacity can be added. Vice-Chancellor Yogesh Singh said the proposals had been cleared by the university’s highest statutory decision-making body and would now be forwarded to the Union Ministry of Education for approval. The new construction plan includes two additional hostel blocks for the Institute of Eminence hostels at the university’s Dhaka Complex, separate boys’ and girls’ hostels at Veer Savarkar College in Roshanpura, Najafgarh, and hostels for men and women at DU’s West Campus in Dwarka and Najafgarh, and East Campus in Surajmal Vihar, Kardardooma. The university is also planning to reconstruct Jubilee Hall and the Postgraduate Men’s Hostel to increase their capacity. Jubilee Hall, established in 1947, currently accommodates 212 students. Under the reconstruction plan, it is proposed to house 3,795 students. The Postgraduate Men’s Hostel, built in 1975 and currently accommodating 100 students, is proposed to have a capacity for 2,337 students after redevelopment. “The university’s earlier hostels were built differently from the conditions expected in the future; therefore, planning is being done with the next 100 years in view,” Singh said, adding that the names of existing hostels would remain unchanged after reconstruction. The new approvals come as DU continues to face delays in implementing previously announced residential projects. Two projects at the Dhaka Complex — a Girls’ Hostel/Studio Apartment Complex estimated to cost ₹233.35 crore and a Hostel-cum-Residential Block pegged at ₹318 crore — remain pending. A university official told HT that both projects were expected to be completed by December 2028. The Nirbhaya Residential Accommodation Project, also located at the Dhaka Complex, has seen its estimated cost increase from ₹272 crore to ₹400 crore. Funding from the Union Ministry of Women and Child Development is yet to be released, the official said. “We have made several attempts to reach out to the women and child development minister, but the funds are yet to be released,” a senior university official told HT on condition of anonymity. Delhi University has more than 251,000 students, including around 71,600 undergraduate students admitted in recent years, while roughly half of its students come from outside Delhi, according to reports. Before the latest proposal, the university’s official hostel infrastructure across its colleges and departments offered around 7,224 beds — approximately 3,688 in undergraduate college hostels and 3,536 in postgraduate university hostels, as per reports. The proposed capacity of 21,895 students would significantly expand this infrastructure if all the projects are completed. However, these are planned seats, not accommodation currently available to students. Even if the entire proposed capacity is delivered, many students from outside Delhi are likely to continue relying on private paying guest (PG) facilities and rented accommodation. Safety concerns have also drawn attention to the conditions in which students live outside university hostels. On September 6, a five-storey building in Delhi’s Satya Niketan neighbourhood reportedly collapsed, killing seven people and leaving several others critically injured. The 40- to 50-year-old building, locally known as “Hostel Daze”, was reportedly being used as a private boys’ PG accommodation and housed students because of its proximity to DU’s South Campus. The incident has underscored the importance of safe and affordable student housing, although the extent to which it influenced the university’s latest decisions has not been established. To the average observer concerned with the future of American democracy, it might be easy to conclude that religion has been part of the problem — particularly over the last few years. Right-wing religious leaders, including the leading Southern Baptist televangelist Robert Jeffress, have endorsed “Christian nationalism”; other evangelical pastors and conservative Catholic intellectuals have been openly pondering if America should become more of a theocracy; Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who once called for an “American crusade,” evoking bloody medieval religious campaigns, has referenced Christian theology in statements about the Iran war.
Maybe secular liberals can’t save democracy
The solution to some of American democracy’s biggest problems might be something old and controversial: more religion.
To critics, these examples show that American religion is becoming an active threat to pluralism and tolerance — the ideas that make American democracy work.
But what if the solution to this anti-democratic slide is also religion — more religion than the US currently has?
Key takeaways
- The authors of a new book argue that declining levels of religiosity have worsened polarization, which has led to a backslide in democracy.
- To reverse this trend, the authors suggest everyone, but particularly liberals and secular people, engage with religion more and take lessons on debate and disagreement from faith traditions.
- For those who do identify as religious already, this would mean participating in organized religion; for those who are not religious, this would mean approaching religion and religious people with more openness and curiosity.
- This argument has limitations, but there are signs it is becoming more widespread, including the rise of religious Democrats and the pope’s recent comments.
A new book by two thinkers from opposing ends of the ideological spectrum argues that declining levels of religiosity across the board, but particularly among liberals, have deepened political polarization, which in turn has corroded democratic norms. Now, they argue, one of the most effective ways for liberals to stand up for democracy is to engage with religious communities and their scriptural traditions with more respect, openness, and curiosity. The authors also urge liberals who are believers themselves to embrace organized religion and return to it themselves.
Conservative evangelical Christian Matthew Kaemingk and liberal Muslim writer Shadi Hamid argue in Can Religion Save Democracy? that there’s a necessary and unique role that religious institutions and organized religion must play in American public life. Religion serves a fundamental regulating purpose, tempering emotions, fundamentalism, and nihilism. And when that fades away, those base instincts and emotions get channeled into our politics.
They write:
As Americans exit churches in droves, they’re not leaving behind their religious passions. Instead, they’re transferring those passions to the political battlefield. In this new post-religious context, Christian faith and Scripture function less as moral constraints within evangelical circles and more as political cudgels to use against one’s opponents.
“We’re not trying to convert [nonbelievers],” Hamid told me in an interview. “Believing is one thing, but believing that religion can play a positive role is another. And we want to encourage secular readers to embrace the second proposition, even if they don’t believe religion is true or don’t believe God exists.”
What happens when religion recedes from the public square
At the core of Kaemingk and Hamid’s argument is a simple case: There is an innate religion-shaped hole in people in the 21st century, which has been slowly replaced with politics, unbridled passions, and secular ideologies. The loss of religion hasn’t meant a loss of religious convictions, but instead has meant the rise of a new fanaticism, either secular or fundamentalist, while depriving everyone of the good things that organized and institutional religion can do.
It’s not a completely novel argument; it’s a combination of St. Augustine’s famous line that “our hearts are restless until they rest in [God]” and of the political scientist Robert Putnam’s modern case that churches and religious communities provided the third spaces that fostered civic partnership, trust, meaning, and belonging.
But they also connect these lines of thinking to what the Dutch philosopher Abraham Kuyper used to argue around the turn of the 19th century: that all people are religious, and that something very similar to religious fervor quietly powers all political movements. Religion is “pervasive, public, and pluriform” — an essential part of being human, whose absence leaves nihilism, fear, and distrust in isolated, but still fanatical, individuals.
“If Kuyper is correct that all human beings desire ultimate belief and belonging, then erasing or sequestering religion won’t extinguish our spiritual passions. They will simply shift elsewhere,” Kaemingk and Hamid write. And that shift has been toward politics, candidates, elections, and secular “creeds” that provide identity, belonging, moral certainty, and salvific promises without the accountability, guidance, and caution that religious traditions can provide.
It’s not hard to find examples of what Kaemingk and Hamid mean here. From 2016 to 2024, many observed elements of quasi-religious fervor in movements powering Trump and Woke 1.0. Trump’s strongman appeal generated a cult of personality around him, while anti-Trump resistance efforts and progressive social movements often took on qualities people also found quasi-religious: in-group markers, language, and customs, BlueAnon theories. What’s left is a stalemate, with more conservative religious believers bunched up on one end, and nonreligious but equally passionate citizens on the other end.
Kaemingk and Hamid argue that people on the left often respond by denigrating religion and religious people, dismissing those who try to defend or practice it in the public square, or forcing them to adopt secular language and thinking instead of letting religious people bring their full selves to the public space. But the way out of this current stalemate, Kaemingk and Hamid suggest, is for people on the left to be open, curious, and respectful with the devoutly faithful, whether they’re neighbors or candidates running for office.
“For that audience, my desire is to say, ‘Hey, you don’t have to believe in religion, but you can recognize the positive aspects of religion,’” Hamid told me.
That involves practical, daily activities and more high-minded appeals. In regular life, the authors recommend prayer, or prayer-like practices for nonbelievers, to help better understand and forgive opponents. They suggest there can be benefits for both nonreligious and religious people to meditate on scriptural and theological teachings about forgiveness, debate, disagreement, salvation, and why earthly politics shouldn’t be taken so seriously.
And they urge liberals in particular to reengage with religious communities and congregations. Religious liberals should avoid isolation or solitary, individualized faith, the authors recommend, and instead return to congregations and specific churches or places of worship to become part of a community and find purpose. For nonreligious liberals, Kaemingk and Hamid suggest they reexamine their own ideological priorities and be open to the possibility of being wrong on some of them, and potentially engage with organized religion to better understand a religious worldview.
Kaemingk and Hamid offer a specific challenge for liberals and secular Americans that might seem a bit unsavory: They have to realize that they are not blameless for the polarization and radical religious fervor that exists right now through their dismissal of organized religion. Their earlier denigration of organized religion around the turn of this century (think of the New Atheist movement), combined with many leaving institutional churches or failing to participate in religious life, has all contributed to the capture of these institutions by unsavory political opponents, or helped in the decline of more moderate congregations. And any attempt to stop this continued slide away from pluralistic democracy hinges on a collective effort between religious and nonreligious Americans to reverse these trends.
This argument has its limitations
Here’s an obvious question: If religion is so good at moderating people, why hasn’t it been able to temper emotions among the religious already? The most loyal Republican voters over the past few cycles have tended to be evangelical and nondenominational Christians, followed by white Catholics — both of which tend to report above-average levels of religious participation. They’ve stuck with Trump and the GOP over the last decade, which has been defined by polarization, authoritarian policies, and even moments of political violence, that both Kaemingk and Hamid say religion can fix.
Here’s an obvious question: If religion is so good at moderating people, why hasn’t it been able to temper emotions among the religious already?
More generally, while there is evidence to suggest that evangelicals who leave their churches become more cynical and individualistic — a point in Kaemingk and Hamid’s favor — there’s not much evidence to suggest that the converse is true: that religious participation has actually tempered emotions, passions, and politics. Instead, there’s a case to be made, as the writer Robert P. Jones laid out recently, that the opposite seems to be true: The most religious folks tend to still be the most likely to support harsher Trump-era policies.
Hamid acknowledged that this is a challenge, but argued this isn’t about the religion itself — rather a Trump-specific phenomenon: “Many evangelicals have let partisan loyalties take precedence over religious commitments,” he told me. “This is the distorting effect that Trump has had on the evangelical movement.”
He emphasized that evangelicalism has suffered because many of the most fervent MAGA supporters who identify with that religious movement are not actually very religious. “Evangelicals aren’t going to church as much as they used to on average,” he said. “There has been a kind of process of de-institutionalization in the kind of Protestant domain. And the people who tend to be more fervent MAGA supporters tend to go to church less.” He compared the level of evangelical support that Ted Cruz and Trump got in 2016: Trump had an upper hand among unchurched evangelicals.
Beyond this, the practical reality is that, as things stand today, religiosity does not seem likely to bounce back to the levels it was at two decades ago — at least, not without the help of secular Americans.
Still, it’s an attractive idea, and it’s not hard to see why people might be open to it. Even Democrats themselves seem to understand that writing off religious voters for years was a bad idea. Some of the most promising Democratic candidates in red states in upcoming midterm elections are religious, including Texas Senate nominee James Talarico and Kansas Senate nominee the Rev. Adam Hamilton. A dozen other pastors or believers are running in down-ballot races across the country, while potential 2028 presidential candidates like Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro talk openly about their personal faiths, the role of organized, institutional religion, and seem comfortable doing so.
“It’s promising,” Hamid told me about this trend. “Part of what we argue in the book is that Americans should be able to bring their full convictions into the public arena. If they’re editing themselves or suppressing their religiosity out of fear of alienating constituencies, that’s not good for democracy.”
And Kaemingk and Hamid also have a very influential intellectual ally in this mission: Pope Leo XIV just made a similar case in France for secular liberals to reexamine their understanding of religious liberty and how to balance it against the rise of right-wing religious politics.
“A Christian engaged in public service and guided by the light of his or her conscience, illumined by faith, cannot be considered a proselytizer or a threat to the unity of the nation,” he said in Paris, appealing directly to France’s fiercely secularized civic leaders. “Indeed, authentic secularity does not exclude religion but is capable of valuing it as an educational resource.”
Aboard a plane back to Rome, Leo continued, arguing that religion must have a role in the public square and pointing to the decline of religion in Germany as something that may have facilitated the rise of a far-right movement that cloaks itself in religious language.
“It would be interesting to study, analyze if and how there may be a relationship, for example, between the growth of these groups on the far right,” Leo said mid-flight, “...with some expression of a combination of these far-right points of view with a certain kind of religion, which…is not an authentic expression of Christianity.”
This may be an unsavory ask for liberals and secularists most upset about creeping religious nationalism in the Trump administration and around the country. The recent creation of a new Office of Religious Affairs in the Pentagon, the invocation of God and Scripture to support military action and immigration enforcement, and the attacks on the wave of religious candidates running as Democrats this year all make it understandable why there may be hesitancy in accepting this challenge. But Kaemingk and Hamid are undeniably right about one thing: In a diverse and pluralistic nation, we have no choice but to live with each other.

IMF chief urges US to rein in $40 trillion debt as poor countries ‘pay the price’
Rising debt levels and global inflation, partly resulting from high energy costs due to the Iran war, have pushed interest rates to multidecade highs

The U.S. and other wealthy nations must urgently tackle rising global debt that is placing immense strain on low-income countries and the wider financial system, the head of the International Monetary Fund warned on Wednesday.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. policymakers acknowledge that the federal deficit and the national debt, which now stands at more than $40 trillion, are too high. She said economic expansion alone will not solve the issue.
Disruptions in financial markets continue as bond yields rise, driven by investors requiring higher risk premiums.
"We believe that growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments," Georgieva said during the autumn meeting of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.
Pointing out that further steps are essential, she added, "There is no magic," and said: "You have to go in a direction of tightening, bringing it down, bringing the deficit down."
‘Fiscal consolidation’ faces challenges
Rising debt levels and global inflation, partly resulting from high energy costs due to the Iran war, have pushed interest rates to multidecade highs, adding to the burdens of the world’s poorest nations.
Efforts to bring debt under control with what Georgieva and other experts call “fiscal consolidation” have suffered setbacks from heavy spending during the COVID-19 pandemic and since.
“Fiscal risks are rising, and a proper reaction is largely absent in many countries,” said Rodrigo Valdes, director of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs Department. “And in major advanced economies, the effect of fiscal indiscipline does not stop at the border. It travels to the rest of the world.”
“Among the world’s poorest countries, interest payments have reached historic highs relative to revenue, and declining amounts of aid are creating gaps that some countries have been unable to finance,” the IMF's latest Fiscal Monitor said.
That is forcing countries to make hard choices between supporting their most vulnerable people and meeting their debt repayment obligations.
“The Global South is paying the price for rising interest rates in wealthier countries,” U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said at an event on the sidelines of the IMF meetings.
“We need a new deal on debt, a deal that supports countries to repay over longer time horizons and, crucially, refinancing with better rates to give developing countries precious fiscal space,” he said.
Nations need help with job creation and investment
The median developing country pays three times as much in interest as developed countries, said Alexander De Croo, former Belgian prime minister and administrator of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
On average, nearly 10% of government spending goes toward debt repayments. High fuel and fertilizer prices, the effects of the El Niño weather phenomenon and rising borrowing costs have left many low-income countries with little room to recover.
“I mean, we don’t see really a light at the end of the tunnel,” De Croo told The Associated Press.
Creating jobs is another top priority, particularly as the growing use of artificial intelligence threatens to make many traditional occupations obsolete. More than 1.2 billion young people are expected to enter the global workforce over the next decade or so, while forecasts suggest only 400 million net new jobs will be created.
The UNDP this week announced its “Jobs for Prosperity” initiative to bring together governments, development banks — such as the World Bank — and private businesses to encourage investment in sectors such as tourism, healthcare and food processing.
The initiative and related efforts will help countries attract investment by strengthening governance and policies and developing pipelines of “investible projects,” De Croo said. “These are things that are feasible. It’s been proven that you can do it in many places of the world,” he added.
Separately, the IMF, Bank of Thailand and World Bank Group announced a “Bangkok Blueprint” on Wednesday to combat cybercrime, financial fraud and online scams.
The announcement came a day after cyberattacks caused refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France.

Picture a baby sleeping in a crib.
Every second, her brain is forming more than a million new neural connections. The scaffolding for language, memory, attention, and thought is going up in real time, wire by wire. We don’t yet know who she will become; yet much of her future self depends on what reaches her now, in the earliest months of her life.
We accept that the brain is shaped by developmental plasticity, developing and adapting in response to experience and environment. Yet medicine tends to frame conditions affecting the brain across the lifespan, from autism and ADHD to Alzheimer’s disease, as primarily genetic or social in origin.
Until we understand the biological mechanisms that translate experience and environment from birth into lasting changes in brain development and function, we are operating with only part of the picture. The cost of that missing piece may be trillions of dollars and millions of lives each year.
The question is: What are the biological systems involved in brain developmental plasticity?
Researchers have identified the window between conception and a baby’s second birthday as a critical period of brain development. Genetics, nutrition, parent-child interaction, and sleep all matter, but growing evidence suggests the developing brain also takes its instructions from somewhere perhaps unexpected: the gut microbiome.
The gut microbiome is more than a passenger in early life. It may be one of the biological systems through which brain developmental plasticity operates. When that system is functioning well, the brain receives signals it has evolved to expect during critical windows of early development. But what if those signals never arrive, or arrive at the wrong time? And what if environmental factors we know shape neurodevelopmental outcomes partially do so by disrupting those signals?
Research is linking early gut microbiome disruption to differences in socialization, learning, and memory. Disruption describes a microbiome that develops off course: It can be short on the beneficial bacteria and key functions that a developing brain expects, weighted toward harmful ones, or maturing too slowly or quickly. Variables that are common practice in modern medical and food systems, like cesarean birth, antibiotic usage, formula feeding, and maternal BMI, can contribute to this disruption. Scientists are investigating whether these accumulating pressures on the developing gut microbiome may contribute to rising neurodevelopmental differences, like autism with high support needs.
This is the premise of FORM, a $50 million Wellcome Leap program designed to rigorously investigate links between the early life gut microbiome and neurodevelopmental challenges, including autism with high support needs. The aim is to conduct this much needed research in parallel with the development of new product opportunities that could improve developmental resilience and reduce neurodevelopmental and co-occurring difficulties before they emerge, by promoting a well-functioning maternal and early infant microbiome.
The consequences of early gut microbiome disruptions may not stop at childhood. Researchers at Washington University found markedly different gut microbiomes in people at the earliest preclinical stages of Alzheimer’s, differences correlated with amyloid and tau accumulation before any cognitive symptoms appeared. Scientists at New York University and Rutgers have proposed that this trajectory may begin in infancy, with early antibiotic exposure being one factor that can initiate a cascade that contributes to Alzheimer’s decades later. Both lines of work are early, unanswered questions remain, and neither establishes causation yet. But together they suggest the early-life gut microbiome may be less a chapter in child development than a strand that runs through an entire life.
To be clear about the science: On autism, debate continues and causation is not established. On dementia, the research is only now emerging. We need more rigorous, large-scale research into the gut-brain axis across the life course, conducted in partnership with communities with lived experience to ensure research is socially trustworthy. And we need the infrastructure to act on what we already know. Right now, we are not even close.
By investing in capabilities that can measure and potentially modify key gut microbiome functions in early life, we can ask not just how to react to differences and disease once they appear, but whether supporting developmental resilience from conception through to age 2 can set children up for lifelong brain health.
During this period, the mother’s body and the infant’s body are one system. We treat them as two.
This division makes administrative sense. It makes almost no biological sense.
We know that immune, inflammatory, metabolic, and stress signals influence brain development in a child before and after birth. We also know that factors ranging from infection and antibiotics to nutrition, socioeconomic position, and chronic stress can shape neurodevelopmental outcomes in a child across this same period. Many of these same factors also shape the maternal and developing infant gut microbiome.
So, what if they converge on a common biological pathway? Sitting at the crossroads of immunity, inflammation, and metabolism, the maternal and infant gut microbiomes may help translate environmental influences into the biological signals that shape brain development across pregnancy and infancy, one connected window of developmental plasticity.
This is not an argument against antibiotics, caesarean births, formula, or any other feature of modern life. Nor is it a story about medicine harming children. It is a story about how the science of brain development is outpacing the clinical systems built to act on it. The conditions that shape the microbiome are rarely individual choices made in isolation. They are societal forces that may influence one of the earliest biological systems involved in an infant’s brain development.
Yet our clinical systems still treat maternal health and infant health as separate worlds. Connecting maternal and infant care — shared records, joint protocols, and gut health on the prenatal and postnatal agenda — is the most immediate structural change we can make.
One reason the early childhood brain development window closes without intervention is that our diagnostic tools were not built to look through the mother-child nexus.
Neurodevelopmental screening in the United States typically begins between 9 and 30 months. Providers rarely diagnose autism or neurodevelopmental delay before ages 3 to 6, and the behavioral assessments they rely on detect difficulties when they have already occurred. We are too late in addressing the underlying biology and miss the key windows of developmental plasticity. What we need are objective biological biomarkers that catch gut microbiome and brain vulnerabilities months or decades before differences manifest — and years or decades before dementia.
Getting there requires not just better instruments. It requires a shift in how providers and parents understand brain conditions: not as purely behavioral, detectable only once a toddler shows difficulties, but as biological vulnerabilities that take shape much earlier in life.
Tools to identify a disrupted maternal and infant gut microbiome are already being developed, but screening without a protocol for what to do next is incomplete medicine. We need to fund the full pipeline: validating the diagnostics, building clinical capacity to deploy them, and ensuring that children with disrupted gut microbiomes have real options to restore resilience before early disruption translates into potentially different neurodevelopmental outcomes or later cognitive disease.
Worldwide, $1.7 trillion is spent annually on brain disorders. Nearly all of it goes to people already in crisis, past the point where the underlying biology could have been redirected, whether in infancy or in adolescence or midlife. Early investment won’t erase those costs, but it would reduce the cost later in life — including the projected global cost of dementia, which is rising toward $2.8 trillion by 2030.
Making that case rigorously is itself part of the work. Without serious health-economics research on early intervention, microbiome-based tools will stall on the way to clinical adoption because no one has yet shown what they save in terms a reimbursement system understands. The Davos Alzheimer’s Collaborative works to close that gap, making the case that brain diseases including Alzheimer’s must be met with prevention and detection across the life course, now starting as early as maternal health and the infant gut microbiome.
Now let’s focus back on that baby in the crib.
She is being shaped right now by organisms she will never know exist, through a process medicine has only begun to map. The gut-brain conversation sounds abstract until you consider what it may mean in practice: The architecture and resilience of her neural scaffolding, built in her first years, may influence whether she can still recognize a face across a room at 80.
Holly Baines, Ph.D., serves as program director for Wellcome Leap’s FORM, a $50 million program researching the role of the maternal and developing infant gut microbiome in neurodevelopment. George Vradenburg is a veteran corporate leader turned global health advocate, driving Alzheimer’s research, prevention, and policy change through UsAgainstAlzheimer’s, the Davos Alzheimer’s Collaborative, CEOi, and Business Collaborative for Brain Health.

Kobe – An after-school program in Kobe is helping children with developmental issues build confidence and independence through theater activities, a relatively unusual approach in Japan.
The provider of the after-school program, Hokagorubi, offers creative activities through improvisational plays. It was established by Masatoshi Odaira in 2020 after he gained experience in theater as a university student and later taught drama to students at a special-needs school.
According to Odaira, children who had difficulty maintaining posture or speaking clearly often became more confident and expressive after performing on stage. This made him believe that theater can “have a therapeutic effect.”
In late July, ahead of a stage performance, nine students at Hokagorubi rehearsed a play set at an airport and centered on a young travel enthusiast. Although some forgot lines or encountered difficulties, the participants communicated with and supported each other.
Currently, Hokagorubi has 39 students ranging from elementary school first-graders to high school seniors, including those with autism spectrum disorder or attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. Some refuse to attend school.
It holds three performances a year, with participants divided into six groups. Each group is responsible for writing scripts, directing productions and creating props.
A 14-year-old participant said, “I enjoy improvisational performances as they allow me to express myself freely” and “I hope to continue taking part.” When he feels anxiety, he impersonates an anime character and talks to himself in the bathroom. His mother said that the theater program “helps foster self-esteem by providing a place where participants can take on roles and express themselves.”
Nabi Ito, a lecturer specializing in contemporary theater at the University of Osaka, said that theater can make communication easier for children who struggle with conversation because scripts provide a framework and such children can act as someone else.
Odaira said that a performance should be considered a success as long as it reaches its conclusion, even if participants encounter difficulties on stage.
“I hope children will gain positive experiences in conversation and communication while acting and develop confidence in interactions with others,” he said.

Time and time again as we celebrate achievements in health care, a measurable pinnacle of which could be the Nobel for Physiology/ Medicine, a sobering dose indicating the power of pathogen is delivered to us. This time, with the reported case of all things, the plague, in Russia. This week we discovered that the entire issue is mired in mystery, with not much information being shared by the nation. What was clear during the COVI-19 pandemic was the absolute criticality of sharing information globally, but with every squeak about the break out of infectious disease. In fact the Pandemic Agreement includes an aspect of Pathogen Sharing and Benefits among member nations. However, practically, sometimes nations find it difficult to easily share information with the global community.
Initially, the WHO cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. A WHOOfficial said the global organisation doesn’t know exactly how lab worker in Russia died in plague case. Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the agency doesn’t know the “causative agent” behind the woman’s October 2 death, and urged Russia to share more information. The EU also urged Russia to be ‘transparent’ on plague reports - The Hindu
On its part, in tersely-worded statements, Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, does not link the case to pneumonic plague, maintaining that “extensive” testing found no evidence the lab worker’s illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Russia earlier said she died of pneumonia — a “typical” acute respiratory viral infection — and its health authorities have found no cases of plague recently. Moscow also denied sanitary measures over plague reports.
For an idea of what we actually know for sure now, do read this explainer: Pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia?
In addition, there was a fresh scare from Ebola-affected Africa: Kenya confirms first Ebola case imported from Congo after patient dies in Nairobi. Why is this significant? I explain here: Ebola death recorded in Kenya after victim travelled from DRC. The victim had been living in DRC for years, and was reportedly already ill before he took a road trip, and then, a flight back home to Nigeria. He was admitted to a hospital in Nigeria by a relative, but succumbed to his illness. This is the first case of an Ebola death that has occurred in a country, outside of the DRC and Uganda, during the outbreak raising significant concern regarding transmissibility for public health authorities. Kenyan authorities have called for stricter controls at the airports and also undertaken efforts to spread awareness and urge citizens to test if they notice symptoms. While the WHO has not issued a travel ban to the affected countries, self declaration by travellers has become mandatory at all international ports.
The past week also saw some hectic health-related activity in India. The most significant among them was easily the Supreme Court calling for a cap on trade margin for all essential medicines and medical products, as Aaratrika Bhaumik reported. As the government declared that it had proposed a 30% trade-margin cap on patented and non-patented cancer medicines, but top court asks why a margin cap cannot be extended to all medicines and medical products; the court says the government has to ensure that DPCO-approved medicines, whose price is legally regulated, reach patients. That is jumping the gun though, first read Bindu Shajan Perappadan’s article: Centre to cap trade margins on non-scheduled cancer drugs to 30% of MRP.
She also reported on the Centre’s direction to the States toDisplay rates of healthcare services prominently. Clearly visible display will enable patients to take informed decisions, build trust, prevent billing-related disputes; the Health Ministry also urged clinical establishments to display package rates for international patients visiting India on medical and Ayush visas. Another significant decision taken in the country last week: NMC brings doctors’ digital patient acquisition under ethics rules. In regulatory terms, the Centre proposing tighter curbs on advertising of prescription drugs was also a development of note.
Moving on to mental health issues, Afshan Yasmeen reported a NIMHANS study that found loneliness linked to psychological distress, excessive series watching among parents of children who had emigrated.The study examined 64 ‘empty-nest’ parents aged between 45 and 65, whose adult children had emigrated and lived away from home for at least two years.
Athira Elssa Johnson wrote on Treatment-resistant depression and what happens when antidepressants do not work, while Dr. Sowjanya Gunukula took us through Dental anxiety, particularly important, because here, fear becomes a barrier to care.
Looking at the Indian health care system and the larger stage, Rajendra Pratap Gupta argues that to retain and grow its advantage, India needs a smarter healthcare margin policy, explaining the role of MRP in the sale of drugs and health care consumables. A lesson or two here for India’s drug price regulators, surely.

Qantas flight grounded after bedbug outbreak
- Published
A Qantas flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled on Saturday, after an outbreak of bedbugs on the plane.
During the previous flight on Friday - a nearly 17-hour journey from Perth to Rome - some passengers had complained that they were being bitten by bugs, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.
They were reportedly given antihistamines to help ease the itch of the bites, but supplies ran out.
The Boeing 787 Dreamliner had to be grounded for "a deep clean", a Qantas spokesperson told the BBC.
"We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday's Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue was identified on a small number of economy seats," the spokesperson said.
All affected customers were provided with accommodation and were rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, the carrier said.
Bedbugs are small, wingless parasites that can live on clothes, furniture and bedding. Their bites can be itchy but they do not usually cause more serious health problems, the NHS website says, external.
But they can be difficult and expensive to get rid of. Treatment includes washing all bedding, clothing, and household materials like curtains on a hot wash and tumble dry, or they can be put in plastic bags in a freezer for three or four days.
Bedbugs causing travel chaos is not unusual - less than two weeks ago, several Southeastern train services in England were cancelled after drivers discovered the creepy-crawlies in their cabs.
In 2017, British Airways apologised to a family travelling from Vancouver to London, after they were left covered in bug bites from an overnight flight.
And Turkish Airlines faced with a PR nightmare last year after the New York Times reported, external of several instances of bedbug infestations on its planes - and allegations at the time that the airline did nothing about it.

For Asian Games gold medallist Pranavi Urs, meeting her idol Rory McIlroy was a dream come true. The 23-year-old got to spend time with the six-time major champion at the Delhi Golf Club here on Wednesday, exchanging notes on the highs and lows of competing at the highest level.

GB men 'on back foot' as women take silver

Great Britain's Joe Truman said team-mate Matt Richardson's withdrawal was "not ideal" and they had started "on the back foot" as they exited in the first round of the men's team sprint at the World Track Cycling Championships.
Richardson was pulled from the competition on Monday amid allegations of misconduct.
The 27-year-old, who had also been expected to contend for medals in the individual sprint and keirin, said he would co-operate with a British Cycling investigation into the allegations.
His withdrawal overshadowed preparations for the event in Shanghai, though Britain's women did secure silver in the team sprint.
Emma Finucane, who is Richardson's partner, Sophie Capewell and Rhianna Parris-Smith finished fastest in qualifying, and beat France but lost to hosts China in the gold-medal race.
The men's team - Truman, Ed Lowe and Harry Ledingham-Horn - finished fifth in the qualifying stage but were beaten by fourth-placed Australia in the opening round of head-to-head races.
"We came with a bit of a last-minute change, obviously," said Truman. "We all said this morning we're here just to ride our bikes.
"We're on the back foot a bit but let's just put our best foot forward, put a time on the board at the start of Olympic quali and we got a time to be proud of.
"None of us are riding in ideal circumstances but we're professional athletes and so it's what we train to do - we train to race when it's not perfect - so I think we did OK. We're looking ahead to the next couple of years and think we're in a great spot."
Elsewhere on day one, Britain's women and men progressed as first and second fastest respectively in qualifying for the team pursuit events.
Meanwhile, Abigail Miller finished 17th of 24 riders in the women's scratch race.

Six-time major champion Rory McIlroy has backed the DP World Tour’s decision to bar players who sign up for LIV Golf from competing in its events from next year.
“The DP World Tour (known earlier as the European Tour) are well within their rights to change the rules and regulations. This is the way to protect their business and to make the tour as strong as possible,” McIlroy said at a press conference here on the eve of the DP World India Championship.
In a statement to the BBC, DP World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings said, “Players need to make a choice” — an ultimatum to those contemplating their future in the rival league, which is now facing financial turmoil.
A vocal critic of LIV Golf, McIlroy added, “The DP World Tour have made a good decision. The golf landscape has now got to the point where guys are going to have to make a decision on what is important to them and what they really want to do.”
One of the modern greats of the game, the Northern Irishman may have achieved almost everything there is to achieve on the golf course, but his hunger for success remains undiminished.
McIlroy spoke of his desire to win the Race to Dubai — the season-long competition to crown the European Tour’s leading player — for a record eighth time. He is currently second in the standings behind Patrick Reed, with only a handful of tournaments remaining.
“At this stage of my career, it’s always nice to get to this part of the season and have a chance to win the Race to Dubai. Eugenio (Chacarra) jumped me last week in Spain. Patrick isn’t playing so well, so this is a really good opportunity to cut into that lead this week to try and win my eighth Race to Dubai,” he said.
The 37-year-old has little intention of easing up. With another Ryder Cup on the horizon next year, McIlroy is already looking ahead.
“It’s a Ryder Cup year next year. I want to make that team. I want to contribute. I want to earn more points for Europe. The bulk of our play is in North America (on the PGA Tour), and I still want to do well over there. I have a lot of plates spinning, which is a good thing. No matter where I play, I have always got something to strive for or achieve,” he said.

Iowa, Nebraska and six other states are suing OpenAI for endangering children
The lawsuits cover everything from the design of ChatGPT to the company's recent issues with rogue agents.
In a coordinated effort, eight states have filed lawsuits against OpenAI alleging the company has violated state-level consumer protection laws and endangered children. As Reuters first reported, Attorneys General from Iowa, Nebraska, Kansas, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana each filed in their respective state courts, but with the shared goals of changing how OpenAI develops its models and advertises their capabilities, and forcing the company to pay for the harm it's allegedly caused.
The lawsuits claim OpenAI is misleading customers about the safety of its AI products, not just in their capacity to provide incorrect information or potentially enable users to harm themselves and others, but also because AI agents themselves are capable of breaking the law. For example, both Iowa and Nebraska cite OpenAI's now multiple instances of rogue agent behavior, including the Hugging Face hack. They also point to instances of ChatGPT allegedly enabling a teen's death by suicide and the chatbot providing incorrect medical information that led to a user's overdose, incidents that have also led to separate wrongful death suits against the company. Some states also take issue with OpenAI retaining data from underage users.
Engadget has asked OpenAI to comment on the state lawsuits. We'll update this article if we hear back.
The desired remedies for OpenAI's behavior vary from state to state due to the patchwork nature of consumer protection and child protection laws in the US. Outside of financial penalties, the states want OpenAI to clearly disclose the risks of its products, stop practices the states consider deceptive and comply with existing laws. Some states, like Arkansas, are also asking the court to halt "testing of advanced AI models until adequate safeguards are implemented."
OpenAI has rolled out a series of parental controls and child protection features to try to address some of the most immediate risks posed by its chatbot. It also backed the Kids Online Safety Act, a bill that, if made law, could introduce several mandatory design changes to the company's products. The company's efforts to address the potential for its AI to break rules and "escape containment" have been harder to pin down, though. OpenAI announced it would slow the development of its frontier models in August to ensure their safety and the company signed on to a voluntary safety pact with other AI companies organized by the White House in September. It's not clear if either of these changes have actually made the company's AI development process safer.

Libya executing people based on secret trials and confessions extracted under torture, group says
Libya has executed at least 31 people since late August, marking the first known executions since 2010, according to Human Rights Watch
CAIRO -- CAIRO (AP) — Libya has executed at least 31 people since late August following military trials, marking the country’s first known executions since 2010, Human Rights Watch said Wednesday.
The rights group said it had documented the executions carried out by the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA) as of Sept. 10. It warned that at least 50 other people held at Gernada military prison were at imminent risk of execution.
The LNA, also known as the Libyan Arab Armed Forces, is an east-based military force commanded by Gen. Khalifa Hifter that controls eastern and southern Libya.
“The Libyan Arab Armed Forces are putting people to death after secret trials built on confessions allegedly extracted through torture, in courts that Libya’s own Supreme Court has said should not be trying civilians,” Bassam Khawaja, HRW’s deputy Middle East and North Africa director, said in a report. “Every execution carried out under these conditions is an irreversible injustice.”
Human Rights Watch called on the army to immediately halt executions and impose a moratorium on the death penalty.
The LNA military prosecutor announced in late August that a firing squad executed 10 people after they were convicted of murder and terrorism-related charges, according to the rights group.
Many of those executed were arrested in Derna and Benghazi cities during or after conflicts between the LNA and opposing armed groups between 2014 and 2018, according to the Wednesday report.
In September, Amnesty International reported that military courts in eastern Libya had convicted hundreds of civilians between 2018 and 2021 in secret trials targeting people accused of criticizing the LNA. At least 22 were sentenced to death during this period. The group also said torture was reportedly used to extract confessions.
International rights groups have repeatedly criticized the detention and, in some cases, execution of people after unfair trials. Amnesty International has said Libya retains the death penalty for a wide range of offenses, with courts in both the east and west continuing to impose death sentences for murder following “grossly unfair trials.”
Libya was plunged into chaos and division after a NATO-backed uprising that toppled and killed its longtime autocrat Moammar Gadhafi in 2011. The country has been divided for years between rival administrations in the east and west, each backed by armed groups and foreign governments.

The Sentinelese, living on North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal, are one of the most isolated peoples on earth.
Part of an archipelago governed by India, it is prohibited by law to venture within 5km of their island. And when a missionary did manage to land on the beach in 2018, he was killed by bow and arrow.
Yet none of that was to deter influencer Mykhailo Polyakov, who last year filmed himself arriving on North Sentinel Island, and leaving a can of coke on the beach.
Features writer Elle Hunt documents the rise of a new breed of influencer, travelling around the world, and streaming to millions their attempts to contact the uncontacted – despite the warnings of indigenous rights groups that the consequences could be fatal, both for the social media stars and the communities they risk exposing to disease.
Helen Pidd also speaks to Ecuadorian indigenous rights activist María José Andrade Cerda about the rights and wrongs of this new world.

In October, rumors circulated that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration did not extend an invitation to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, an international body that aims to preserve democracy and human rights across the globe, to observe the 2026 midterm elections.
The OSCE explains that its goal in observing elections is to "assess the extent to which fundamental freedoms are respected in the campaign and if the elections are characterized by equality, universality, political pluralism, confidence, transparency and accountability."
Social media users who shared the claim noted that it was the first time since 2002, when the OSCE first started observing U.S. elections, that the group had not received an invitation. One post featured an image of Trump with text reading, "Trump demands 'secure' elections, yet rejects independent scrutiny and offers no explanation. Perhaps security was never the point."
The rumor circulated after Trump's Department of Justice said it would deploy its own election monitors, sparking concerns from Trump's opponents.
The claim was true.
In a statement posted to its website Sept. 23. the OSCE confirmed that the U.S. had not invited it to observe the 2026 midterm elections.
"The decision not to invite the OSCE to observe the 2026 midterm congressional elections in the United States is regrettable, particularly given the long-standing co-operation with the country in the field of election observation," the organization said.
They wrote that the decision was "not in line with the 1990 Copenhagen Document," which the group describes as an outline of basic human rights and freedoms that "broadens the scope of human rights matters to include election commitments" and "recognizes that the presence of international observers can enhance the electoral process."
The OSCE confirmed in its statement that the 2026 midterms marked the first time it was not invited to observe a federal U.S. election since the group first began observing elections in the country in 2002. That year, the OSCE sent representatives to the Florida gubernatorial election. 
The 2002 observation occurred after the contentious 2000 presidential election between George W. Bush and Al Gore that resulted in a recount in Florida. The matter ultimately ended up with the Supreme Court, and the United States didn't see a president-elect officially declared until that December.
According to a 2004 article by the Commission on Security and Cooperation in Europe about the history of the U.S. inviting OSCE to observe elections, following its 2002 observation in Florida, OSCE observed the 2003 California gubernatorial recall election that actor Arnold Schwarzenegger won. 
OSCE said it has observed 12 federal elections, including six midterms, since 2002.
The CSCE wrote in 2004 that the U.S. had formally invited observers to its elections in 1996, 1998, 2000 and 2002, noting that 2002 was the first election that OSCE had observed. 
In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections in November, Trump continued his attempts to implement voting restrictions and pitched giving Americans $5,000 each if Republicans won, sparking opposition from critics.
A White House official told Snopes via email that "no other nation has done more to advance the cause of human freedom and representative government" than the United States and added, "American elections will be administered, participated in, and observed by American citizens."
The White House did not deny that it had declined an invite to OSCE observers and provided no explanation for departing from decades of precedent.
We reached out to the OSCE and the Justice Department for further comment and will update this article if we receive responses.
For further reading, we fact-checked a claim that Trump thanked billionaire Elon Musk for artificially increasing votes for Republicans ahead of the 2026 midterms.

The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine is expected to begin in the Democratic Republic of Congo by the end of October, World Health Organization experts said Tuesday.
The DR Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,000-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,000.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the outbreak.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will go through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
"We have got strong reassurances that... it should be starting before the end of this month," said Anthony Scott, chair of the WHO's Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunisation (SAGE).
The group said insights that Ervebo might offer cross-protection against Bundibugyo were no match for evidence from standardised vaccine trials.
The so-called Tumaini trial in the DRC -- a single trial framework that can test the efficiency of multiple vaccines -- should also eventually incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are moving through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.
Need for data
The Tumaini trial "will generate urgently-needed data on the efficacy of Ervebo against Bundibugyo virus disease, and will help formulate the policy decisions we need", Scott told a press conference.
"In addition, we welcome the accelerated development of vaccines that are specifically targeting Bundibugyo.
"They're both progressing rapidly through early clinical development."
SAGE said it was deeply concerned about the ongoing challenges in controlling the Ebola outbreak.
"The key elements here are insecurity and population displacement, and they're hindering access to care, disrupting surveillance, and delaying critical research, including, from our perspective, research on vaccine trials," said Scott.
Kate O'Brien, director of the WHO's immunisation department, said a WHO technical advisory group would be meeting to review evidence from the small-scale trials of the Oxford and Moderna candidate vaccines.
She suggested the Oxford jab could drop into the broader Tumaini trial fairly swiftly -- as doses are ready to roll -- if the safety and the immunogenicity data from the first trial is "positive and reassuring".
Therefore "everything is lined up for at least two products to be moving quickly", she said.
The medical charity Doctors Without Borders is conducting a data-gathering study -- not a full clinical trial -- of Ervebo's effectiveness in frontline health workers in DRC provinces hard-hit by the Bundibugyo outbreak, with the jab being offered to volunteers as an interim measure.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.
Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.
The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.
In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.
Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.
The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.
In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

FIFA will propose to its members a $6.35 billion development fund for the next four-year cycle, including a boosted amount of $25 million for each national association, two people with knowledge of the plan and a letter reviewed by The Associated Press confirmed Tuesday.
Football’s world governing body planned to use the financial success of the latest World Cup to enhance investment in the sport’s development across 211 FIFA member associations, confederations and other stakeholders. Originally, each association was to receive $10 million for the four-year period.
FIFA planned to distribute more than $3.5 billion from its financial reserves which were boosted with the success of its 48-team World Cup, said two officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the proposal had not been announced.
FIFA estimates approximately $15 billion in revenue in the 2022-26 cycle, including the men’s World Cup hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico, significantly above projections, both people told AP.
The proposal comes as European football leaders seek a candidate to try to oust Gianni Infantino as FIFA president. Infantino’s divisive World Cup private investment plan — that was scrapped within days of being revealed in July — prompted UEFA to act.

Infantino, who became FIFA president in 2016, is seeking reelection next year.
On Sept. 28, the leaders of football’s six continental confederations received a letter from Infantino with the plan, which is expected to be finalised at the upcoming FIFA council meeting and approved at its congress in March. The AP has reviewed the letter.
“Taken together, your submissions confirm broad agreement on the central objective: FIFA’s financial success must serve football and all FIFA’s 211 member associations,” Infantino said in the letter.
“I am confident that together we can reach a sustainable and properly supported outcome for FIFA’s member associations and for football in every part of the world.”
One of the people with knowledge of the proposal said continental confederations made the suggestion for FIFA to use its reserves in the plan, which now offers $99 million for each of the six confederations.
UEFA announced in August it was preparing a criminal complaint against Infantino in Switzerland for possible financial mismanagement in the World Cup sell-off deal and has asked courts in the United States to authorise discovery of evidence.
UEFA’s 55 members account for more than a quarter of FIFA’s 211 member federations who can vote in the election on March 18 in Rabat, Morocco.
Any candidate to challenge Infantino must enter the race by a Nov. 18 deadline.
Infantino indicated last month he would be open to an independent review of FIFA’s governance system and signaled a willingness to consider reforms.

Fifa to offer extra £2.6bn for football development
- Published
Fifa is set to propose a $3.4bn (£2.6bn) increase in the amount of money it hands out for football development across the world.
World football's governing body wants to release the money from its reserves in a move which would more than double the level of planned distribution funding for 2027-2030.
It says it has been able to release the extra cash because of the commercial success of this summer's World Cup.
The proposal will be made at a meeting of Fifa's council on Thursday and comes at a time when the organisation is under pressure following president Gianni Infantino's aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan.
Infantino wanted to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors but faced huge criticism for the proposal, with Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation questioning his position.
Uefa and Concacaf wrote to Infantino in September calling on Fifa to pay at least $10m (£7.5m) from its cash reserves to each of the 211 member associations.
In a letter then sent to Fifa's six continental confederations, Infantino - who will be standing for re-election for a fourth time in March 2027 - said he would support "the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered".
Fifa will now offer extra money from its reserves in addition to the current $2.7bn (£2.05bn) budgeted to be paid to all 211 member associations, the confederations, regional associations and certain non-Fifa affiliated associations.
In total, Fifa will now be spending $6.35bn (£4.83bn) on football development for the 2027-2030 cycle, with a focus on investment and development of women's and youth football.
The breakdown is as follows:
• $25m (£19m) per member association
• $99m (£75m) for each of the six confederations
• $8.25m (£6.3m) for each of the 13 zonal/regional associations
• $1.1m (£836,000) for 100 member associations for travel and equipment solidarity
The terms of the distribution would be as follows:
• One third would be allocated to women's and youth football development
• One third would be allocated to infrastructure (of which there shall be equal access to women's and youth football)
• One third would be allocated to projects
The plan, including the eligibility, application, approval, disbursement, control and audit requirements, will be finalised by the Fifa council at its next meeting in December 2026.
It will all be subject to approval by the 77th Fifa congress in March 2027.
Proposed Fifa disciplinary code change over Balogun
BBC Sport understands there is a proposal on the table at the council to change the disciplinary code and prevent a repeat of the Balogun situation, an unprecedented scenario which meant the US striker did not miss a game after being sent off in the World Cup.
If approved, it will be expressly noted in the regulations that an automatic one-match ban for a red card cannot be suspended.
Questions have been raised over the process which led to Balogun having his ban suspended at the World Cup.
US President Donald Trump said he called Infantino to get the ban rescinded, which raised serious concerns over political interference.
A proposal has been put forward to add to Article 27 of the regulations a list of instances whereby a ban cannot be suspended.
This would include an automatic one-game ban for a red card.
