Jaipur, Oct 14: An Air India aircraft from Frankfurt to Delhi was diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday morning following a hijack alert, according to sources.
However, the alert turned out to be false.
The flight AI2030, operated with a Boeing 787-9 aircraft, made an emergency landing at the Jaipur International Airport and was taken to an isolation bay for security checks, the sources said.
The flight had 293 passengers and 13 crew members on board.
Assistant Commissioner of Police, Malviya Nagar, Shiv Dayal told PTI that airport authorities had informed police about the emergency landing of the flight following a threat.
Police sources said security personnel checked the aircraft in the isolation bay.
"The flight landed at around 9.35 am. The flight was taken to the isolation bay within ten minutes for checking," the sources said.
As per the initial information, the pilot pressed 'Squawk Code 7500', which indicates unlawful interference, when the aircraft was in the Mumbai Flight Information Region (FIR). Subsequently, the plane was diverted to Jaipur, the sources added.
Jaipur airport management said security checks were conducted and later passengers were de-boarded and taken to the terminal building.
"The passengers were brought to the terminal building, and later their boarding began for the same plane for departure for Delhi. All are safe, and there is no situation of panic," airport sources said.
After the checks, the flight is now set to depart for Delhi, the sources said.

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?
- Published
Imagine a world where Manchester City had not used "sham contracts" to build a team capable of winning three Premier League titles, one FA Cup and three EFL Cups.
If City were the winners, then there had to be losers.
Not just those teams who finished runners-up or lost cup finals.
The potential impact runs much deeper and includes missed Champions League qualification, relegation and Premier League prize money.
Thirty-five other teams played in the English top flight between 2009 and 2018.
And every one could in some way claim to have been left financially out of pocket.
City, of course, continue to deny any wrongdoing and they have appealed. But as it stands they are guilty of all charges related to inflating their sponsorship income to the tune of £830m, plus another £90m in expenses.
Strip that money out and it changes the whole complexion of the competition.
BBC Sport has crunched the numbers to assess the potential financial impact on the top flight.
How the figures are worked out
When Sheikh Mansour bought Manchester City in 2008 they were far removed from the club you see today.
Since finishing fifth in 1991-92, the last season before the formation of the Premier League, City's highest placing had been eighth in 2004-05.
The Abu Dhabi money poured in via what the Premier League's independent commission described as a "disguised funding scheme". It took the club's sponsorship revenues from being on a par with Stoke City in 2008-09 to eventually overtaking those of Manchester United.
City finished fifth in 2009-10. Since then, not once have they finished outside the top four in the Premier League.
Did this money deny other clubs a place in the competition, and other kinds of success?
This article is not trying to set out how much compensation a team might be able to claim.
Nor is it saying any one team would definitely have avoided relegation or reached the Champions League.
It is about chance, the possibility that a very different City team would have taken to the field without the hundreds of millions pumped in by the club's Abu Dhabi owners.
It has not considered potential future earnings from success, including sponsors' bonuses and further prize money.
Nor has it factored in players who may feel they have missed out on salary increases, or triggered payments, for how their club might have performed.
This is purely about domestic impact:
- Lost prize money by league placing
- Missed potential Champions League earnings
- Europa League payments
- Loss of Premier League status
- Impact of cup final defeats
- What Manchester's 'super-profit' deal with City owners has paid out so far 
  - Published8 hours ago
- Were any current Man City players signed during charges period? 
  - Published3 hours ago
How City gained £1.17bn, and others may have lost £844m
The full impact of City's behaviour on other clubs could be calculated at £844m.
- £188.2m in Premier League placing money
- £349.7m in relegation costs
- £217.8m in missed Champions League prize money
- £88.3m related to domestic cup competitions and the Europa League
We calculated these figures by taking published prize money from the relevant seasons.
For Premier League place money, each team that finished below City is considered to have potentially missed a payment for one place.
For relegation, this is the minimum value of being in the Premier League for the next season, minus the received parachute payment.
For the Champions League, we took City's earnings from the following seasons and deducted the impacted teams' Europa League prize money.
But City also earned prize money themselves during this period.
Across the competitions, City were paid £1.17bn:
- £812.3m from the Premier League - total income from prize money and broadcast revenues
- £363.4m via the Champions League
- £900,000 from the FA Cup victory
- £300,000 from the three EFL Cup victories
The most impacted: How Spurs could have missed out on £120m
"We have lived through a period of deception," former Tottenham Hotspur boss Mauricio Pochettino said last month.
"No type of punishment will make it possible to repair what was done."
You can see his point. Spurs finished one place outside the Champions League positions in four (although one only was under Pochettino) of the eight seasons in which City qualified for Europe's elite competition.
BBC Sport took City's earnings from the Champions League in the following season, and deducted Tottenham's Europa League prize money.
Over the four seasons Spurs missed out, Manchester City earned £148.2m from the Champions League, with Tottenham taking £29.9m from the Europa League.
The 2014-15 campaign led to the biggest deficit, as City finished second in the Premier League and Tottenham came fifth. City received £71.2m for reaching the Champions League semi-finals in the following season, but Spurs were only paid £17.7m from the Europa League - a difference of £53.5m.
Spurs also finished behind City in the Premier League table six times, with the cumulative prize money difference worth £6.6m.
The north Londoners did benefit in the 2013-14 season, as they only qualified for Europe because City beat Sunderland in the final of the EFL Cup.
Spurs gained £5.1m from their 2014-15 Europa League campaign which would not have been possible without City's success.
Taking into account all competitions, that produced a net financial loss for Spurs of £119.9m.
Did City's EFL Cup win cost Liverpool £37.8m?
The 2015-16 EFL Cup final proved to be decisive for Liverpool's hopes of European football.
Jurgen Klopp's men lost to City on penalties following a 1-1 draw. The Europa League place transferred to the league, and went to West Ham United.
Liverpool only finished eighth, which was not enough to qualify for Europe.
Had Liverpool won the final, they would have entered the Europa League, and this provides a key financial comparison.
Manchester United won the Europa League in 2016-17, receiving prize money of £37.8m. As part of that amount, the Red Devils' market pool payment, which is based upon the value of the television rights, was £26.6m.
While we cannot say for certain that Liverpool would have won the Europa League, they were a club of similar stature to Manchester United, which provides a comparison.
The market pool share may also have been slightly lower with both Liverpool and Manchester United involved.
Together with Premier League place money of £10.6m - Liverpool finished below City in all nine relevant seasons - the total financial impact on the Merseyside club was £52.3m.
As for the FA Cup, City won it just once in the period they were scrutinised over, beating Stoke in 2010-11. The difference in prize money was £900,000, with the runners-up going into the Europa League.
Everton were denied Europe five times
Everton missed out on the Champions League once, in 2013-14, and on four other occasions they finished one place below the final Europa League spot.
The Champions League place is calculated to be worth £32.6m - the £39m earned by Manchester City minus the Toffees' £6.4m winnings from the Europa League they competed in instead.
The combined impact on missing out on the Europa League four times is £23.2m.
Add on the £10.6m from Premier League prize money, and the total financial effect is £66.4m - making Everton the third-most impacted club.
Did two relegations cost Hull City £99m?
While parachute payments provide something of a cushion, relegation from the Premier League is still a considerable financial hit.
Could the teams who finished in 18th place, one spot from safety, argue that they might have stayed up but for City?
There are a couple of ways of looking at this.
Firstly, the results against City who took at least four points off every 18th-placed team other than Birmingham.
Secondly, the mere fact that City were able to assemble a squad far better than their finances should have allowed. Could they otherwise have been involved in relegation battles?
Again, this is not to say City would have been relegated. It is about chance.
BBC Sport has taken the total prize money earned by the team finishing in 20th in the following season. That suggests a minimum return for having stayed in the top flight.
Deducted from that is the first season of parachute payments to give a net amount.
Hull were relegated twice in the period, costing the Tigers £93.78m.
The Tigers finished below City in the table four times, adding £5.2m in place money to the sum.
It leaves the East Yorkshire club as the second-most impacted on £99m.
Swansea are fourth in the table with £63.1m. Of that total, £54m is from relegation and £9.1m in place money from the seven seasons the Swans were in the top flight.
Newcastle suffered relegation by finishing 18th in 2015-16, costing them a projected £60.4m, of which £7.9m was place money.
Norwich (£43.8m), Wigan (£39.6m), Burnley (£31.1m), Bolton (£26.4m) and Birmingham (£25.1m) also suffered relegations in 18th place.
The loss of Champions League money
Alongside Tottenham, four other teams missed out on Champions League football by one place across the eight seasons when City qualified.
The biggest impact was on Chelsea, who finished fifth in 2017-18.
City earned £79.2m from reaching the quarter-finals of the Champions League, with Chelsea getting £39.4m from winning the Europa League. That left Chelsea with a deficit of £39.8m.
Also just missing out on the Champions League were Everton (5th in 2013-14, £32.6m deficit), and Arsenal (5th in 2016-17, £22.1m deficit).
The only team not to experience much of a financial impact were Manchester United, who were fifth in 2015-16.
City got no further than the round of 16 in the Champions League, earning £42.6m, while United won the Europa League that season, receiving £37.8m. It left the Red Devils with a deficit of £4.8m.
The cumulative cost of league places
In the Premier League there is no specific prize pot for being crowned champions.
Broadcast revenue is allocated on a merit basis by final league position.
It is a 1+1 system, so the club in 20th get the base payment. Then the team in 19th get the base payment two times. For 18th, it is that base amount three times, and so on.
It means that the only financial difference, in prize money at least, for the team finishing runners-up in one of Manchester City's three title-winning seasons is one base payment.
Could any team claim they might have finished one place higher?
The value of a Premier League place rose sharply in line with the broadcast deals over the period of City's offences.
In 2010-11 it was £755,881 per place, and by 2016-17 it was up to £1.94m.
If any compensation were to be considered, Everton, Liverpool and Stoke City would have the biggest claim of £10.7m, having finished below City in all nine seasons.
West Brom and West Ham's total is £9.9m, with Swansea on £9.1m.
At the other end of the scale are the seven clubs who spent one season in the Premier League, including Blackpool (£756,756), Portsmouth (£800,424) and Huddersfield (£1.93m).

Despite the expansion of Starlink and other communications satellite services, most of the world’s Internet traffic still travels through subsea cables crisscrossing the ocean floors. Those fiber-optic cables coexist with a network of oil and gas pipelines and submarine power cables—and all these crucial links connecting countries and continents now face growing sabotage risks as gray-zone warfare and open conflicts have become widespread.
The rising risks to the world’s invisible infrastructure beneath the waves are the main subject of a new book by Elisabeth Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative. Her book, titled Undersea War, explores the modern rise in suspicious incidents in which ships dragging their anchors for unusually long periods have cut or damaged undersea cables and pipelines from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean.
Braw acknowledges that about 60 percent of undersea cable damage is primarily due to human error during fishing and shipping activities, when weighted nets or anchors drag across the seabed. Natural hazards such as storms and undersea landslides also account for a smaller proportion of such incidents. In total, between 150 and 200 cables are damaged each year and usually repaired quickly.
But international tension between superpowers and open war in Europe and the Middle East have led to increased scrutiny of cable-cutting incidents, with governments investigating and sometimes prosecuting crews for allegedly causing deliberate damage to subsea cables. One of the more notorious incidents documented in the book is the “Christmas Day massacre” of 2024, when a Russian-linked oil tanker named Eagle S dragged its anchor across the seabed for about 56 miles (90 kilometers), cutting or damaging four data cables and the Estlink 2 submarine power cable connecting the Baltic and Nordic power grids.
One of those data cables had also previously been severed by the Chinese cargo ship Yi Peng 3 just one month earlier in November 2024, when that ship damaged two data cables in the Baltic region. That ship’s crew was not prosecuted by European authorities, whereas the Finnish government has attempted to prosecute three senior officers of the Eagle S.
On the other side of the world, the captain of the Chinese-owned ship Hong Tai was convicted by a court in Taiwan of severing an undersea telecommunications cable in February 2025 and sentenced to three years in prison in June 2025. The island democracy’s legislature later amended its laws to increase penalties for intentional damage to undersea cables or pipelines and allow for up to seven years in prison.
This year has seen several notable incidents involving both overt and covert threats to undersea infrastructure, including Iranian efforts to impose fees on operators of undersea cables running through the contested Strait of Hormuz. Separately, a joint operation involving the UK, Norway and the United States confronted Russian submarines that were practicing using a new technology to disable undersea cables in Arctic waters near Norway’s Svalbard archipelago.
What happens when the Internet’s undersea backbone, not to mention crucial energy infrastructure, is no longer protected by near-universal international agreement? Ars spoke with Braw to find out more. (The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.)
Elisabeth Braw is the author of the book Undersea War.
Credit:
Hachette Book Group (cover art) / Annabel Moeller (author photo)
Elisabeth Braw is the author of the book Undersea War.
Credit:
Hachette Book Group (cover art) / Annabel Moeller (author photo)
Ars Technica: Right now there’s so much suspicion and tension around undersea infrastructure. But it does seem like for quite a few decades, even during the Cold War, there was a broad international framework that mostly worked where countries generally agreed not to mess around too much.
Braw: Exactly. It worked for so long, and that’s why it’s so frightening to see that system that really depends on everybody doing the right thing and being a good seabed citizen, as it were, may not work for that much longer.
Ars Technica: I know it’s not really any single factor, but I’m curious what you would highlight as the key contributing factors to why we’re seeing a breakdown in that general agreement.
Braw: If you think about the absolutely crucial nature of subsea cables and pipelines, especially subsea cables… if they were to be disrupted for even just a minute, it would cause massive disruption to not just the New York City area, but also New York as a financial hub. It would cause operational losses, but also the loss of all that money that goes through the cables every second of every day.
So if you think about the utter importance of subsea cables to modern societies and modern economies, then that makes them incredibly attractive as a target. Whereas during the Cold War, we had telephone cables, but there weren’t that many of them, and we didn’t use them as much. Yes, they were used for international phone calls, and there were also telegraph messages that could be sent. But nobody sent telegrams around the clock, and nobody made international phone calls around the clock. So they were there, but they were just less crucial.
Also, despite it being a Cold War and a very dangerous few decades, there was some sort of agreement that when you sign a treaty, you uphold it. In fact, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea was adopted in 1982 during the height of the Cold War. So there was a commitment to creating some sort of rules of the road.
Today that commitment is, I don’t want to say it’s vanishing, but it’s declining among key countries in the world. And at the same time, we are seeing Russia has discovered that it’s really quite beneficial to use non-military means to weaken other countries, and this is something that Russia has come to specialize in, and other countries may yet come to specialize in. That makes the cables around the seabed highly attractive as a target.
Ars Technica: There was even recent reporting on how NATO countries apparently foiled a Russian attempt to practice undersea cable sabotage, although that incident took place back in the spring.
Braw: The fascinating thing about subsea cables and pipelines, but especially subsea cables, is not just that we are utterly dependent on them. They don’t sit only within countries’ territorial waters. They connect countries, so they are in international waters [where] countries don’t have jurisdiction. The oceans are a global commons, and that’s where cables live, and that’s why it’s so utterly important for countries and everybody using the oceans to take care around them so that they don’t get damaged.
Then what we have seen in the past few years is that, all of a sudden, merchant vessels in the Baltic Sea and off the coast of Norway and in Taiwanese waters, all of a sudden, they got extremely sloppy and dragged anchors for long stretches, which is something that is not supposed to happen as a seafarer. You should know whether your anchor is dragging on the seabed or not, and you know where the cables are.
So this is not supposed to happen, and yet it happened not just once, not just twice, but several times, and caused considerable anxiety, obviously, in the countries affected. It also caused considerable expenses to the operators because they have to get the cables repaired, and in the case of the electricity cables, it’s extremely expensive to repair them and takes a very long time.
We don’t know what has caused these merchant vessels to drag their anchors across the border sea and damage cables, and we may never know because it’s not like those crew members are going to tell us what happened. We just know that these incidents were extremely suspicious.
But then we have what you just brought up, that Russia and other countries may develop tools to damage other countries’ subsea cables using submarines or gadgets or drones attached to submarines, and that’s where we are today. That might yet happen, and that’s why it’s always so concerning when Russian research vessels loiter around subsea cables. What are they doing there? What is it that they are looking at? What is it they are measuring?
China does the same thing. It sends research vessels that loiter in other countries’ waters for long periods of time. And you’re supposed to inform the country in whose waters you are conducting research that you are conducting research and what the nature of your research is, but China doesn’t do that. So what is it that these research vessels are doing? What is it they are researching?
This is all in the context of increasing geopolitical tension, and by the way, also rapid expansion of submarine fleets: Western ones and the Russian one and the Chinese one. But also the expansion of other undersea equipment, gadgets, drones, and so forth.
Ars Technica: Another point your book touched on was everything that’s been happening around the Strait of Hormuz, and how we have seen Iran either threaten to put a fee on companies that want to run undersea cables through there, or threaten to attack them. At the same time, it sounds like a number of companies have rethought undersea cable projects that were intended to run through that region.
Braw: This is another fascinating aspect of the situation for subsea cables. So in the Persian Gulf, in the Strait of Hormuz, there are subsea cables, and they are indispensable not just for the countries connected by them, but also for other nearby countries. For example, one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic or digital connectivity goes through the Persian Gulf. So it just illustrates how important these cables are, and not just to countries that are immediately connected.
In February of this year, the situation was that three cable projects were about to be launched or were being conducted. Then the war began, and you can imagine that when missiles are flying, drones are flying around, it’s impossible to install cables on the seabed. Because if you think about ships, that is dangerous enough, but ships are moving. Installation ships are stationary. You really are like a sitting duck, and so those projects had to be suspended or abandoned and the companies declared force majeure.
But we need subsea cables. So what will happen as the world becomes more contentious, as there are more conflicts, or as more conflicts erupt? How are cable installation crews and cable repair crews supposed to do their work when there are various projectiles and other weapons flying around them or next to them on the ocean? This is where geopolitics is truly clashing with modern economies, and at the front line are cable installation crews and repair crews.
And then you asked about the toll that Iran said it was going to impose. This was a new and, I have to say, unsurprising twist on the Iran war. So everybody has heard about the fact that, a few weeks into the war, Iran said it was going to charge tolls on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and that is a violation of UNCLOS, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Iran said it was going to do that anyway, and Iran could claim that it didn’t need to uphold UNCLOS, which it has signed but not ratified. But until February, it had upheld UNCLOS, and shipping had worked well in the Strait of Hormuz.
Then in March, Iran could say that it wasn’t bound by UNCLOS anymore because the US and Israel had violated the UN Charter by attacking it. So why should it uphold UNCLOS? And this is the dangerous situation we’re in, where countries can say, “Well, why should I uphold my treaty obligations when such and such country isn’t upholding that?”
So what Iran said a few months into the war—after having imposed tolls on shipping for a while—was that it was going to charge tolls on the subsea cables in the Strait of Hormuz. And yes, it is a violation of UNCLOS. But it could say, “Well, the US has violated the UN Charter, so we get to do as we like too.”
If you think about the implications of that, it’s not just implications for cable operators in the Strait of Hormuz. How would they make payments to Iran? How would that work? And if they don’t make payments, what would happen? But it’s also a question for other cable owners. What if other countries say, “Well, there are cables in our water, so we are going to charge a toll because countries aren’t adhering to UNCLOS anyway, so we might as well.”
It’s not just that you know the world was harmonious, and all of a sudden there were some suspicious cable incidents. It is that the order on the ocean—and even on land too—is deteriorating, and in the midst of all that we are experiencing suspicious cable incidents.
Ars Technica: These undersea cables are obviously of great national interest to governments and may require even military protection in some cases. But at the same time they’re being developed by private operators, including a lot of tech giants. We just saw Meta announcing it was going to lay the first petabit capacity cable across the Atlantic, and that’s part of a much broader buildout of undersea cables. What does this private ownership but public interest collision mean for who takes responsibility, especially as there are increasing threats?
Braw: It’s such an important question. Ever since the first cables were laid on the seabed, they have been privately owned. The cables that then joined them were also privately owned. Then, in the 1900s, postal services in different countries took over the operation of cables. So many cables were state-owned.
Then later in the 1900s, we started seeing more privately owned cables again. And today, virtually all cables are privately owned, typically by consortia. But shorter cables are often owned by one company. And a crucial development is what you also mentioned, that the hyperscalers are building their own cables for their own traffic. So, these are private operators, but [the cables are] critical national infrastructure. And what governments want may be different; in fact, it is different from what operators want.
So people often ask me, “Shouldn’t operators install more cables to make sure that they always have cables that are operational?” And yes, you can say they should, but each cable is an expense in the installation and the operation of the cable. Companies will look at figures and the hard facts, and are likely to conclude in many cases that the risk of their cables being damaged in some malicious way is smaller than the expense of adding more cables, and that’s a commercial calculation, right? Whereas for national governments, it would clearly be in their interest and they would want to see more redundancy. But they don’t own the cables, and commercial operators exist to make money.
The only other alternative is for governments to subsidize new cables. And I write about this in the book as well, what happened with the Matsu Islands [governed by Taiwan]. But we don’t have that sort of money to create backups for every cable on the seabed. So this is the clash, as it were, the interests of cable owners and the interests of national governments.
Ars Technica: It was interesting to see how that first cable, when it was laid, was used to send a message of hope and peace. And then there were also newspapers declaring that having this near-instant communication across the oceans would basically usher in an era of world peace. So again, viewing this technology as finally bringing about world peace when clearly it hasn’t done that.

US President Donald Trump could disrupt the 2026 midterm elections through a series of actions ranging from allegations of voter fraud and federal investigations to immigration enforcement near polling places and disputes over election results, according to a Reuters investigation.
Reuters said it interviewed more than 50 election officials, voting experts and election lawyers, and reviewed Trump's public statements, court filings and federal agency actions to identify nine potential flashpoints before and after Election Day.
The November midterm elections will determine control of the US Congress and several key state offices.
Here are the nine key risks to the US midterm elections identified by the Reuters investigation report.
Trump could renew unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud, illegal voting or manipulated voting machines. Reuters noted that similar allegations following the 2020 election fuelled efforts to overturn his defeat and led to harassment of election workers. Experts say such claims could trigger legal challenges even if they are subsequently disproved.
The administration could pressure state officials, legislators or election authorities to reject certified results or delay certification based on fraud allegations. Reuters cited Trump's efforts to overturn his 2020 defeat, including his call to Georgia's secretary of state to find enough votes to reverse the result.
Federal agents could seek court-approved warrants or subpoenas to obtain ballots, voting machines and election records. Such seizures could disrupt vote counting, compromise the chain of custody and delay certification. Reuters cited the FBI's January raid on election offices in Georgia's Fulton County, where agents seized records from the 2020 election.
The Justice Department plans to deploy 1,000 election monitors, nearly twice the 590 deployed in 2024. While the department says they will protect voting rights and ensure compliance with federal law, some officials fear monitors could exceed their traditional role by seeking access to voting equipment or interviewing voters.
Immigration enforcement operations near polling places could discourage people from voting, particularly in immigrant communities and Democratic-leaning areas. Legal experts say deploying armed federal agents directly at polling stations would likely violate federal law, although immigration agents could conduct operations nearby.
Trump could seek to invoke the Insurrection Act to justify military deployment by citing alleged election-related unrest or interference. Experts warn that troops near polling stations could intimidate voters and suppress turnout. Federal laws restrict military involvement in domestic law enforcement and prohibit voter intimidation.
Trump could declare a national emergency over alleged voter fraud or foreign interference to justify greater federal involvement in elections, potentially including demands for hand-counting ballots. Legal experts say emergency powers would not allow him to take over election administration, which largely falls under state authority, but such a move could trigger litigation and delays.
The Justice Department could investigate or prosecute election administrators over alleged failures to prevent noncitizens from voting or maintain accurate voter rolls. Officials fear that subpoenas, interviews and document demands could drain resources and intimidate election workers, even without convictions.
Republican congressional leaders could face pressure to delay or challenge the seating of Democratic winners in closely contested races. Although legal scholars consider outright refusal to seat certified winners unlikely to succeed, delayed certifications and unresolved disputes could leave seats vacant when the new Congress convenes on January 3, potentially affecting control of the House.

A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?
- Published
Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement.
Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time.
But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017.
Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed.
That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work.
Morocco never found the requisite finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town.
For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with.
The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub.
At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership.
"It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.
He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision".
"Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past.
"It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity."

From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed.
He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped.
And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal.
Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka.
The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change.
President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa.
Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return.
"We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events."
Why is Rwanda a controversial choice?
Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.
Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion.
The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation.
But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.
The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia.
Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda.
Saudi Arabia will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034. Boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi Arabian finance. Golf came close to being torn apart by Saudi money and the establishment of the rival LIV tour.
F1 is not blind to such issues. Its own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders to address any issues that arise.
It also says it focuses its efforts "in relation to those areas which are within our own direct influence".
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."

Netflix to lay off 1,000 staff in steepest cuts since 2022
- Published
Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.
The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.
Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".
The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.
In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".
Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount.
Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources."
Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon".
The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October.
Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.
The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series.
It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films.
However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer.
He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau.
"Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said.
The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

The Edits Film Festival concluded in Mumbai with filmmaker Farah Khan as the special guest, alongside jury members Ahsaas Channa, Dolly Singh, Nikhil Taneja and Rajeev Masand. The event also saw the participation of over 100 content creators, with Ishank Gupta, Sanya Rohillaa and Ahsan Vazir announced as the festival’s top three winners.
Farah Khan credits Gen Z for inspiring her spontaneous approach to content creation: “I don’t overthink what I post”
The winners were recognised for their storytelling and use of Edits, Instagram’s video-editing app, to create their submissions. The festival invited creators to turn unpolished videos from their camera rolls into edited content, encouraging them to experiment with different storytelling techniques and editing features.
Submissions opened in August, giving participants 45 days to create and submit their work. The festival’s official selection showcased a range of approaches to storytelling, while the top three entries stood out for their creativity, restraint and editing skills. The winners were selected by jury members Ahsaas Channa, Dolly Singh, Nikhil Taneja and Rajeev Masand.
Speaking about the initiative, Ankit Rihal, Head of Global Partnerships, Meta, India, said, “Enabling creators with the right tools, platforms and opportunities is central to what we do. The festival opened up new creative possibilities, encouraging creators to experiment with features they hadn't used before and tell stories in fresh ways. We're thankful to our jury members and to Farah Khan for the invaluable perspective she shared on her storytelling journey.”
Farah Khan on content creation and storytelling
Farah Khan attended the festival as a special guest and spoke about her approach to filmmaking and creating content for digital platforms. Having worked on feature films for theatrical audiences as well as short-form videos for Instagram Reels, the filmmaker discussed how she approaches the two formats.
Explaining her approach to social media, Farha said she prefers to keep her content spontaneous rather than plan every detail. She also credited Gen Z with influencing her outlook towards creating and sharing videos. She stated, “People assume there's a big plan behind it, but I don't overthink what I post. Gen Z has inspired me — they're so nonchalant about it, no second-guessing. Be it a clip from my show, a random chat or a bit of mischief on the spot, everything is spontaneous for me. I think relatability and realness, with a bit of humor, are what audiences actually respond to on Instagram.”
The filmmaker’s comments highlighted the role of authenticity and humour in connecting with audiences on social media. The festival brought together creators and industry professionals to recognise emerging talent and encourage experimentation with digital storytelling tools.

On 10 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) organised a major protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which protesters claim led to arbitrary voter deletions. In response to the demonstrations, authorities imposed a security crackdown, shutting down dozens of metro stations, cancelling trains, and enforcing prohibitory orders across the capital. Police have detained thousands of individuals, including political figures like Arvind Kejriwal, Pinarayi Vijayan and Mamata Banerjee, as well as CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who were later released.
Against this backdrop, a video (here & here) is being shared on social media with the claim that it shows protesters at Jantar Mantar demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing the October 10 CJP protest at Jantar Mantar, demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
Fact: The video was uploaded on 20 July 2026 and shows an earlier protest demanding Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation. It is unrelated to the October 10 CJP protest. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the same video (archive), uploaded to the Facebook page of Samar Moto Vlog on 20 July 2026. According to the post, the video shows a protest at Jantar Mantar on 20 July 2026, demanding the resignation of then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
This indicates that the video is unrelated to the CJP protest held at Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026. Delhi Police also stated that the video was an old one from July 2026 and urged users to refrain from spreading misinformation. We have previously debunked several old and unrelated visuals falsely linked to the October 10 protest.
To sum it up, a video from July 2026 is being falsely shared as footage of the October 10 CJP protest at Jantar Mantar.

In 2020, the police department of picturesque Covington, Georgia, paid Flock Safety, the surveillance technology company, $40,000 to maintain 20 cameras around the city. The next year, it paid the same amount.
In 2022, that cost went up to $81,250. Fifteen new “Falcon” cameras, which Flock says have more sophisticated technology for reading license plates, accounted for $37,500. Another $3,750 went toward installing the new cameras, and the rest was spent maintaining the initial fleet.
Then, in 2024, the department paid Flock $113,225. Of that, $87,500 was to maintain its existing 35 cameras, a rate it agreed to pay for the next five years, and the remainder went toward eight new Falcon cameras. The next year, Covington paid Flock $159,000 for a combination of camera maintenance and enrollment in its Drone as First Responder program, which uses drones to fly to emergency scenes and stream footage back to the police station.
It’s unclear how much Covington will wind up paying Flock in 2026, but through August, it has paid $201,000—$100,000 to maintain its existing cameras, $800 to replace one, and another $100,200 for new software products. The Covington Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Overall, Flock is a small fraction of the Covington police department’s $12,488,733 budget for June 2025 to July 2026. But amid fierce blowback about Flock’s surveillance practices, contracts with the company are now being scrutinized in cities across the country. Flock did not provide a comment for this story.
WIRED obtained documents via public record request from a dozen Flock customers across the country and compared them to publicly available information from more than a dozen others. The documents shed light on how much Flock can actually cost communities, the way many of those deals are structured, and how the deals can expand over several years—leaving taxpayers on the hook year after year, with no end in sight.
“Once you let police officers try a tool,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, “it becomes really hard to get the political will and motivation to take that tool away from them.”
How Flock Gets in the Door
When Flock was founded in 2017, it originally sold its license plate readers to private homeowner associations (HOAs). By the time the company decided to sell to police departments in 2019, it had an in: Rather than starting a camera network from scratch, police could start by accessing the cameras that HOAs were already using.
A version of this story played out in Alpharetta, Georgia. In 2020, the city’s police department paid Flock $17,680 for five Falcon cameras and logins for Flock software called Wing, which can extract vehicle and license plate data from off-brand camera footage. The next year, when Alpharetta bought a few more Flock cameras, a payment justification noted that “several” local private homeowner associations had already purchased Flock and granted them camera access.
“We are looking to add more city cameras into the Flock system,” the justification read. According to the city, “other vendors” would “not integrate with our existing Flock system.”
Over the next several years, Alpharetta expanded its work with the company significantly. By 2025, the city’s annual Flock bill had ballooned to $381,000.
As in other industries, companies that sell technology to police often use financial incentives to get customers in the door. Clearview AI, Ring, and Taser have all ponied up enticing offers to agencies around the country.
“A lot of these police surveillance vendors have learned the lessons of general old salesmanship,” Guariglia tells WIRED. In other words, deals and discounts work.
In some cases, this looks like new and increasingly expansive Flock products. In 2025, for instance, Alpharetta paid for an upgrade to the Elite Package of FlockOS, which Flock describes as a real-time crime-center platform. Other products are first offered with a free trial; Alpharetta took advantage of one 90-day window last year to try a new product dubbed Nova.
Flock also expands its contracts by offering discounts if departments sign a multiyear contract. In 2024, Alpharetta locked into a five-year contract with Flock that would cost $254,250 the first year and $238,000 for each successive year. The agreement was $232,500 less than five one-year agreements, which could be subject to higher rates.
The Alpharetta Police Department declined to comment.
Five-year agreements are common among Flock customers, which the company has sometimes marketed as a “price-lock promotion.” In a November 2023 email, Flock customer success manager Gwen Saltal used this framing to offer a five-year deal to New York’s Albany County Sheriff’s Office.
“As you may be aware, on April 1st, the cost of new Falcons went from $2,500 to $3,000, which will apply for future renewal terms on existing cameras as well,” Saltal wrote. “If you would like to lock in your current camera rates, Flock is offering a 5-year contract to hold that pricing.” The Albany County Sheriff’s Office did not respond to a request for comment.
In other cities, Flock won long-term contracts because it offered a convenient product bundle. (This is far from exclusive to Flock; Motorola, for instance, recently inked a $54 million agreement with Louisiana for a slate of policing technology.)
Guillermo Mixer, the police chief of the central California city of Greenfield, reported in a January city council meeting that the annual cost of the city’s surveillance system was $112,900, spread across five contracts with three companies: Flock, the surveillance camera company SurveillanceGrid, and the drone company Paladin.

Mixer proposed ditching SurveillanceGrid and Paladin and instead locking into a five-year contract with Flock. The annual cost would be $136,940—about $24,000 more than its level of spending at the time. He noted, however, that the price included three new cameras and access to Flock911, which transmits 911 call data to responding officers, as well as drones from Aerodrome, a company Flock acquired in 2024.
A proposed order form listed dozens of other Flock products and services included in the contract, though it’s unclear how many of those were new additions.
In the end, Greenfield’s city council unanimously approved Mixer’s repackaged Flock contract. Mixer and the Greenfield Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
What Your Money Gets You
WIRED reviewed a July 2022 “Public Sector Price Sheet” for Flock products for the Fort Lauderdale Police Department in Florida. Though it was generated for one specific agency, it reflects the approximate price ranges WIRED observed in Flock purchase orders around that time from around the country.
Historically, Flock has placed agencies into one of 14 pricing “buckets” for its software, depending on their size. Agencies in “Bucket 1” have one to 15 sworn officers and could pay as little as $2,000 or as much as $115,500 for Flock software, depending on whether they get a basic package or select multiple add-ons. The costs by bucket incrementally increase until Bucket 14—which is for state and federal agencies, or local forces with more than 3,000 officers—which the sheet says gets “custom” rates.
Hardware, meanwhile, tends to be sold at flat annual rates. According to the pricing sheet, individual license plate readers and surveillance cameras cost $3,000 to $5,200 per year, not including the cost of initial installation—which can run between $150 and $2,750 upfront.
The pricing sheet puts Flock’s individual gunshot detectors at $8,500 to $35,000 annually, depending on their range. The cost for its individual drones, meanwhile, is $50,000 to $150,000 per year, and Flock’s two “mobile security trailer” offerings cost $20,000 and $25,000 annually. Fort Lauderdale police did not respond to a request for comment.
Though prices vary depending on the size of a purchase and individual negotiations with a city, Flock’s pricing appears to be comparable to its competitors. Axon recently quoted Denver $150,000 to install 50 cameras across the city and maintain them for one year, while Motorola recently charged Manti, Utah, $4,704 for a single license plate reader.
Flock also has a pricing plan for replacing damaged or stolen products—a particularly relevant concern amid a national wave of vandalism targeting Flock cameras. Per Flock contract conditions, the company retains ownership of the products it sells to cities. This means that when people damage or destroy cameras, cities are on the hook for the cost. (It also means that if a city decides to end their Flock contract, they have to give the equipment back.)
According to Flock’s website and invoices reviewed by WIRED, the company has flat rates for replacing damaged or stolen products: $800 for cameras, $500 for poles, and $1,300 for both. (This is up from its 2021 pricing, according to documents from Anderson County, South Carolina, when its replacement cost was $500 for cameras and $150 for poles.)
Some cities have gone out of their way to draw attention to the fiscal toll of replacing damaged Flock equipment—sometimes overstating the cost in the process.
Police from Winona, Minnesota, and Rutherfordton, North Carolina, have said that camera replacements cost $3,000 and $3,500 each, respectively—or $2,200 and $2,700 higher than the listed cost. And in Derby, Kansas, after a man damaged 10 Flock cameras, local police claimed that he caused $26,000 in damages. But depending on whether he damaged the poles, replacements likely would have cost $8,000 to $13,000. Police from Winona, Rutherfordton, and Derby did not respond to a request for comment.
Flock’s pricing, ultimately, is much lower than other department expenses—like police helicopters, which can cost tens of millions of dollars annually, or hiring more police officers.
Still, when compared to other technology-related expenses, Flock spending can stand out.
In Pasadena, Texas, which has a population of about 148,500, the 2026 police budget allotted $427,133 for Flock, $500,842 for body camera software, and $500,000 for "Motorola maintenance." These were, by far, the most expensive technology purchases. Most of the other purchases had budgets of less than $100,000. The Pasadena Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Why Some Customers Are Ditching Flock
Across the country, cities big and small have chosen to increase their Flock spending significantly over just a few years.
Savannah, Georgia, for instance, paid $33,000 for Flock in 2020 and $193,500 in 2025. Snellville, Georgia, paid Flock $5,000 in 2021 and 2022; in 2025, it paid $163,275. This year, as of August, the city has paid Flock $138,934.94. The Savannah and Snellville Police Departments did not respond to requests for comment.
However, in some cases, Flock’s pricing eventually proved to be prohibitive.
Jack Hall—the sheriff of Lorain County, Ohio—recently announced that the county would be canceling its Flock contract. Hall said that Flock planned to raise Lorain County’s two-year rate for 15 cameras by 17 percent. For him, it was too much.
Hall and the Lorain County Sheriff’s Office did not respond for comment.
Killingworth, Connecticut, also decided to end its relationship with Flock. The town paid $14,600 last year for four cameras. Killingworth first selectman Eric Couture noted “privacy concerns” related to Flock and said that it didn’t provide much to police relative to its cost.
Couture told WIRED that Flock’s cost wasn’t entirely prohibitive. But, he added, the cameras “did not add any utility” for the town’s “resident state trooper.”

Air France has confirmed it is complying with new Israeli restrictions that bar flight crew members from certain nationalities from operating flights to Israel, a policy that reportedly affects citizens of 31 countries, most of them Muslim-majority nations, including Pakistan, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Algeria and Tunisia.
“Like all airlines, Air France is required to comply with the entry regulations established by the authorities of the countries it serves, both for its customers and employees,” the airline told Al Jazeera in a statement.
“The staff concerned have been informed of the new regulations implemented by the Israeli authorities for flights to Tel Aviv,” it added.
Israel’s directive affects crew from 31 countries
According to Israeli broadcaster N12, Israel’s Ministry of transport and road safety informed foreign airlines on October 1 that pilots and cabin crew operating flights into Israeli airspace must not hold the nationality or dual nationality of countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel.
The directive reportedly covers 31 countries, many of them Muslim-majority nations. The list includes Pakistan, Iran, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Algeria, Tunisia and Niger.
The move came a day after an Omani co-pilot allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv and crash it into Israel’s Ben Gurion airport on September 30, according to Emirati and Israeli authorities. The co-pilot is accused of attacking the aircraft’s Indian pilot, who has been recovering in hospital.
The restrictions could affect dozens of airlines operating flights to, from or over Israel.
Other airlines confirm receiving directive
Czech airline Smartwings confirmed it had received the Israeli directive, but said its operations had not been affected so far.
“We received the directive from the Israeli authorities in September 2026. We have carefully reviewed the directive and continue to monitor and comply with all applicable requirements issued by the relevant authorities. At present, the directive does not have any impact on our operations, crew management procedures, or the deployment of crew members on flights to and from Israel,” Smartwings spokeswoman Vladimira Dufkova told Al Jazeera.
United Airlines said it had nothing to share but did not confirm whether it had received the directive or changed crew assignments.
An internal memo to Air France pilots and cabin crew, seen by French investigative publication Mediapart, warned that “failure to comply with this directive would expose Air France and the employee to potential sanctions”. However he memo could not be independently verified.
The restrictions have raised concerns over possible discrimination against airline employees based on nationality and could expose carriers to legal challenges under French employment law, according to legal experts cited by Al Jazeera.
Paris-based anti-discrimination lawyer Clara Gandin said the restrictions could put Air France at odds with French employment law by treating employees differently based on nationality.
“The measure rests on a collective presumption which amounts to a discriminatory bias: Every national of these 31 countries, most of them Arab or Muslim-majority, is treated as a potential security threat,” Gandin told the outlet.
“Article L1132-1 of the French Labour Code prohibits any discriminatory measure based on a person’s actual or perceived nationality, in particular regarding assignment, pay and discipline,” she added.
Gandin said the policy could also amount to indirect discrimination based on origin and possibly perceived religion, given that most countries on the list are Arab or Muslim-majority.
According to legal experts, Israel’s authority to regulate access to its airspace and territory raises a separate question from whether airlines complying with the directive could breach employment laws in their home countries.
Vincent Correia, a professor of air law at McGill University in Canada, said international aviation law recognises state sovereignty over territorial airspace.
He also pointed to Article 13 of the 1944 Chicago Convention, which allows countries to enforce rules governing the admission of passengers and crew.
He said crew members from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were already barred from flying there, making the new directive relevant mainly to dual nationals.
Gandin, however, said a country’s authority to impose entry restrictions did not automatically exempt airlines from their obligations under applicable national laws.
She said Air France could choose not to operate routes under the restrictions or challenge the directive through the French government, the French Civil Aviation Authority or the European Union.
Affected employees could seek damages, while trade unions could initiate legal proceedings, she said. Gandin also warned that the policy could raise concerns under data protection laws if airlines collected information on employees’ nationality without a direct and necessary link to their jobs.
According to Mediapart, Air France had considered asking crew members to voluntarily disclose whether they were affected by the directive.
The Alter union, which represents flight deck crew, reportedly persuaded management not to proceed, arguing that the measure would amount to “discrimination based on nationality”.
The wider impact on international airlines remains unclear. Correia warned that similar restrictions adopted by other countries could complicate crew scheduling and airline operations.

The Rejinagar and Nandigram by-elections in West Bengal concluded on October 9, Friday, with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) clinching victory in both seats. BJP’s Shankharavh Sarkar won in Rejinagar and Hasirani Rath won the Nandigram seat.
Polling in both the assemblies were, however, marred by allegations of electoral malpractices, with the Congress demanding repolling.
Amid these allegations, digital censorship emerged as another flashpoint, with social media content documenting alleged electoral malpractice and vote rigging being restricted in India. The restrictions also added to concerns over the growing suppression of online criticism of the ruling party. For the past couple of months, Alt News has reported extensively on this social media censorship frenzy in India.
On October 7, the Facebook page of the Murshidabad district wing of the West Bengal Pradesh Congress (@DCCMurshidabad) was restricted under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules. The page remains unavailable at the tome of this article being written.
ALSO READ: Bengal bypolls: Facebook restricts local news pages covering Opposition campaign in Rejinagar
On the same day, prominent local news outlet NBTV Bangla’s (@nbtvbngla) Facebook page was also restricted in India for seven days following the same notification. With over five lakh followers, the outlet reported critically on issues of the government or law enforcement in the context of the Nandigram and Rejinagar bypolls.
Alt News learnt that the two videos uploaded by the Facebook page of NBTV which were restricted in India directly addressed allegations of voting malpractices in the Rejinagar by-election.
The first of the two videos — both of which are still accessible on Instagram — shows a woman claiming that voters in Rejinagar were being intimidated away from the polling booths. A man also appears in this video, alleging that not even 10 voters had been able to cast their votes.
View this post on Instagram
Another video shows allegations being levelled by voters of the Mirzapur Gram Panchayat area in Rejinagar. “Who I choose to vote for is entirely my own decision. They marked our fingers with ink and sent us home, even though we had not yet cast our votes,” a man appearing in the video claims.
View this post on Instagram
“It is not the first time this has happened. Several of our social media posts have been restricted in the past,” Zeba Noshin, a reporter at NBTV, told Alt News.
Notably, the notices received by Congress’ Murshidabad district page and NBTV Bangla state that the account had been restricted pursuant to legal requirements. This indicates that the restrictions followed a legal request or official complaint concerning the content on these pages, rather than being flagged by Meta’s own content-moderation process.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
A video uploaded on Facebook by Bengali digital media outlet Inscript.me was restricted in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000 on the day of the polls, October 6. A representative of the platform told Alt News that the banned video was regarding allegations of rigging in Rejinagar.
The title of the video visible on the notice sent by Meta reads, “People of Rejinagar allege rigging in byelection”.
On October 9, another Facebook post by Inscript.me, a report on Rahul Gandhi’s detainment by Delhi Police during the protests demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, was also restricted.
A Facebook user named Diya Maity also alleged that her page with close to 2.5 lakh followers had been restricted for seven days. She was also posting content on the alleged election rigging in the Rejinagar constituency.
Rigging, Malpractices & Intimidation: Opposition
The October 6 bypolls were necessitated in Murshidabad’s Rejinagar and East Medinipur’s Nandigram, after AJUP chief Humayun Kabir and Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari chose to vacate these two seats respectively, having secured victory in two constituencies apiece.
Suvendu Adhikari’s home constituency, Nandigram has a Muslim population of around 27 per cent. He vacated this seat, and retained Bhabanipur, where he defeated former chief minister Mamata Banerjee.
The demography is entirely different in Rejinagar, with Muslims accounting for around 69 per cent of its electorate. Kabir won both Nowda and Rejinagar and subsequently vacated the latter, where his victory margin was more than 58,000 votes. His son, Golam Nabi Azad, was contesting the seat vacated by him.
Opposition leaders repeatedly alleged that the BJP was manipulating votes and applying pressure tactics in the lead up to the polls. On the day of polling, the AJUP chief was taken into custody by the police after a heated altercation. He was released from the Rejinagar police station after spending 12 hours in custody.
